Mr. Earle (according to Order) reported from the LymcRegii Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it Ele^lon* appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Lyme Regis, in the County of Dorset, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read: And the Report, and Resolution of the Committee, are as follows; viz.

Upon the Petition of Henry Holt Henley, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of John Burridge, junior, Esquire, to serve for the Borough of Lyme Regis, in the County of Dorset; and also, the Petition of divers Inhabitants of the Borough, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others, who have a Right to vote at the Election of Burgesses, to represent the Borough in Parliament, praying Relief against the Pretentious of Mr. Henley to be one of the Representatives for this Borough:

That the Committee proceeded to examine the Merits of this Election, so far as the same were referred to them.

The House having adjudged, that Mr. Burridge, being Mayor of this Borough at the Time of the Election and the proper Officer, to whom the Precept was directed, was not capable of being elected, and returned, for the same Borough;

The Counsel for Mr. Henley proceeded to make good the Allegation in his Petition that he was duly elected.

And they alleged, that the Right of Election is in the Mayor, capital Burgesses, and Freemen, of the Borough.

That the Poll, as between Mr. Henley and Mr. Burridge, was,

Kennedy* A Petition of Sir William Dudley, Baronet, and Dame ElUt* Elizabeth, his Wife, only Daughter and Issue of Sir Richard Kennedy, of Mount Kennedy, in the Kingdom of Ireland, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that in 1706 Sir Richard Kennedy, being feiled of an Estate Tail in the Manor of Mount Kennedy, and other Lands in Ireland, by Deed and Recoveries barred the Estate Tail, and limited the same to the Use of himself in Fee; and by his Will devised the same to the Petitioner, Dame Elizabeth, and her Heirs; and in 1710 died: That in 1713 Elizabeth Jones, the Petitioner's great Aunt, informed the late Queen, that Sir Richard Kennedy's Estate, during the Life of Sir Wm. Kennedy, was forfeited, and vested in the Crown, by the Outlawry of Sir William, 6th and 7th Gul. Regis, for being in the Rebellion in Ireland, which Outlawry being before the said Recoveries, they did not bar the Right of the Crown, during Sir William's Life; but no further Proceedings were had on the said Information, during the Queen's Life: That in 1724, upon the Application of Robert Jones, Son of the said Elizabeth, a Commission was granted, to inquire into the said Forfeiture; and he obtained a Cujiodium of the said Estate, and came into Possession; and has received the Rents and Profits ever since, without paying any of the principal Sums, which are Incumbrances thereon prior to the Crown, or any Interest for the fame: That the said Estate, if continued in his Possession, will produce nothing to the Publick, but will tend to the Ruin of the Petitioners, and their Children: And, in regard it is directed by Acts of Parliament, that the said forfeited Estate should be sold for the Benefit of the Publick, the Petitioners pray, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for veiling the said forfeited Estate, during Sir Wm. Kennedy's Life, in Trustees, to be sold, subject to the Incumbrances thereon prior to the Forfeiture, and that the Petitioners, paying a valuable Consideration, may have the Preference in such Purchase, or may have such other Relief, as the House shall think fit.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, that this same having been represented to his Majesty, his Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that his Majesty gives his Consent, that this House may do therein as they think fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition; and that Sir Wm. Tonge, Lord Limerick, and Mr. William Fortescue, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of all the insolvent Debtors confined in the Debtors Castle of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; Potion, setting forth, that the Petitioners are many in Number, being Grafiers, Farmers, Tradesrnen, Gentlemen, but mostly those belonging to the Woollen Manufacturevwho, by the Decay of that Trade for many Years pad, are reduced to great Poverty: That many of the Petitioners, when first arrested, were fair Dealers, and in tolerable good Circumstances, and have offered great Competitions* to their Creditors, who would have all their Debts, or none; so that the Petitioners differed themselves to be brought to Gaol, the better-to enable them to make an equal Dividend amongst all their Creditors; so that by their Creditors rigorous Proceedings many are in Execution, who have wasted their little Substance, and are forced to lie on Pads of Straw upon the cold Ground:

That their Apartments, being very narrow and close, have caused great Sickness among them; so that within Two Months lately they have buried 17 Persons, and it is no. Surprize to bury Two in a Day now, many of whom have been starved, notwithstanding the Country's Charity may seem great: And praying the House to take their calamitous Circumstances into Consideration, and release the Prisoners in all the Gaols of this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Petition of the Master, Wardens, and Ccfurt of Assistants, of the Company of Tilers and Bricklayers, of the City of London, in behalf of the said Company; and also the Petition of John Brown, late Master of the Corporation of Tilers and Bricklayers of London, and JoJepk Welsh, one of the late Wardens, and several other Liverymen of the said Corporation, whose Names are thereunto subscribed; were referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in Ids Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table; where the same was read: And the said Report, and lle-fblutions, are as follows; viz.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said several Petitions, and had heard Counsel thereupon.

That, upon the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. tVaxam and Mr. Scott, Brick-makers, were examined; and said, that the Time limited by the Act of Parliament, of the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty, for digging and tarn-ing the Earth to make Bricks with, is from the First of November to the First of February; which Season very often proves so wet, that the Turning is of no Service:

That the Earth of which Bricks should be made, ought to be turned twice, and to lie One Month after the second Turning at least, before it be used; and the Bricks would be considerably better, and more durable, than they can be expected now to be, as the said Act limits.

That the Petitioners proceeded to examine as to the Size of Bricks.

Mr. Waxam, Brick-maker, being examined, said, that the Size of Bricks, as by Act of Parliament directed to be made, is Nine Inches long. Two Inches and a half thick, and Four Inches and One Quarter wide; which arc so heavy, that they will not bear their own V\reight, till they can be dried, fit to be burnt; betides they take up a greater Quantity of Coals, and are considerably longer in burning, than if they were less:

That if Bricks were to be but Eight Inches and a half long. Two Inches and a half thick, and Four Inches wide, they would be firmer, and more fit for Use, than the Size mentioned by the said Act; and would be better to be handled by the Workmen, and be of more Service to the Public, in their Buildings, and more Work Could be done in a Day with these, than with them that are made as the said Act directs.

Mr. Churchill and Mr. Godfrey, Bricklayers, laid, that, if Bricks were not to be under Eight Inches and Three Quarters, when burnt, they would be of much more Benefit to the Public, in building, than now they are; and would dry in less time; and stand better in the Ciamps; and be cheaper, than at present can be afforded.

Then the Committee examined the followingWitnesses as to the Use of-Spanish.

Mr. Godfrey and Mr. Barrett said* that, if they were to be allowed, in the making of One hundred thousand of Bricks, One-fifth Part Spanish, the Bricks would be more firm than they are now, and produced Two Bricks, both grey Stocks, the One made as the Act directs, the other mixed with Spanish, and that in the burning of Ten Thousand of Bricks, made without Spanish, they can scarceget Four thousand Stock Bricks; which is a considerable Lois; and that Twenty-five Load of Spanish is as little as can be made use of, in the making of One hundred thousand of Bricks.

Mr. Walknger laid, that he bought Bricks Of Mr; Barrett, which were made according as the Act directs j but they were so bad, that he could not go on with his Building, and was forced to get Bricks at another Place, to finish what he had begun; and was informed, that they were made with Spanish; but disposed of the Building, for fear the Foundation should give way.

Mr. Scctt, Brick-maker, being examined, said, that if a Quant ity of Spanish was allowed to be used in the making of Bricks, they would be firmer, and of more Service, than it is possible they can be at present without Spanish:

And, in the burning of Bricks, if they were allowed to make but Two Outsides, instead of Four, as the said Act directs, and to put Stock Bricks and Place Bricks both in One Clamp, but to be separated, and not intermixed, nor surrounded, with Place Bricks, both the one and the other would be fitter for Service, than they are* now.

And being asked, if he had not used some Mud, instead of Spanish; he said, he had once made Trial of ir, and no oftener; and the Experience he found by it, was, that it gave the Bricky, made use of for fronting, a much better Colour than Spanish did.

That the Petitioners, in order to prove the Frauds, committed by the Master and Wardens of the Company of Tilers and Bricklayers, called

Mr. Barrett \ who said, that Mr. Bilbey, and several other Brick-makers, who made use of Spanish, contrary to the Act of Parliament, had and could afford to fell much cheaper than those Persons who conformed to the said Act.

Mr. Bilbey, Brick* maker, being examined, said, that he had made about Six hundred thousand of Bricks with Spanish, for his own Use; and being summoned to attend the late Master, Wardens, and Court of Assistants, on the Seventh of September last, they acquainted him, they were well informed he had made use of Spanish, contrary to the Act of Parliament; for which the Court fined him, as the said Act directs; and on the Eleventh of December following, the present Master and Wardens summoned him, to pay the Searchers Money; acquainting him at the same time, there was a Fine set on him, for making Bricks contrary to the said Act: Upon which he produced Coni rafts, that he had fold the Earth, and was only the Maker; upon which the present Master and Wardens mitigated the Fine to Twelve Guineas, which was paid the same Day, as appeared by the Company's Court Book, which was produced.

Mr. Morrice, being examined, said, that he was summoned by the said Company, to pay a Half-peny a Thousand to the Searchers, as isusual: The Master and Wardens told him, they were informed, he had made use of Spanish; he acquainted them, they were for his own Use, and not for Sale: Neither did he pay any Fine, or had Leave from the Company to dispose of them; but paid the Search.

And being examined as to his making Bricks with Spanish for Mr. James Brown; he said, he did, but was only an Agent; and what carfle of themj knows not,

Mr. Fish, being examined, said, that Mr. Mallaud had made Sixteen hundred thousand of Bricks, or more, with Spanish: That he is his Neighbour, and has loft Five hundred Pounds, because he would not make Bricks contrary to the said Act; and Mallaud, making them with Spanish, has drawed most of his Customers from him, by reason he could afford to fell cheaper, than he did; and that People came far and near to buy them; and, if some Remedy is not taken, to prevent chefe ill Practices, the fair Trader will be ruined, and those Persons, which use Spanish, will get most Money: And cannot say Mallaud had Leave from the Company for so doing; but knows Mallaud was summoned, to pay a Half-peny a Thousand: The late Master and Wardens acquainted him, that they were well informed, lie used Spanish; and fined him £. 600 on the Seventh of September last; and on the Eleventh of December following the present Master and Wardens received no more,' in full of that Fine, than Thirty Pounds, as appeared by the Court Book of the said Company of Bricklayers.

Mr. Moreton said; that he being at their Court af the same time, told them Mallaud was a great Aggressor, and that he ought to pay severely; but Mr. Brown made Answer, that a small Fine was sufficient now, and a greater hereafter.

That upon the second Petition, the following Witnesses were examined as to the use of Spanish; viz.

Mr. James Brown, Bricklayer, said, that there is a great deal of Difference in the Spanifit, used now, and that which was formerly used in the making of Bricks for the building the Royal Exchange, which was the first Use of Spanish, and at that time only consisted of clear Sea-coal Ashes; and the Reason, why it is not now so good, is, that the Houses being strewed with Sand, and fivept into the Dust Tub, and mingled with the Ashes* has occasioned the Brick-maker to put a larger Quantity of Spanish, to increase the Force of the Fire, which the Mixture of Sand has abated:

Another Sort, which is called Spanish, is the Slop and Dirt of the Streets, of which some is carried to the Du hg-hills, and the other Part carried off immediately from the Streets, and mixed with Brick Earth, without letting it dry, to have itidean fifted; but the high Duties, and Price of Coals, has obliged them to have recourse to these Shifts, to save Fire:

And laid, that Bricks might be made-without Spanish, provided the Brick-makers would give longer time for the drying; and that Bricks, made with natural Earth, would be much the best, they requiring twice the time drying, than when Spanish is used, and will take more Coals ,tp burn them. Breeze being too weak a Fire.

And being examined as to the Size of Bricks; said, that, if Bricks were made of natural Earth, without Spanish, that Eight Inches and Three Quarters was a sufficient Length, Four Inches and One Eighth wide, and Two Inches and a half thick the outside, they being heavier, than Bricks made with Spanish; so that Prentices, and tveak Workmen, could not work up such a Quantity, as they now do.

Being asked as to the Price cf Bricks; said, that Place Bricks were delivered in London, before the patting of the late Act, at Fourteen Shillings a Thousand; and immediately, on the passing of the said Act, the Brick-makers raised the Price to Sixteen Shillings a Thousand upon all their Stock in hand; and, after the new Bricks came to Market, they raised them to Twenty, and Twenty-one, Shillings a Thousand:

And laid, that he made full-sized Rubbing Stock Bricks according to the said Act, which are all burnt in Kilns;

Aftd that, upon the whole Matter of the said Petitions, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Master and Wardens of the Company cf Tilers and Bricklayers, appointed to put in Execution an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty's Reign, intituled, "An Act to prevent Abuses in the making of " Bricks and Tiles, and to ascertain the Dimensions " thereof, and to prevent all unlawful Combinations f‘ amongst any Brick-makers, or Tile-makers, within 15 u Miles of the City of London, in order to advance or ennance the Price of Bricks, or Tiles," have not executed the same duly, so as they ought to have done.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Power of imposing Fines be in the Master, Wardens, and Assistants, of the Company of Tilers and Bricklayers, or the major Part of them assembled.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the more effectual preventing Frauds and Abuses in the making of Bricks, and Tiles, within 15 Miles Distance from the Cities of London and Westminster, Power be given to the Justices of the Peace, at their respective General or Quarter Sessions to appoint Searchers, who shall have equal Authority with those, appointed by the said Company of 1'ilers and Bricklayers.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all bad Bricks shall be broke and destroyed at the Charge of such Brick-maker who shall be convicted of making the same.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, itgreed imto-by the House.

Mr. Earle (according to Order) reported from the Buck-Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the w County of Bucks, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's*!'able; where the same was read: And the Report, and Resolution of the Committee, are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of iVm. Gore, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Richard Hampdeny Esquire, to serve for the County of Bucks:

That the Committee proceeded to examine the Merits of this Election.

In order to prove the Poll, the Petitioner's Counsel called

Mr. Hayden, Clerk of the Peace for this County; who produced 18 Paper Books, which, he said, were delivered to him by the Under-sheriff, as the Poll Books, taken at the Election: That they were taken at different Places, some by the Sheriff's Agents, and others by Agents for the Candidates; but he could not distinguish, or lay, which of them made the Sheriff's Poll.

And none of the said Books being either sworn to by the Sheriff, or attested by him;

The Committee did not think, they had sufficient Evidence to proceed upon; and came to the following Resolution; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee That Richard Hampden, Esquire, is duly elected aKnight of the Shire, to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Bucks.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

Mr. Hampden was heard in his Place: And then he withdrew.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Resolution be re-committed;

The House divided.

Treaty with Mr. Treasurer acquainted the House, that his Majesty sPam* had commanded him to lay before this House, Copy of the Act for the Execution of the Preliminaries, signed at the Pardo, March the Sixth, 1728, N. S‘. and Translation thereof.

And he presented the same to the House.

And the Titles thereof were read.

the Translation of the A cl for the Execution of the Preliminaries is as follows; viz

Whereas certain Difficulties have arisen upon the Execution of the Articles, which are called Preliminaries, and which were signed at Paris the last Day of May, and afterwards at Vienna the 13th Day of June, in the Year 1727, by the Ministers respectively furnished with sufficient Powers: And whereas by a certain Declaration, made by the Count de Rottembourg, with the Consent of all the Parties, and approved, the aforesaid Difficulties have been happily adjusted; of which Declaration, and of the Acceptation thereof by his Catholick Majesty, as the same was exhibited, and subscribed by the Marquis de la Paz, in his Name, and by his Command, the Tenor here follows:

Whereas, since the signing of the Preliminaries, certain Difficulties have arisen between the con trading Parties, in relation to the Restitution of Prizes, that have been taken on either Side, and namely, that of the Prince Frederick, and its Cargo, belonging to the South Sea Company, seized and detained by the Spaniards at Vera Cruz; which Difficulties have delayed the Execution of the Preliminaries, the exchanging of the Ratifications with Spain, and the opening of the Congress; his Bri-tannick Majesty, to facilitate Matters, as much as lies in his Power, and to remove all Obstacles, that obstruct a general Pacification, has declared, and given his royal Word, to the most Christian King, that he will, without Delay, fend Orders to his Admirals Wager and Hojier, or, the chief Commander in his (lead, to withdraw from the Seas of the Indies, and of Spain, and that he consents,

that the counterband Trade, and other causesof Complaint, which the Spaniards may have in relation to the Ship Prince Frederick, shall be difeuffed and decided in the Congress; that all the respective Prelensions on each Side shall be produced, debated, and decided, in the same Congress; that therein shall likewise be difeufled and decided* whether the Prizes, taken at Sea on each Side Vox.. 21.

shall be restored.; and that his Britannick Majesty will abide by what shall on all this be regulated:

On my Part I promise, in the Name of the King my Matter, by virtue of the Orders, and full Powers, which I have received for that Purpose, that this Discussion, to be made at the Congress, shall be faithfully executed; that the Exchange of the Ratification shall be performed without delay; and that the Congress shall meet infallibly, and the fooneftthat shall be possible, according to what shall be agreed by the Ministers of the contracting Parties, who shall happen to be at Paris, provided his Catholick Majesty will give his royal Word,

x.

To raise immediately the Blockade of Gibraltar, by fending back the Troops to their Quarters, by causing the Cannon to be drawn off, the Trenches to be filled up, and the Works, made on occasion of this Siege, to be demolished, by re-establishing every thing on each Side conformably to the Treaty ot Utrecht:

2.

To fend, without Delay, his Orders, clear and express, for delivering up forthwith the Ship Prince Frederick, and her Cargo, to the Agents of the South Sea Company, who are at Vera Cruz, that, when they shall think fit, they may fend her to Europe, and to restore the Commerce of the English Nation in the Indies, according to what is stipulated by the Assiento Treaty, and agreed by the ad and jd Articles of the Preliminaries:

5.

To cause the Effetfts of the Flotilla to be immediately delivered to those, to whom they belong, and those of the Galeons, when they shall return, as in Time of Freedom, and of full Peace, according to the jth Article of the Preliminaries:

4-

That his Catholick Majesty do engage in the same Manner, as his Britannick Majesty has engaged above, to abide by all, that shall be regulated by the abovesaid Discussion and Decision of the Congress. Given at the Pardo this 4th of March, 1728.

(L. S.) Rottembourg.

I, the under-written Marquis de la Paz, declare, by express Order, in the royal Name of the Catholick King my Matter, and in consequence of his full Power, that his Majesty, out of his ever constant Desire to facilitate the Negociations for an universal and lasting Peace, is come into an Acceptation of, and does effectually admit, and accept, the Proposal, lately made by the Count de Rottembourg, Minister Plenipotentiary of his most Christian Majesty, according to what is here next above inserted. In witness whereof I sign this present Declaration, and put thereto the Seal of my Arms. At the Pardo, the 5th of March, 1728.

(L. S.) The Marquis de la Paz.

We, the under-written Ministers Plenipotentiaries, duly authorized, to the end the above-written Declaration and Acceptation may obtain the most full Force and Vigour, have signed this special Instrument of Consent and Approbation, in the Name, and by the Command, of our respective Matters, and have affixed our Seals thereto. Given in this Palace, called the Pardo, the 6th Day of the Month of March, in the Year 1728.

H. Count of Kiniigegg, B. Keene, Rottembourg,

(L. S.) (L. S.) (L. S.)

The Marquis la Paz} F. Vander Meer.

That it likewise appeared to the Committee, that the Parish Church of St. George, Hanover Square, was con fecrated by the Lord Bishop of London on the Eighteenth Day of March, which was in the Year of our Lord 1724, and the Easter Day following was on the 28th Day of the said Month, in the Year 1725.

That Application was made to the Commissioners of the Land Tax, at their first general Meeting last Year in the Exchequer Chamber, to apportion a distinct Part of the Tax upon the Parish of St. George, Hanover Square, separate from that of St. Martin\ but the said Commissioners refused so to do, the Question being put for that Purpose, and carried in the Negative by a great Majority; and no distinct Sum hath hitherto been allotted upon the Parish of St. George, separate from that of St. Martin.

Neither did it appear to the Committee, that any Demand had been made for that Purpose, excepting last Year.

That, as to the Quotations from the several Acts, for granting an Aid to his Majesty by a Land Tax, for the Years 1725, 1726, and 1727, whereof different Parts of Clauses, relating to the Duty of Commissioners in distributing the several Proportions of the said Tax, are mentioned by the Two Petitions respectively, the Committee referred to the said Acts.

That it appeared to the Committee, that the Commissioners of the Land Tax, at their general Meetings, had proportioned the Land Tax to the several Divisions, in like Manner, as had been practised since the Statute, of the 4th of William and Mary, before the above-mentioned Act, of the 6th of the late King, for rebuilding St. Martin's Church, passed:

And, that particular Assessors and Collectors had been appointed by the Commissioners of the Land Tax of the Parish of St. Martin, for the out Wards, which now constitute the Parish of St. George, Hanover Square.

That the said Afl'efiors and Collectors were Inhabitants of the Parish of St. George; and that they were appointed at a Meeting, where one of the Commissioners, dwelling in the said Parish, was present.

That Evidence was likewise produced before the Committee, to prove, that several Houses in the Parish of St. George, Hanover Square, are more favourably rated to the Land Tax, than other Houses in St. Martin; and that the Rents of several Houses in St. Martin s Parish are diminished, some before, and many since, the new Buildings were erected in and about Hanover Square.

And several of the Witnesses imputed the Decreaseof Rents in St. Martin's Parish to the Increase of Buildings in St. George's Parish.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting an Aid to his Majesty by a Land Tax, for the Service of the Year 1728, is committed, that they have Power to receive a Clause, or Clauses, to oblige the Commissioners for the City of Westminster, and Liberties thereof, and Offices executed in Westminster hall, to ascertain the Proportion of the Land Tax, to be charged upon the Parish of St. George, Hanover Square, distinct from the Parish of St. Martin in the Fields.

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday next, at Twelve of the Clock, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Biff, for granting

A Petition of sundry Owners, Freighters, and Masters, Encouraging of Ships, trading from and to the Port of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners have for many Years paR Rruggled with very great Losses and Hardships, by the impressing Seamen from on Board Merchant-ships, by the total Decay of the Cargo, if loaded with peiifhable Commodities; which is not only a Loss to the Freighter, and Commerce of the said City, but to the Nation in general, by giving Foreigners an Opportunity to supply the Markets: That the impressing Seamen, and the long Time they are continued in the Service, unpaid their Wages, mufl expose their Families to great Necessities, and be a Discouragement to the Seamen, and occasions them to leave the Service of their Native Country, and con&questly lays the Merchant under a necessity of raising their Wages; which is a great Clog to the Employment of our Freight Ships, the great Nursery of our Seamen, and, if not timely prevented, may prove the Ruin of che best Part of our Navigation;

That, since his Majesty has from the Throne recommended to the House the Increase and Encouragement of Seamen, and that they may be invited, rather than compelled, into the Service, the Petitioners pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and give such Relief as ill all be thought moR convenient, far the Pie-femtion and Improvement of Trade and Navigation.

A Petition of the Cordwainers* and Curriers, of the Borough of Bodmyn, in the County of Cornwall, was preferred to the House, and read; letting forth, that the Petitioners} have been great Sufferers, for Years past, in their Trade, by the great Scarcity of Leather, occasioned by the vast Exportation thereof, whereby Leather is advanced to more than double the Price it formerly was sold at, and they cannot get sufficient to employ themselves; lb that they, and their Families, must be ruined, if a speedy Remedy be not found out, to prevent the Exportation thereof; which, the Petitioners apprehend, is owing to the great Drawback allowed to the Exporters, who also go to the Tanners Yard, contrary to Law, and engross the belt Leather; so that there is scarce any fit for working, to be had: They are also Sufferers by the Loss in Weight of Leather, having found Hides to Ihrink Six or Seven Pounds from their first Weight; which would be righted, if brought to a proper Market, and there tried, and learched, to the Statute; another Grievance the Petitioners labour under, which is by the Butchers gafliing and cutting of Skins, and refuse Persons authorized to come into their Shops, where they fell them contrary to Law: And praying, that the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and relieve them therein.

Ordered) That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Digby reported from the Committee to whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Tradesmen, and others, living in, and near, Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, and also the Petition of several of the Trustees named in an Act, palSed last Session of Parliament, for repairing the Roads leading from Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, to and from several Places therein particularly mentioned, and also of several other Persons living in, and near, the said Town of Birmingham, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, were referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and found the same to be as follows; viz.

Mr. Wm. Twamlcy, Mr. James Furr eft, and Mr. John Wilks, were called; and, being examined, said, that the Road desired to be repaired, leads from Great Bridge to Ccaljley, where great Plenty of Coals are, and joins to one of the Roads directed to be repaired by tire Act passed in the last Session of the last Parliament of his late Majesty, for repairing the several Roads leading from Birmingham to several Places in the Act mentioned; and the same is become so very ruinous, by reason of heavy Carriages frequently going that Way, that Horses and Cattle canont pass and repass in the Winter Season without great Difficulty.

That the same Witnesses gave Evidence, the Statute-work had beenconstantly done by the Parishes wherein this Vol. 21.

Road lies; and, if n^ore was done, than is required by Law, it would not be sufficient to repair the lame; and, this Road being so bad all the Winter, a great many Persons using Coals are obliged to go to another Place for what they want, where they are forced to give double the Price they usually paid.

Mr. Twamley laid, that, if this Road was repaired, which is no more than Two Miies, the Price of Coals would be abated; for Coals which Two Years ago were sold at Four Pence, and Four Pence half-peny, per Hundred Weight, are now fold for Eight Pence per Hundred Weight; and the Persons who have Coals at other Places, keeping the Price of them very high, has impoverished Abundance of poor Families employed in the Iron Manufacture, and increased the Poor's Rates to above Three hundred Pounds/w Annum; and that, by this advanced Price, he now pays Nine Shillings pet Week more for.Coals, than he used to do; but if this Road was amended, Coals might be had at the same Price they were formerly.

Mr. John Wilks, one of the Trustees in the late Act of Parliament, for repairing the Road near Birmingham; Aid, that he and his Co-trustees are willing that Part of the Moneys arising by the Toll collected by the said Act* should be applied for repairing this Road, being no more than Two Miles in Length, if they may be impowered by Parliament so to do.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for impowering the Trustees appointed to put in Execution Part of an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Roads leading from Birmingham, in the County of Warwick, to and from several Places in the said Act mentioned, to repair the Road from Great Bridge, in the County of Stafford, to Coalefley, in the said County: And that Mr. Digby, Mr. Peytoe, and Mr. Plumer, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the insolvent Debtors, confined in the Debtor* Prison of Woodstreet Compter* in behalf of themselves, Petitions, and many Thousands of Prisoners in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that though they are willing to deliver up all they have to their Creditors, yet they refuse to accept of the fame, resolving rather have their Persons confined, whose Liberty might be serviceable to the Publick j but their Imprisonment is become a Burthen to the several Parishes to which they belong: That, since his Majesty's Accession to the Throne has filled the Hearts of all other his Subjects with Joy, the Petitioners hope the Government will not leave so many Thousand Debtors as there are in Gaol, to despair of Mercy: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Relief of insolvent Debtors.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the several Person in White Chappel Pri-fbn, in behalf of themselves, and several Thousands imprisoned Debtors in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners had great Hopes whilst the late insolvent Act was depending, that the same would have extended to relieve all Debtors, without any Limitation of a Sum, or that the Creditor should be obliged to maintain the Debtor, whilst in Gaol, upon Refusal to accept of his All; but that Act limited a Sum ofj£. 100. due to any one Creditor; whereby the Petitioners, who owed above that Sum, were deprived the Benefit thereof, and are in a worse Condition than Bankrupts, or other Prisoners who had not so considerable Dealings in the World, and may be made serviceable to the Publick: And praying, that, if their Creditors will not accept the Surrender of all they have, upon Pain of Death, that they may be obiged to maintain them in Prison.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

AN ingrossed Bill from the Lords, intituled, An Act to enable the Guardians of the Lord George Ben* tineke, Second Son of Henry, late Duke of Portlandy to make Leases of certain Houses, Grounds, and Tenements, in Soho, during the Minority of the said Lord George, for making Provision for his Maintenance, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, was read the First time.

A Petition of the Cordwainer. % and Curriers, £dV. be-longingto the LeatherTrade in the Borough of Tobies, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners have for several Years past been great Sufferers in their Trade, by reason of the Exportation of vast Quantities of Leather; which renders it so scarce, that they cannot get sufficient to carry on their Business, and so dear, that it is double the Price it used to be at; which Scarcity, and Dearness, is occasioned by the great Drawback the Exporter is allowed, who engross all they can, by going to, and buying at, the Tanners Yards, contrary to the Act 90 Anna Regina: The Petitioners are also Sufferers by the Butchers cutting and gashing the Hides and Skins, contrary to Law, which obliges them to bring the Skins to a proper Place, to be viewed, and searched, which would prevent that Abuse; but they fell them at their Shops, in Defiance of the Law: And praying, that the' House will take their Grievances into Confederation, and apply such & Remedy, as shall prevent the like for the future.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.,

Gaols of this Kingdom, on Account of the Penalties irt curred, and Duties owing, for clandestine Importations, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, having, by their Errors, fallen under the Severity of the Law, are, by long Confinement, with their unhappy Families, reduced to the greatest Necessities, and many thousand others, equally guilty with the Petitioners, have absconded and left their Families, to avoid the Terrors of the Petitioners Punishment; which is a Detriment to our Woollen Manufactures, the Fishery, and Trade in general, especially his Majesty's Service, tire greatest Part of them being seafaring Men: And, as the Petitioners are incapable of making any Reparation for their Faults, Extent, and long Imprisonments, having swallowed up what little Substance they had, which many of the Petitioners offered to Composition, they humbly pray the Companion of the House, to release them from the Duties, and several Penalties, incurred by their clan* destine Importations, and their present Confinement, which can have no other Consequence, than the Ruin of themselves, and their innocent Families.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 13th of March instant, proceeded to examine the Matters of the said Petitions:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners called

Mr. Robert Salmon*, who, being examined, said, that he knew very well the Road between St. Margaret's Church, in Rochester, and Maidstone, which leads through several Parishes, and contains above Eight Miles: That the same is in so bad and ruinous Condition, especially in the Winter Season, that it will cod at lead Fifty Pounds a Mile to amend it; and that many Parts thereof are (o narrow, that Coaches and Carriages cannot pass by one another; nor can a Horse pass by a Coach or Carriage in some Places.

That the same Witness, being examined as to the Condition of the Road from Maidstone to Mailing Heath, leading through Barming Woods, laid, That Road is about Two Miles, but so deep and bad, that it is not passable for Coaches and Carriages; and that it will cost near One hundred Pounds a Mile to repair it: And said further, that, if a draight Koid was made, the Road would be nearer by half a Mile.

That Mr. John Reeves, Mr. Wm. Cruttenden, Mr. Joseph Smalwell, and IVManjer, being severally examined, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Robert Salmon: And Joseph Smahvell added to his Evidence, that the repairing of the Road between Rochester and Maidstone would cost between £. 60 or^. 70 a Mile.

Mr. Smalwell, being examined as to the Condition of the Road, leading from Maidstone to Wrotham Heath, said, that the same is so bad, that it is almost impafiable; and that the Statute-work is not near sufficient to repair it.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing and enlarging the Road, leading from St. Margaret's Church, in Rochester, to Maidstone, and from thence to Mailing Heath, through Barming Woods, in the County of Kent, and that Mr. Finch, Mr. Whitworth, and Mr. Glanville, do prepare, and bring in the fame.

A Petition1 of the Cordwainers, and Curriers, and others, concerned in the Leather Trade within the Town and Parish of Tiverton, and Parts adjacent, in the County of Devon, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners have for several Years past been great Sufferers in their Trade, by reason of the Exportation of vast Quantities of Leather; which renders it so scarce, that they cannot get sufficient to carry on their Business, and so dear, that it is double the Price it used to be at; which Scarcity, and Dearness, is occasioned by the great Drawback the Exporter is allowed, who en-grofsall they can, by going to, and buying at, the Tanners Yards, contrary to the Act 90 Ann<e Regina: The Petitioners are also Sufferers by the Butchers cutting and galhing the Hides and Skins, contrary to Law, which obliges them to bring the Skins to a proper Place, to be viewed, andsearched, which would prevent that Abuse; but they fell them at their Shops, in Defiance of the Law: And praying, that the House will take their Grievances into Consideration, and apply such a Remedy, as shall prevent the like for the future.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table*

Smallet: That the said Election was on the 9th Day of September last; and the Commissioners from Glasgow, Rutherglen, and David Colquhon from Dumbarton, appeared at the Town-house of Dumbarton, which was the proper Place of Election, and demanded Admittance; but the said George Smallet, having the Night before placed a Guard of armed Men in the Town-house, and having another Guard of the Town Officers, and others, along with him, thought fit to post himself, with a Halbert in his Hand, at the Door, and taking upon himself to judge, who were lawful Delegates, refilled to admit any, but whom he thought fit, and in particular the said David Colquhon, and likewise refused Entrance to David Hutchinson, who appeared with a Commission to be Common Clerk to the Town of Dumbarton; whereupon the Commissioners for

Marl'd. d- 1728.

Glasgow and Rutherglen insisted, that every Person, pretending to have a Commission to be Delegate, or Common Clerk, should be admitted, that their Right might be determined; which the said Smallet absolutely refused, saying, himself was the legal Delegate for Dumbarton, without so much as (hewingany Commissionl for that Purpose; against which Proceedings the Commissioners for Glasgow, Rutherglen, and the said David Colquhon, protested, and declared, they came there to have given their Votes for the Petitioner; and, giving publik Notice to all then present, withdrew to the nearest convenient House, and chose the Petitioner, and made use of the said David Hutchinson, as Clerk to the Meeting; and the Commissioner from Renfrew refused to concur with Smallet, as apprehending his Proceedings to be arbitrary; but the said George Smallet alone has taken upon him to name Daniel Campbell,

Esquire, to be Member for the said District, and James Duncanfon,2iS Common Clerk of Dumbarton, hath returned him, as duly elected, in Prejudice of the Petitioner: And praying the Relief of the House in the Premises.

Wendover A Petition of the Persons, whose Names are theretmto Election, subscribed, Constables, and Burgesses, of the Borough of Wendover, in the County of Bucks, on behalf of themselves, and many other Burgesses, having a Right to vote in the Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the proper Officers, to make the Return of Members, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, are the Constables, annually chosen at the Manor Court, held before the Steward of the Lord of the Manor of Wendover for the Time being: That the Lord of the said Manor, in 1726, was Richard Hampden, Esquire, and his Steward was Francis Sheldon, Gentleman; but by an Act of Parliament, parted the last Session of King George the First, the said Richard Hampden became diverted of all his real Estates, with the said Manor of Wendover, which are verted in the Trustees, mentioned in the said Act; and at a Manor Court, held before the said Mr. Sheldon, in October, 1726, Jonathan Fofter, and William Christmas, were chosen Constables of the said Borough, and acted as such, in returning the Lord Limerick, and Mr. Hampden, as Members for this present Parliament; and their Time expiring on the 25th of October last, at a Court then held, John Ginger, junior, and Wm. Trott, were elected Constables, and had the Staffs delivered them, and acted, and ought to act, as Constables for the whole Year ensuing: That Mr. Hampden, being elected Knight of the Shire for the County of Bucks, as well as a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Wendover, did, on the 13th of March last, make his Election, to serve for the said County of Bucks; and thereupon a new Writ issued, for electing a Burgess for Wendover, which ought to have been returned by the said John Ginger and Wm. Trott; but John Hamilton, Esquire, intending to set himfe'lf up as a Candidate for the said Borough at the new Election, caused another Court of the said Manor to be held, in an illegal Manner, within Fourteen Days after the said former Court, before John Geary, Gentleman, as Steward to Mr. Hampden, and procured Thomas Penning, and Wm. North, junior, to be chosen Constables: That on the 131h of March last the said Mr. Hamilton, by Bribery,-and other corrupt Practices, procured himself to be elected a Member, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, and is returned as such by the said Benning and North, who refused several of the Petitioners Votes 2 And praying, that the Election and Return of the said John Hamilton, Esquire, may be declared void.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Mr. Compton reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of his Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the County of Bedford, met at their General Quarter Sessions of the Peace* holden at Bedford for the said County, the Fourth Day of October, 1727, and the Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, and other Inhabitants, redding near the Parishes of Newport Pag-nell, Moulfoe, Broughton, Middleton, Keynes, and Waven don, in the County of Bucks, and also of several Waggoners, and Stage-coach-men, in behalf of themselves, and others, were referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 21st of March last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the First Petition: And, to make good the Allegations of the lame.

The Act of Parliament, mentioned in the said Petition, passed in the 5 th Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repairing the Highways between Hockliffe and Woburn, in the County of Bedford, was produced, and Part thereof read; whereby it appeared, that the Toll, by the said Act granted, was made payable for the Term of 21 Years, from the 24th Day of June, 1707; but the Tolls and Profits, arising in the two last Years of that Term, are, by the said Act, directed to be paid to the Lord of the Manor of Battles-don, and the same have been paid to him accordingly, ever since the 24th of June, 1726.

Then a Witness was called, to prove the Condition of the said Highways between Hockliffe and Woburn \ viz.

Mr. Jof. Willoughby: Who, being examined, said, that, although the Money collected by the Tolls, hath been applied, and accounted for, as the Act directs, yet several Parts of the Highways are ftiil very much out of Repair; and that they cannot, by the ordinary Course of the Laws and Statutes of this Realm, be effectually amended, without some further Provision be made, for ra-ifing Money to be applied for that Purpose, Materials fit for repairing the Roads being at a great Distance from the same.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine the Matter of the Second Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, several Witnesses were called; viz.

John Ingram, John Gregory, John Holmes, John Cxcjfi, and Wm. Wotton: Who, being severally examined, said, that the Road, leading from Woburn to Bickford Bridge, leading through the several Parishes of Wavendon, Middleton Keynes, Broughton, Moulfoe, and Newport Pagnell, in the County of Bucks, is become very bad, and dangerous to Passengers; and also said, that the Inhabitants of the several Parirties have constantly. done their Statute-work in the said Road.

And the same Persons gave Evidence, that, if the Inhabitants of the several Parishes, through which the said Road leads, were to do and pay much more, than they are obliged to do andraifeby Law, the same would not be sufficient effectually to repair the Road, so as to make it commodious for Passengers.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the more effectual amending the Highway between Hockliffe and Woburn, in the County of Bedford, and for repairing the Road, leading through Woburn to Tickford Bridge, in Newport Pagnell\ in the County of Bucks; and that Mr. Compton and Mr. Wrigbie do prepare, and brine in, the fame.

A Petition of the Cordwainers, and Traders in Leather, inhabiting in the Borough of Plymouth, in the County of Devon, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, for several Years last past, have been great Sufferers in their Trades, by reason of the great Scarcity, and Dearnefe, of Leather; so that Merchants, who used to export, yearly, above One hundred Dozen of Shoes, do now hardly export any at all, telling the Petitioners that Goods, made in foreign Parts, of our own Leather, are fold cheaper there, than those made here, to the Impoverishment of the Petitioners; the chief Occasion of which they conceive to be, the great Encouragement given to the Exportation of Leather, by Drawbacks allowed to the Exporters, who buy up the same at the Tanners Yard, before the same is duly tanned, and dryed; whereby the Markets are forestalled, and the Petitioners are forced to give the Tanners what Price they please for their Leather: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The House (according to Order) resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Petition of Thomas Hammond, late of London, Merchant, in behalf of himself, and Samuel Woodlaw and Henry Woo din, his Sureties.

That an Act of Parliament passed in the 3d Year of his late Majesty's Reign (which was produced to the Committee) for continuing the DutyofTwo Penies Scots on every Pint of Ale and Beer, fold in the City of Edinburgh, and Privileges thereof, for the Benefit of the said City, and for difeantinuing the Payment of the Dues, commonly called the Petty Port Customs, at Edinburgh, during the Continuance of that Act.

That by the last Clause in the said Act it is provided, and enacted, that the Dues paid, and commonly called or known by the Name of the Petty Port Customs, payable at the Port of tlxe City of Edinburgh, should be difeon-tinu.ed and cease, during the Continuance of that Act.

That, in the Ninth Year of his said late Majesty's Reign another Act passed, which was also produced to the said Committee, for enlarging the derm granted by the said Act, made in the 3d Year of his said I ate Majesty's Reign, and for making the said Act more effectual.

And in the said Act, of the Ninth Year of his said late Majesty's Reign, there is the like Clause, for difeon-tinuing the Payment of the Petty Port Customs, during the Continuance of that Act.

That it appeared to the Committee, that some Doubts and Questions have arisen in relation to the true Meaning of the Clause in both Acts, touching the Petty Port Customs, there being noDiftinct ion, or Enumeration, of such of the Petty Port Customs, as were by the said Acts to be discontinued, or such, as were to be continued.

Sir William Yotige reported from the Committee, ap- National pointed to draw up a Representation, to be made to his Debt. Majesty, upon the Resolutions of the House, the Twelfth of March last, and upon the Debate of the House, laying before his Majesty a particular Account of the national Debts, discharged, and incurred, since the Twenty-fifth Day of December. 1716, distinguished under their proper Heads and Services, with a State of the Sinking Fund, and of the publick Credit; that they had drawn up a Representation accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Tabic; where the same was twice read, and amended, and is as follows; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

Your Majesty's most dutiful and faithful Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, having, in Duty to your Majesty, for the Sake of Truth, and for the better Information and Satisfaction of all your good People, taken into their Consideration the State of the national Debt, in regard to what Debts have been discharged and paid off, since the Establishment of the Sinking Fund for that Purpose, and what new Debts have, within the said Time, been contrafted and incurred, beg Leave, with all Duty and Submission, to lay the same before your Majesty in this our most humble Representation.

The national Debt of this Kingdom, contrafted in carrying on Two long and expensive Wars, before the happy Accession of your Majesty's late royal Father to the Crown of these Realms, as it was a Matter of the last Consequence to the Nation, was become the Care and Concern of all, whowished well to our present and future Prosperity. This produced several Considerations in Parliament, to find out, and settle, some Means of putting this great Debt into a Method of being gradually reduced and diminished; and the Sinking Fund was at last happily established, to general Satisfaction. This Fund became immediately the favourite Article in all parliamentary Considerations, relating to the publick Revenues, and was considered as a national Interest, worthy of the highest Regard and Attention; which was, by all possible Means, to be cherished and improved, and the Produce of it set apart, and kept distinct, from all other Services and Purposes, and was appropriated by Parliament, to pay off and discharge national Debts, incurred before the Twenty-fifth Day of December, 1716.

Hence arose that Distinction in the publick Revenues, which has ever since been so far continued, and kept up, that the Nation has seemed to have Two different Interests; one, in the Produce of the Sinking Fund, for the Discharge of the national Debt, another, in the annual Supplies, granted to the Crown, for carrying on the current Service of the Year.

But several Controversies having of late Years been started, concerning what real Benefit had accrued to the Nation from the Produce and Application of the Sinking Fund, if considered and compared with new Debts, iup-posed to have been incurred within the same Time; the Commons of Great Britain, truly sensible of the Weight of this national Debt, a Burthenof itfelfsufficient to create some Uneasiness in the minds of the People, without the Help of any Aggravations, or Misrepresentations, thought it a Duty incumbent upon them, so far to enter into the

Consideration

i Geo. II. ' 8° JpHlis

i2i

Copsideration of this important Affair, as to examine, and state, how much of the national Debt, incurred before the Twenty-fifth of December, 1716, had been actually paid off, or discharged, and what new Debts had been really contrafted and incurred in Support of the Publick, and in carrying on the current Service of the several Years, since that time.

It is well known, with what Content and Chearfulriefs your Majesty's Subjects have all along paid and contributed towards the annual interestof this national Debt, contracted and incurred in securing to them the inefti* mable Blessings of your Majesty's most auspicious Reign, and the Protestant Succession in your illustrious Family, and in Defence of their Religion, Liberties, and Properties, which they always thought, could not be purchased* and preserved, at too dear a Rate; ari$y from the Time they had the Comfort of having a Sinking Fund settled and established, that gave them the Prospect and Hopes of seeing this great Debt gradually reduced, and discharged, it was a Satisfaction* that rendered the Burthen easy and light; and your People seemed even to forget the great Expence they had been at, happy in the tree and full Enjoyment of all that was dear and valuable to them, the Fruit'and Return of so much Treasure, necessarily and usefully employed.

notwithstanding this flourishing State of the publick Credit, and the good Effects of this happy Situation, there were not wanting those, who attempted to disturb the Quiet and Satisfaction, that almost universally prevailed in the Minds of your People, by publishing and promoting, with the greatest Industry, most notorious Mifreprelen tat ions of the true State of our Debts, and of the Provisions made for the Discharge of them; and by infusing groundless Jealousies and Insinuations, as if the Produce of the Sinking Fund had been but little and inconsiderable, or that by wrong and imprudent Measures, bad Economy, Neglect, or Mi ('management, unnecessary Expences had been made, and new Debts contracted, that not only equalled, but exceeded by several Millions, the Amount of the old Debts, that had been discharged.

These artful Insinuations and M ifrepre fen tat ions served to a double Purpose, to make our Fellow-subjects restless and uneasy under their present Difficulties, by persuading them, they were endless, and inextricable; and, at the same time, so apprehensive of new Engagements, that they might be prepared rather to suffer all Sorts of In-fults and Injuries, than by endeavouring to do themselves

Justice, to enter into new Expences; every-where repre-lented as destructive and intolerable.

This prevailing Mischief called for an imniediate Remedy, and made it necessary to enter into a strict Disquisition of the Truth and Certainty of these Affairs, that your Majesty might be truly informed, and your faithful and well-affected Subjects have the Satisfaction to fee, how grofly the World had been imposed upon by these ground less Mifreprelen tations 5 and that your Enemies might be convinced, that the Wealth and Power of Great Britain is not so exhausted, as to render this Nation, under your Majesty's happy Government, less considerable and formidable, than in the 'time of any of yctfr royal Predecessors.

We observed, that what gave any Foundation for the Belief of these notorious Falflhoods, was, the Liberty which some misinformed, or ill-designing*Personshad taken from the several Alterations, which had been made of late Years in the Shape or Denomination of our publick Debts, to make and publish imaginary States of the Whole of those Debts, by putting fictitious Values upon them, at theit own Will and Pleasure, and from thence making Balances, that might serve their Purpose, but were not really true.

But the Difficultiesof making up this Account in that Manner, with any Certainty, made us carefully avoid going into a Method, which might be afterwards liable to Cavil and Disputes, according to the Humour, Caprice, or private Opinion, of every Man.

That wemight therefore avoid, as much as possible, any Doubt or Perplexity, we proceeded to state the Truth of this Past in a Method, that was plain, obvious, and intelligible to the meanest Capacity; and took an Account of the several national Debts, incurred before the Twerity-fifth Day of December, 1716, which, since that time, had been actually paid off, or discharged, and also an Account of the several national Debts, that, since that time, had been contrafted or incurred, and were still subsisting; upon comparing of which together, it will appear, whether the national Debt is, since the Establishment of the Sinking Fund, increased, or decreased, and so what Amount.

Having now gone through this Enquiry with as much Care and Exactness, as wos possible, we beg leave, in the most dutiful Manner, to lay before your Majesty Two Accounts; the First containing the several particular Articles of national Debts, incurred before the Twenty-fifth Day of December 1716, and since discharged; which is as followeth:

From these Two Accounts, we presume most humbly to represent to your Majesty, that the several national Debts, incurred before the Twenty-fifth Day of December, 1716, which have been since discharged, after deducting the before-mentioned Sum of £.22,357, do

amount in the Whole to the Sum of Six millions Six hundred and Twenty-six thousand Four hundred and Four Pounds, Sixteen Shillings, and Nine Pence Half-peny; and that the several national Debts, incurred since the said Twenty-fifth Day of December, 1716, and now subsisting, amount together to the Sum of Three millions Nine hundred Twenty-seven thousand Nine hundred Eighty-eight Pounds, Seven Shillings, and One Peny Three Farthings.

Which being deduded out of the Amount of the Debts discharged, the Difference is so much real Decrease of the national Debt since the Twenty-fifth Day of December, 1716, being Two millions Six hundred Ninety-eight thousand Four hundred and Sixteen Pounds, Nine Shillings, and Seven Pence Three Farthings.

And, that the State of the new-con traded Debts may appear in a true Light, we think it necessary, for the better Information of your Majesty, to distinguish them under Vol. 21.

the proper Heads of Services, for which they were contracted, and, by way of Explanation, to observe, that a considerable Part of the new-contracted Debt, amounting to the Sum of £.703,740. 6s. 2\d. was occasioned by the annual Provisions, made by Parliament for making good the yearly Deficiencies of the General Fund to and for the Year ending at Michaelmas, 1726, pursuant to the Directions of the Ad establishing the General Fund, the Surplus whereof compotes Part of the Sinking Fund; and by these Means the Sinking Fund h*s received annually some Proportion out of the Supplies of the Year:

And, that the further Sum of £.290,029. has been raised by new-contracted Debts, and is included therein, for making good at several Times the Deficiencies of the original and additional Funds of the South Sea Company;-which Two Sums, amounting together to the Sum of £.993,769. 6j. z\d. having been applied towards making good Deficiencies of the General Fund, and other Funds, established before the 25th Day of December, 1716, ought to be distinguished from the national Debt incurred since that Time;

And further, to obviate any Objections that may be made to the Rating of the Account of national Debts, contracted and incurred since die Twenty-fifth of December, 1716, and still subsisting, it is proper to observe, that no Notice is taken therein of the Debts by Loans, or Exchequer Bills, on the annual Land Taxes, or Malt Duties; because, as those Loans, or Bills, are weekly discharged out of the Produce of those Taxes, and asroften as any Deficiencies happen thereon, they, as well as the Deficiencies of Grants, are not suffered to remain as Debts, but are constantly from Year to Year, discharged, by being made Part of the Supplies, granted for the current Service of the subsequent Years; and accordingly Provision has been already made for such of them as can be anyways ascertained, out of the Supplies for the Service of the Year 1728; therefore, they were not proper to be brought into this Account.

Having thus humbly represented to your Majesty the true State of the Decrease of the national Debts since the 25th Day of December, 1716, and the Establishment of the Sinking Fund, with the Occasions and Services for which the several new Debts have been incurred, we beg Leave, by this our humble Representation, to lay before your Majesty the Ci re urn (lances this Nation was in, with regard to the national Debt, before the Establishment of the Sinking Fund, and what happy Consequences have arisen from the Establishment thereof.

At the Accession of your Majesty s late royal Father to the Throne of these Realms, a great part of the publick Debts confided of absolute Annuities, granted for very long Terms of Years, which were only to be discharged by the wearing out of those Terms; other great Parts thereof were the capital Stocks of the Bank, the South Sea and India Companies, at very high Interest; other Debts were charged upon particular Funds, appropriated to pay off and discharge the principal Moneys, with Interest, at very high Rates, in course, to Multitudes of People both at home and abroad; other great Parts thereof were in Exchequer Bills, circulated and exchanged at very high Rates for Interest, Premium, and Charges; and the Debts of the Army, which were very considerable, were not then liquidated, nor had any Provision at all then been made for the Discharge of them: Besides this, the Funds themselves, appropriated for these Debts, were most of them deficient; so that, if these Debts had been differed to continue in this State, so far would they have been from being lessened to any Degree, that new Burthens mufthave been laid on the Nation, for securing the Debts unprovided for.

Soon after his late Majesty's Accession, an unnatural Rebellion broke out, during which, not only ail Thoughts # for any Method for the more speedy Payment of our Debts were of Necessity suspended, but new and heavy

Fears of the People removed, but the Parliament immediately began to set about the great Work of putting the national Debt in a Method of being sooner discharged with Honour and Justice; and, in the Year 1717, the Foundation was laid, by establishing the Sinking Fund; the Consequences and Advantages whereof will befit appear, by considering, what it is, and by what Means it was perfected.

The only Methods, that could be thought of, for paying off the national Debts, must be, either by improving and augmenting the Produce of the Funds, already settled for the Payment of the Principal and Interest, or by granting new Taxes and Impositions upon the People, or by a Reduction of the Interest, made payable on the several Debts; and, as the first Method would have been found not diffident to answer this desirable End, and the Second would have been very grievous and burthensome to the People, the principal Merhod, that was then thought expedient, and most free from Objections, was to reduce the high Interest, and other Charges, payable on all the publick Debts: But, as great Part of those Debts were not subject to any Power of Redemption, and as none of them werer redeemable, but on Payment of the principal Money, it manifestly appeared, that such a Reduction could never be made, without the voluntary Consent of the Proprietors of such, as were irredeemable, or a legal Tender ro the others of their principal Money; both which seemed at that time almost impracticable; but, by an extraordinary Zeal and Application to the publick Service, this Difficulty was surmounted, with respect to the whole of the Debts, that were then redeemable, by procuring, not only the voluntary Consent of the South Sea Company to the Reduction of the Interest on their whole capital Stock, then confiding of Ten Millions, from £.6. to £.5. per Cent, and of the Bank to a like Reduction on an Annuity, then payable to them in respect of a Sum of upwards of £.1,7 75>000. and to a great Abatement in their Allowances for circulating Exchequer Bills, then amounting to more than£.4,500,000. at an annual Charge of above £.7. per Cent. but also by engaging those Corporations to furnish sufficient Sums for paying the principal Money to such of the Proprietors of other redeemable Debts, amounting to more than Nine Millions, as would not voluntarily choose to accept an Interest at £.5. per Cent. for the future.

This Provision being made, the Act passed in the Third Year of his late Majesty's Reign, for establishing the General Fund; whereby the Proprietors of certain Debts therein mentioned, all carrying an Interest at £.6. perCent. had their free Election, either to accept an Interest at £,5. per Cent. per Annum, or to receive their principal Money; and so general was the Satisfaction of all the Proprietors, that few and very inconsiderable Sums were demanded to be paid off; but the principal Sums, that were voluntarily reduced to £.5. per Cent, amounted to £.9,392,311. 4s. *i\d. or thereabouts; and by this Method more than £.25,800,000. was at once voluntarily reduced from £.6. per Cent. or upwards, to £.5. per Cent. which was an annual Saving of above £.320,000.

By the same Act, not only the Surplus of this General Fund, but the Surplusses of several other Funds, were appropriated to the Discharge of national Debts, contrafted before the Twenty-fifth of December, 1716: And this was the Beginning and Establishment of the Sinking Fund.

From this happy Event arose such general Satisfaction in all Degrees of People, that though the Interest of the publick Debts was reduced, and the Proprietors received a less Income from them, than before, yet their Security for their Capital being so much mended, the Rate or Price for the Purchase of these Debts soon advanced to a much higher Value, than they were at before the Reduc-and it was easy to foresee, that, in Process of Time,

But now, at length, net only the Reduction from £. 5. to £. 4. per Cent, settled by the South Sea Ad, has taken place, but a voluntary Reduction hath also been made, by the Bank of England, from £. 5. to £. 4. per Cent. Interest or Annuities, for Two principal Sums belonging to them, amounting together to upwards of £. 3,775,000. and by these several Reductions a further Addition is made to the Sinking Fund of more than £.377,000. per Annum, from Midsummer last: By all these Means, and by the Savings of Interest of the Debts, that have been already discharged, and by several wife Provisions for the Improvement of the Funds themselves, this Sinking Fund is risen to, and may be reasonably estimated at £. 1,200,000. per Annum, or thereabouts; and will be every Year increasing from the further Savings of the Interest of the remaining Debts, from time to time, as they shall be paid off.

But, if any thing were further necessary to demonstrate the immediate and certain Advantages, that have accrued to the Publick from the Methods used and established to discharge the national Debts, it is sufficient only to refled, that the Interest of the greatest Part of the Debt, being now actually reduced from £. 6. to £. 4. per Cent. makes a Saving of One-third of the Interest of such Debt; which, being in the Hands and Possession of the Government, and applicable, from time to time, to the Discharge of the Principal, makes a Gain and Profit to the Publick, equal to the Discharge of One-third of such Principal.

And, if the Amount of the Produce of the Sinking Fund did appear originally to be about £. 400,000. per Annum only, the Produce of the said Fund being now raised to about £. 1,200,000. per Annum, the Addition of £. 800,000. per Annum to the Sinking Fund, which is just so much gained by the Publick, if valued at Twenty-five Years Purchase, at which Rate all Annuities are now currently fold, makes a real Profit to the Publick, amounting to Twenty Millions.

This is the happy State of the Sinking Fund, taken separately, and by itself; but, if we cast our Eyes upon the State cf our publick Credit in general, it must be an additional Satisfaction to us, that by preserving the publick Faith inviolable, by the Discharge of the old Exchequer Bills, and the Reduction of the high Interest on all our (landing Debts, the whole Credit, that is taken on^the annual Funds, for carrying on the current Service of the year, is and may be supplied for the future at £. 3. per Cent, or less, for Interest, Premium, and Charges, by Exchequer Bills, created, just as the Occasions of the Publick require, without any Loans, or being obliged to any Persons for Money to be advanced, or lent, on the Credit of them; and so far is the Publick from being under the former Necessities of allowing extravagant Interest, Premiums, or Discounts, for any Money they want, that the only Contest now among the Creditors of the Publick is, that every one of them desires to be the last in course cf Payment*

Permit us then, Mofl: gracious Sovereign, to congratulate your Majesty on the comfortable Prospect we hdve now before us, if, notwithstanding the many Difficulties this Nation has laboured under since the happy Accession cf your Majesty V late royal Father to the Throne, notwithstanding the unnatural Rebellion, which soon after broke out, and the many heinous Plots and Conspiracies, which have since been formed and carried on for overturning the Religion and Libertieaiof our Country, and the Protestant Succession in your mofl: illustrious Family, the many Disturbances, which have arisen, and the uncertain and embroiled Condition of the Affairs of Europe, not a little fomented and encouraged by the false Intelligence, and malicious Insinuations, which have been industriously fptead abroad by your Majesty's and our Enemies, of the uneasy and perplexed State of our Affairs at home, as if that had rendered it almost Vol. 21.

Aprilis. 125,

impossible for this Nation, effectually to exert themselves in Defence of their own just Rights and Possessions, and for establishing, and securing, the publick Peace and Tranquillity; if, notwithstanding these and many other Difficulties, which we laboured under, and while the Sinking Fund was yet in its Infancy, and so much less than it now is, we have been able to diminish the national Debts so much already, what may we not hope for in regard to a mote speedy and sensible Discharge of them for the future, now the Sinking Fund is so greatly increased, and our publick Credit in so flourishing a Condition

The finishing and perfecting this great Work seems to be a peculiar Glory reserved for your Majesty's Reign. From your known Goodness and Wisdom, the present Age may promise themselves the certain and immediate Benefit of your Majesty's particular Regard to the publick Credit, and your universal Care and Concern for the Ease and Happiness of your People, which our latest Posterity mull remember, and acknowledge with Duty and Gratitude.

Fulham Mr. Vincent reported from the Committee, to whom and Putney the Petition of the Commissioners and Trustees, appointed Bddge. by an Act of Parliament, passed in the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty's Reign, for building a Bridge cross the River of Thames, from the Town of Fulham, in the County of Middlesex, to the Town of Putney, in the County of Surrey, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk'sTable; where the same was read i and the Report, and Resolutions of the Committee, are as follows; viz.

That the Committtee had, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 3d Instant, examined the Matter of the said Petition, which the Committee found to be as follows; viz.

That the Book, wherein are entered all the Proceedings of the Commissioners and Trustees, appointed to put the said Act in Execution, was produced; whereby it appeared to the Committee, that several Propofols had been made by Workmen, for building the Bridge.

The First. Proposal, that was made to the Commissioners and Trustees, and which was produced, and read, to the Committee, was by Thomas Phillips, Carpenter; who proposed to do the Carpenters Work, necessary towards building the Bridge, for £. 7,106. 12 s. and to keep the Wood-work in Repair for 12 years, at £. 80. per Annum.

The next Proposal, that was made to the Commissioners and Trustees, was by Andrews Jelfe, Mason, which Proposal was produced and read to the Committee, who proposed to do the Masons Work for £. 1,766. and to keep the same in Repair for 12 Years, at £. to per Annum.

Then was produced, and read, to the Committee, the Proposal of John Mist, Paviour; who proposed to pave the said Bridge for £. 693. 18 s. and to keep the same in Repair for 12 Years, the First Year to have One Pepper Corn, and the Eleven succeeding Years £.30. per Annum.

That the several Sums mentioned in the several Pro-pofals, amounted in the whole to £. 9,566. 10 s.

That, in order to ascertain, what Damages will accrue to the Owners and Proprietors of the Horse Ferry, by erecting the said Bridge, it appeared to the Committee, that Juries were impannelled, according to the Act: of Parliament; and the Verdicts of those Juries were produced to the Committee, who have ascertained the Damages to be £. 9,655. 10s.

And it appeared to the Committee, that the Damages, which will be sustained by the Watermen of Fulham and Putney, who claim a Right to the Sundays Foot Ferry, will be £. 62. per Annum, exclusive of the aforesaid Sum

or jC* 9>^ss- 10 s-

That, as the present Act now Hands, the Commissioners and Trustees are not sufficiently enabled to carry on the Work; neither can they raise any Money by any Contributions of their own, they being retrained from lending or advancing Money, upon the credit of the Act; but, if they were enabled to do it by way of Loan, or Annuities, by the Alignment of the Tolls in perpetuity, as other Persons can and may do, it would very much tend to the carrying on and compleating the Undertaking.

That the Petitioners fully proved the Allegations of their Petition; and the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, unless Leave be given to the said Commissioners and Trustees to grant Annuities, by Assignment of the Tolls in perpetuity, they will not be enabled to raise a Sum sufficient for erecting the said Bridge.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Commissioners and Trustees ought to have a Power of lending or advancing Money, in the same manner as other Persons, towards erecting the said Bridge.
