Address on Answer.

Mr. Speaker reported, that he did, with the House, Yesterday attend his Majesty, and presented to his Majesty their humble Representation; and that his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer ‘thereunto; viz.

Gentlemen,

I cannot but be very.Well pleased with this Represen-‘ tation, which must give general Satisfaction to all my People, by removing those groundless Jealousies and Apprehensions which have been propagated and dif-perfect throughout the Kingdom.

The happy Effects of the flourishing State of the publick Credit are too* sensibly felt, and seen, not to be confessed and acknowledged by every body:

And the Provision made for gradually discharging the national Debt, is now become so certain, and considerable, that nothing, but some unforeseen Event, can alter or diminifti it; which gives us the faired Prospect of seeing the old Debts discharged, without any Necessity of incurring new ones:

And you may beaflured, that tt shall be my particular Care and Study to maintain and preserve the publick Credit, to improve the Sinking Fund, and to avoid all Occasions of laying any new Burthens upon my People*

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return the most humble Thanks of this House to his Majesty, for his most gracious Answer to their Representation.

Montgomery - Mr. Earle, according to Order, reported from the Election, Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the double Return, and Election, for the Town of Montgomery, in the County of Mont* gomery, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Report, and Resolutions, are as follows; viz.

Upon the double Return of William Corbet, Esquire, and Robert Williams, Esquire, to serve for the Town ' of Montgomery, in the County of Montgomery, and the respective Petitions of the said Mr. Corbet and Mr. Williams;'mutually complaining of the Return, and Election, of each ocher; and also the Petition of several Burgesses of the said Town of Montgomery, and several Burge lies of the Boroughs of Llanidloes, Poole, and Llanvylling, in the County of Montgomery, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and other Burgesses of the said Three Boroughs, complaining that due Notice of the Election was not given to the Burgesses of the said Three last mentioned Boroughs, and that, although their Votes were taken, yet they were unduly prevented joining in the Return of Mr. Williams, which they would have done; and also complaining of the Return of Mr. Corbet, as by the Burgesses of Montgomery only:

The Committee have inspected the said Double Return, and have examined the Merits of this Election.

The Return is by Two several Indentures; viz.

That of Mr. Cdrbet is by Edward Botterell, Esquire, one of the Bailiffs of the Borough of Montgomery, and the Majority of the Burgesses of the said Borough;

And the Return of Mr. Williams is mentioned to be made by John Greenly, Esquire, one of the Bailiffs of the said Borough of Montgomery, and many Burgesses, as well of the said Borough, as of the several Boroughs of Poole, Llanidloes, and Ltanvylling, some of which Burgesses are named in the Body of the Return; and the Return is mentioned to be signed and sealed by the said Bailiff and Burgesses, but is executed by the Bailiff only.

The Counsel for Mr. Corbet insisted, that the Right of Election is in the Burgesses of the Borough of Montgomery only, notwithstanding the last Determination of the House to the contrary.

The Counsel for Mr. Williams, and for the Petitioners in favour of the said Three Boroughs of Poole, Llanidloes, and Llanvylling, called the Out Boroughs, insisted, that the Burgesses of the said Three Out Boroughs have a Right to vote in the Election, equal with the Burgesses of Montgomery.

And the Counsel for Mr. Corbet called the following Witnesses: viz.

Moses Powell; who spoke for 50 Years; and said, the Right of Election was always taken to be in the Burgesses of Montgomery only; and that Mr. Herbert's Election to the Convention Parliament was by thofeBurgeffes only; but there was no Opposition; none of the Out Burgesses claimed then, as he saw; and that he had heard several ancient People, who are since dead, say, that the Right of Election was in the Burgesses of Montgomery: That Price Devereux, Esquire, was, after the Convention, elected by the Burgesses of Montgomery only; but that no Oppofi-tion had been since the Convention.

Being cross-examined, he said, he had heard of a disputed Election in King "James the 2d's Time; when Mr. Williams was chole by the Burgesses of Montgomery, and Mr. Herbert by those of the Out Boroughs:

That Mr. Dcvercux, was chose Three times; and the Second time he gave^.10. to each of the Out Boroughs, to vote, and sign the Return:

That he did not remember any contested Election; nor did he know that ever any Burgesses of the Out

Boroughs voted, or offered to vote.

Morrice James spoke for 46 Years; and said, that Mr. Charles Herbert was returned to the Convention Parliament by the Burgesses of Montgomery only; and that he had heard several old People say, that the Burgesses of Montgomery had paid their Members Wages, and that they only had the Right of Eiefition: That the Burgesses of the Out Boroughs had voted: Thar, when Mr. De-vereux flood, the Bailiffs desired the Out Burgesses might vote, that he might be returned by them all: That he heard Mr. Devereux say, he would rather have One Burgess of Montgomery, than Twenty of Pool: That there was no Opposition in the Election to the Convention Parliament; Six or Seven from Pool then offered to vote, and were refilled: That Out Burgesses were taken against Mr. Mason in 1705, when he, and Mr. Vaughan, flood.

Richard Powell lpoke for 60 Years; and laid, that his Mailer, Mr. Whittingham, the Town-clerk, told him, that the Ele<ftion of Mathew Priie, Esquire, about 50 Years since, was by the Burgesses of Montgomery only: That Mr. Lloyd, in Opposition, brought some Men from Pool; but their Votes were refused: That he had heard, old Men lay, none had a Right to vote, but the Burgesses of Montgomery; and that they had coJlcdted Money at Montgomery, in King Charles the Second's Time, for the Burgesses Wages; but none was collected of the Out Burgesses.

Charles AJpfon, Esquire, said, that he served for Montgomery about 25 or 2 6 Years since, and demanded his Wages of the Bailiff of Welsh Pool, who refused to pay; but he owned, he had no Certificate: That he excused thofirof Montgomery, became they were his Friends: That Vqi. 21.

be did not believe, the Out Boroughs had a Right to vote: Montgomery That Mr. Vaughan, and the Out Boroughs petitioned Elation, against him; and the Petition was heard, and the Right of the Out Boroughs was not questioned, because they agreed:

That the Bailiffs of Montgomery sent the Serjeants, to give Notice of the filedion to the Out Boroughs, and some of them were admitted at his Eiefition; and he had beard, their first Claim was in King James the id's Time.

The Counsel for Mr. Corbet admitted, that the Three put Boroughs, before named, were ancient Boroughs before; the Statute of the 27 Hen. VIII. but infilled, that they had only a conditional Right of voting, in case they paid to the parliamentary Wages; which they not having done, they had no Right to vote.

The Counsel for Mr. Williams, and for the Burgesses of the said Three Out Boroughs, infilled, that those Burgesses had an equal Right to vote with the Burgesses of Montgomery; and that those Put Burgesses were equally liable by Law to the parliamentary Wages, and mignr be compelled to pay the same; and that they had anciently contributed thereto, when Wages were taken.

A Petition of the distressed iiifolvent Debtors, near Five hundred in Number* Prisoners in the Marshalsea Prison, Southwark, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands Debtors in the several Gaols of this Kingdom, was presented to the House* and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners are in a starving Condition, through the Rigour of their Creditors, who refuse all Offers made to them, althbugh the Petitioners are willing to satisfy them, as fer as their Effects will reach: That, if Starving, or a lingering Death, could be of any Advantage to their Creditors, otherwise than to gratify their Passion, their Conduct could not be blamed; but a Prison will pay no Debts: But the Blessings which attend this Kingdom, by the happy Accession of his present Majesty to the Crown, which gives his People the utmost Joy, so the poor Prisoners, confined in their respective Gaols, hope to partake thereof, with the rest of their Fellow-subjects, by their Releasement: And praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for their Relief.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

, And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, dated the lift Day of Marchfoft., proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petitions;

And, by the Evidence of several Persons, it appeared.

That the Towns of Pooleg Harwich, Portsmouth, &c. are very much impoverished, and the Trade lessened, by reason, that several of the unhappy Inhabitants, who, through Ignorance, or Inadvertency, either run, imported, or bought, Goods, which had not paid the Duties, are now confined in Prison, and very few of them, if any, capable of making any Composition or Satisfaction for the same; and that several of the Persons, having given Bail, are run away5 and most of the People under Prq-fecution are seafaring Men, who, in regard to their own Safety, will in all Probability be induced, if not thereby obliged, to withdraw themselves out of his Majesty's Dominions, as many of them have already done.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to enable the Commissioners of the Treasury, or Lord High Treasurer, for the Time being, to compound with Thomas Hammond,\aXz of London, Merchant, and his Sureties, for a Debt due to the Crown for Customs on Tobacco and Wine, without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for impowering the honourable Charles Howard, Esquire, to raise Money by Sale, or Mortgage, of the Manors of Walden, alias Chipping Walden, Brook Walden, and other Manors and Lands therein mentioned, for payment of the Debts of Charles William, late Earl of Suffolk and Bindon, deceased; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting the real Estates of William Scour field, the elder, Esquire, Catherine, his Wife, William Scourfield, the younger, Esquire, and Anne his Wife, in the Counties Vol. 21.

A Petition of the Merchants, and other Inhabitants, of Newfoundland the Town and Port of Poole, in the County of Poole, *i(hery. trading to, and concerned in, the Fishery of Newfoundland, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that the Petitioners employ about Forty Sail of Ships yearly in the Newfoundland Fishery: That the Fish on the Coastof the old Settlements have altered their Couife, which formerly began in May, when they made 300 Quintals per Boat; but of late Years took no Fish till the latter End of July, and then made but from 70 to 120 Quintals per Boat at the mod, and last Season, in the Bays of Conception and Trinity, did not make above 60 Quintals per Boat, which did not pay above half the Charge of the Outset; and such Fish coming so late in the Season, is generally ill cured, and comes so late to the proper Market, that 'tis a great Damage to Trade; for t he French, at Cape Britaign, and other Places, begin their fishing in April\ and consequently come to Market Two or Three Months before the Petitioners, and fed for a Dollar and Half, or Two Dollars, per Quintal, more, than the Petitioners

Sir Charles turner, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was > referred to consider of that Part of his Majesty's molb gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, which, relates to Greenwich Hospital, the Resolution, they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read* and is as follows \ viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for a greater Encouragement to Seamen to enter voluntarily into his Majesty's Service, his Majesty be impowered to issue and apply any Sum, not exceeding Ten thousand Pounds, out of the Money grahted for the Service of the Navy, for the Year 1728, in Aid of the Fund, appointed for the Support of the Royal Hospital at Greenwich, for the better Maintenance of the Seamen of the said Hospital, worn out and become decrepid in the Service of their Country* and for enabling the Commissioners of the said Hospital to take in ait additional Number of fochdifabled Seamen, pot exceeding Two hundred and Twenty Men, and for other Expences of the said Hospital.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House. ....

A Petition of the Justices, met at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, held for the County of Gloucester on the Thirtieth Day of April, Anno Domini 1728, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that, for want of a Law, to limit the Number of Apprentices, taken by Weavers, and others, concerned in the Woollen Manufacture, their Number is so increased, that the Trade is not sufficient to employ and mantain them, and their Families, who are reduced to great Want, and are become a great Burthen to the Parishes, where to they belong: And praying, that some Provision may be made, for limiting the Number of their Apprentices.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Thursion and Mr. Masham:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for enabling Charles, Duke of Grafton, Lord of the Manor of Grafton, in the County of Northampton, to inclose the common Fields and waste Grounds within the said Manor, in pursuance of several Agreements between the said Duke, and the Reftor and Churchwardens of the Parish of Grafton Regis,*nd to establish the said Agreements; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Mr. Treasurer acquainted the House, that he had a Vol. 21,

Message from his Majesty to this House, signed by his. Message from Majesty: And he presented the same to the House; and the KinS-it was read by Mr. Speaker; and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE, R.

His Majesty being under some Engagements, entered^ into, and concerted, with the Advice and Concurrence of the last Parliament, for securing the Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom, and for restoring and preserving the Peace of Europe; and having been enabled to answer and defray the Charge and Expences thereof, as far as they have hitherto become due and payable; and there being (till wanting a Sum, not very considerable, to perfect and fulfil these Obligations; his Majesty relying upon the Duty and Affection of his Commons, hopes, they will enable him to discharge such Engagements, as Hill remain unsatisfied upon this Head of Service.

Resolved, That this House will. Tomorrow Morning, take his Majesty s most gracious Message into Consideration.

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are there- Stepney new unto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others, Churches, being Gentlemen.Lmdlords, Owners of Estates, Holders of Lands, and Inhabitants, of the Hamlet of in

the Parish of Stehunheath, aliai Stepney, and several Inhabitants, paying to the Church and Poor's Rates, and other Inhabitants, Householders of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the said Hamlet consists of about 1,000 Acres of Land, let at £. 3 per Acre, about 600 Houses, worth, one with another, at £. 3 per Annum, Four Ship Yards, valued at £. 600. per Annum, and some Wharfs: That the Land keeps up to its former Value, but the Houses, and Ship Yards, are funk, within 25 Years, One-half of their former Rent, and now One-third Part are empty, and those inhabited are chiefly by Sailors, Fishermen, and other poor industrious Men, and not above 170 of them are rated to the Poor; so that, was it not for the Land, the Petitioners would not be able to maintain their Poor:

That the Chapel of Poplar was built in the Year 1653, at the Expence of the East India Company, and the then Inhabitants, who were the Petitioners Predecessors, and large Contributors thereto, and divine Worship hath been performed Morning and Afternoon, on Sundays, and on Holidays, and other Prayer Days, weekly, ever fence; and the Inhabitants, and others, referting thereto, have constantly paid the Minister for the Pews, which, with an Allowance by the East India Company, and the Surplice and other Fees, have been a sufficient Maintenance for the Minister: That, should the Sum of £.2,500. be allowed by the Bill, now depending in the House, for making the said Hamlet of Poplar a Parish, for t he better endowing the said intended Church, the Petitioners apprehend, the fame, with the other Fees and Dues, will be a sufficient Provision for the intended Rector, without making any Pound Rate and, if the sum of £. 50. per Annum be raised by the said Bill upon the Inhabitants of Houses, Lands, 13c. in Poplar (considering the Poverty of the People) it will be an insupportable Burthen upon them, and greatly occasion reducing the number of Inhabitants paying to the Poor: And praying, that they may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, against such Part of the said Bill, wherein the Petitioners apprehend themselves to be aggrieved.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confederation of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for uniting the Moieties, or Portions, of the Rectory of St. Dunstant Stepney, alias Stebunheath, and for making one Rector full Incumbent of the said Rectory, and for converting the Chapel at Poplar into a Parish Church, and appointing aDi ft rift, or a new Parish, for the fame, and for the Maintenance of the Ministers of Five new Churches, at Stratford (Bow) Poplar, Spittle* fields, Wapping (Stepney) and Limebeufe, and for reftram-ing the Churchwardens of the said Five new Churches from disposing of the Pews, and Places in Pews, without the Consent of the Vestry, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard by 1 heir Counsel before the said Committee, against the said Bill, if they think-fit.

A Petition of several Justices of the Peace, Deputy Lieutenants, and Gentlemen, having Estates in the Parish of Stepney, alias Stebunheath, and the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot in the said Parish, and Hamlets within the same, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that there is a Bill depending in the House, for uniting the Moieties, or Portions, of the Rectory of St. Dunstan, Stepney, alias Stebunheath, and for making one Rector full Incumbent of the said Rectory, and for other Purposes therein mentioned; in which Bill there is a Clause, that gives a very great Power-to a select Vestry, by debarring the Churchwardens from disposing of Pews, without Leave of the said Vestry; and the arbitrary Power of select Vestries hath always been a very great Burthen to the Petitioners: There is also another Clause, whereby the old Modus, is to be altered of Easter Offerings, small Tythes, and Garden Penies, and, in lieu thereof, the Ministers are to have a Pound Rate upon all the Inhabitants within the Limits of the Five new Parities, mentioned in the Bill, without any Exception: And praying, that the old Modus may be continued, instead of a Pound Rate, and that the Petitioners may be heard by themselves against the said Clauses, before the said Bill do pass.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, had examined the* Matter of the said Petition: And, to prove the Allegations thereof, William Lovelock, Receiver of the Toll, granted by the said Act, was examined, who said, that about Three Weeks after the Turnpike was ertfted, in pursuance of the said Act, at Marshfield, in the County of Gloucester, several Colliers, and other disorderly Persons, came in a tumultuous Manner, and cut down and carried the-Turnpike Gate away, and the Persons, who at tended at the Taid Gate, Were obliged to make their Escapes, for fear of being killed. And the same Evidence said, that the said Gate has been cut down Six or Seven times since by other Persons, who came disguised, and in Womens Apparel, in the same Manner: That now they are obliged to hire Six or Seven Soldiers at a time, to guard the said Turnpike Day and Night; which is a great Expence; and the Pretence they give for cutting down the fame, was, that there was no Act of Parliament for Turnpikes in those Parts, for that the King had not let his Hand to it.

Flint Mr. Earle (according to Order) reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the double Return, and Election, for the Town of Flint, in the County of Flint, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Report, and Resolutions, are as follows; viz.

Upon the double Return of George Wynne, Esquire, and Salisbury Lloyd, Esquire, for the Town of Flint, in the County of Flint; and the Petitions of the said Mr. Wynne and Mr. Lloyd, respectively complaining of the Election, and Return, of each other;

The Committee have inspected the said double Return, and have examined the Merits of this Election,

The Return is, by Two several Indentures, expressed to be made between the Bailiffs, of the one Part, and the Burgesses, of the other Part.

Mr. Wynns Return is executed by David Jones, Gentleman, one of the Bailiffs of Flint, and several Burgesses of the Borough and Liberty of Flint, some of which are named to be of Caerzvys, and Caergurley, and others iworn Burgesses of Flint:

T he Return of Mr. Lloyd is executed by John Jones, Gentleman, the other Bailiff of Flint, and several Burgesses of that Borough.

It was objected, that these Returns are void, because the Sheriff was not made a Party, as required by the Act 6(236 H. VLr. 15.

To which it was answered, that the Returns are not void for that Reason, the Act inflicting only a pecuniary Penalty in that Cafe.

The Counsel for Mr. Wynne alleged, that the Right of Election is in the Burgesses at large of Flint, and of the Four Boroughs of Overton, Rhydlan, Caerwys, and Caer* gurltjr, called the Out Boroughs:

That Persons become Burgesses of Flint by Admission of the Corporation, upon Presentment by the Mayor: That the Constable of Flint Castle, for the Time being, is, by the Charter, Mayor of the Borough; and the Burgesses take an Oath of Fidelity to the King, and to defend the Rights and Privileges of that Borough: xAnd, that Inhabitants of the other Boroughs became Burgesses by Inhabitation.

The Counsel for Mr. Lloyd admitted, that some Burgesses of all the said Boroughs had a Right to vote; but infilled, that the paying Scotland Lot was a requisite Qualification, otherwise they had no Right.

The Counsel for Mr. Wynne examined the following Witnesses; viz. n

Thomas Eyton, Esquire , who spoke for 15 Years; and remembered Two Elections, one ot which was his own, in 1 722; in both which Elections a!J Inhabitants voted, without any Distinction, or Objection; and said, he had Vo La 21*

been informed by ancient Persons, since dead, that , all Inhabitants, being Housekeepers in any of the said Boroughs, had Voces; and that Out Burgesses, being such by Creation, had Votes:

That his Election was conceited; and that his Majority was made by the Burgesses of the Out Boroughs; and he was returned; and there was no Objection for Nonrefiency, or Non-payment of Scotland Lot.

Robert Jones said, that in the contested Election between Mr. Eyton and Mr. Conway, in 1722, all sworn Burgesses were polled, whether relient, or Out Burgesses, and no Objection to any of them; and it was foin 1697, in the contested Election between Mr. Ravenscroft and Sir John Hanmer; the former of which was returned; having a Majority by the Out Burgesses, when the other had the Majority of the refient Burgesses:

That all Housekeepers have Right to vote, without Distinction as to paying, or not paying, Scotland Lot; which Distinction he never heard of till now, though he had known the Borough 31 Years.

Two Returns, one, of the 2d February, 13 Gul.Wl. the other 1 Auptft, i* Anna, were produced, signed by Three Out Burgesses.

And farther,.as to the Right of voting in the Burgesses of the Four Out Boroughs,

John Hughes and Robert Thomas said, That the Burgesses of Overton, being Inhabitants there, had a Right of voting, though they did not pay Scotland Lot.

And Hughes said, they voted in Sir John Hanmers Election.

As to Caergurley.

Griffith Jones and John Hughes were examined: The first spoke for 25 Years, and the other was 65 Years old: And they said that all Inhabitants of that Borough, being House-keepers, had a Right to vote, and had voted in all their Times.

And Davis said, they voted in the contested Election, when Sir John Hanmer flood.

And, as to paying Scotland Lot, they said, they knetv of no such Distinction from any other Inhabitants, with respect to the Right of voting, but that all Inhabitants within the Borough had equal Right.

John Hughes and Richard Jones gave the like Evidence as to Caerwys Burgesses voting.

As to the Rhydlan Burgesses voting.

Henry Lloyd, junior, and Edward Jonet, gave the like Evidence, of all Inhabitants of that Borough voting, and having a Right to vote, without any Distinction, as before given for the other Boroughs.

Some of the Witnesses said, they thought, Servants, Almsmen, and Beggais, if Inhabitants, had a Right to vote:

That in some of these Boroughs they had no Rates to Church or Poor, and in others none till lately.

The Counsel for Mv.Lloyd in lifted, that none but tha Payers of Scotland Lot, had a Right to vote, and that 00 others were Burgesses; and,

That they had no Powers by Charter to create Out Burgesses.

The Committee came to the following Resolution; viz. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right cf Election of a Burgess, to serve in Parliament for the Town of Flint, in the County of Flint, is in the Inhabitants of the Boroughs of Flinty Rhydlan, Overton, Caerwys, and Caergnrley, paying Scotland Lot.

A Question arose, whether the Inhabitants of that Part of the Parish of Overton, which lies contiguous to the Borough., but without the Limits of it, and is called Overtonforreign, and the Inhabitants of Knolton, in the same Parish, had a Right of voting, as well as those, who lived within the Borough.

This Right was denied by the Counsel for Mr. Wynne, but affirmed on Mr. Lloyd's Part.

The Counsel for Mr. Wynne insisted, that the Vill of Overton had Privileges, which Overtonforreign, and Knolton, had not; and that those Places were no Part of the Vill:

Which was denied by Mr. Lloyd's Counsel; who insisted, That those Two Places being in the Parish of Overton, within the Liberty of the Vill, their Privileges were equal with those of the Vill itself.

To which Point the following Evidence was produced; viz.

On the Part of Mr. Wynne,

John Hughes, Robert Thomas, and John Thomas, being examined, laid, that Over ton-forreign, and Knolton, were tio Part of the Borough of Overton:

That the Inhabitants of Overtonforreign, and Knolton, pay the King's Toll at Wrexham Market, from which those of the Vill were exempted.

Hughes said, he had known Overton 40 Years, and remembered a disputed Election, when those of Overton-forreign did not vote.

Being cross-examined, he said, the Rates, and Parish Officers, were the same for the whole Parish of Overton, including Over ton-for reign, with the Vill.

An ancient Table of the Duties, Tolls, and Tallages, paid at Wrexham, was produced;

Wherein it is entered, that such Burgesses who live in the Borough of Oreton, or are Freeholders within the Liberties of the fame, are exempt from Payment of Toll, for such Corn only, as groweth within the said Borough, or Liberties thereof, and for such Cattle, by them bought or sold, as are necessary to be fed* employed, or used within the said Borough:

But that all other Burgesses of the said Borough, not having Land within the lame, or not living the re, are to pay the Tolls:

And for Corn, which did not grow, and for Cattle, which were not used, or fed, upon the Lands of the said Borough, they are to pay the like Tolls which are paid by other Persons.

Richard Jones, who was, Fifty Years since. Toll-gatherer at Wrexham Market, and continued in that Office many Years, said, that the Inhabitants of Overton Vill

were always exempted from the King's Tolls, which the Inhabitants of Overtonforreign. and Knolton always paid; and, todistinguish them, those of the Vill brought Tickets from the Steward of the Manor, testifying their being of the Vill, and those of Overton-forreign and Knolton, had no Tickets.

Thomas EyloH, Esquire, said, that in his Election, in 1722, an Inhabitant of Over ton for reign offered to vote for him; which being objected to by Mr. Conway, the Witness did not inlist: upon the Vote, apprehending, that hone but those who lived within the Vill, had a Right.

He also said, that, upon the best Enquiry he could make, he could never hear, that any voted, or pretended to vote, as Inhabitants of Overton-forreign, or Knolton.

Vill.

On Mr. Wynne's Part,

It was objected, that the Bailiff, John Jones, who returned Mr. Lloyd, was partial and corrupt.

To which the following Wicnefies were examined; viz.

Mr. Thomas Williams, the Town-clerk; who said, that, before the Election began, he was appointed by both Bailiffs to take the Poll, as being the usual and proper Oftiqer in that same: but the next Day Bailiff John Jones appointed John Jones, an Attorney, to take the Poll for him; which Attorney was the former Day appointed to be only his Clerk, to infp.£t the Poll.

That he, Williams, cast up the Poll, after it was over, and declared the Numbers, wherein Mr. Wynne had so great a Majority; notwithstanding which, the said Bailiff John Jones, without objecting to any Votes, and without calling up the Poll, upon Jones, the Attorney, his telling, or whispering, him, that Mr. Lloyd had the Majority, executed a Return of Mr. Lloyd, though he owned a Majority for Mr. Wynne.

He farther said, that before and since the Election, this Bailiff, John Jones, had told him, that he was obliged to make a Return of Mr. Lloyd, who was his Landlord, and had threatened to turn him out of his Farm, unless he returned him; and that Mr. Lloyd had given him Security, to indemnify him.

Tins Witness laid, that both Bailiffs make but one Officer; and that they had nofeparate Authority.

Edward Jones, being examined, confirmed the Evidence, given by the Town clerk, as to the Proceedings at the Election.

A Note, under Mr. Lloyd's Hand, was produced, dated August the 26th, 1727, promising to indemnify John Jones, the Bailiff, from all Costs and Damages whatever, that may be incurred by returning him, as having a Majority of the Five Boroughs.

Which Note was found in Mr. Lloyds Lodgings at Flint, and taken from thence; and was enquireef after by him, when milled, but Was never delivered to the Bailiff.

Agmondcfham A Petition of Charles Hayes, Esquire, was presented to Election. the House, and read; Petting forth, that at the late Election of a Member, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Agmondesham, in the County of Bucks, in the room of Montague Gerrard Drake, Esquire, deceased, the Petitioner, and Marmaduke Allington, Esquire, flood Candidates; and the Petitioner was chosen by a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned; but William Child and William Haley, Constables, and returning Officers of the said Borough, refused the Votes of several, who were duly qualified, and would have voted for the Petitioner, and admitted several to poll for Mr, AUington, who were not qualified, by receiving Alms, and otherwise; and the said Constables have arbitrarily returned Mr. Allington, in wrong to the Petitioner: And praying Relief in the Premises.

After which, his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament* as fob loweth; viz.

The Kine's My Lords, and Gentlemen,

Speech. The Dispatch you have given to the publick Business, and the advanced Season of the Year, make it proper for me to put an End to this Session of Parliament.

The Zeal and Unanimity which you have shewn in all your Proceedings, with regard to the true Interest of your Country, and in Support of the common Cause, have fully answered my Expectations, and will, I am persuaded, give general Satisfaction here at home, and cannot fail of having their due Weight and Influence abroad.

I expect very soon to hear, that the Congress is opened, the preliminary Articles having laid fogood a Foundation fora general Pacification. I hope all Parties will bring with them such favourable Dispositions for finithing and perfecting this desirable Work, that we shall soon fee a happy Conclusion of this important Transaction, with that Satisfaction to me, and my Allies, which may reasonably be expected from the Justice of our Cause, and the mutual Confidence which is established among us.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my Thanks for the effectual Supplies you have raised for the Service of the Year. The prudent Application you have made of the Produce of the Sinking Fund will contribute to the Support of the publick Credit; and the Power you have given me of borrowing Five hundred thousand Pounds, for the Discharge of the Seamens Wages will meet with universal Approbation.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is unnecessary for me to recommend, in any particular manner, to your Care, the Preservation of the publick Peace in your several Stations and Countries. Your own Inclinations will naturally lead you, by a due Execution of the Laws, and a faithful Administration of Justice, to promote upon all Occasions the Welfare and Prosperity of my People.

GEORGE, R.

WHEREAS our Parliament {lands prorogued to 'Thursday, the 5th Day of this instant December; we, with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, that the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said Fifth Day of this instant December, to Tuesday, the Twenty-first Day of January next ensuing; and we have given Order to our Chancellor

Parties to the Treaties of Hanover and Vienna, was approved of by me, and my Allies, not without reasonable Hopes of the Concurrence of the Imperial Court, and the Court of Madrid.

But no definitive Answer being yet returned by either of them, nor the projedtof the provisional Treaty either accepted, or rejected, the Fate of Europe is (till held in Suspense, labouring under Difficulties, that unavoidably attend such a doubtful and undetermined Condition.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, that the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty was pleated to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament, of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House, and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I am sensible, you are met together in Expedlation of being informed of the present Situation of publick Affairs, and of receiving that Satisfaction, which the Expences, already made, and the Apprehension of their being continued for some longer Time, make it just and reasonable for you to desire.

The Execution of the preliminary Articles, and the opening the Congress at SoiJl'o?is, laid a Foundation for you to entertain Hopes of seeing very soon the happy Fruits and Effects of a general Pacification.

But the various and extensive Views, which fell under Consideration, in settling and reconciling the different Interests and Pretensions of so many different Powers, appeared to be a Work of so much Time, and Difficulty, that the Project of a provisional Treaty was thought of, as a proper Expedient; which being concerted and negotiated among the Ministers of the principal Powers,

and that, in our present Circumstances, some may be induced to think, that an actual War is preferable to such a doubtful and imperfect Peace; but, as the Exchange is easy to be made at any time, and as I am confident, I shall not be thought backward in doing myself, and the Nation, Justice, when a proper Occasion calls upon me for it, I hope you will believe, that a just Regard for the Ease and Interest of my People alone prevailed upon me, rather to suffer some temporary Inconveniences, with the daily* Prospect of obtaining a safe and honourable Peace, than too precipitately to kindle a War in Europe, and to plunge the Nation into ftiil greater and unknown Expences. But, how disagreeable soever these Delays may be, nothing is more unjust, than to impute them to my Conduct, or to that of my Allies. No Endeavours indeed have been wanting, to separate and dissolve the happy Union that is established among us; but long Experience, and repeated Proofs of mutual Fidelity, have fb strengthened and cemented this Alliance, founded upon, and united by, common Interest, that all Attempts to weaken it, or to create Jealousies and Diffidence among us, have proved as vain and fruitless, as the Insinuations to the contrary are false and groundless.

It will nevertheless be incumbent upon us to bring this important Transaction to a speedy and certain Decision, that, if a Conclusion can be put to it, consistent with the Security and Preservation of the Rights, Privileges, and Possessions, of Great Britain, and my Allies, the Blessings of Peace may be diffuled throughout Europe, and my Kingdoms again enjoy the happy Effects of a settled Tranquillity; or, if this cannot be had, that the Allies may unite with Vigour and Resolution, and exert themselves in procuring that Justice and Satisfaction, which has been so long delayed. If this should unavoidably be the Cafe, I depend upon the Zeal and AfL-dlion of this Parliament, that they will cheerfully and effectually support me in carrying on a just and necessary War.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I wished, and truly hoped, to have seen the public Expences very much reduced and lessened before this time; but the present Circumstances of Affairs oblige me to a(k of you such Supplies as shall be necessary for answering and defraying the Charge and Services of the ensuing Year, and for enabling me, as Events may require, to act with Vigour, and in Concert with my Allies, who have resolved to make the same Preparations, and to keep on foot all their extraordinary Forces. I will order the proper Estimates to be immediately prepared, and laid before you; and, as the Produce of the Sinking Fund has exceeded our Expectations, I mull recommend it to your Care, to make a further Application of it to its proper Uses.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It cannot be expected, that I should enter into the several Causes and Motives which may have occasioned the present Delays in the Courts of Vienna and Madrid; but if, among other Reasons, Hopes, given from hence, of creating Discontents and Divisions among my Subjects, and a Prospect of seeing Difficulties arise at home, have greatly encouraged them in their dilatory Proceedings, I am persuaded, that your known Affection to me, and a

Election. Rhayder, Knighton, Knucless, and Kevencleece, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that, by the last Resoluti.on in Parliament, the Right of Election of Burgesses, to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Radnor, is in the Burgesses of Radnor, Rhayder, Knighton, Knucless, and Kevencleece: That at the last Election of Members to Parliament for the Borough of Radnor, John Verney, and Thomas Lewis, Esquires, flood Candidates; and Herbert Lewis, Esquire, Brother-in-Law to the said Thomas Lewis, was Bailiff, and the returning Officer; who, several times before the Election, declared, that he would return his said Brother, right or wrong; and, in order thereto, he did, a short time before the Election, make above Two hundred new Burgesses in an illegal Manner, contrary to the Directions of the Charter, and without summoning the capital Burgesses, without whom the Bailiff can do no corporate Act: That such new Burgesses were engaged to vote for the said Thomas Lewis, and such as would not promise, were for that reason not admitted to be lwore, but were menaced in a very opprobrious Manner; and finding that such new-made Burgesses were not sufficient to gain a Majority, several more were made but Three Days before the Election and the Bailiff admitted all the new Burgesses to poll for his Brother, though they were objected to, as being definitive to the Privileges of the legal Burgesses: That, by Custom immemorial, no Person can be made a Burgess of Rhayder, though presented by a Jury, if objected to by any Two Burgesses; yet the Bailiff admitted above a Hundred to poll for his Brother, upon Pretence of their being presented by the Leet about Seven Years ago, though at that time they were all objected to by several Burgesses, and have never since been permitted to enjoy any Privileges, as Burgesses j he also permitted to poll for his Brother several who received Alms; and by Menaces intimidated divers from voting for Mr. Verney, who declared, they otherwise would have done; and, though the said Thomas Lewis had not, at the time of Election, a sufficient Estate to qualify him to be elected, and both he, and his Brother, had Offices in the Custom-house, and the said Bailiff ought not therefore to intermeddle in the said Election, all which was objected by the Burgesses, yet the said Bailiff hath returned his Brother, although Mr. Verney had the Majority of legal Votes: And praying such Relief, as the House shall think meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of John Sinclare, Esquire, was presented td Grithnefii the House, and read; setting forth, that the 31st Day of h eC lon* August, being appointed for electing a Knight of the Shire, to serve in this present Parliament for Caithness,

Patrick Dunbar, and the Petitioner, flood Candidates:

That the Earl of Broadalbine, being Sheriff of the said Shire, was prevailed upon to absent himself from the said Election, and then John Sinclair, having a Prejudice to the Petitioner, and declared, that he would not return him at any rate, claimed toact as Sheriff, and returning Officer, in virtue of a latent Conveyance from the said Earl of Broadalbine, never legally perfected; and, as such, did refuse to produce the Sheriff Court Books, with the Minutes of former Elections, and Rolls of the Freeholders, who used to vote; but Patrick Dunbar, in Combination with John Sinclair, pulled out of his Pocket a Roll, made -up without any Authority, in which several Persons were inserted, that never voted at any Election, and others, that had voted, were left out; which Roll the said John Sinclair did impose upon the Freeholders: That, by Act of Parliament, the Sheriff Clerk, in absence of the Member last elected, is appointed to ask the Voters, who shall be Prefes, and who shall be Clerk; and that James Campbell, the principal Sheriff Clerk, being absent, John

Dunett did appear with a Deputation from him, and offered to act; yet the said John Sinclair took upon him to name Hugh Monro to ask the said Votes, although the Freeholders are entitled to choose their own Clerk, which Clerk is the returning Officer, and the Majority of the Freeholders did elect Benjamin Doul to be Clerk to the Meeting: That the said John Sinclair, Patrick Dunbar, and other Two, who concurred with them, separated from the rest, and, pretending to elect by themselves, made use of the said Hugh Monro, as Clerk; and though the Petitioner was duly elected by a Majority of Nine to Four, of which Four the said John Sinclair and Patrick Dunbar made Two, yet the said John Sinclair and Hugh Monro have returned the said Patrick Dunbar as duly elected, in Prejudice of the Petitioner; and several other illegal Practices were used by the said pretended Sheriff, to accomplish his Design: And praying Redress of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Sir George Oxenden reported from the Committee oa

appointed Yesterday- to draw up an Add ref-, to be -the King'* presented to his Majesty; that the Committee had drawn ^cc up an Address accordingly, which they had direted him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's-Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliarp-nt assembled, beg Leave humbly to return our frncere and unfeigned Thanks for your Majesty's most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We congratulate your Majesty upon the safe Arrival of Iris Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, so much to the1 Joy and Sxtisfadion of your Majesty and all your People.

We are not insensible of the various and extensive Views, which mud naturally arise in settling and reconciling the different Intered and Pretensions of so many different Powers, Parties to the Treaties of Hanover and Vienna; and wc acknowledge, with the utmod Gratitude, your Majesty's great Wisdom and Prudence, in avoiding, as far as was possible, all Occasions of Difficulties and Delays, by concerting the most expeditious Methods of concluding with Honour and Justice the Negociarions depending at Soiffbns.

We have the Happiness to fee your Majesty indefatigable in the Pursuits of the Interests of your People, accommodating and composing the Publick Differences, declining the Temptation of military Glory, and chusing rather to secure to yotir Subjects their just Rights and Possessions by the milder Arts of Moderation and Forbearance, than to plunge the Nation unnecessarily into infinite and unknown Expences.

But your faithful Commons are so fully convinced that your own Honour, and the Honour of your Kingdoms, are Confident ions so dear to your Majesty, and so infc-parable from your royal Mind, that we can, with the greatest Confidence imaginable, intirely rely upon your Majesty's undoubted Valour and Resolution, to do vourself and the Nation Justice, whenever a proper Occasion calls upon you for it; and we cannot in the lead Doubt, from your Majesty's constant and dye Regard to the Rights, Privileges, and Interests of your People, but that your princely Care will equally extend itself to the securing our Commerce, and obtaining a just Satisfaction for the many and great Losses sustained by your Subjects.

The mutual Harmony and Fidelity fofirmly established and subsisting between your Majesty and your Allies, cannot fail to create in your Commons the higbeft Satisfaction; and it is with Pleasure we observe, that all Endeavours and Attempts to separate and dtffolve thb happy Unton, of such Consequence to your Kingdoitis,

and

2 Geo. II.

and so essential to the preservingjhe Peace and Tranquillity of Europe, haveproved vain and unsuccessful.

We beg Leave to allure your Majesty,. that we will, with the greateftChearfulness, raise the Supplies necessary for answering and defraying the Charges and Expences of the ensuing Year, and will not salt to make the proper Disposition of the growing Produce of the Sinking Fund; and if, after all your Majesty's unwearied Endeavours to procure a l'afe and honourable Peace, a Rupture should become unavoidable, your Majesty may depend upon the Zeal and Affection of this House effectually to i'upport your Majesty in carrying on a just and necessary War, and enable you to with Vigour, in Conjunction with your Allies, as future Events, and the Circumstances of publick Affairs, may require.

And; as nothing can be more injurious to your Majesty's Honour, and the Interest and Reputation, or your People, than the vile and detestable Practices of those who, by giving Hopes of Discontents, Divisions, and Difficulties, anting here at home, encourage the dilatory Proceedings, that have hitherto retarded the Conclusion of this important Transaction, we look with the utmost Abhorrence upon the Authors and Contrivers of such base and unnatural Artifices, who iuggeft the Means of distressing their Country, and clamour at the Inconveniences, which they themselves have occasioned. This makes it highly incumbent upon us to give your Majesty the most unfeigned Assurance, that this House will, by an unshaken Duty and AffeClion to your Majesty, and by a steady Perseverance in Support of your Government, convince the World, that no false and groundlefe Insinuations, no wicked Designsand Intrigues, whatsoever, shall be able to alter, or diminish, that Harmony, and good Understanding, between your Majesty and yopr Parliament, which our Inclination, xDuty, and Interest, call upon us inviolably to preserve.

That the said Election was on the 9th Day of September,

1727; and the Commissioners from Glasgow, Rutherglen, and David Colquhon from Dumbarton, appeared at the Town-house of Dumbarton, which was the proper Place of Election, and demanded Admittance; but the said George Smallet having, the Night before, placed a Guard of armed Men in the Town-house, and having another Guard of the Town Officers, and others, along with him, thought fit to poll himself, with a Halbert in his hand, ac thedoor, and takingupon himself to judge who were lawful Delegates, refused to admit any but whom he thought fit, and, in particular, the said David Colquhon, and likewise refused Entrance to David Hutchinson, who appeared with a Commission) to be Common Clerk to the Town of 22 Dumbarton

Dumbarton; whereupon the Commissioners for Glasgow and Rutherglen insisted, that every Person, pretending to have a Commission to be Delegate* or Common Clerk, should be admitted, that their Right might be determined; which the said Smallett absolutely refused, saying, himself was the legal Delegate for Dumbarton, without so much as shewing any Commission for that Purpose: Against which Proceedings the Commissioners for Glasgow, Rutherglen, and the said David Co/quhon, protested, and declared, they came there to have given their Votes for the Petitioner; and giving publick Notice to all then present, withdrew to the nearest convenient House, and chose the Petitioner, and made use of the said David Hutchinson as Clerk to the Meeting; and the Commissioner from Renfrew refused to concur with Smallett, as apprehending his Proceedings to be arbitrary; but the said George Smallett alone has taken upon him to name Daniel Campbell, Esquire, to be Member for the said DistridV, and James Duncanfotiy as Common Clerk of Dumbarton, hath returned him, as duly eiedleJ, in Prejudice of the Petitioner: And praying the Relief of the House in the Premises.

{ at the Guild-ball of Raverford-west; at which Time and Place the Petitioner had a great Majority of legal Votes, and was by the Sheriff declared to be duly elected; but a Poll being demanded, it was granted, and proceeded in for several Days; all which Time the said Sheriff was wholly influenced by Mr. Campbell, and used all possible Means, by frequent and unnecessary Adjournments, to protract the Poll, and weary out the Petitioner's Voters; and he absolutely refused to swear his Clerks, for taking the Poll impartially; notwithstand-ingwhich Practices, the Poll ended with ^Majority for, the Petitioner, though the Under- flu-riff under pretence of another Poll, carried on by him in a Garret, contrived to be filled with the Friends of Mr. Campbell\ to which the ' Petitioner, nor his Friends, could not come, and without the Consent of the Petitioner, or any Inspection of the fame, declared he had been taking a Poll in another Place, and that Mr. Campbell had the Majority thereby; and the High Sheriff returned Mr. Campbell accordingly, though no other Place of polling was mentioned, when the Poll 1 was demanded by Mr. Campbell, and this Poll, if any, was intended as a Colour, to justify the returning of Mr. CampbeU: And praying the House to take the Fasts into Consideration, not only for the Petitioner's Relief, but to prevent the Violation of all other Elections. 1

Supply- Sir Charles Turner (according to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to repoit to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Fifteen thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service for the Year 1729, beginning from the First Day of January, 1728.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sutn not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per Month, be allowed, for maintaining the said Fifteen thousand Men for Thirteen Months, including the Ordnance for Sea Service.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Two hundred and Six thousand and Twenty-five Pounds, Ten Shillings, and Five Pence, be granted to his Majesty, for the Ordinary of the Navy (including Half-pay for Sea Officers) for the Year 1729.

The full of the said Resolutions being read a Second time;

Resolved\ nemine contradicente, That (he House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That Fifteen thousand Men be employed for Sea Service for the Year 1729, beginning from the First Day of January, 1728.

The rest of the said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ways Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning

and Means. nex^ resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Wallingford A PET IT IO N of John Tuckwell, William Bradford, Election. Richard Dunn, Edward Bradford, William Gunn, and

James Bonnet, in behalf of themselves, and of several other of the Inhabitants of the Borough of Wallingford, in the County of Berks, having a Right to vote for Burgesses, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that George Lewen, William Hacks, Isaac Leheup, and Richard Bigg, Esquires, were Candidates at the last Election of Burgesses, to serve in this Parliament for the said Borough: That Mr. Lewen, by most notorious Bribery, and other illegal Practices, by himself, the Mayor, then *7

being Town-clerk, and other Agents, and by using Menaces to many of the Eledors, and by promises of distributing Charities, did procure great Numbers of Votes for him; and many Persons were admitted by the Mayor to vote for him> who had no Right; and by such undue Means the said Mr. Lewen hath procured himself to be returned, as duly elected, although he was altogether a Stranger to the Eledors till a very few Days before the Election: And praying the Consideration of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Richard Bigg, of Bear Court, in the Wallingford County of Berks, Esquire, was presented to the House, Election. and read; setting forth, that at the lad Election of Burgesses, to serve in this Parliament for the Borough of Wallingford, in the said County, George Lewen, William Hacks, Isaac Leheup, Esquires, and the Petitioner, flood Candidates: That it appeared upon the Poll, that Mr.

Lewen had 95 Votes, Mr. Hucks 93, Mr. Leheup 55, and the Petitioner 53; and thereupon Richard Wing, Mayor of the said Borough, has thought fit to return Mr. Lewen and Mr. Hucks, to serve for the said Borough; but Mr.

Hucks, by Bribery, Threats, Promises, and other unjust and illegal Practices, did seduce divers of the Eledors to vote for him, who would otherwise have voted for the Petitioner; and the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Voters, and ought to have been returned: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as shall be agreeable to Justice.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Sir James Najmyth, Baronet, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that on the 8th of September, 1727, a Precept issued in the Name of the Earl of March, Sheriff'Principal, for the eleding a Knight, to lerve in this present Parliament for the Shire of Peebles, when the Petitioner, and John Douglas, Esquire, Brother to the said Earl, flood Candidates: That the said Mr. Douglas, and his Brother, being resolved to impole Mr. Douglas on the Electors, did, by Threats, and otherwise, overawe the Eledors, and produced a pretended Roll of Eledors, made up at a packed Meeting, called by the said Sheriff, wherein were contained the Names df divers Persons not qualified to vote, and others, who had a Right of voting, were utterly omitted; which Roll was the only Rule by which the Meeting was constituted; to which the Petitioner, and other Freeholders, protested, for that several of them were left out of it, who had been inrolled, and voted, and also had represented the Shire in Parliament, both before and since the Union; by which illegal and arbitrary Proceedings, Mr. Douglas has gotten a Majority of the pretended EJedors, to colour a Return in his favour; for which Purpose they chose Alexander Williamson, one of their own Number, as Clerk, who hath returned Mr. Douglas, though the Petitioner was duly elected by a Majority oflegai Votes, and ought to have been returned: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and give such Relief therein as shall be thought fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Alexander Duncan, of Lundie, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Laws of Scotland have declared in what Manner the Rolls of the Freeholders of each County should be made up, and that none should have a Vote in the Election, but such as are so inrolled: That at the last Election of a Member, to serve in this Parliament for the County , of Forfar, the Petitioner, and several Freeholders of the said County, insisted, that, if there was any Roll made up according to the said Law, the same should be produced, or, if there was none, they should then proceed to make up and adjust one: That there was no Roll produced, and therefore the Petitioner, and the other Freeholders, proceeded to make up a regular Roll; and the Freeholders, so inrolled, unanimously voted for the Petitioner to be Commissioner to Parliament for the said County, and directed their Clerk to certify the same to the Sheriff accordingly; but James Scot, of Logie, with some others, pretending to be Freeholders, though they had neither been formerly inrolled, nor did then produce any Evidence of their Freeholds, took upon them to constitute a Meeting, and admitted several Persons to vote, as Freeholders, who were not such, and have made a pretended Election of Mr. Scott; and the Sheriff Depute hath returned him, though the Clerk did return Vol. 21.

the Petitioner to the Sheriff, as duly elected, and, as such, he ought to have been returned; in Violation of the Rights of the Freeholders: And praying such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Robert Swafey, Joseph Curtis, John Way, Hairy Moss, Richard Hall, Lionel Parsons, Samuel Rates, William Bishop, Thomas Hardy, Benjamin Hallett, John Hill, Henry Jacob, Anthony Morris, William Gully, and William Kenway, on behalf of themselves, and many others, that have a Right of voting for eleding Members to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Bridport, in the County of Dorset, was presented to the House, and read; and accordingly the Bailiffs, with Mr. Bowles and Mr. Pelham, returned, but, without calling, or adjourning, the Assembly, withdrew themselves into another Room, and made sass: the Door, and, having tarried there some time, the said Bailiffs returned, and declared Mr. Bowles and Mr. Pelham to be duly elected: That the Petitioners have since obtained a Copy of the said Poll, and find, that they, with about One hundred more qualified Persons, are rejected, under a Pretence, that the Right of Election, is only in the Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot, contrary to the Right of Election settled by the House, and tending to destroy the fundamental Privileges of the said Borough: And praying such Relief in the Premises ^s shall be thought meet.

Sir Charles Turner (according to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions they had directed him to report to the House , which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table , where the ferrie were read, and are as follow $ viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Number of effective Men, to be provided for Guards and Garrisons in Great Britain, and for Guernsey and Jersey, for the Year 17 2 9, be (includ ing One thousand Eight hundred and Fifteen Invalids, and Five hundred Fifty-five Men, which the Six independent Companies coniiftof, for the Service of the Highlands) Twenty-two thousand Nine hundred Fifty-five Men, Commission and Non-commission Officers included.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seven hundred Eighty-four thousand Nine hundred Eighty-three Pounds, Twelve Shillings, and One Peny Half-peny, be grafted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the said Twenty-two thousand Nine hundred Fifty-five effective Men, for Guards, Garrisons, and other his Majesty's Land Forces, in Great Britain, Guernsey and Jersey, for the Year 1729.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a^um, not exceeding One hundred Sixty thousand Three hundred and Fifty-seven Pounds, One Shilling, and Five Pence Half-peny, be granted to his Majesty, for maintaining his Majesty's Forces and Garrisons in the Plantations, Minorca, and Gibraltar, and for Provisions for the Garrisons at Annapolis Royal, Placentia, and Gibraltar, for the Year 1729.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twelve thousand Eight hundred Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, for Out-pensioners of Chelsea Hospital, for the Year 1729.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Twenty thousand Seven hundred Thirty-nine Pounds, Four Shillings, and Seven Pence Half-peny, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying several Extraordinary Expences and Services iricurred, and not provided for by Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Fifty-seven thousand Pounds, be granted to his Majesty, upon Account, to reduced Officers of his Majesty's Land Forces and Marines, for the Year 1729.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Eighty-one thousand Seven hundred Twenty-eight Pounds, One Shilling, and Three PeDce Half-peny, be granted to his Majesty, for the Charge of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, for the Year 1729.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Sum, not exceeding Eight thousand Five hundred Twenty-one Pounds, Two Shillings, and Two Pence Half-peny, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the extraordinary Expence of the Office of Ordnance, for Land Service, not provided for by Parliament*.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put ^hereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, 20

the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, which by an Act of Parliament, of the First Year of his Majesty's Reign, have Continuance to the Twenty-fourth Day of June, 1729, be further continued, and charged upon all Malt, which shall be made, and all Mum, which shall be made or imported, and all Cyder and Perry, which shall be made for Sale within the Kingdom of Great Britain, from the Twenty-third Day of June, 1729, to the 24th Day iof June, 1730.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, a Duty of Six Pence per Bushel be laid upon all Corn and Grain, used in diddling, not malted.

Whittlesey A Petition of the Land-owners, and Proprietors of

Drainage. J0w Lands, and Fen Grounds, in the Township of Whittlesey, within the Ifleof Ely, in the County of Cambridge, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and all others the Owners and Proprietors of low Lands, and Fen Grounds, lying in the said Township, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the said low Lands, and Fen Grounds, containing about Seven thousand Acres, have, till lately, been very good, and yielded great Profit, by Corn, Grain, and Hay, and feeding Cattle and Sheep; but for more than Seven Years past have been so often drowned, and surrounded with Waters, that they have yielded little or no Profit, and cannot be drained, for want of convenient Outfalls, and Drains, to discharge the Waters into the common Rivers, whereby the same may be conveyed from thence to Sea: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bil! for draining the said low Lands, and Fen Grounds, in the said Township, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And it is referred to Mr. Bromley, Mr. Shepheard, Lord Marquis of Hartington, Mr. Townshend, Mr. Sandys, Sir Charles Turner, Sir John Rufhout, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Pelham, Mr. Jacomb, Mr. Byng, Mr. Scrope, Mr. Ongley, Mr. Metcalfe, Mr, Par-Vol. 21.

A Petition of the insolvent Debtors in the Fleet Prison, Debtor's in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands in the Petition, several Gaols of the Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that all the insolvent Acts, that have passed, have been with a Proviso, That the Debtor, who did not owe above^. 50. or £. too to any one Person, should be discharged; whereby those Persons who have been very considerable Dealers in Life, were excluded, and are now most miserable, and their Families reduced to great Necessities: That in the 22d and 23d Carol. 2tVl, an Act passed, for the Relief of insolvent Debtors, without Limitation of a Sum: and the Gaols are now fuller than they were then: And praying, that an Act may pass, for Relief of insolvent Debtors, without the Limitation of a Sum, upon surrendering their All lor the Benefit of their Creditors.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table. Ditto, A Petition of the Constable, and Assistants, confined Debtors in the Poultry Compter, London, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Debtors of the said Gaol, being in'Number One hundred and Twenty-nine, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, by their long Confinement, are become mere Objects of Pity, and are utterly unable to satisfy the Demands of their cruel Creditors, to whom they are willing to surrender up their All for Satisfaction; who will not accept of the fame, and discharge them: And praying, that, on delivering up all their Effects to their Creditors, they may be discharged, or that their Creditors may be obliged to maintain them in Prison.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table. Ditto. A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors, Freemen, and Widows, of the City of London, confined in the Prison of Ludgate, was presented to ihe House, and read; setting forth, that after all just Endeavours to satisfy their Creditors, even to the delivering of their whole Substance, they have not been able to gain their Liberty; so that by their long Confinement they are reduced to the lowed State of Misery, and many of them have already perished for Want: And praying the Consideration of the House, and such Relief, as shall be thought fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in Cambridge Ditto. Castle, belonging to the County of Cambridge, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that there are now but 14 Prisoners in the said Gaol, feme of them having been in several Years, and are in a starving Condition: And praying such Relief, as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That the Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 7th Instant, proceeded on the several Matters, mentioned in the said Petition, and examined the following Witnesses; viz.

Henry Carter, Samuel Worrel, Churchwardens; William Majon, Esquire, Mitchell, and William Taylor:

Who severally said, that there is a Church built by the Commissioners for building Fifty new Churches, and a Piece of Ground, 800 Feet long, and 100 Feet broad, inclosed for a Church-yard, in the Centre of the Hamlet of Spittlefields, which have been ready for Consecration a considerable time: That the said Hamlet hath been by the said Commissioners allotted, as a District for a new Parish; and the Inhabitants have f>r many Years pad chose their own Officers, and maintained their Poor among themselves, which are numerous; and that there are near 2,500 Houses in the said Hamlet:

That the Parish Church of Stepney is above a Mile and a half from the said new Church; and although there are Two Tabernacles in the said Hamlet, for Pertormance of divine Service, which are supported by a voluntary Contribution of the Inhabitants, amounting to upwards of £. 200. per Annum, yet all the Inhabitants cannot go to the Tabernacles, they being in a ruinous Condition, and not large enough to contain one Half of those Inhabitants; and one of them is held only for a Term of Years, now near expiring:

That the Inhabitants are obliged to carry their Children to Stepney Church, to be baptized, or pay considerable Fees for the Minister to come home, winch amounts to a very large Sum of Money in the Year; and there being no Burying-place belonging to the said Hamlet, but that at Stepney, the Inhabitants are forced to carry their Dead to be buried there; whereby the Burying-places are very much filled with dead Corpses, inso much, that they arc frequently digged up, before they are mouldered away, to make Way for new Burials: That the Inhabitants of the said Hamlet are at a very great Expence, to the Amount of 2 or £.300.per Annum, in carrying the Burials to the said Church-yard; and the Expence even of their pensionary Poor amounts to a considerable Sum yearly.

The same Witnesses also gave Testimony, that a Pfo-posal wasunanimously agreed at a general down meeting of the said Hamlet, to allow the Minister for the said new Church £. 125. per Annum, to be raised by the Burials, and what they hoped, would be allowed out of the Money, appropriated for endowing the new Churches; and, if the said Sum falls Abort, it was agreed to be made good to such Minister out of publick Moneys, that should be remaining in the Churchwardens Hands; which, with the other Surplice Fees, amounting to upwards of £. 70. per Annum, they conceived, would be a fitting Maintenance for the Minister of such new Church.

Mr. Alderman Perry reported from the Committee* to Wiping whom the Petition of the Churchwarden, Constable, new Church. Overseers of the Poor, and other ancient and principal Inhabitants, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants, of the Hamlet of Wrapping, Stepney, in the County of Middlesex, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 12th Instant, proceeded on the several Matters, mentioned in the said Petition, and examined the following Witnesses; viz.

Samuel Cow per, Overseer; Henry Rayne and John King, Gentlemen: Who, being severally examined, said, that there is a Church built by the Commissioners for building 50 new Churches, and a Piece of Ground, 600 Feet long, and 200 Feet broad, inclosed for a Churchyard, in the Centre of the Hamlet of Wapping (Stepney) which have been ready for Consecration a considerable Time:

That the said Hamlet hath been by the said Commissioners allotted as a District for a new Parish; and the Inhabitants have, for many Years past, chose their own Officers, and maintained their Poor among themselves, which are numerous ;and that there are upwards of 2,500 Houses in the said Hamlet:

That the Parish Church of Stepney is a Mile and half distant from the said new Church; and that there is no Chapel, or Tabernacle, for Performance of divine Service in this Hamlet; and that the Inhabitants of the Parish are so very populous, that the said Parish Church will not hold a Fiftieth Part of the Inhabitants of the Parish:

That the Inhabitants are obliged to carry their Children to Stepney Church, to be baptized, or pay considerable Fees, for the Minister to come home, which amounts to very large Sums of Money in the Year; and, there being no Burying-place belonging to the said Hamlet, but that at Stepney, they are under a Necessity of carrying their Dead to be buried there; which is very much filled with dead Corpses, and are frequently dug up, before they are mouldered away, to make room for new Burials; and the Inhabitants are at upwards of £. 200. per Annum Expence upon account of the said Burials.

The same Witnesses also gave Testimony, that a Fro-posal was made, and unanimously agreed to, at a publick Meeting of the said Hamlet, to allow the Minister of the said new Church f. 100. per Annum, to be raised by the Burials, and also what, they hoped, would be given out of the Money, appropriated for endowing the new Churches; and, if the said Sum falls short, it was agreed to be made good to such Minister out of the publick Moneys, that should be remaining in the Churchwardens Hands; which, with the other Surplice Fees, amounting to upwards of £. 70. per Annum, they conceived, would be a fitting Maintenance for the Minister of the said new Church.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring a Bill for making the Hamlet of Wrapping, Stepney, in the Parish of Saint Dunstan Stebunheath, alias Stepney, in the County of Middlesex, a distinct Parish, and for providing a Maintenance for the Minister of the new Church there; and that Mr. Alderman Perry, Mr. Brereton, Mr.

Alderman Child, and Mr. Bertie, do prepare, and bring m, the fame.
