Shepards- Mr. reported from the Committee, to whom

fbord, &c. the Petition of the Justices of Peace, Gentlemen, and

Hoads. others, living in, and near the Highways, lying between Shepards-shord and Horfiey-upright Gate, leading down Bagdon Hill, in the County of Wilts, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; that the Commirtee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations of the fame, the Petitioners first laid before the Committee an Act, passed in the Parliament, holden in the nth Year of her late Majesty's Reign, whereby several Tolls and Duties were granted, for repairing the said Highways; which Act was to continue in force for the Term of 21 Years, from the palTing thereof.

And then the Petitioners called Mr. Anthony Brooks; who, being examined, said, that at the Time the said Act passed, the Highways, thereby directed to be repaired, were so very bad, a considerable Sum of Money was laid out, in order to make the same passable in all Parts.

And then he produced to, and laid before, the Committee, the Accounts of what Money had been collected, and paid, by virtue of the said Act; which Accounts appear to be reeuiarly passed according to the Directions of the said Act.

That it appeared to the Committee, that there is {till due on the Credit of the said Act the Sum of £. 1,000. or thereabouts, carrying Interest; and the Income of the Toll amounts to no more than £. 155. per Annum; so, if the Toll should be applied towards discharging the said Debt, little or nothing could be laid out, during the Continuance of the Act, in repairing the Roads.

That the same Witness gave Evidence, that gteat Care had been taken to amend the said Roads; and that the Statute-work had been done by the Inhabitants of such of the Parishes, as lie therein; notwithstanding which, many Parts of the Highways continue bad:

That it will be very expensive to repair the Roads, proper Materials for amending the same, lying at a great Distance from the said Roads: And he also said, that in the Winter Season Bagdon Hill, Part of the said Road directed to be repaired, is' so bad, that Coaches and Waggons cannot get up the fame, without some Assistance; which is chargeable to the Owners and Drivers thereof.

That it also appeared to the Committee, that the said Highways cannot be effectually repaired, and so kept, for the Accommodation of Travellers, without the Term, so granted, as aforesaid, be enlarged, and the Act made more effectual.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term granted by an Act, passed in the Parliament, holden in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of the late Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for repairing " the Highways between Shepards-shord and Horsley-€t upright Gate, leading down Bagdon Hill, in the " County of Wilts, and other ruinous Parts of Highways thereunto adjacent," and for making the said Act more effectual; and that Mr. Holland, Sir Richard Lane, Mr. Duckett, Mr. Heathcote, and Mr. Andrews, do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

Lichfield, Mr.' Le*vefon Gower reported from the Committee,

*c. Roads, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders,

Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, of the ancient Market Town of Stone, in the County of Stafford, as also the Petition of the Bailiffs, and Citizens, of the City of Lichfield\ in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said City, were referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Tabic; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Orders of the House, have proceeded on the Matter of the said Petitions, and the Allegations thereof; and, in order to prove the fame, examined Witnesses; viz.

Mr. Robert Barbor; who said, that he is well acquainted with the Road between Canna/ls Gate and the Tow a of Stone, mentioned in the first Petition; and that in many Places the same is worn very deep with heavy Carriages; and, although large Sums of Money have been laid out, by Contribution, for the repairing the said Road, and the Statute-wwk constantly done, yet that has not been sufficient to put, and keep, the same in Repair:

Tha|t iiy several Places between Cannalls Gate and Stone, and at Darlajton, about a Mile from thence, there are several hollow Ways, which render such Parts of the Road impassable, when any Quantity of Snow falls; and, for that lieafon many Coaches, usually travelling that Way, have left (he Road, and Post-boys with Packets have not been able to pass:

That many Inhabitants in that Part of the Country in a great measure depend upon Travellers.

Mr. Theophilus Levet said, that the Road between Lichfield and Stone are very bad, and, there being lb many deep Hollows therein, the Statute-work is not sufficient to repair the fame; and that, in the Time of deep Snows, he has known several Post-boys fall into those Hollows, whereby, and by meeting with Carriages therein, they have been greatly delayed: t

That the Road from Lichfield, through Tezvno.lt r Lane, to High bridge, about Four Miles from Lichfield, is so bad, that it is almost impassable for Carriages in the Winter Season; and that, by reason of the Badneis of the Road, the Corn, grown in such Part of the County, as usually supplied the City of Lichfield, cannot, without great Difficulty, be brought thither, and therefore the same is carried to other Markets:

That the Roads, leading from Lichfield, off Ogley-hay and Wood-End, in the Parish of Shenfton, and also the Roads from Lichfield to Burton upon Trent, are very ruinous, and icarce passable in the Winter Sealon, although the Statute-work hath been constantly done, and near £.100. within Five Years last past hath been raised by voluntary Contributions, and laid out in such Parts of the Road, as leads from Lichfield to Burton; yet the same has proved in effectual towards putting the said Road in Repair:

That, if the said Roads were put into good Repair, there would be an easy Communication by Land Carriage between the Two navigable Rivers of Severn and Trent, to the great Benefit of the Trade, of the Kingdom in general.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Roads, leading from Cannalls Gate to the City of Lichfield, and from the said City to Stone, and from thence to Swinnerton Heath, and also from Burton upon Trent to the said City, and from thence to Wood-end and Ogley-hay, and also from the said City to High Bridges, in the County of Stafford, and County of the City of Lichfield*, and that Mr. Leveson Gozver, Mr. John Chetwynd, Mr. Baptist Leve/on Gower, Mr. Pturner, Sir Walter Bagot, Mr. Walter Chetwynd, and Mr. Ward, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

fible, inso much that Death itself is more preferable, than a lingering starving Life in Prison, they having spent that little Substance they had, when first imprisoned, for their Subsistence, which they would willingly have given to their hard-hearted Creditors, towards Satisfaction of their Debts; but they would not accept of the fame: That this Prison, and, as the Petitioners are informed, all the Gaols in England\ are now fuller, than ever, of poor Debtors; and all the insolvent Acts, lately passed, have been limited with such Restrictions, that those, who have been the most considerable Dealers to the Publick, could not have the Benefit thereof: And praying, that some Expedient may be found out, for making those Hands useful to the Publick, who, with their Families, are, or soon will be, a Burthen by their Confinement, the Petitioners being willing to deliver up all their Effects to their Creditors, for their Discharge, or that they may have such other Relief, as the House shall think fit.

Mr. Conduit reported from the Committee, to whom Westminster the Petition of several Persons, whose Names are there- Streets, unto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others, inhabiting in the City of Westminster, and the Liberties thereof, and the Parts thereunto adjoining, was referred;

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Tabic; where the same was read; and the Report, and Resolutions of the Committee, arc as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition, and the Allegations thereof; and, in order to prove the fame, examined the following Witnesses; viz.

Christian Cole, Esquire, one of his Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the County of Middlesex, said, that the Streets are in a very dirty and ruinous Condition, for 3 M want

h Coogk

want of being better paved and cleaned: That if the Laws now in being, for paving the Streets, were put in Execution, the same would not be sufficient to keep them well paved, because the present Laws do not limit the Inhabitants, either as to Materials, or the Time of paving, or the observing a due Level: '

The several Kennels are very deep, and dangerous, and cannot be altered, but by paving a whole Street at once; which cannot be done by the Laws in being:

That there are at present Three different Jurisdictions relating to the paving and cleansing the Streets; the Crown Office, the justices of the Peace, and the Borough Court of Westminster: That the Justices of the Peace had gone in a Body, and viewed several Streets, and lined the Inhabitants, bjut could not cause the Pavements effectually to be amended:

That it is a cctptoon Custom for an Inhabitant, after his Door is new paved, to agree with a Paviour for the keeping his Pavenfent in Repair; and indemnifying him from all Fines, for Seven Years, for Four Pence for each Yard Square per Annum/:

That, if the Streets wefe to be paved by Persons, not employed by they Proprietors of the Water-works, it would hinder the bad Pavements, which frequently happen by mending and laying down frefti Pipes, which are/generally laid too near the Surface of the Street Humphry Thayer, Esquire, et at.* severally said, that the Streets are very badly paved and cleansed; and that the Laws, now in being, are mot sufficient for the well paving and cleansing the fame:‘That the using bad Materials, and not observing a due Level, is the main Qaufeof the badnest of the paving of the Streets; and that there is no Law now in force, to oblige the Inhabitants to observQ a due Level:

That the Proprietors of the Water-works lay down the Pavement, broke up by them, with any Rubbish, instead of Gravel: That, where the Ground.is wet, by the ouzing of their Pipes, they pave upon the wet G«ound, which gives way, and causes Holes in tire Pavemdnt; and that the Paviours, employed by the Proprietors of the Water-works, fed, they could not afford to pave the Streets for what the Proprietors paid them, if they did not know, it would be necessary to new-pave again in a short Time, and that they should be paved over.again:

That in sortie Streets the Inhabitants.are obliged to hire Persons to cleanse the Streets . at an extraordinary Price* over and above the Scavengers Rates; and that the Money, raised for the Scavengers, is not duly applied, nor accounted for,

The" Allegations of the Petition having been fully proved, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; v/z.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That one Cause of the Badness of the Pavement of the Streets is the not observing a due Level.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this'Committee, That one other Cause of the present ill Condition of the Streets arises from the Badness of the Materials, and ill Porting of the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That one other Cause of the ill Condition of the Pave-,ment of the Streets is the breaking up, and repairing, the same in an improper and unworkmanlike Manner by the Proprietors of the several Water-works, v Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration Tomorrow Morning, and nothing to intervene.

M R, Alderman Child reported from the Committee, Bricks and to whom the Petition of several Persons, whose Tilesmaking. Names are thereunto subscribed, being Brick-makers,

Bricklayers, or others concerned in building, in the City of London, or within Fifteen Miles thereof, and also the Petition of the Master and Wardens of the Company of Tilers and Bricklayers of the City of London, in behalf of the said Company, and also the Petition of several Brick-makers, and others, concerned in Building in and about the City of London, and Parts adjacent, in behalf of themselvrt, and others; were referred, that the Committee' had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Report, and Resolution of tile Committee, are as follows; viz.

That the Committee have examined the Matter of the said several Petitions, and have heard Counsel, ant} examined Witnesses, thereupon.

Upon the first-mentioned Petition, the following Witnesses were examined, viz.

Henry Cock, Brick maker; who said, that he had, since the Act, of the 12th Year of his late Majesty', paid a Fine of Five Pounds to the said Company of Tilers and Bricklayers, imposed upon him by them, for burning Ten thousand Bricks, made before that Ad:

That he also paid another Fine of Twelve Pounds, imposed upon him by the Company, for making Bricky with Spanish, although they were made pursuant to a Contract with a Gentleman; but owned, 'he disposed of some of them for his own Use:

That he gave a Note for Four Guineas to Holmes, one of the Wardens, for his Favour, in order to mitigate the last mentioned Fine to Twelve Pounds; but he confessed, . the Note was given without the Knowledge of the Master and the other Warden.

Robert Tmfiall, Brick-maker, said, that the Master and Wardens of the Company fined him Thirty-five Pounds, for making Thirty dive thousand Bricks mixed with Spanish; which Fine was afterwards mitigated to Ten Pounds, which he paid.

Mr. Thomas IVaxam, Brick-maker, said, that he made his Bricks conformable to the Directions of the late Ad'; and finding his Trade decrease, and his Neighbours Trade increase, in regard they could undersell him, because of their mixing Spanish with their Earth, he informed iheMasterand Wardens of the Company thereof, and desired them to put the Ad in Execution; where to the Master, and Holmes, then one of the Wardens, replied, very shortly. That he might make such Bricks too, if he would do as other People did; and that, if he would trust to the Honour of the Company* they would be easy in the Fines.

He confessed, that Bricks, made with Spanish, can be afforded much cheaper, than without, are better, and are burnt with less Charge.

John James, Bricklayer, said, that since the late Ad Contracts are frequently made for making Bricks with Spanish, contrary to the Ad; for which some small Fines have been imposed on some by the Company, as will be to the Ruin of the fair Traders, if a Stop be not put to the Partiality of the Company therein.;

Arthur Bilbey, Brick-maker, said, that since the late Ad he had made Bricks with Spanish, and for some of which he had been fined Twelve Pounds by the Master and Wardens; but that they afterwards told him, that Bricks were the better for Spanish, and, as Bricks, were Very much wanted, they would indulge him in the Use of it, to serve the Town.

Upon the last mentioned Petition the following Wic-neifes were examined; viz.

Quarters long, and Four Inches broad, and Two Inches and a half thick, they would be more serviceable, and could be afforded cheaper, and be burnt with much less Charge, than those of the Dimensions prescribed by the said Act.

Francis Brewit and John Ford, Bricklayers, said, that better Bricks were made before the late Act, than since: That lessening the Size of Bricks from the Standard of that Act: may make them less serviceable in repairing old Buildings, but will in other Helpers j make Bricks more serviceable in the general; and* that the bell Bricks are made with some Spanish.

A Petition of the Merchants and Traders in Tobacco, in the City of Bristol, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that, since the Ad, prohibiting the Importation of stript Tobacco, which is the best and most valuable Part of that Commodity, the Tobacco Trade has been carried on with great Difficulty, and Loss, and large Quantities of unwholesome Stems used, to the Injury of his Majesty's Subjects: That the said Prohibition is a great Prejudice to the Trade in general: And therefore praying Liberty to import stript Tobacco, or such Relief, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Council and Burgesses of the Colony of Virginia, is referred 5 and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of the several Merchants, and Traders in Tobacco, of and in the Port of Liverpoole, in the County Palatine of Lattcaster, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Prohibition to import Tobacco stript from the Stalk, is found to be very detrimental, and a great Discouragement to that Branch of Trade: That the Importers are loaded with the prime Coll of the Stalk in the Plantations, Freight from thence, and Customs for it here, and, when separated from the Leaf, cannot be exported; whereby they are great Sufferers; and, that the uling Stalk, instead of Tobacco, will ruin the Trade: And therefore praying the Consideration of the House, and such Relief, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Council and Burgesses of the Colony of Virginia, is referred 5 and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A PETITION of the poor insolvent Debtors in his Majesty's Gaol the Castle of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners, by long Confinement, are reduced to a starving Condition, and are utterly incapable of paying their Debts: And praying Relief of the House in their deplorable Circumstances.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table. A Petition of the poor insolvent Debtors in the Gaol at Halifax, kept for the Manor of Wakefield, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that most of the Petitioners have been close Prisoners for Two Years last past, through their Misfortunes in the Woollen Manufacture, which was their whole Dependence, and is at a very low Ebb; and Provisions being very dear, so that the Petitioners have nothing but Stone Walls to look on, for their Subsistence, there being no Allowance to the said Prison, nor can they obtain any from the Towns, whereunto they did belong, and mull inevitably starve, unless speedily relieved, Five of them being dead in a short Time; and the Petitioners are willing to deliver up all they have, to satisfy their Creditors: And praying such Relief, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table. A Petition of the poor Prisoners in his Majesty's Gaol of Rothwell, kept for the Honour of Pontefratt, and of Halifax, for the Manor of Wakefield, both in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that several of the said Prisoners have died in Gaol for Want, having no Relief from the County, nor any Subsistence of their own; and their Debts are but finall; so that if the House will not take their deplorable same into Consideration, they must inevitably perish: And praying Relief in the Premises, they being great Objects of Charity.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table. the said Arthur Dillon, was preferred to the House, and read; setting forth, that under a Settlement, made by the said late Lord Dillon in November, 1688, of several Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, in the Counties of Mayo, Roscommon, and West Meath, in Ireland, Richard, now Lord Viscount Dillon, is Tenant for Life, Remainder to his first and other Sons in Tail Male, Remainder to the said Arthur Dilkn, with like Remainders to his first and other Sons in Tail Male: That the said Arthur Dillon the Petitioner's Father, having been outlawed, or attainted, for High Treason, on Account of thfe late War in Ireland, his Remainder for Life did, by Force of the said Outlawry, and several Acts of Parliament, become vested in the Crown, subject to such Dispositions as should be made thereof in Parliament; whereby the Petitioner, the next Remainder Man in Tail, expectant upon the Determina* tion of the said forfeited Estate for Life, would be precluded from taking immediately upon the Death of the present Lord Dillon without Issue Male, if it should happen in the Life of the said Arthur; the Apprehension of which Contingency, though very improbable, prevents the Petitioner's making such Jointure, or other Marriage Provision, as should certainly take Effect upon the Death of the present Lord Dillon without Issue Male: That the Petitioner, or his Brothers, having never been guilty of any Crime of a treasonable Nature, and having in most dutiful Manner made their Submission to his Majesty, humbly hope, from his gracious Acceptance thereof, that his Majesty will look upon them as proper Objects of his royal Clemency: And therefore praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to enable the Petitioner, and his said Brothers, to take the Premises immediately after the Death of the said now Lord Dillon without Heirs Male of his Body, as fully and effectually, as if the said Arthur Dillon were dead, and had never been outlawed, and to make Provision for the Daughters of the said now Lord Dillon, in case he should die without Issue Male.

A Petition of thfe poor distressed Debtors, confined in Dehtori the Prisonof Newgate in the City of Bristol, in the behalf Petition!, of themselves, and many Thoufonds imprisoned Debtors in the several Gaols in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that there are great Numbers of unhappy Persons confined for Debt, who are no ways capable to relieve themselves; and often great Numbers die in a languishing Condition, though all the Gaols in England are now fuller than ever; and indigent Persons, before they come there, too often spend what little Substance they have, by seeing Attorneys, and Bailiffs; but, if the Law were put on such a Footing, as not to confine the Person, the Creditors would sooner come at their Debts; and this is the general Practice of foveral States of Europe: And praying, that they may be discharged from their Imprisonment, upon delivering up all they have, for the Benefit of their Creditors.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of all the insolvent Debtors, confined in the , Castle of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners are many in Number, chiefly belonging to the Woollen Manufacture, who, by the great Decay of that Trade for many Years, and others by Lbfles and Misfortunes, are reduced to great Poverty, and have offered great Compositions to their Creditor*, who would have all, or none, though the Petitioners arc willing to part with all their Effects, to their Satisfaction:

That many of the Petitioners are in Execution, and have been confined for Four or Five Years past, whereby they have wasted their Substance, which their Creditors might have had; so that they are now forced to lie on Pads of Straw, on the cold Ground, and their Number is now lo increased, and the Gaol so narrow, that they are obliged to make Platforms of Boards, and lie upon one another, like Coffins in a Vault, though some of them are strong, in the Prime of their Years, and fit to serve their Country:

And praying such Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And the Petitioners, to make out the Allegations thereof, called

Mr. Robert Barber; who, being examined, said, that he knows the Road, leading from the Town of Stone, in the said County of Stafford, to the End of the said County, in the Post Road towards Chester; and that there are several deep hollow Ways therein; and that in the Winter Season, and when there are deep Snows, Travellers cannot pass and repass without Danger: And he said, he has known the Post frequently go a great way about, to avoid those hollow Ways.

And he further gave Evidence, that the said Road cannot be repaired by the Laws now in Force; and, if more was done on that Road, than required by Law, it would not be sufficient to repair the fame.

Ordered, That it be an Inllrudion to the Gentlemen, who are appointed to prepare, and bring in, a Bill for repairing the Roads, leading from Cannals Gale to the City of Lichfield, and from, the said City to Stone, and from thence to Swinnerlon Heath, and also from Burton upon Trent to the said City, and from thence to Wood-end, and Ogley-hay, and also from the said City to High Bridges, in the County of Stafford, and County of the City of Lichfield, that they do make Provision in the said Bill, for repairing the Road from the Town of Stone to the End of the County of Stafford, in the Post Road towards Chester.

Debtors A Petition of the Prisoners for Debt within his Petition. Majesty's Prison of the King's Bench, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands other Insolvents, confined in this Kingdom, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Calamities of the Petitioners, occasioned by their long and expensive Confinement, render them the greatest Objects that ever were relieved by Parliament, the Prisons throughout the whole Kingdom, and this in particular, being now more crouded than ever; and they have the doleful Prospect of seeing many of their Fellow Sufferers end their Days in want, having received no Benefit by the late insolvent Acts, by reason of the limited Sum, and Time, therein specified; yet the Petitioners are willing to surrender up their All, for the Satisfaction of their Creditors, who refused to accept thereof: And praying, that, on delivering up all their Effects to their Creditors, they may be discharged, or have such other Relief as the House shall think fit. Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Turkey A Petition of the incorporate Company of Clothiers in

Trade. the City of Worcester, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the great Burthen of the Poor cannot be expressed, which increases daily under the Decay of their Woollen Manufacture, inso much, that their Poor's Rate amounts to at lead 8 s. in the Pound, besides other Charities: That they were unwarily milled to petition against the 7/^;Trade, and, fmce the obtaining the Bill relating thereto, their Trade bath gradually decreased: That the Turkey Merchants export, under the Name of Worcesters> Cloth of less Value and Goodness, made in other Parts of the Kingdom; which Practice has occasioned the total Lossof their Trade at present, and will, if not prevented in time, bring Disgrace and Ruin to the whole Woollen Manufacture of this Kingdom: That the Petitioners conceive, that, if Liberty were given to the Italian and other Merchants to export their Cloth, as formerly, and the Trade to Turkey laid open, and a Stop put to the Exportation of other Cloth, under the Denomination of Worcesters, their Trade might again flourish, and their Poor be relieved: And praying the Consideration of the House, and such Relief as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and Fullers, of Turkey the Clothing Trade in the City of Worcester was presented Trade, to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Clothing Trade of the said City, which is mostly for Turkey, has for many Ages been the Support of many thousarxJ Families in the County of Worcester, and many Weavers and Walkers in the said City lived in good Fashion, paying Scotland Lot, and bearing Parish Offices, with the rest of their Neighbours; but now they are all reduced ro the lowest Degree of Poverty and Beggary, for want of Trade, occasioned, as they conceive, by the Turkey Merchants monopolizing to themselves the Liberty of buying their Cloths just when, and at what Price, they please so that the greater Part of their Master Clothiers have left off their Business, and the few, that keep on their Trade, though Men of great Fortune, are often reducing the Labourers Wages to Four Pence a Day; so that they must be a Burthen to their respective Parishes: And praying the Compassion of the House to find out some Relief, suitable to their Distress, and prevent their Ruin.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Petition of the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City, of Worcester, is referred; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the lame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

of January, in the second Year of the Reign of our Sovereign Lord George the Second, of iBritain, France, and Ireland, King, Defender of the Faith, isle, and of the Grand Jury at the same Quarter Sessions, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, that the Provision, made by an Act, of the Eleventh Year of his late Majesty's Reign, for the better regulating the Manufacture of Cloth in the West Riding of the County of York, for sealing and damping the Woollen Cloths by the Mailer, Owner* or Occupier, of Fulling-mills, has been found insufficient to prevent Ibme Frauds and Abuses in the Woollen Manufacture, intended to be prevented by the said Act; and that the evil Combinations and Practices of many Millers, and Clothiers, have been the Occasion of other Frauds and Abuses in the said Manufacture, and, particularly, of damping the Cloth at such Mills to be of greater Lengths, than the true Lengths thereof: That the growing, or Ihrinking, of the Cloth, or other Alteration thereof, in a small Time after its being taken out of the Stocks, not 9nly renders the Convictions of the Miller,

Sof Abuses, very difficult, but frequently exposes ir Miller to be convicted of wrong damping such Cloth: That the Petitioners conceive, that, if Inspectors were appointed, and such Regulations provided, as in the Act, of the Thirteenth Year of his late Majesty's Reign, for the better Regulation of the Woollen Manufacture, many Abuses might be prevented: And therefore they pray, to have such Inspectors, or such other Remedy, as the House shall think fit.

jtqgjryjnto Mr. Oglethorpe, from the Committee, appointed to wbuieof enquire into the State of the Gaols of this Kingdom, acquainted the House, that the Committee had entered upon their Enquiry into the State of the Fleet Prison; and had directed him to report to the House, how highly the Warden of the said Prison had misbehaved himself upon that Occasion: And he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That, upon the Receipt of a Letter this Morning, being the 28th Day of February, 1728, from Sir Rich, Baronet, complaining of severe Treatment from Mr.

Bambridge, Warden of the Fleet, since his Examination before the Committee, the Committee thereupon examined the said Sir IVm. Rich, and found.

That, so soon as the Committee adjourned Yesterday, lie, the said Sir William, had his Legs loaded with Irons, and Handcuffs put on, by an Agent of the Warden's, Yoi. 21.

much straiter than those, that were on i before his Examination; so that his Wrists were much fwuln, and he was in Torture all Night. ....

Mr. Bambridge being called in, and examined, what Induced him to Change Sir Witt. Ric Handcuffs, and put on straiter, by which he was in great Pain and Torture all Night;

The said Bambridge answered, that one of the Handcuffs Was broke Yesterday; and that he bad no other Reason for changing the m.

That, upon the Inspection of the Committee Yesterday, it appeared, that the Handcuffs, which Sir Rich bad on, before he was brought to the Committee, were found and good, and after they were weighed, were returned unbrqken to Mr. Bambridge, or his Agents.

That it further appears to this Committee, that the changing the Handcuffs of Sir William Rich, and the ill Treatment he has met with from the Ward n, and his Agents, was the consequence of Sir William Rich's having given Evidence to this Committee, and was in order to intimidate others from giving further Evidence to this Committee.

Resolved, nemine contradicetite. That Thomas Esquire, Warden of his Majesty's Prison of the Fleet, having misused, in a very cruel and barbarous Manner,

Sir William Rich, now a Prisoner in his Custody, for having given Evidence before a Committee of this House, is guilty of a high Indignity to r: is House, a Contempt of the Authority, and a Breach of the Privilege, thereof.

Ordered, nemine contradicente, That the said Thomas

Bambridge be, for his laid Offence, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

Mr. Alderman Barnard reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants and Traders of the City of London, whose Names are thereunto fub-Icribed, in behalf of themselves, and other Merchants and Traders of the said City, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table; where the same was read; and the Report, and Resolutions, are as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition: And the Petitioners, to make out the Allegations thereof, called Mr. Samuel Bonham; who said, that he is concerned in several Ships, that trade to Guinea: notwithstanding he gives them full River Pay, when the Ship has come to Gravesend, and paid his Men what was due to them, and cleared the Ship, they have refused to proceed on their Voyage, without advancing their Wages ;, and have often taken his Boat, and gone ashore, and returned no more, but left the Boat behind: That he has been put to great Expence and Trouble in getting others in their Read before he has done which, the Wind has fluffed, and he has like to have loft his Voyages; and often, when his Ships have come into the West his Men have run

away, after they have received their Wages as diretfted by Law; and he has been forced to give ft. 20. a Man for the Run home; which Run has not exceeded above Eight or Ten Weeks; and has often been threatened, and has been sued by such Deserters for Wages.

Mr. 'Thomas Sand ford(aid, that Seamen refule to enter into Contracts to perform the Voyage, as formerly they did; and when he has agreed for Half-pay in the River, and lb much per Month during the Voyage, yet, when he has come to clear his Ship, they have infilled upon whole River Pay; and, for fear his Ship should lole her Voyage, he has complied therewith; yet, notwithstanding all he could do to them, they have left his Ship, and he has been at great Trouble and Expence in getting other Men, and in danger of losing his Voyage: And he apprehends, by the Laws now in being the Mailers have no Power to oblige them to Hay on board, to discharge their Duty; which he looks upon to be a very great Hardship to the Navigation of Merchant Ships.

Mr. Henry Gough laid, that he is concerned in the Shipping, trading to the East Indies: notwithstanding the y give Seamen the River Pay, and, at the clearing of Ships, Two Months Pay Advance, yet, when they come to clear the Ship, they have of late Years run away from them, and pot them to great Charge and Trouble in getting others in their room; and that they have Two Ships at present, have loft the Opportunity of failing, upon the same Occasion, which if they fliou/d lole the Season, it would be ft. 2,000. Damage to the Owners, besides 20 or ft. 30,000. Damage to the Company; and, when the Ships return home, the Seamen run alhore, and will not stay to unlade the Ships; which obliges the Owners to hire Men, which they call Lumpers, to do it; who, being a Set of idle pilfering People, do Heal their Goods, and frequently occasion 2 or ft. 300. Lois to the Owners, besides a great Detriment to the Revenue.

Mr. Joseph Groves laid, that they are very much troubled with Seamen deferring at the Clearing of their Ships, and put togfeat Charges in getting others in their room; and, when the Ships come abroad, the Men have left the Ships and been absent Three, Six, and Nine,

Months; and yet have come, and infilled to come home in the Ship; and the Mailer has been obliged to bring them, for fear of coming into Trouble for leaving them in foreign Parts; and, when they have come home, they have infilled upon their w hole Pay, during the Time they were absent, having been informed, that they could oblige the Mailer to pay it; and which they have been forced to comply with.

Privilege. Mr. Earle (according to Order) reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter touch-in the Complaint, that Mr. Thomas Jufon, Rector of ‘ Wanfted, in the County of Essex, William Hatton, John Brooks, and Rickard Spencer, had, in a forcible Manner,

' entered upon Part of the Possessions of the Right honourable Richard, Viscount Cajllemain, in the Kingdom of Ireland, a Member of this House, at Wanfted aforesaid,

and had cut down a Fence, and committed Spoil, in Breach of the Privilege of this House, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table, where the same was read; and the Report, and Resolutions of the Committee, are as follows; viz.

That the Question was. Whether Mr. Jufon, the present Rector of Wanfted, had cut down a Hedge-row of White Thorns, near adjoining to the Church-yard of Wanfted, but on the Outside of the Pale of the said Chui'ch-yard.

The Counsel for the Lord Cajllemain alleged, that his Lordship was seised in Fee of a Field, called Seven Acre Field, which was planted all round with a Hedge, and Trees, for Ornament: That the same was planted by the Ancestors of the Complainant on their own Ground: That their own Servants and Workmen have always taken care of fplicing and pruning the fame, and have accordingly

paid for the said Work; and that the said Hedge was about Forty Years growth. To prove which, he called Robert Taylor; who said, he knew Mr. Jufon; and that he law him, with an Ax in his Hand, with Two of his Servants, one on each Side, the Twenty-third of January last, cutting down the Hedge of White Thorn: That Mr. Jufon was chopping a Standard: That one of the Servants was named John Brooks; and believes, the other was his Coachman, Wm. Hatton: That on the Twenty-fourth of January, the next Day, he saw Mr. Jufon, and his Coachman, pitching up the Buthes, and cut Wood, into a Cart with Two Horses; and one Spencer was there loading the lame; and that Spencer drove the same off the Ground:

Said also, that he had been Servant in the Family about Twenty Years: That his Father and Grandfather were so before him: That Sheep were formerly kept in this Field: That the Ditch was made next to the said Field, to keep the Sheep and Lambs from the Hedge: That this Seven Acre Field, Twenty-three or Twenty -four Years ago, was an Orchard; and that some of the Trees were cut down, to make Vifto's to the House: And fays, he remembers the fplicing the Hedge; and that there was a Pale round the Church-yard, which was broke down about Fifteen Years ago: That one Allison undertook the doing of it; and that the Paling was very bad at the West End of the Church: That the Pale at the West End was nailed on the Inside, with the Points towards the Hedge, because of the Growth of the Hedge, which was very thick at Bottom; all the rest of the Pales were nailed on the Outside, with the Points towards the Church-yard; and that the Pale was always esteemed the Bounds of the Church-yard.

Being cross-examined, he said, the Pale was always esteemed the Bounds of the Church-yard: That he knew Mr. Harkey and Mr. Pound, former Ministers of this Church, who never took any Care of the Hedge; but has heard his Father, and old People say, Lord Cajllemain's Family did: Remembers the Pale round the Church-yard about Twenty-five Years: That the Parish always repaired it: That between the said Pale and Hedge it was in some Places a Foot and Half wide, in others Two or Three Feet.

William Philips said, he has known the Hedge in Dispute Thirty-seven Years: That it was made and fpliced by one Charles Russell, Servant to Sir Josiah Child, at Seven Pence per Pole: That he was paid for his Work by Sir Josiah's Bailiff; and that he saw the Money paid: That John Faux, Richard Faux, and Edward Stebbings, made the Fence, to preserve the Quick-set, at Three Pence per Perch: That he saw the Money paid by Sir Josiah's Bailiff; and that the Ditch was made on the same Side as the Seven Acre Field, and was flung up in that Manner, to preserve the Quick-set:

That he worked with one William Lee, who told him, he planted the Quick-set, and he did it by Order of Sir Joshua Child:Says, that he has known the Place ever

since 1683: That the Church-yard Pale was repaired by the Parish; and that one JBoundley had done it about Twenty Years, and the Parish paid him Twenty Shillings per Annum.

Being cross-examined, he believes, the Hedge was planted on Sir Josiah Child's Ground; and that the Parish did not do any thing to the Hedge; and that the Pale Hands in the same Place as in 1683.

Philip Gray said, he knew the Seven Acre Field next the Church-yard; remembers the planting the Hedge without the Church-yard; the Pale was Handing before the Hedge planted: Does not remember any Ditch before the Hedge planted, but that the Earth was thrown from the Pales to the Quick-set, to preserve it: That the Field was planted Three Parts round with the same fort of Hedge.

Being cross-examined, he said, he believed, the Pale was set to the Extremity of the Ground belonging to the Church-yard:

Says, he has known the Hedge about Forty Years: That the Pale flood there, before the Hedge was planted:

The House proceeded (according to Order) to take into Consideration the Report from (he Committtee, to whom the Petition of the Council and Burgesses of the Colony of Virginia, and also the Petition of the Merchants of the City of London, trading to and Maryland,

and also the Petition of the Merchants, and Traders in Tobacco, in the City of Bristol, and also the Petition of the several Merchants, and Traders in.Tobacco, of and in the Port of Liverpool, in the County Palatine of Lan~ cafer, were referred.

And the Report was read, and is as follows;

That the Committee had taken into Consideration the said Petitions, and examined the following Witnesses; viz.

Mr. John Randolph, Agent for the Colony of Virginia; who said, that the People of Virginia and Maryland are chiefly subsisted by the Tobacco Trade, and, having no Manufactures of their own, are clothed with the Manufactures of this Kingdom, and are also supplied with all Sorts of Household Goods, Utensils of Trade, and other Merchandize, fit and necessary for them, from hence, which amounts to a very great Value yearly:

That the Exportation of the British Manufactures to those Countries doth wholly depend upon the Price of Tobacco, and, if by any Hardship laid upon them, they become unable to furnish themselves with Necessaries, as in some Years they have been, they mult of Necessity employ themselves in Manufacture of Woollen and Linen 9f their own, which would be a considerable Loss to the Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom:

That the Clause in an Act of Parliament, passed in the Ninth Year of his late Majesty's Reign, whereby the Importation of Tobacco, ftvipt from the Stalk or Stem,

Vo i. SI.

is prohibited, obliges the Planters to throw away the under and lhattered Leaves, of the Tobacco Plant, which is computed to be at lead One-fifth Part of the whole, when, by taking out the Stalk, it might be made very fit for the Markets here; but, for want of the Liberty of importing, it is become useless to them, unless they fell it at low Prices to them, who run it ashore; and, besides, they are under a Necessity of fending great Part of the Remainder of the Plant in such a Shape, as is not fit for the home Consumption; in Consequence whereof, the Planters are prevented from having their Returns so foots, as their Occasions require, the Merchants are obliged t keep great Quantities of Tobacco in their Wareltoufes; and several Persons, who formerly sent considerable Cargoes to Virginia, for purchasing Tobacco, have left off Trade on account of this Prohibition:

That the priceof Stalks in London is from tajr. to 18 per Hundred Weight: That they are manufactured by the Retailers, and mingled with the pure Tobacco; so that. the Importation of them cannot be any Addition to the Revenue; but must rather be a Lelfening, seeing that Sort of Tobacco will not consume To f*ft, nqr is so pleasenr, as the pure Leaf without any Mixture:

That the Quantity of Tobacco imported isconsiderably increased; but that is owing to the Increase of People in those Countries,' from the' Importation of Slaves, and Convicts, and not to the bringing in of Stalks. ‘

Mn James Bradley said; that, if this Clause be repealed, it can be no Detriment to the Revenue, because that depends intirely on the home Consumption; and it cannot be imagined, that the taking of the Stalk out can make it either less liked, or burn longer; but, on the contrary, it is evident, that the Stalk, manufactured with the Tobacco, will make it burn much longer in the Pipe, and lef6 acceptable to the Consumer:

That the repealing of this Clause can be little or no Detriment to the Poor, employed in the (tripping of-Tobacco here; for the Quantity of stript Tobacco, imported, before the Clause took Effect, did not exceed 8000 Hogsheads per Annum, and One Stripper can (trip 10 oik.of Tobacco per Diem-, which, computing the Hogsheads at 800 lb.per Hogshead, 200 Persons or thereabouts can strip the whole Quantity imported in One Year; and at least Half that Number will be employed in the picking, and laying straight, the stript Tobacco, and making it fit for the Knife.

Colonel Spotjwcod said, he had been near 15 Years there, and was sometime Commander in chief; and did observe, when Tobacco was low, it did not make sufficient Returns, but was generally brought in Debt; and* if the Clause be not repealed, the People will make their own Manufacture, which at present they have all from hence, and are depending upon; which will be

a very great Detriment to the Manufactures here: There is a Necessity, for that Reason, to give an Encouragement to the Tobacco Trade:

That he is well allured, if the Clause was to be repealed, there would be an Increase of One Tenth, in the Tobacco, and they could furnish net Tobacco sufficient for the home Consumption: That the Colony is at present in a low Condition, from the Want of a Consumption here: That the Increase of the People within these few Years last past has been the Occasion of fbmuch being imported* and makes the Planter enlarge the Plantation, though it is very often to his Ruin; but, if a good Commodity was made, they would be the sooner paid for it, and the Return would be much the quicker.

That it also appeared to the Committee, that the encouraging the Tobacco Colonies, is a general Good to the Kingdom, as it is a very great and beneficial Branch of its Trade; and the Planters at this Juncture are in great Need of Relief from the Hardships they lie under; and that the Clause, complained ofi is a principal Causa thereof.

A Clause in an Act, made in the Ninth Year of his late, Majesty's llcign, cap. 21. prohibiting the Importation <*jf Tobacco, stript from the Stalk, or Stem, was read.

Gosport A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are there-new Chapel, unto l'ubscribed, being Inhabitants, and Freeholders, paying Scotland Lot, in and about the Town of Gosport, in the Parish of Alverstoke, in the County of Southampton, in behalf of themselves, and many poor Families living

in the said Town, waspresented to the House* and read; setting forth, that a Petition is depending in the House, that a Bill may be brought in, for laying a Tax upon all Coals, which shall be imported at Gosport, for a Provision for a Minister, and keeping the Chapel there in Repair: That the Chapel was built by voluntary Subscription, and at the Time of the Consecration, in 1696, Fees were vested in the Minister there, amounting to not less than £. too. per Annum, one Year with another, and are now enjoyed by the present Rector, besides 10 for the Use of the Pall, now engrossed by him, which was formerly the Property of a poor Widow; notwithstanding which, the Petitioners for the said Bill suggest, there is no Provision for a Curate, although his Salary, at the Consecration of the said Chapel, was settled only at £. 20. per Annum: That about Three Years ago a very heavy Rate, of above £.700. was raised by the Inhabitants, for

rebuilding the Parish Church of Alverstoke; and the Town, through the Want of Trade, and daily Increase of the Poor, is fallen above one half in the Value of the Rents; lb that the Poor's Rates have amounted to above £. 500. per Annum for several Years pall; and, should the said Tax be laid, many Tradesmen, that use great Quantities of Coals, and several other considerable Families, have determined to leave the Town: That a very able Divine, formerly Curate of the said Chapel for several Years, now fixed in a Living of above 80. per Annum, has offered £. 40. in Money, and to resign his present Incumbency, if the Rector's Son, who now officiates, would accept thereof, in Exchange for the Chapel, which is but one Mile and an Half, and the Way always very good, from the said Parish Church: And it is observed, that those who petition for this Tax, are the moll wealthy Persons in the Town, and very able to maintain a Minister, and repair their Chapel, as they have hitherto done: And praying, that they may be heard by Counsel against the said Petition, before a Bill be brought in, pursuant to the Prayer thereof, or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief, as the House shall think fit, not One-fiftieth Part of the Inhabitants of the Town of Gosport knowing any thing of the said Petition, when presented.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, who have thereunto subscribed their Names, Inhabitants of the Borough of Gosport, in the County of Southampton, on the behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Borough, presented to this House on the Twenty-eighth Day of February last, ..... be received.

Sir George Cooke said, that to his Knowledge, he never entered any Clerks in his Office, but such as had served their Time, Or were well recommended by Pradifers, that he knew, or the Master with whom they served their Clerkship:

That the Clerks who are entered in his Office, claim a Privilege of not being-sued.but in that Court: That, if any one isfued in any other Court, he may plead his Writ of Privilege; and, if he is' sued in any other Court, he mud have a Copy of the Writ, and then plead it fub pede figil/i;

That he has not above a Thousand Clerks entered in his Book: That he does not-know all his entering Clerks by Name, but several of them by Person j and that entering Clerks are exempt from pacing Fees, when sued: That the several Prothonotaries tax Attorneys Bills in their respective Offices: That, before Bills-have been taxed, the whole Money has often been brought into Court; and sometimes tie has taxed- Bills,-Without the Money being brought into-Court:

Mr. John Ward produced a List from the Warrant of Attorneys Office of all the sworn Attorneys on the Rolls for Thirty Years: That he believed, there might be about 420 in all.

Mr. Samuel Clarke produced a List of the Clerks of Edward Ventris, Esquire, chief Clerk of the King's Bench, as also a List of the Attorneys of the Court of King's Bench:

And, being examined, said, that none ought to prac-tife, but such as are sworn Attorneys; but believes, there are a great many, that practise in others Names, though they are not allowed so to do, and who never were entered Attorneys in that Court, but ad only by Collu* lion; and that there is no Power to restrain them from so doing: That no Person ought to sue out a Bill of Middlesex, but such as are (worn Attorneys:

That the Sheriffs Officers often take out Writs, and put an Attorney's Name thereto, without the Knowlege of the Attorney; and all Attorneys and Clerks, who are sworn, are privileged by their Courts; but Solicitofs, who practise in others Names, are not: That none are admitted Attorneys in the King's Bench, without a Certificate of their having served Five Years at lead to k Clerk or Attorney of that Court: That the Judges and Serjeants Clerks have a Privilege of being (worn; and none but the sworn Clerks belonging to the Office, can make out a Judgment or take out a Writ.

Mr. John Croft, Deputy to the Master of the Bill of Middlesex Office, said, that he believes, there are several Persons that take out Writs, that are not Attorneys; and that the several Offices never refuse any Person that comes to (ign their Writs; but there is always an Attorney's Name to the Writ; and they never inquire, whether they' are sworn Attorneys or not: Has often known Sheriff

Officers take out Writs: That Officer always keeps an Account of the Number of Writs, that are issued:

Has known 1,100 issued in a Vacation, and about 3,000 in a Year.

Mr. William Spicer produced a List of the Attorneys and Clerks, in the Office of Pleas in his Majesty's Court of Exchequer; and said, that there are Three Sorts of Processes, a Subpoena,a Quominus, and a Summons; and that they are obliged to grant a Process to any Person who comes for it. /

- Mr. William Tu/ly'said, That he has heard, that there are a great Number of Persons who call themselves Pfcotbonotaries' Clerks, that have the same Privilege of practising as fwora-Clerks. That he has heard, several broken Tradesmen and Bailiffs, do practise as Attorneys, and often set People at Variance, and have got £. 10. or £. ao. of each Party, by being concerned, and, before the Maitter comes to a Trial, make the Affair up between their Clients for a-Bottle of Wine, and a Treat: Believes, many practise in the Name of others, to avoid the Duty of the Six Pound Stamp: That several practise, in the Town' and Countty, who are not sworn Clerks, nor ever served any Clerkship, and ought not to practise; but practise only as being entering Clerks, and have a Writ of Privilege, not to be sued in any other Court, but such 4s they belong to: That the Prothonotaries Clerks formerly never entered up Judgments, but such as were actually seated Clerks in the Office, as likewise in the King's Bench: That he believes, there are some Thousands of entering Clerks:

Mr. Richard Marriott, one of the Attorneys in the Office of Pleas in his Majesty's Court of Exchequer, said, that the Cods of that Court, upon a Judgment of Default, are always taxed by the Mader, which generally amount to about £. i and no Difference in the Taxations, whether the Judgment is for great or smallSums: That, where the Judge, in case of a Trespass, or for Battery, certifies for under 40 s.the Cods are usually taxed at 16 or £. 17. Gentlemen,

I have always had the greatest Regard and Concern for the Commerce and Navigation of my Kingdoms: I am fenlibly affected with the Losses, sustained by my trading Subjects: I have, upon all proper Applications, given the strictest Orders, for procuring just and reasonable Satisfaction; and you may be affined, that I will {till use my best endeavours to answer the Desires and Expectations of my People upon an Affair of so much Importance.

Re/o/ved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return the most humble Thanks of this House to his Majesty for this most gracious Answer.

Mr. Oglethorpe, from the Committee, appointed to en- Enquiry inu quire into the State of the Gaols of this Kingdom, made the State of a Report of some Progress, which the Committee had made in their Enquiry into the Stateof th Prison, with the

Resolutions of the Committee thereupon: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered the fame, with Two Appendixes, in at the Clerk's Table; where the Report was read, and is as followeth; viz.

The Committee, having, in pursuance of the Order of this House, of the Twenty-fifth Day of February, 1728, to enquire into the State of the Gaols of this Kingdom, adjourned to the Fleet, and at several Times examined into the State of that Prison, have made some Progress therein, which they have thought fit to lay before the House.

The Committee find, that the Fleet Prison is an ancient Prison, and formerly used for the Reception of the Pri-(oners, committed by the Council Table, then called the Court of the Star-chamber, which exercised unlimited Authority, and inflicted heavier Punishments, than by any Law were warranted.

And, as that afliimed Authority was found to be an intolerable Burden to the Subject, and the Means to introduce an arbitrary Powerand Government, all Jurisdiction,

Power, and Authority, belonging unto, or exercised in, the same Court, or by any the Judges, Officers, or Ministers, thereof, were clearly and absolutelydiflblved, taken away, and determined, by an Act, made in the Sixteenth Year of the Reign of King Charles the First:

And thereby, the Committee apprehend, all Pretences of the Warden of the Fleet, to take Fees from Archbishops,

Bishops, Temporal Peers, Baronets, and others of lower Degree, or to put them in Irons, or exact Fees, for not doing so, were determined and abolished.

That, after the said Act took place, the Fleet Prison became a Prison for Debtors, and for Contempts of the Courts of Chancery, Exchequer, and Common Pleas, only, and fell under the same Regulations, as other Gaols of this Kingdom.

That by an Act, of the 2 2d and 23d of King C/wr/w the Second, the future Government of all Prisons was vetted in the Lords Chief Justices, the Chief Baron, or any Two of them, for the Time being, and the Justices of the Peace in London, Middlesex, and Surrey, and the Judges for the several Circuits, and the Justices of the Peace for the Time being in their several Precincts; and, pursuant thereunto, several Ordersand Regulations have been made (the last of which is hereunto annexed in the Appendix, marked Letter^) which the prefers Warden of the Fleet hath not regarded, or complied with; but hath exercised an unwarrantable and arbitrary Power, not only in extorting exorbitant Fees, but in oppressing Prisoners for Debt, by loading them with Irons, worse than if the Star-chamber was dill subsisting, and contrary to the great Charter, the Foundation of the Liberty of the Subject, and in Defiance and Contempt thereof, as well as of other good Laws of this Kingdom.

It appears by a Patent, of the Third Year of Queen Elizabeth, recited in Letters Patents bearing Date the Nineteenth of King Charles the Second, that the Fleet Prison was an ancient Prison, called Prisona de la Fleet, alias, the Queen s Gaol of the Fleet; and that certain Constitutions were then established, by Agreement between Richard Tyrrell, Warden, and the Prisoners of the Fleet, and a Table of Fees annexed, in which the Fees to be paid by an Archbishop, Duke, Marquis, Earl, or other Lord Spiritual or Temporal, are particulaly mentioned, and the Fine ascertained, which they are to pay for the Liberty

of the House, and Irons; artd that there Conditiltions and Orders were confirmed by the said Letters Patent of King Charles the Second; which Letters Patent grant the Office of Warden of the Fleet, and of the Keeper of the old Palace at Wesimnfter, the Shops in certain

Tenements adjoining to the and other Rents and

Profits belonging to the Warden, to Sir Jeremy and his Heirs for ever; and the said Sir Jeremy rebuilt the said Prison at his own Expence, as a Consideration for the Grant thereof; but the said Prison, and the Custody of the Prisoners being a Freehold, and falling by Descent, or Purchase, into the Hands of Persons incapable of executing the Office of Warden, was the Occasion of great Abuses, and frequent Complaints to Parliament, till at length the Patent was set aside.

And a Patent for Life was granted to Leigh-

ton, Esquire, in Consideration of his great Pains and Expences in suing the former Patentees to a Forfeiture; and, he soon dying, John Huggins Esquire, by giving 5,000. to the late Lord Claredon, did, by his Interest, obtain a Grant of the said Office for his own and his Son's Life.

That, during the Time the said Huggins possessed the said Office of Warden of the Fleet, Thomas , a Prisoner in that Pril'on, charged with £. 40,000. Debt, the greatest Part thereof to the Crown, escaped, having the Liberty of the Rules by Permission of the said for which Escape Huggins pretends, he hath obtained a Quietus 1 and, since that Time, Joseph Fains, charged with £.10,000. Debt to the Crown, having like Liberty of the Pules, also escaped.

That Thomas Dumay made several Voyages to , whilst a Prisoner in the Fleet, and in Custody of the said Huggins, and there bought Wines, some of which were delivered to the said Huggins; and Dumay drew several Bills, whilst in Frcmce, to the Value of £. 320. on Richard Bishop, one of the Tipstaffs of the said Prison, who paid £. 300. and the said Huggins paid the rest: That by the punctual Payment of the said Bills, Dumay acquired a Credit in France, and drew for a further Sum, and then returned to England; and, when the Bills came for Payment, the said Richard Bishop refused to accept them; and the Merchants upon Dumay' % Return, endeavouring to get the Money of him, who was the Drawer of the Bills, found him a Prisoner in the Rules, and had no Remedy.

The said John Huggins owned to the Committee, that so many Prisoners had escaped, during the Time he was Warden, that it was impossible to enumerate them, he having kept no Lilt of the Persons lb escaped.

He also owned to the Committee, that in his Time Oliver Read made his Escape, when there was a great Funeral, and, whilst the Doors were open, he went off: That afterwards being retaken, he, the said,

sent him to a Spunging-house, kept by Richard Corbett, one of the Tipstaffs belonging to the said Prison; where he was locked up, ironed, and ftapled down, by his Order, though not condemned by any Court of Justice.

That it appeared to the Committee, that in the Year 1725, one Mr. Arne, an Upholder, was carried into a Stable, which stood where the strong Room on the Mailer's Side now is, and was there confined, being a Place of cold Restraint, till he died; and that he was in good State of Health, before he was confined to that Room.

That the said John Huggins growing in Yeats, and willing to retire from Business, and his Son not caring to take upon him so troublesome an Office, he hath for several Years beeen engaged in continual Negotiations about the Disposal of the said Office; and in August last concluded a final Treaty with Thomas Bamb and Dougal Cuthbert, Esquires, and for £. 5,000. to be paid unto him, obliged himself to ItiiTender the said Patent for his and his Son's Life, and procure a new Patent for the said Bambridge and Cuthbert; which the said Huggins did accordingly obtain; and Cuthbert paid in Money, or gave good Security to pay £. 2,500. for one Moiety of the said Office of Warden, and Bambridge gave Land and other Security, which the said Huggins was then content with, for £. 2,500. being for the other Moiety of the said Office,

That, upon Inspection and Examination On the com- Enquiry into monSideof the Prison, in the Three Wards; called the Upper Chapel, the Lower Chapel, and Julius Cafar's, 0 a* *" Ninety-three Persons were confined, who are obliged to lie on the Floor, if they cannot furnish themselves with Bedding, or pay 1 s. per Week to such Prisoner as is so provided.

That the Lyons Den and Womens Ward, which contain about Eighteen Persons, are very noisome, and in very ill Repair.

That there are several Rooms in the Chapel Stairs, for each of which £.5 a Year is now paid, but did formerly belong to the common Side, and for which nothing was paid, until charged by Mr. Huggins, at 3 a Year each; and on this Floor there are several Persons who are uncertain, what Chamber Rent they shall be obliged to pay, and are at the Mercy of the Warden.

That in some Rooms Persons, who are lick of different Distempers, are obliged to lie together or on the Floor:

One, in particular, had the Small Pox, and Two Women were ordered to lie with her; and they pay 2 10 per

Week each for such Lodging.

That in all the Rooms, except very few, the Furniture is provided by the Prisoners, and those which are furnished by the Warden, are extremely bad.

That there was a Regulation by the Judges in Trinity Term, 1727, by which the Warden ought to furnish all the Rooms, and in such same the Prisoners to pay 2 s. 6d. per Week for each Room so furnished; but now there are several Rooms, in each of which :keie are Two, Three, and Four Beds, and in each Bed Two, and f 'mutinies Three Persons, who pay 2 s. 10 deach per Week lor such Lodging.

That the Walls which secure the Prison, are 25 Foot high, with Pallisadoes on the Top, and in good Repair; and no seeming Possibility for any Prisoner to escape.

That at the End of the Place called the Bare, a Watch-house was built about a Year since, wherein are kept several Mulkcts and Bayonets, as are like wife several others in a Room fronting Fleet Ditch-, whereas formerly only Pikes and Halberts were kept in that Part of the Prison, which is called the Lodge.

That several Men, called Watchmen, and under the Pay of Mr. Bambridge, belong to the Prison, one of which Bambridge ordered to fire upon Captain Mackpkeadris, upon the Dispute, which happened between them; but the Watchman fearing the Consequence, refused to obey him.

That the Windows of the Prison are in very bad Repair, to the great Prejudice of the Health of the Prisoners, though by a late Order of the Judges, they ought to have been kept in good Repair by the Warden.

That there are Three Houses adjoining, and belonging to the Prison, which are kept as Spunging-houses, by Tenants to Mr. Bambridge, as Warden; in one of which, kept by Corbett, 26 Prisoners are confined.

That many of thele Prisoners pay 2 a Day for the Use of a Room in this House, and for Firing 1 s. and the other Prisoners n. a Night for a Bed; but, notwithstanding such Payments, they are obliged to lie Two or more in the same Bed: The Sums paid by these Twenty-six Prisoners, Two at 2 s. per Day, and Twenty-four at 1 s. for the Use of the Lodgings only, being in, the Whole £, 1.8r. amount yearly to £511. besides the Money paid for Firing, at 1 s. a Day, by such as have any, and 1 s. a Day for their Board.

Some of these Prisoners, not being able to pay the is. a Day for eating, procured Necessaries to drels their own Meat; but Corbett, the Tipilaff, would not suffer them so to do, and they are under the Necessity of being supplied by their Friends, or starve.

And that in about Two Years Time one Gentleman paid £. 30. for obtaining Day Rules.

That an Act having passed in the Sixth Year of the late King, for the Relief of insolvent Debtors, Mr. Fytche did thereupon declare, in the Name of the said Mr. Huggins who had directed him so to do, that unless every Prisoner within the Rules would give him Two Guineas, they should not be lifted, in order to be discharged, in pur-luance of that A<f!; for that he, the said Huggins, would refui'e to (wear them his Prisoners, as that Act required, and would not suffer his Deputy to do it; but a List was delivered of about Twenty Prisoners then in the Rules, who were discharged, having given Two Guineas each to Huggins, for inferring them in the Lift, and for swearing them to be his Prisoners; and Three hundred Prisoners were carried up to Guild-halt, in order to their Discharge, but some were refuted to be lifted, and loft the Benefit of the Act, because they had not Money enough to pay for being put into the Lift.

That Mr. Huggins being examined touching an Instrument, signed by him in November, 1724, appointing Richard Corbett one of the Five Tipstaffs of, or belonging to the Fleet Prison, acknowledged, that he had no Power, by virtue of any Patent from the Crown, to constitute such Tipstaff; but that, when he came to his Office, he found, that such an Officer had been so constituted, and he took that for a Precedent to do the fame.

That there are Five Commitment Books, wherein the Names of all Prisoners, committed to the Prison, are,

or ought to be entered: The Commencement of the Date of the first Book is the 26th of March, 1708, and the last the 6th of May, 1728, to this Time.

There is one Book, wherein the Names are inserted of those Prisoners, who are removed to the Fleet by Habeas' Corpus, beginning in Michaelmas Term, 1727, to this Time.

There is one Declaration Book, wherein the Names of those Creditors are inserted, who declare against their Debtors, beginning the 23d of , 1728, to this

Time.

There is one Lodge Book, wherein the Prisoners Names are entered, when they come into the Prison, beginning November, 1728.

There is one Security Bond Book, without Date.

That he, the said Mr. Huggins, on , Sunday,

and Monday the First, Second, and Third of March, r 728, since the Committee was appointed, did exonerate, or discharge out of the Commitment Books, One hundred and Nineteen Persons, for several Sums, amounting to about £. 17,099. 6j. 7 d.

He owned, that he has in his Custody Fifty-two Discharges more, which ought to have been long since discharged, and amount to very great Surm of Money.

That by the Dates in the Lilt, which Mr. Huggins delivered to the Committee, of One hundred and Nineteen Persons lb discharged, and the Fifty-two to be discharged, it appeared, that many of them ought to have been discharged in the Years, 1718, 1719, 1720, and so on to this Time.

That there are Two Escape Warrants, one of which the Judge grants, the other the Warden; that, which the Judge grants, carried the Prisoner to , there to

remain during Life, unless the Debt be paid; and that,' which the Warden grants, is on some Information, or Pretence, that the Prisoner is out of the Rules, and so remands him to the Prison.

One ill Use, which is made of keeping the Prisoners so long on the Commitment Book, is, that the Warden may, at his Pleasure, issue his Escape Warrant against any such Person, continued on the Commitment Book, and carry him to the Spunging-house, or to the Prison, and there detain him, until he squeezes from him all the Money, that can possibly be got.

Another ill Use and Inconveniency is, that Persons, who have been Seven Years, or more, out of the Rules, or out of the Prison, their Names remaining in the Commitment Book, return, after having contrafted new Debts, and so become Prisoners again fraudulently, to obtain the Benefit of the usual Acts for Relief of insolvent Debtors.

And, notwithstanding the Payment of such ‘large Fee$, in order to extort further Sums from the unfortunate Prisoners, the said Bambridge unjustly pretends, he has a Bight, as Warden, to exerc'rfe an unlimited Power of changing Prisoners from Room to Boom, -of turning them into the common Side, though they have paid the Matter's Side Fee, and inflicting arbitrary Pumthments, by locking them down in unWholcfome Dungeons, and loading them with torturing Irotis; fottie Instances of which follow; viz*

Jacob Mendez Solas, a Portvjgueft, was as far as it appeared to the Committee, one of the first Prisoners for Debt, that ever was loaded with Irons at the FA The said Bambridge one Day called him into the'Gate-house of the Prison, called the Lodge; where‘he caused hint to be seized, fettered, and carried to s, the Spunging-

house, and there kept for upwards of a Week; and, when brought back into the Prison, Bambridge caused him to be turned into the Dungeon, called 7he Strong Rotfw, of the Matter's Side.

This Place is a Vaiitt, like those in which the Dead are interred, and wherein the Bodies of Persons dying in the said Prison, are usually deposited, till the Coroner's Inquest hath patted upon them: it hasno-Chimney, nor Fire-place, nor any Light, but what comes over the Door, or through a Hole of about [Eight] Inches square: It is neither paved, nor-boarded, and the rough Brides appear both on the Sides, and Top, being neither wainfeotted.

nor plaittered: What adds to the Dampnds and Stench of the Place, is, its being built over the common Shear, and adjoining to the Sink and Dunghill, where all the Nastiness of the Pris in is cast. In this miserable Place the poor Wretch was kept by the said Bambridge manacled, and shackled, for near Two Months. At length, on receiving Five Guineas from Mr. , a Friend of Solas's, Bambridge released the Prisoner from his cruel Confinement; but, though his Chains were taken off, his Terror dill remained; and the unhappy Man was prevailed upon by that Terror, not only to labour gratis for the said Bambridge, but to swear also, at random, all

that he hath required of him: And this Committee themselves saw an Instance of the deep Impression his Sufferings had made upon him; for, on his furmifing, from something said, that Bambridge was to return again as Warden of the Fleet, he fainted, and the Blood started out of his Mouth and 'Nose.

Captain John Mackpheadris, who was bred a Merchant, is another melancholy Instance of the cruel Vie the said Bambridge hath made of his affirmed Authority. Mackpheadris was a considerable Trader, and in a very flourifiling Condition, until the Year 1720, when, being bound for large Sums to the Crown for a Person, afterwards ruined by the Misfortunes of that Year, he was undone. In Jane, 1727, he was Prisoner in the Fleet-, and, although

he had before paid his Commitment Fee, the like Fee was extorted from him a Second time; and he having fiir-niflied Room, Bam bridge demanded an extravagant Price for it, which he refused to pay; and urged, that it was unlawful for the Warden-to demand extravagant Rents, -and offered to pay what was legally due: notwithstanding winch, the said Bambridge, affi-sted by the said Jam A Barnes, and bther Accomplices, broke open his lloom, and took away several Things of great Value, amongst others, the King's Extent in Aid of the Prisoner (which was to have been returned in a few Day's, in order to pro-cutethe Debt to the Crown, and the Prisoner's Enlargement) which Bambridge ft ill detains: Not content with

this, Bambridge locked the Prisoner out of his Room, and forced him to He in the open Yard, called The Bare. He fat quietly under his Wrongs, and, getting some poor Materials, built a little Hut, to p rot eft himself, as well as Jie could, from the Injuries of the Weather. The said Bambridge, feeingbt« Unconcernedness, said, " Damn him, " he is ealy !' I will put him into the Strong Room before " Tomorrow ;v and ordered Barnes to pull down his little Hut.: Which was done accordingly. The poor Prisoner, being in an ill State of Health, and the Night rainy, was put to great Distress. Some time after this he was, about Eleven a Clock at -Night, attaulted by bridge, with several other Persons, his Accomplices, in a violent Manner; and Bambridge, though die Prisoner was unarmed, attacked him with his Sword, but by good Fortune was prevented from killing him; and several other Prisoners coming out, upon the Noise, they earned Mackpheadris, forSafety, into another Gentleman's Room: Soon after which; Bambridge, coming with one Savage, and several others, broke open the Door; and Bambridge strove with his Sword.to kill the Prisoner; but he again got away, and hid himself in another Room. Next Morning the said Bambridge entered the Prison with a Detachment of Soldiers, and ordered the Prisoner to be dragged to the Lodge, and ironed with gre-.it Irons: On which he desiring to know, for what Cause, and by what Authority, he was to be so cruelly used, Bambridge replied. It-was by his own Authority; and, damn him, he would do it, and have his Life! The Prisoner desired, he might be carried before a Magistrate, that he might know his Crime, before he was punished; but Bambridge refuted; and put Irons upon his Legs, which were too little, fothat, in forcing them on, his Legs were like to have been broken, and the Torture was impossible to be 'endured; lUponwhich the Prisoner complaining of the gricvous'Pain, and Straitness of the Irons, Bambridge answered. These evil Practices of letting out Prisoners, extorting exorbitant Fees, suffering Escapes, and exercising all Sorts of Inhumanity, for Gain, may in a great measure be imputed to the Venality of the Warden's Office; for the Warden, who buys the Privilege of punishing others, does consequently fell his Forbearance at high Rates, and repair his own Charge, and Loss, at the wretched Expence of the Ease and Quiet of the miserable Objects in his Custody.
