That there is no Fee due to the Warden, upon his accepting Security, on the Prisoner's having the Benefit of Day Rules.

That there is no Fee due to the Warden for Lodging and Chamber Rent, where the Prisoner has not actual Possession of the Chamber; but there is due to the Warden for every Prisoner or Prisoners his or their Lodging or Chamber Rent is. 6 d.per Week, such' Lodging or Chamber being furnished - — 2

That there is clue to the Minister, that officiates, and performs divine Service, within the said Prison, for the Time being, from every Prisoner within the Walls of the said Prison, or without the Walls, or within the Rules, Four Pence per Week, to be paid to the Warden for the Use of such Minister:

And that no such Minister, or any other Clergyman, being a Prisoner within the Walls, or Rules, of the Fleet, do presume to marry any Person, without Licence, within the Prison, or Rules, of the Fleet; and that the Warden, and his Officers, do use their utmost Vigilance to prevent all such Marriages.

That there is no fresh Commitment Fee due to the Warden, upon the Prisoner's bringing himself back to the Fleet by Habeas , when the Warden himself had removed him thence by Habeas Corpus; and that there is no Fee, Gratuity, or Reward, due to the Warden, for his returning a Habeas but

there is a Fee of 5 r. A,d. due to the Clerk of the Papers, for the Allowance of every Writ of Habeas Corpus, and 4/. for the Return of the first Cause, and zs. for every other Cause, and no more - n

That, when a Prisoner dies in the Fleet, the Warden shall detain the Body no longer, than till the Coroner's Inquest be finished, which shall be done with all reasonable Speed; and immediately afterwards the Body shall be delivered to the Prisoner's Friends, or Relations, if they desire it, without Fee or Reward.

That it is the Duty of the Warden, and belongs to him, to keep the Prison House, and Windows, in necessary and good Repair, and to keep the Bog-house, and Dunghill, as clean, and free from Stench and Noilomnefe, as possible.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords desire a Conference with this House immediately, in the Painted Chamber, upon the Subject-matter of the last Conference.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Ordered, That the Committee who managed the last Conference, be the Committee to rnanage this Conference.

And being returned;

The Lord Malpas reported, that the Managers had met the Lords at the Conference, which was managed, on the Part of the Lords, by the Lord President; who acquainted them, that the Lords had desired this Conference, to communicate to this House an Address to his Majesty, which the Lords had agreed upon, grounded upon the Resolution of both Houses; to which Address the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House: And he* read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the said Report was read.

And the said Address is as follows , viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and in Parliamentafsembled, have, upon mature Deliberation, come to the following Resolution, which we humbly beg Leave to lay before your Majesty;

Resolved, By the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in Parliament assembled, That they do intirely rely upon his Majesty, that he will, for the maintaining the Honour, and securing the Trade of this Kingdom, take effectual Care, in the present Treaty, to preserve his undoubted Right to , and the

Island of Minorca.

And the said Address being read a Second time;

Resolved, That this House doth agree with the Lords in the said Address.

And then the Blank therein was accordingly filled up by the Clerk with the Word " Commons."

Resolved, That a Conference be desired with the Lords upon the Subject-matter of the last Conference.

The House (according to Order) proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee to whom the Petition of the incorporate Company of Clothiers in the City of Worcefte and also the Petition of the Weavers, Walkers, and Fullers, of the Clothing Trade, in the City of Worcester, and also the Petition of the Mayor, Justices, and Grand Jury, of the City and County of the City of Worceft, in General Quarter Sessions, held by Adjournment, were referred.

And the Report was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petitions; and, to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners called the following Witnesses; viz.

Mr. Joseph Turner, Clothier; who, being examined, laid, that since the Act passed, whereby the Italian Trade is restrained, they have felt a sensible Decay of their Trade, and it is now in a very low Condition: The Merchants who formerly bought the Worcester Cloths, now buy a fort of Cloths which are considerably worse, and can be afforded a great deal cheaper than theirs, and are exported by the Merchants under the Denomination of Worcester Cloths; which is very prejudicial to their Trade:

Turkey ' That the Price of Wool ih Worceferpiire is much lef-Trade. fened, since the Italian Trade has been restrained, the Turkey Merchants not buying the fine Cloths now, as they used to do when the Trade was open, but have since bought the low-price Cloths, made at other Places: The Cloth which was formerly sold at 1 per Yard, they now (ell for 11 s. and good Cloths have been

(bid to the Turkey Company for per Yard: There is also a Difference of 6 or 7 s. less in making a Piece of Cloth now, than there was 10 Years ago; and the Length of the Cloths, when made, is about Yards; and they are frequently sold to the Merchants wet, who have them stretched 10 Yards longer; which is the Merchant's Profit, but a great Prejudice to the Cloth; and, unless the Merchants have that Advantage, they will not buy the Cloth.

And he said, about Seven Years ago he paid or 5 jr. in the Pound to the Poor, but within these Three Years bast hath paid full 8 s.in the Pound; and, should t continue so much longer, Numbers of Families who save helped to fbpport the Poor, will be in want of it themselvesj but, if the Trade was free and open, it would make them flourish again.

Mr. John Poole said, that from 1715 to 1720 upwards

of 4,000 Cloths were made for Turkey yearly, at which time there were near 80 Clothiers, and about 40O Looms; and at present there are about 20 Clothiers* and 190 Looms; and that each Loom gives Employment to 40 or 50 People: That Two Men, and a Quil Boy, are a Month in weaving a Cloth, the Workmanship of which costs 25 r. the Cloth on the Loom is near 12 Quarters wide* which loses one half in the milling of it; and that there is Cloth now at Blackwell Hall, which has been there Seven Years; and believes, the Reason is, for want of an open Trade.

William Drew and John , Weavers, said, that

about Seven or Eight Years ago they used to get 7 or 8 a Week each with more Ease, than they can get 4 a lDay each now; and, when they came to the Trade, there was about 80 Clothiers, and above 300 Matter Weavers, in and about the City of; and that the Trade

has been decaying ever since the Peace of Utrecht.

Mr. Thomas Bingo said, he was an apprentice to a Fine-drawer in London, and has fecn Cloths come to the Packers, and ordinary Ones, which, when tilletted by them, have been sealed, and a WorcesterMark put upon them, with the Contents, and Colour, which have not been Cloths, and not so good as those Cloths; and this was practised for Four or Five Years, as he remembers; which is very prejudicial to the Trade: That he now

pays ior. in the Pound to the Poor; and, without speedily relieved, this will be their Ruin.

Mr. Turner said, they fell their Goods at Three Months Credit to the Merchants, who very often keep them out of it 18 Months; which is a great Hardship upon them.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to this Resolution; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations contained in their Petitions.

Groundage, for Ships, Boats, and Vessels, within the said Limits of Sheerness and H

And Robert Dawfott, Serjeant at Mace to the said Mayor and Citizens upon the said River, within the Limits and Bounds aforesaid, commonly called the principal Water Bailiff, declared, he had received tire said Duties for the Mayor and Citizens for about Eight Years past.

And it was also proved to the Committee, that, when the native Crops of Oysters are not thought sufficient for the Maintenance of the said Dredgers, and their Families, other Oysters, and Brood, are bought, and laid in the said Fishery, with Money, borrowed by Part of the said Oyster Dredgers, intended to be raised again by mutual Collections out of such Oysters, when dredged again; and that some of the said Dredgers refuse to pay any Contribution thereto, yet take their Shares thereof} and that one Year with another the Sum of £. 800. is laid out, when there is Occasion, to store the said Fishery with such Oysters, and Brood.

That it further appeared to the Committee, upon the Examination of the said Witnesses, that the Number of the said Dredgers are of late increased from about One hundred to Three hundred Persons: That very great and wilful Waste and Spoil has been, and is, made by many disorderly Persons amongst the said Dredgers, in taking Oysters at improper Sealons, together with the Fry and Brood Oysters, which tends to the utter Loss and Destruction of the said Fishery; and that some Doubts having arose, touching the Powers of the said Mayor and Citizens, and the said Jury, at the said Courts, they have been discouraged to proceed against such Offenders.

That it likewise appeared to the said Committee, that the Lord Mayor of London, and his Officers, from Yenleet Creek, as far up the Medway, within the said Limits, as a Bound Stone standeth near Cockhamwood, on the North Side of the said River, have exercised a Jurisdiction of Conservancy for floating Fish, and have taken away unlawful Nets, found there; and that the free Fishermen of the River Thames do take floating Fish in common with the free Fishermen of Medzvay, as far as the said Bound Stone; but it appeared, as well by the said Witnesses, as by several other Witnesses, being very ancient free Fishermen of the River Thwho frequently take floating Fish in the Medway, that the Fishermen of the River Thames never, in their Time, or any others before them, as they ever heard of, dredged for Oysters in the said River Medway, or claimed any Right so to do; but said, the dredging Oysters, in the said Fishery was peculiar to the free Dredgers thereof; and, if the Fishermen of the Thames have taken any Oysters there, it has been secretly, and when discovered, they have been obstructed, or punished for so doing.

And it further appeared by the said Witnesses, that Oyster Dredging is a separateTrade from other Fishing.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, that Leave be given to bring in a Bill for regulating, well ordering, governing, and improving, the Oyster Fishery in the River and Waters thereof, under the Authority of the Mayor and Citizens of the City of Rochester, in the County of Kent.

And the House being moved accordingly}

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for the more effectual preventing, and further Punishment, of Forgery, Perjury, and Subornation of Perjury, and to make; it Felony to steal Bonds, Notes, or other Securities, for Payment of Money; to which the Lords defije the Concurrence of this House:

And also, the Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting in Thomas Lamplugh, Clerk, and his Heirs, the Rectory of Felkirk, in the County of being Leasehold for Three Lives, comprised in his Marriage Settlement, and for settling other Fee-Ample Lands and Tenements in Potto, in the same County, of better Value, in lieu thereof; to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew*

The Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon' Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Resolved \That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for the better suppressing of Piracy, and for giving all Prizes, taken from the Enemy, to the Captors.

The Order being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty;

Ordered, That the Account of the Money, paid into the Exchequer for the Duty on Victuallers, from the Commencement thereof, distinguishing each Year, and also an Account of What‘ Exchequer Bills have been made out upon the Credit of the Act for laying the said Duty, how much paid off, and what Sum now remains 16

ported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the more effectual preventing Bribery and Corruption in the Elections of Members to serve in Parliament, was committed, the Amendments, the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk's Table; where the said Amendments were once read throughout, and then a Second time, one by one, and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House;

Mr. Oglethorpe, by Direction of the Committee appointed to enquire into the State of the Gaols of this Kingdom, acquainted the House, that Richard , a Tipstaff to Thomas Bam bridge, Warden of the Fleet Prison, had spoken Words refleding upon the Proceedings of the said Committee, and the Authority thereof.

Resolved, That Richard Corbet, a Tipstaff to Thomas Bambridge, Warden of the Fleet Prison, having spoken Words refleding upon the Proceedings and the Authority of a Committee of this House, appointed to enquire into the State of the Gaols of this Kingdom, is guilty of a high Contempt of the Authority of this House, and a Breach of the Privilege thereof.

Ordered, That the said Richard Corbet be, for his said Offence, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

Ordered, That the Bill be re-committed.

Ordered, That the Bill be re-committed to the same Committee:

And they are to meet this Afternoon, at Five of the Clock, in the Speaker's Chamber.

The other Orders of the Day being read

kefohed, That this House will, upon Monday, the Fourteenth Day of April next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for indemnifying Persons who have omitted to qualify themselves for Offices or Employments within the Time limited by Law. and for allowing further Time for that Purposej and for repealing so much of an Act of Parliament, passed in the First Year of his late Majesty King George the First, as requires Persons to qualify themselves for Offices or Employments within Three Months, and for limiting other Times for such Qualifications.

Mr. Speakei left the Chair.

Mr. Winnington took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Wednesday Morning next.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A PETITION of the Mayor, capital Burgesses, and Assistants, together with the Merchants, Serge-makers, Fullers, and other the principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Tiverton, in Devon, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousand poor Labourers in the Woollen Manufacture in the said Borough, and in the Parts adjacent, was presented to the House, and read complaining of the great Decay of the'AVoollen Manufacture, and the Increase of their Poor; which the Petitioners attribute to the running of Wool from Ireland into foreign Parts; whereby Foreigners, mixing the same with their own Wool, otherwise useless, are enabled to rival the W oollen Manufactures of this Kingdom, to the great endangering the Lois thereof: And therefore praying such Redrels, as to the Uoufethall seem fit.

3" Eliz. It appeared by the Charter, that the Bailiffs,

and their Successors, for the Time being, together with others, to be nominated, appointed, and authorized, within the Borough of Tamworth, and the Precind and Liberty of the fame, for the future may and shall be Justices of the Peace of the said Borough for and concerning all Matters, which to Justices of the Peace do belong to be enquired into, heard, and u. termined, within the aforesaid Precind of the said Borough, and all and singular the Matters, arising within the Liberties thereof, in as ample Manner and Form, as other Justices of the Peace in any County of England may do, or have accustomed or ought to do.

Nicholas Parker, Town-clerk, gave Evidence for 40 Years, that the Bailiffs are always looked upon as the head Officers in Tamworth, and have always acted as such; and that they have always signed the Rates:

That the Justices have signed the Rates since the Year 1722; and that tome Inhabitants have paid to the Bailiffs Rates, and some to the Justices:

That some have refused to pay to either; but he knows of none, that are capable of paying, but what are rated upon the Bailiffs Levy.

The Counsel for the Petitioner insisted, that the Lift of Thirty-ieven Voters, refused by the Bailiffs, are rated in the Justices Rates, and are good Votes.

Which being objected to by the fitting Member's Counsel, the Ad 43 Eliz. c. 2. Sedtions x. 8. and 10. were read; whereby it is enacted, in

Section 1. That the Churchwardens of every Parish, and Four, Three, or Two, substantial Householders there, as shall be thought meet, having respect to the Proportion and Greatness of the same Parish and Parishes, to be nominated yearly in Easter Week, or within the Month after Easter, under the Hand and Seal of Two or more Justices of the Peace in the same County, whereof one to be of the Quorum, dwelling in or near the same Parish, or Division, where the same Parish doth lie, shall be called Overseers of the Poorot the same Parish:

Section 8. That the Mayors. Bailiffs, fcfc. of every Town corporate within this Realm, being Justices of the Peace, shall have Authority within their Jurisdiction:., as well out of Sessions, as at their Sessions, it they hold any, as is therein appointed to Justices of the County, or in their Quarter Sessions, to do and execute all the Purposes in the said Act:

Section 10. If there happen to be no Nomination of Overseers yearly, as is before appointed, that then every Justice of Peace of the County, dwelling within the Division, where such Default of Nomination shall happen, and every Mayor, Alderman, and head Officer, of the City, Town, or Place corporate, shall forfeit for such Default Five Pounds to the Poor.

To the honourable the Commons, in Parliament assembled:

A Memorial in relation to the Order of the House, for laying before them an Account of the net Produce of the Civil List Revenue from 1724,

to Lady-day, 1727, as also in relation to the Order,

for laying before the House an Account of what Orders, or Directions, have been sent to the said Commissioners, for altering the Charges of Management of the said Revenues.

We have received his Majesty's Commands to lay before this honourable House, an Account of the grots Produce of that Part of the Civil List Revenue under our Management, with all Deductions, for Charges of Management, or any other Account whatsoever, before the same was ]vaid into the Exchequer, with an Account of the net Produce from Michaelm1724, to Lady-day, 1727, distinguishing each Year, and from 1727, to Midsummer, 1728, with Copies of all Orders, or Directions, sent to us, for altering the Charges of Management, during the said Times.

We humbly represent to this honourable House, that we have given Directions to our Clerks, to make up the said Accounts with all the Expedition that is possible; but the Period, for making up Accounts in this Office, being fixed, from the Commencement of the Duty, at Midsummer, it will be impracticable to make up the Accounts from Michaelmas, 1724, to 1727, with-

out Splitting above Six thousand Vouchers, which is a Work, that will require Three Months at least to complete: And we herewith humbly lay before this honourable House the Account ordered, from Midsummer, 17 27, to Midsummer, 1728; and we humbly certify, that we have not received any Orders or Directions whatever, for altering the Charges of Management, during the said Times; but that the said Charges have and are continued to be made in the Manner always practised in this Office.

A Petition of Jeremiah Dummer and Jonathan Belcher, Esqtiires, Agents for the Colony of Connecticut, was pre-finted to the House, and read; setting forth, that in the Bill now depending in the House, for Preservation of his Majesty's Woods in America, and for Encouragement of the Importation of naval Stores fro*n thence, ami toen.. couraoe the Importation of Masts, Yards, and Bowsprits

House of Commons, which requires an Account of how much of the Sum of ,£.79,022. 4 9 allowed for

Drawbacks on Goods exported, on the new Subsidy, between Midsummer 1727, and Midsummer 1728, was for Goods entered before Midsummer 1727* direct us,

without Lois of Time, to prepare the said Account; in Answer thereto we humblyTeport,

That

2 Geo. II. 230 Jpr 345

Drawbacks That by the bed Judgment we are capable of making, the Drawbacks for Goods, entered before u 1727, may amount to about half the said Sum; but the exact Sum cannot be ascertained, for the following Reasons:

ift, The Debentures containing great Quantities, and great Variety, of Goods, which paid, and secured, the Duties, at Several Dates before, and since, the 24th of 1727, which Dates are all expressed in the Debentures, but referring to the whole Quantities in general, and not to the particular Quantities, which paid the Duties at each respective Date, it was therefore not practicable for the Officers, from the said Debentures, or from the First Certificates, from whence they were made out, to compute, how much the new Subsidy amounted to for the Goods, entered before the said 24th of , distinct and Separate from what was entered afterwards.

The Merchants Importers, who, after mixing and Sorting Goods of Several Dates; and then felling particular Parcels thereof to those who export them, not l>eing able to distinguish in their Affidavits the particular Times, When each Parcel paid Duties Inwards, yet being certain, in general, of the Goods having paid the Duties, they therefore, in the said Affidavits, recite, and refer to, all the Several Dates of their Entries, relating to the Goods in the Debenture, that they may be justly entitled to the Drawback; wherefore, the Merchants themselves not being able to make the Di(lindion, now required, though they make due Proof of their having paid the Duties, it is impracticable for Such Conriputation, and Distinction, thereof now to be made.

adly, On former Deinifes of the Crown, and Expirations, and Ke-commencements, of the Customs, and other Duties, the Debentures have been constantly made out, and paid, in this Method, by Orders of your honourable Board, grounded on Directions from the Treasury, and agreeable to the Opinions of Several Attorneys-gener.il; and as the Time, for Merchants to draw back their Duties, is now enlarged to Three Years, it makes it more impracticable to change it; because, as the Moneys paid by them, are by Law weekly Sent to the Exchequer by the Receiver-general, and made use of there for the publick Service, long before they come to claim their Drawbacks, to which they have always a Title till the Expiration of the said Term, they therefore can be no otherways paid, than out of the growing Receipt j and, should any Delay thereof, or Obstruction, be made, it would put an intire Stop to Trade, the Merchants having by Law a Right to their Drawbacks, an<£ whenever demanded by them, the same is always payable out of the gross Produce of the said Duty, before any Appropriation of the net Produce can take place.

Your Honours having likewise directed us to prepare An Account of how much of the Sum of £. 102,012.

" 4-f. 9 id.(landing out in Arrears on the new Subsidy at " Lady-day 1727, has been paid for Drawbacks on Goods " imported before Lady day 1727, distinguishing what " was paid before Midsummer 1727, and what since, and " how the remainder had been accounted for," wehumbly acquaint you, that there are the same Difficulties in computing, and distinguishing, the several Drawbacks, in order to explain, how much related to Goods imported before Lady-day 1727, as are set forth in our Answer to the Order above-mentioned; which renders an Answer to so much of this Order, as relates to the said Drawbacks, likewise impracticable. As to the Close of the said Order, which requires an Account, how the Remainder has been accounted for; it being impracticable to make out the Amount of the Debentures, it is therefore not possible to know, how much the Remainder amounts toj but, whatever it amounts to, except so much thereof, as has been paid into his Majesty's Exchequer since Lady-day 1727, it consists either in Bonds of Merchants, not yet due and recovered, of small Sums, resting in Out-port Collectors Hands, not yet remitted by them, or of Bills of Exchange, not yet become payable; all which, as it Voi. 21.

comes to the Receiver-general's Hands, is weekly paid into the Exchequer, the Receiver-genera l and Collector inwards having no Money remaining in their Hands on the said Branch, which flood out at Lady-day 1727.

All which is humbly submitted.

A Petition of the Matter, Wardens, and Assistants, of WocUta the Incorporation of Weavers, Fullers, &c.together with Minufednre, the principal Merchants, and Traders in the Woollen Manufacturee, of the City and County of Exon, was pre-lented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the chief Support of their Western Pans is the Woollen Manufacture, which hath principally been carried on with Irish Wool; but, notwithstanding the wliolefome Laws, already made, to prevent the running of Wool, both wrought and unwrought, from Inland to foreign Parts, yet that pernicious Practice is carried on to such a Degree, that for these late Years there has been but very finall Quantities of Wool imported from Ireland to which Deprivation hath so funk their once flourn'hing Trade, that, unless some speedy Care be taken to prevent this growing Evil, the English Manufacturee is in danger of being Joft, or at lead reduced to a low Ebb: And praying, that some effectual Me&furcs may be speedily taken, to prevent the running of Wool, and Woollen Goods, from Ireland to foreign Parts.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Clothiers, Drugget-makers, arid

Hollers, of the Town of Ringwood, in the County of

Southampton, on the behalf ot themselves, and several Hundreds more, concerned in the Woollen Manufactory in and about the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Exportation of Irish,

Wool into foreign Parts is of the moll destructive Consequence to the Trade of this Kingdom, thereby enabling foreign Nations to be our Rivals, which, without British or Irish Wool, the Petitioners conceive, is impossible to be done; and thereby our own Pcor want Employment, and are a Charge to their respective Parishes: And praying, that effectual Measures may be taken for putting a Stop to the pernicious Practice ot running Wool from Ireland to foreign Parts.

Ordered, That the said Petition do Jie upon the Table.

neither are they allowed to load at Newcastle without one: That he never knew of any other, betides Harmin and Turpin, denied Coals, for want of a Certificate: That all Ships, he is concerned with, keep their Turn: That he has asked several Ships, if they would go to work; but was answered, they were not in Turn: That Ships out of Turn will work, if they would give 6 d. per Chaldron extraordinary: That he

has heard, that there are great Complaints, about the City, of the Badness of Coals, and more now, than formerly.

Mr. Willyford being asked, whether he knew of any Agreement, entered into by the Coal-owners; he an-lwered. No:

That they generally buy Coals unseen, and if they do not prove so good, as expected, they generally abate something; and, if the Coals have proved good, has paid 3 d. perChaldron extraordinary: That, if a Ship in

Turn fells at 27;. the other Ships do the fame: That his Servants, and the Meter, are the Judges of the Goodness of Coals: That he always alks a Matter, what he will have, but never mentions any Price, that he will give; but it is customary to ask, if Coals are dry, and found; and, if they do not answer, then they generally abate 3 d.per Chaldron: That it is usual to pay One-third in Money, some Part into the Custom-house, and the rest give a Note for, payable in Forty Days: That about April, 1725, he was lent down the River by his Father, to fee, if any Ships were at work after Twelve of the Clock: That there were Ships then at work: That they had Orders given them to leave off; and believes, they might do so: That the Lightermen generally meet every first Wednesday in the Month, about One o'Clock,

and every Morning, upon the Keys.

Mr. William Ward said, that he has kept an Office

about Five Years, as an Undertaker, for hiring Labourers to unload Ships: That they had a Book some Part of last Year; but the present Book begins about the Seventh of Mareh.h. % wherein he enters all Ships, belonging to the Coal Trade, that come up the River: That about Twelve Months ago, when Coals were from 20 to 21 6 he

heard several Matters say, that they were under very great Hardttiips, and much reduced; so were obliged to think of Rules, for some Regulation: That 6 or 7 Matters of Ships met, and complained to one an'other of their Hard-ships; and then agreed amongst themselves, that Ships should keep Turn: That they came tohim, and desired him to keep a Register Book for them; which at first he refused, but, at the Request of one Mr. Thomas , was

prevailed upon to keep it; and that he keeps it now: That at the first Beginning Ships took their Turn, as they patted by Greenhith, and do lo now: That about the Be-

ginning of March last, 3 3 Sail of Ships came up the River, and, he being out of the Way Three Hours, half of them fold out at 28 s. per Chaldron: That he endeavoured all

he could to keep down the Price of Coals, the Wind being the contrary Way: That, when Ships are unloaded, the Matters come, and pay one Peny per Chaldron which was for the Trouble, the several Agents would have, in attending the Matters, and being Witnesses to their several Bargains and Agreements with the Lightermen for their Coals, who for want of such Witnesses, have suffered many Hardships, it being customary for the Lightermen, to buy Coals at one Price, «nd pay another; and then he has a Certificate granted, wherein is certified, that he has unloaded and conformed here: That the Use of the Certificate is to convince the Owners of Ships, that the Matters had kept their Turn, and to satisfy the Fitter and Coal-owners, what Quantity of Coals they delivered: That the Coal-buyers and Lightermen are opulent, and a few in Number; who meet, and let what Piice they please on Coals: That they have their monthly, weekly, and daily Meetings, and have come to several Resolutions: That the Lightermen generally buy Coals upon Honour, and then pay the Matters what they please for them: That they pay Part in Money, for the Expence of the Ship, Part in a Note, upon Demand, for the Duty, and the rest in a Note, payable in Forty

*5

Days, for the Stock; never give Notes for Value received, and sometimes not to Order: That the Matters scruple to make any Agreement, without proper Witnesses: There are Six Persons, who belong to the Office, viz. Mallory Peirfon, Esquire, Mr. John Gibson, Mr.' Benjamin Horn, Mr. Joseph Merry man, Mr. James -ston, and Mr. William Ward, who are to fee, that Turns are kept, and to be Witnesses to all Agreements: That the Lightermen had rather never buy Coals, than hav&" Witnesses to any Agreement; That in December last there was a very great number of Ships in the River, and in November Coals were offered at 25 per Chaldron: That it was agreed upon, that he and Mr. John Hurston should go into the North, to consult with the Owners of Ships, not to fend their Ships up: That they called at all the Sea-ports, as they went: Some sent their Ships, and others would not: That several Matters of Ships desired them to endeavour with the Coal-owners at,

not to load any Ships before the 15th of; but

they would not agree thereunto; and the Fitters would not agree to help them in anywise: That he believes, 400,000 Chaldron of Coals per Annum are brought to London: Believes, many Ships never take any Certificates; and has heard, a Ship has been refused Coals, for want thereof; but has known several Ships been loaded without Certificates; That the Matters of Ships have had strict Orders from the Owners, to keep their Turn: That he has granted Certificates to some, who have worked out of Turn: That the first granting of Certificates was about last Michaelmas: That the Ship-owners along the Coast were requested, nr t to let their Ships go to Sea till the 15th of March: That he applied to the Coal-fitters, and to Coal-owners, in the Capacity of Ship-owners, and they agreed, that, if possible, they would influence the Matters, not to go to Sea till the Third of March: That he was instructed to apply to the Coal-owners, not to load any Ships, without they had Certificates from his Office, that they had kept their Turn, according to the Direction of the Ship-owners; but was answered, that they could not come into it, because the principal Coal-owners were at , and he mutt: apply to them: That it is a Method of the Owners of Ships at Yarmouth to keep a Book; and the Matter, when he has fold his Coals, at his Return gives an Account to the Book-keeper, who enters it: That he came to London the Nineteenth Day of , and applied

to several Gentlemen, who vend about Two thirds of the Coals, that are brought to London; who told him, they could not agree to it, for they had writ to their Agents, to load all, that demanded: That there is no Penalty, if any Person fells his Coals without the Consent of others: That there was no Agreement, to enhance the Price of Coals: That he applied to the Coal-owners, not to load without a Certificate; which they would not agree to: Believes, the Matters generally keep the Certificate.

Mr. Ward produced a Book, and a File of Letters; which were read. Mr. Wm. Dickenson laid, that in his iaft Voyage, which was in April, he fold One hundred Chaldron to James Roberts, junior, and Eighty Chaldron to John;

and Robertsafked him, who he had fold the rest to: He answered, to one Tickner: And he said he was no Lighterman; so, if he had them, he would have none; So he got Tickner to relinquish, and he fold them to others: And, if Housekeepers buy, they are obliged to employ Lightermen.

Mr. James Roberts owned, he told Mr. Dickenson, as aforesaid; and generally bought Mr. Dickenson's. Coals, when he came to London.

John Tickner, Dealer in Coals, and Dickenson, made a Bargain for 80 Chaldron, at 27 6 and Roberts said,

if he had any, he would have none of them: That he generally employs Lightermen; yet they will not buy of any Master, that deals with him: That Mr. Parry and Mr. Beaty suffered by being denied to work with them: That Lightermen receive a Premium of Six Pence per Chaldron, which he can't have, as being no Lighterman: That the Lightermen can fell cheaper, than he, by reason of the Premium: That the best Coals pay Premium, as well as the worst.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that several Agreements and Combinations have been entered into by the Matters and Owners of Ships, using the Coal Trade from Newcastle upon Tine, and Places thereto adjacent, unto the Port of London, and other Parts of this Kingdom, and also by the Lightermen of the said Port, which said Agreements and Combinations are illegal, and tend to the enhancing the Price of Coals, to the Oppression of the Poor, the Prejudice of several Manufactures, and to the lessening the publick Revenue.

That Sir Philip Meadoivs, then Knight Marshal of the King's Houllioid, did, by Deed Poll, given under his Hand and Seal the 25th of November, 1720, constitute John Darby, Gentleman, Deputy Marshal of the Mar-

shalfea

a Geo. II. 146 Maii. 377

fhaljea of the King's Houftiold, and Keeper of the Pri-fbns aforesaid, during the Term of his natural Life.

And tire fard Knight Marshal, by Articles of Agreement indented, bearing even Date with the said last mentioned Deed Poll, declares the Conditions, under which the said John Darby is to enjoy the said Offices; and, among others, that, if the said John , without the Knight Marshal's Consent in Writing, shall at any Time let to farm the said Offices, or any of the Fees, Profits, Advantages, or Benefits, thereof, the said Grant shall cease, determine, and be void.

That John Darby, contrary to the said Conditions, hath let the Profits of the said Offices, without Consent of the said Knight Marshal; and by Indenture of Lease, bearing Date the aid Day of March, 1727, did grant, and to farm let, to William Ail on. Butcher, the Mar* Jhalfea Prison for £. 140. per; and by the fame

Lease did let the Benefit of the Lodging of the Prisoners, and other Advantages, for the further yearly Rent of £. 260. to be paid to him, clear of all Taxes, for the Term of Seven Years.

That to make the Profits of the Prison arise, to answer the said exorbitant Rents, no Kind of Artifice, or Oppression, hath been unpraftifed.

It appears, upon the Examination of many Witnesses, that, on the entry of Prisoners into the said Prison, Money has been extorted from them, for obtaining the Liberty of going to the Mailer's Side, though the said

Darby acknowledged, he had noRight toanyFees, till the Prisoner was discharged: And, in order to create a greater Profit, by vending Liquors, and Food, the Servants of the Keeper have obstradled the bringing in ne-Ceflary Liquors, and Provisions, contrary to the express Words of the Act of Parliament, of the Twenty-second and Twenty-third Year of King 2d; and have

often, under the Pretence of searching for Liquors, treated very ruddy and indecently, Women who came to relieve and support their Husbands, labouring under the Hardships and Necessities of the Gaol: And they raile the Price ot Liquors and other Necessaries, inso much that the necessitous Prisoner is obliged to pay Three Pence per Quart for worse Beer, than he can buyout of the Prison for Two Pence Half-peny: And they have also encouraged a Praft ice among the Prisoners, of forcing those, newly committed, to pay Garnish, and of levying Fines upon each other, under frivolous Pretences; the Money arising from which is to be spent at the Tap-house; so that he, who is moll aftiye in exact ing it, is favoured, as the greatest Friend to the House. This Method of levying Garnish Money, and Fines, is so publickly allowed, that there are Tables hung up in each Room, of the Rated Garnish Fees, some of which amount to 7 some to more; and, if the unhappy Wretch, which is the general Cafe, hath not Money to pay them, tire Prisoners strip him in a riotous Manner, which, in their Cant Phrase, they call letting the black Dog walk.

This (hews the Inconveniency of the Keeper's having the Advantage of the Tap-house; since, to advance the Rent thereof, and to consume the Liquors there vended, they not only encourage Riot and Drunkenness, but also prevent the needy Prisoner from being supplied by his Friends with the mere Necessaries of Life, in order to increase an exorbitant Gain to their Tenants.

And these Extortions, though small in the Particulars, are very heavy upon the unhappy Prisoners, many of whom are so poor, as to be committed for a Debt of One Shilling only; for, by the Usage of the said Court of Record, Processes are issued for the smallest Sums; and, though the Cause of Action is but One Peny, a Process is issued, t he Process is returned, and the Proceedings are carried on, till such Time as the Colls amount to above 40 s. and thereupon the Debtor is thrown into Prison; and, by adding the Colls to the Debt, the late Act of Parliament, against frivolous and vexatious Arrests, is eluded: Nor is it probable, that he can be from thence released; for, if he was incapable before to pay the Cause of Action, he must be much more so, when the Colls are

Vol. 21.

added thereto; and, if his Creditor then relents, he is detained for the Gaoler's Fees, and Colls of Suit, infinitely greater than the original Debt.

It appeared to the Committee, that there was no Lift of Fees publickly hung up in any Part of the Prison, though required by Law: As to which the said John Darby being examined, he acknowledged, that no such-Lift of late had been hung up; but he delivered to the Committee a Paper, which, he informed them, was a Schedule of Fees, established by the Judges the Court of the King's Palace of Westminster the 17th of December, 1675, hereunto annexed in the First Appendix, marked with the Letter A; which Fees seem very exorbitant, in regard there are different Fees paid by the same Prisoner to the same Officer, and the whole amounts to more than is proportionable to the Smallness of the Sums, for which Processes are issued out of that Court.

Upon Inspection of the several Parts of the said Gaol, the Committee find, that the said Gaol is divided into Two Divisions, viz. the Mailers Side, and the common Side; and that a Part thereof is only fenced in with a few weak old Boards: That there are several Rooms on the Matter's Side kept empty, some with but One or Two Persons in them, and others at the same time crouded to that Degree, as even to make them unhealthy; particularly, in one of the Rooms in a Part of the Prison called the Oake, Nine Men are laid in Three Beds, and each Man pays 2 s.6 d.per Week; so that Rootnfingly produces jC.x. 2 s.6d. per Week: But a more particular

Account of the number of Prisoners in each Room, and of the Sums they are to pay for Chamber Rent, will appear by the annexed Appendix B.

It appeared to the Committee, that the Gaoler of the said Prison, out of a View of Gain, hath frequently refused to remove lick Persons, upon Complaint of those who lay in the same Bed with them; a particular In-Itance of Which follows:

Mrs. Mary Trapps was Prisoner in the and

was put to lie in the same Bed with Two otherWomen, each of which paid is. 6d. per Week Chamber Rent: She fell ill, and languished for a considerable Time; and the last Three Weeks grew so offensive, that the others were hardly able to bear the Room: They frequently complained to the Turnkeys, and Officers, and desired to be removed; but all in vain: At last (lie smelt so strong, that the Turnkey himself could not bear to come into the Room to hear the Complaints of her Bedfellows; and they were forced to lie with her, or on the Boards, till (he died.

And the Committee, inspecting the various Parts of the Gaol, saw a Prisoner, who kept his Bed with a Fillula, and Two other Persons obliged to lie with him in the same Bed, though each paid 2 s. 6 per Week; yet they even submifted to such Rent, and Usage, rather than be turned down to the common Side.

The common Side is inclosed with a strong Brick Wall'; in it are now confined upwards of 330 Prisoners, most of them in the utmost Necessity: They are divided into particular Rooms, called Wards; and the Prisoners belonging to each Ward, are locked up in their respectiveWards every Night; most of which are excessively crouded. Thirty, Forty, nay Fifty Persons having been locked up in some of them, not Sixteen Foot square; and at the same time that these Rooms have been so crouded, to the great endangering the Healths oft he Prisoners, the largest Room in the common Side hath been kept empty, and the Room over George's Ward was let out to a lay lor, to work in, and nobody allowed to lie in it, though all the last Year there were sometimes Forty, and never less than Thirty-two, Persons locked up in George's Ward every Night, which is a Room of Sixteen by Fourteen Feet, and about Eight Feet high: The Surface of the Room is not sufficient to contain that Number, when laid down; so that one half are hung up ihHammocks, whilst the other lie on the Floor under them: The Air is so wasted by the Number of Persons, who breathe in that narrow Compass, that it is not sufficient to keep them

The crouding of Prisoners together in this Manner is one great Occassion of the Gaol Distemper; and, though the unhappy Men should escape Infection, or overcome it, yet, if they have not Relief from their Friends, Famine destroys them: All the Supporti'uch poor Wretches have to subsist on, is an accidental Allowance of Pease, given once a Week by a Gentleman, who conceals his Name, and about Thirty Pounds of Beef, provided by the voluntary Contribution of the Judge and Officers of the Marshalsea, on Monday, and; which

is divided into very small Portions, of about an Ounce and an half, distributed with One Fourth-part of an Half-peny Loaf: Each of the Sick is full served with One of those Portions, and those that remain are divided amongst the Wards; but the Numbers of the People in them are so great, that it comes to the Turn of each

All the Charities belonging to the Prison were formerly received by a Steward, chose by the Prisoners on the common Side; and the said Prisoners had a common Seal belonging to them, kept by their said Steward; and they were divided info Six Wards, each of which chose monthly a Constable; and the said Constable signing a Receipt, and sealing it with the said common Seal, was a full Discharge to the Persons paying the Charities.

In 1722 Matthew Pugh was chosen Steward by the Prisoners, and, at their Request, approved by Sir John Bennet, then Judge of the Marshalsea Court. Pugh discovered several Charities, which had been before concealed, and applied them to the Use of the Prisoners; and in 1725 he acquainted the then Constables, that John Darby, and his Servants in the Lodge, had got Possession of the old common Seal, and that Edward Gilbourne, Deputy Prothonotary of the said Court, had the Possession of another Seal, with the same Impression, which he had Reason to believe was made use of t? affix to Receipts for Charity Money, to the great Fraud and Oppression of the poor Prisoners: Upon which the said Constables agreed to be at the Expence of rftaking a new Seal, with this Addition, " Marfiialft a Prison, 1725 and they also bought

a Chest, with Seven different Locks and Keys, so that the Chest could not be opened without all the said Seven Keys, one of which was lodged in the Hinds of each Constable,

The Committee saw in the Womens Sick Ward many miserable Objects lying, without Beds, on the Floor, perishing with extreme Want; and in the Mens Sick Ward yet much worse: For along the Side of the Walls of that Ward, Boards were laid upon Treftles, like a Dresser in a Kitchen; and under them, between those Treftles, were laid on the Floor, one Tire of sick Men, and upon the Dresser another Tire, and over them hung a Third Tire in Hammocks.

The Custom of this Court formerly was to foil all the Places belonging thereto, and the very Counfol, and Attorneys, purchased the Liberty of pleading, and pradfifing, in this Court; for which the first gave as far as £. 1,000. the latter as far as £. 1,500. each; One Moiety of which Sums was for the Benefit of the Lord Steward, and the other Moiety for the Knight Marshal.

As the present Enquiry is not into the Nature hnd Practice of this Court, the Abuses of which well deforve a particular Enquiry, the Committee do not enlarge upon the ill consequences of such Corrupt Sales; but cannot forbear to observe, that the first who stemmed this Tide of Corruption, was his Grace the Duke of Argyle, then Lord Steward, who, disdaining to share the Spoils of the Unfortunate, scorned to take any Money arising from the Sale of Offices, and made an excellent Precedent, very much disliked by the practising Part of the Court, that of appointing Officers for their Merit, not for their Money. Upon the Death of Sir John Bennett, his Grace, without Fee or Reward, appointed Sir John nall Judge of the Court, and followed the same Method in disposing of the other Offices of the Court.

The Duke of Dorset, now Lord Steward, was very much importuned by the Officers of the Court to permit the Practice of felling, as formerly; but, being resolved not to give way to it, yet willing to be eased of their Importunity, he let them know, that he would fell the Place of one of the Counsel, then vacant: The Sum, he fold it for, was One hundred Pounds only, to George,

Esquire, which his Grace ordered to be applied *to dif-Voi. 21.

mit to give to such Persons, for their Pains, all the Moneys collected by them, provided they bring in Two Baskets only of broken Victuals per Week, or, in lieu thereof, pay Two Shillings; and even this disadvantageous Agreement is not complied with; for the Prisoners are Months together without hearing any thing at all of their Basket Men.

So that the good and charitable Intentions of Mankind are wickedly perverted, and rendered ufoless, and of no avail, to the poor Prisoners, who can neither come out to be relieved, nor can those, who come to relieve, have easy access to such poor Wretches, nor distinguish the Impostors from the Unfortunate.

The only effectual. Way to distribute such Charity rightly seems to be, to foe some Prisoner of each Ward, who is not in the Keeper's Interest, and from such Prisoner to know the most necessitous.

The above-mentioned Practice of farming and defrauding the Begging Box is not peculiar to this Prison of the Marshalsea only :. The poor Prisoners in the Fleet

Prison are abused in the same manner.

In this Prison of the Marshalsea, Pirates are kept, as well as Debtors; and the first, who are generally a very desperate and abandoned Sort of People, are fullered to mix with all the unhappy Debtors of the common Side; which may be of dangerous Consequence: For this being a Prison for the poorer Sort, in which great Numbers of poor Sailors are commonly confined, the Conversation of these Pirates, and their Boasts, how riotously they Jived, whilst at Sea, may instil Inclinations of following the same wicked Practices. desperate People hath already had some Influence upon the poor Debtors, and was, in part, the Occasion of fevered of them attempting to escape j to which Hunger and extreme Want being added, some of them became so desperate, that, after having fasted Four Days, and seeing no Hope of Relief, they attempted to break through the Prison Wall, and were taken in the Attempt.

This gave the Gaolers a pretence to exercise their greater Cruelties. All the Persons, so attempting to escape, were called into the Lodge by the said Acton, one by one, and there examined. One of them was seen to go in perfectly well, and, when he came out again, he was in the greatest Disorder: His Thumbs were much swollen, and very fore; and he declared, that the Occasion of his being in that Condition was, that the Keeper, in order to extort from him a Confession of the Names of those, who had assisted him, and others, in their Attempt to escape, had ferewed certain Instruments of Iron upon his Thumbs, so close, that they had forced the Blood out of them, with exquisite Pain: After this he was carried into the strong Room; where, besides the other Irons, which he had on, they fixed on his Neck and Hands an Iron Instrument, called a Collar, like a Pair of Tongs; and, he being a large luity Man, when they ferewed the said Instrument close, his Eyes were ready to start out of his Head, the Blood guihed out of his Ears and Nofc, he foamed at the Mouth, the Slaber ran down, and he made several Motions to speak, but could not: After these Tortures, he was confined in the strong Room for many Days, with a very heavy Pair of Irons, called Sheers, on his Legs.

It has been usual in this Prison for the Keepers unlawfully to assume to themselves a pretended Authority of Magnates, and not only to judge and decree Punishments arbitrarily, but also to execute the same unmercifully. Numberless are the instances of their immoderate beating poor Debtors, at their Pleasure; inso much, that the very Name of the-Instrument hungup in the Lodge, for beating the Prisoners, became a Terror to them.

The various Tortures and Cruelties, before-mentioned, not contenting these wicked Keepers in their said pretended Magistracy over the Prisoners, they found a Way of making within this Prison a Confinement more dread-ful than the strong Room itself, by coupling the Living with the Dead; and have made a Practice of locking up Debtors who displealed them, in the Yard with human Carcases. One particular Instance of this Sort of Inhumanity was of a Person, whom the Keepers confined in that Part of the lower Yard, which was then separated from the rest, whilst there were there Two dead Bodies, which had lain there Four Days; yet was he kept there with theha Six Days longer; in which Time the Vermin devoured the Flesh, from the Faces, eat the Eyes out of the Heads of the Carcasses, which were bloated, putrified, and turned green, during the poor Debtor's dismal Confinement with them.

The great Business depending in the House of Commons, having often required the long Attendance of the Members of this Committee, the Committee have not been able to go through the Examinations, which they had entered into, upon the various Complaints laid before them, of cruel beating, ironing, torturing, and murdering, Debtors, too (hocking, and two numerous, to be thoroughly examined in so short a Time, as the Remainder of this Session of Parliament allows.

One cruel and barbarous Instance, among others, which appeared to the Committee, they cannot omit; viz.

In the Year 1726, Thomas a Carpenter, not having any Friends to support him, was almost starved to Death in the Prison; upon Which he attempted to get over the Prison by a Rope, lent him by another Prisoner: In the Attempt he was taken by the Keepers, dragged by the Heels into the Lodge, barbarously beaten, and put into Irons, in which he was kept several Weeks. One Afternoon, as he was quietly standing in the Yard, with *7

his Irons on, some of the said Alton's Men called him into the Lodge, were Alton was then drinking, and merry, with Company. In about Half an Hour Bliss came out again crying, and gave an Account, that when he was in the Lodge, they, for their Diversion (as they called it) fixed on his Head an Iron Engine, or Instrument, which appears to be an Iron Scull-cap, which was ferewed so close, that it forced the Blood out of his Ears and Nose. And he farther declared, that his Thumbs were at the same time put into a Pair of Thumb-screws, which were ferewed so tight, that the Blood started out of them: And from that Time he continued disordered to the Day of his Death. He was let out of the Prison, without paying his Debt; and, at his going out, Alton desired, that all, that was pad, might be forgot, and that he would not bear him any Ill-will. This miserable Wretch was put into St. Thomas's Hospital for Help, but died very soon.

The Committee observe,

That, though in this Prison there are many Rooms Intirely empty, yet in other Rooms the Prisoners are crouded together, to the utter Destruction of theit Healths, and the endangering a general Infection:

That, notwithstanding Thirty and Forty Prisoners wer locked up together in One Room, yet the said Darby, the Keeper, did certify to the Committee, that the said Prison of the Marshalsea was sufficient commodiously to contain the Number of Prisoners thereto committed:

That the Charities have not been accounted for, but have been scandalously perverted, while great Numbers have perished in the Prison through mere Want;

That many Prisoners have died daily in the said Prison, as well those in Execution, as others, and no Coroner's Inquest hath fat upon their Bodies.

The said William Alton, being examined, at first de-

nied, but, after being confronted with several Witnesses, acknowledged, that he had had Thumb-screws in his Possession, and pretended, he had given them to the Gaoler at York. He positively denied the having any Iron Instrument, or Cap. for the Head; and yet afterwards directed the Turnkeys, where to find the Iron Scull-cap before mentioned, and it was produced to the Committee.

The Committee also found several very heavy Iron Bars, Shackles, Fetters, and Handcuffs, for the miserable Prisoners in the said Marshalsea Prison.

The unwarrantable letting to Farm the Benefit of keeping these Prisoners, hath unjustifiably increased the Profits of the Prison, to the greater Oppression of the Prisoners. The said William Al, to whom the Profits of the said Prison are let by the said John Darby, hath, in this First Year of his farming the fame, invented new oppressive Methods, to make his Profits double those of the preced i ng Year.

It the Gaolers are not punished for these their wicked Devices, and due Care be not taken, to prevent the like barbarous Practices for the futufe, the poor Prisoners, who may happen to survive these Cruelties, must be more miserable than can be expressed.

The Committee, apprehending the Conclusion of this Session to be now lo near, as to prevent their proceeding to farther Enquiries, have thought it their duty at this Time to lay a State of these Fadts before the House; hoping, some effectual Provision will be made in the next Session of Parliament, for remedying the great Grievances before mentioned, for better Regulation of Gaols, and for inflicting proper Punishments upon Gaolers for Cruelties to their Prisoners.

And the Committee have come to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That William Alton, Clerk of the Prison of the Marshalsea, and Farmer of the same Gaol, and the Profits thereof, by Lease from Mr. John Darby, the Keeper of the said Prison, hath been guilty of many high Crimes and Misdemeanors in the Execution of his Office, and hath arbitrarily and unlawfully loaded with Irons, tortured, and

( ' destroyed,

2 Geo. II. 14

destroyed, in the most inhuman, cruel, and barbarous Manner, Prisoners for Debt under his Care, in high Violation and Contempt of the Laws of this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it appears to tHis Committee, That the Charities, given by well-disposed Persons, for the Relief and Sustenance of the poor Debtors, confined in the said Prison of the Marshalsea, are notoriously and scandalously misapplied; and that the Keeper of the said Prison, and his Dependents, and Agents, instead of distributing the said Charities to the said poor Debtors, have most unjustifiably possessed themselves thereof, and wickedly perverted the same to their own Uses, to the great Fraud and Oppression of the said poor Prisoners in general, and

Mail. 381

to the darving many, who have perished in the said Prison, for want thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Mr. John Darby, Keeper of the said Prison of the Marshalsea, having contrary to, and in Defiance of, the Law, let to farm his said Gaol, and Office, and the Profits thereof, unto the said William and having grofly

neglected his Duty, in not preventing, or remedying, the said Inhumanities, Cruelties, Frauds, and Abuses, is guilty of a high Misdemeanor in his Office, and a notorious Breach of his Trust, in contempt of the Law, and to the great Oppression and Ruin of many of his Majesty's Subjects.

Appendix, C.

Palace Court, 30th July, 1725.

Enquiry into , Upon Information given to this Court by the Keeper the Sate of of the Prison thereof, that one Matthew Pugh, who has Gaols.) for some Time pad received for the Prisoners of the said Prison, the Gifts and Legacies belonging to them, has under that Pretence, very often behaved himself very turbulently in the said Prison, frequently occasioning Disturbances amongst the said Prisoners; and because of the impudent Behaviour of the said Matthew Pugh, as well in this Court, as the Office of the Prothonotary thereof; it is this Day ordered, that the said Matthew Pugh be no longer permitted to have Accels to the Prison of this Court, upon the Pretence aforesaid; and that the Prisoners of the said Prison be at Liberty to appoint another Person, to receive the Gifts and Legacies belonging to them.

By the Court.

Gilbourne.

Farther, in relation to the Fleet Prison.

The Dispatch, which your Committee found themselves obliged to give to their former Report, relating to the Fleet Prison, prevented their inserting several Fads, which in the Course of their Examination havefince con e to their Knowledge in a fuller Light, and which they think proper to lay before the House, by way of Supple-ment to their said former Report, as followeth; viz.

It farther appeared to the Committee, that Mr. mentioned in the said former Report, whilst he was in the Tap house of the said Fleet Prison, during the War-denship of John Huggins, Esquire, and behaving himself quietly, was suddenly seized by James Barnes, Agent for Huggins, and, without any Reason given, was forced into the strong Room, or Dungeon, on the Matter's Side; which Dungeon, being then but lately built, and fodamp, that the Drops hung upon the Walls, was very nauseous, and unwhollome. In this Place was this unfortunate Man locked up, and never once permitted to go out; but by an Accident, on a Sundry, the Door being opened, he ran into the Parlour, adjoining to the Chapel, during the Time of divine Service. He had then no Covering upon his Body, but the Feathers of a Bed, which Bed was thrown in to him by a Prisoner, into which he crept, to defend himself from the Cold; and the Feathers stuck and were clotted upon him by his own Excrements, and the Dirt, which covered his Skin.

He was immediately seized, and carried back into the said Dungeon; where, through the Cold, and' the Restraint, and for Want of Food, he loft his Senses, languished, and perished.

notwithstanding the miserable Condition of this Man, and the Applications, which were made to Mr. Huggins, then Warden, who law this miserable Object lying naked in the said Dungeon, and unable to speak, but lifting up his Eyes to Mr. Huggins,j the said Huggins bad no -Companion on him, but caused the Door to be close locked upon him.

Oliver Reed, another Prisoner in the Fleet Prison, was loaded with Irons by the Directions of Mr.;

who confessed to the Committee, that he sent for the Fetters ana Manacles~from Newgate, and ordered them to be put 'on the Hands and Legs of this ymfortunate "Debtor! wltoin October last was put into another £>ungeon -and; way continued there, till your Committc went to view The Gaol, where he was forced to lie on a small Bed, -with Chains of Forty PoTinds Weight, which even Bam-- thought too heavy, and applied to Huggins for

lighter. Reed had nothing but a thin ragged Blanket, to cover his naked Body, in the most piercing Weather of the last hard Winter; and within Three Yards of him was a Window, treble barred, without Glals or Shutter; under which Window was a Heap of the most noisome Offals, to feed the Dogs, there kennelled; And the Place was the more unwholsome, because of a Necessary-House in the same Room, the Stench whereof,n{aa so intolerable, that your Committee could not continue in the

Room Six Minutes, to examine t! is unhappy Person, whose great Sufferings, under the Warden's cruel Usage of him, were far greater than your Committee can express. ‘

It appears also to the Committee, that the said Mr. Huggins hath, in Combination with Richard Bishop, his Tipstaff, consented to let out several Prisoners, whom they call by a cant Name, Pidgeons, to go into foreign Parts, as well as into several distant trading Counries at home, and furnished them with a lham Credit, to buy Goods; which beir.g consigned to the said Bishop, he took out CommilEons of Bankruptcy against the Persons, so let. out of Prison, and fraudulently employed, as aforesaid, and thereby cheated the Creditors, who dealt with them, of their Goods, to a very considerable Value; and that a Waggon Load of scarlet Cloth was brought away from the Owner, on such false Credit; but the Owner, pursuing it, seized the Cloth, as they were unloading it, upon Ludgate Hill.

And farther it appears to your Committee, that, during the said Mr. Huggins's Wardenship, several Writs of Habeas Corpus ad testijicandum, were surreptitiously taken out by his Direction, to protect Prisoner, who desired to go to any Part of the Kingdom, on Pretence of giving Evidence at some Trial, or at some Assizes; for which Liberty Huggins received large Sums of Money; and even those Writs have had Blanks left in them, to insert a pretended Cause; and, to avoid Suspicion of such Writs being colluftve, Huggins, by Letter under his own Hand, and now in the Hands of your Committee, pretended to caution his Servants not to be concerned in taking out such Writs; And by the said Letter it fully appears, that this wicked Practice was for Lucre only; and such Liberty, thus given, was to Prisoners committed for very large Sums.

Your Committee, notwithstanding their Diligence and Zeal in the Premises, have not been able to come at a true Account of the Charities, given for Relief of the Poor Prisoners in the Fleet Prison; but your Committee have no Reason to believe, there is in that Particular Jess Iniquity in the Warden's Management, than in the other Practices, whereof the following may serve as an instance: Lieutenant Robert FitzSimmonds, being discharged by the

Plaintiff's Executors on the 12th of 1728, lay then in Prison for his Fees only; about which time a Gentleman came to the Fleet Prison from an unknown Lady, to discharge all such Prisoners, as remain there for Fees only, provided the same exceeded not the Sum of Three Guineas each, or that the Warden would discharge such Prisoners of all Fees and Demands for that Sum. Upon which, Mr. 'Thomas Bambridge, then. Warden, sent for

Twelve Prisoners, and gave the said Gentleman a List of their Names with his full Demands on them severally, which were considerably more than Three Guineas each: However Bambridge, in Compliance with the Lady's great Charity, and in regard to the poor Prisoners, consented to accept the Three Guineas for each Prisoner, in full Discharge of all Demands, alluring tire said Gentleman, that they should be discharged on that Condition. Whereupon he paid Bambridge, in the Presence of the said Twele Prisoners, Thirty-six Guineas for their Discharge; but, as soon as the Gentleman's Back was turned, Bambridge infilled on all his former Demands to the full, and vyould not suffer them to go out of Prison, till they had given him Notes for what exceeded the Three Guineas.

Mr. Fitz-Simmonds, one of these Prisoners, was forced to sign a Note, drawn by Bambridge himself, payable to William Pindar, one of his Accomplices, or Order, for Twenty-seven Pounds, Ten Shillings; and the other Eleven of the said Prisoners were forced to do in the same Manner.

It also appears to the Committee, that the first bringing of Soldiers to the Fleet Prison, to put in Fear, and to insult the poor Debtors, was in the Time, when Mr. Huggins was Warden.

The Committee think it proper to lay before the House the same of Sir IVm. Rich, Baronet, a Prisoner for . Debt in the Fleet Prison; viz.

It appeared to the Committee, that Sir IVm. Rich removed himself by Habeas Corpus from , where

he lay for Debt, to the Fleet Prison; but, instead of being admitted, as he desired, into that Prison, he was carried to, and confined at, Corbett's Spunging-house for a Fortnight, at very great Expences-, and, though he often applied to be put into the Prison, it was refused, unless he would pay £.5. to the Warden, as a Commitment Fee, and also for. per Week for his Lodgings; which exorbitant Demands he was obliged to comply ‘ with, not being able to support and pay the heavier Extortions of the said Spunging-house.

In about Ten Weeks after Sir s Removal, Mr.

Bambridgebecame Deputy Warden; to whom Sir William applied for a Chamber at a less Rent, which he obtained, at 3 s. 6 d. per Week, on payment of Pour Guineas.

After Sir William had been in this new Chamber about Three Weeks, William Pindar, the Chamberlain, came to him, and demanded the Rent of 3 per Week,

which was paid; but Sir William not being able to pay all the Arrears of the great Rent, due for the former . Chamber, a Message came from Mr. Cambridge, that he wanted him in the Lodge; but Sir William conceiving, ' it was the Part of Mr. Bambridge to come to him, if lie had Business, answered to that Effect; thereupon James Barnes, Corbett, and others, armed with Pikes, and Halberts, required Sir William to go and wait upon Mr. Bambridge-, but Bambridge, immediately following his laid Messengers, met Sir William upon the Stairs, seized him by the Collar, and, the rest of s Followers

a (lifting, dragged Sir William into the Lodge, and soon after procured him to be removed by Habeas Corpus to the King's Bench Prison, where he remained Twelve Months, and was afterwards brought back to the Prison, by another Habeas Corpus, and carried again to Corbett's Spunging-house, in order to extort a farther £.5. as a Baronet's Fee, for his Commitment, though Sir William offered to pay the Fee, settled by the Court of Common Pleas, of £. a.4 s. d.

After Ten Weeks Stay at Cor belt's. Sir Wiilium, late at Night, was ordered into the Prison, and, by the Consent of one of the Prisoners on the Matter's Side, went into his Room; where the said Prisoner permitted him to have Part of, his Bed, and, desiring his Stay, said, he would raise Money to pay the Warden.

Soon after this the said Bar came into the Room, to turn Sir William out by Force; and the Reason being asked, Barnes answered shortly, lie would -not stand arguing with him; and then put a red hot Poker to Sir William's Bread, and swore, if he did not pay the Money, or go down immediately, he would run the Poker into his Body.

Then came in Two Men, fike Russians, armed with - Muskets, and Bayonets fixed on them, and forcing the Standers-by out of the Room, Barnes run at Sir William with the said red hot Poker, which Srr William having the good Luck to put by, ,on that Disappoint-

The Appendix. I

Perrin's Cafe,

As it relates to John Huggins, Esquire, Warden of the

Fleet,

That in Easter Term, 1714 Esquire,

Warden of the Fleet, for a Sum of Money, and upon a Security Bond, wherein the said Thomas Perrin, together with Benjamin Robinson , and Three other Persons, as his Securities, were bound for his Lodging without the said Prison, permitted him the Liberty aforesaid.

That the said Sureties were Persons of no Account, or Substance: That the said Perrin, with the Privity, and express Consent, of the said Huggins, went often at large, out of the Rules, without any Day Rule, or lawful Licence so to do.

That on the itth of August, 1714, the said Perrin went over to Holland, having first employed the said Warden to solicit a Matter, then depending before the Commissioners of the Customs, upon a Reference on a Petition of the said Perrin, praying, that his same might be considered with relation to the said Debts, and have his Liberty, on giving Security to return to Prison, when required.

That the Warden undertook the Care and Negotiation of the said Business, and, the better to carry on the fame, corresponded with the said Perrin, when in Holland , who, on that Account, and for his Liberty, remitted, by Bills, and otherwise, considerable Sums of Money, which the Warden received.

That afterwards the said Warden, fearing a Prosecution for the Escape, sent over Mr. Robinson into Holland, to remind Perrin of his Promise to return to the said Prison of the Fleet before the next Term, promising him, the said Perrin, by Letters, and upon Oath before a Matter in Chancery, that he, the Warden, would not seize his Person in the mean Time, and that, whatever the said Robin-

n

Jan undertook for him, the Warden, touching the same and Favour of Perrin, he, the said Robinson, should fee faithfully performed.

That, in pursuance thereof, it was agreed between the said Robinson and Huggins, Perrin should have Liberty to transact his Affairs at large, so as he returned to Prison before next Term; and, for his Security, in that behalf, the Warden offered to trust Perrin intirely, not doubting Perrin's Honour* and gives, in one of his Letters, this Reason , viz. that Perrin came once before from Holland, to surrender himself, to save his Bail.

Whereupon Perrin came back to London without any Seizure, Recaption, Restraint, or Molestation of his Person; and, for his Security on that behalf, the Warden offered, and did give, Perrin a general Release; and by this Deed, bearing Date 20th October, 1714, released to Perrin all and all Manner of Actions, Cause and Causes of Action, Suits, Bills, Bonds, Writings obligatory, Debts, Dues, Duties, Accounts, Sum and Sums of Money, Judgments, Executions, Extents, Quarrels, Controversies, Trespasses, Damages, and Demands, whatsoever.

That on the 22d of October, 1714, Perrin returned to the Rules of the Prison, goes under the Key, to save the Warden, as if in Execution for the said Debts, and for the pretended Damages by Means of the said Escape into Holland, although that was all settled betwixt and the Warden, and his Right of Seizure and Recaption released also.

That Perrin remained in the Fleet until on or about the Second of April, 1716; but some short time before consults the Warden about a new-intended Voyage to Holland, in order to raise more Money for the said Warden, by applying to Messieurs and Son, his old

Correspondents, and by endeavouring to fall into Bufi-nels, toexercisehis Industry, for the Benefit of the Warden* which he so effectually brought about, that he remitted to the said Warden near i,oco. which came safe to the Warden's Hands.

That Huggins, to prevent his being sued, as he pretended, immediately proposed to the Commissioners of the Customs, that they would be pleased to say, that the Crown had gained One thousand Pounds more, than if Perrin had not escaped; and, after he had prevailed with the Solicitor so so do, they drew up a Report, and transmitted it to the Treasury, signed by the Commissioners of the Customs.

The Affidavit, mentioned in the said Cafe.

John Huggins, Warden of the Fleet, maketh Oath, that 'Thomas Perrin, of London, Merchant, shall peaceably and quietly, without Interruption or Molestation, hold and enjoy to himself the Liberty of the Rules of the Prison of the Fleet, without any future Charge whatsoever and this Deponent will not permit or suffer the said Thomas Perrin, under any pretence whatsoever, against his Will, to be confined within the Walls of the said Prison nor shall the said Thomas Perrin be removed to any other Prison by or through the Means or Procurement of this Deponent, or Habeas Corpus, or otherwise, to any of his Majesty's Prison or Prisons, Place or Places of Confinement, so far as to the utmost of his, this Deponent's, Power, can be prevented and, in case a Habeas Corpus be brought to Effect, so as that the said Thomas Perrin should be removed, he, this Deponent, will use his utmost endeavours to bring him back to the Rules of the Fleet, that he may enjoy the Liberty aforesaid, or to procure for him the Liberty of the Rules, at this Deponent's own proper Charge and Expence, and so to be continued to him under Moses Cooke, Esquire, the present Marshal, or any other Marshal, so long as the said Thomas Perrin shall continue to be a Prisoner; so that he may, either at the King's Bench or Fleet Prisons, enjoy the Liberty proposed, notwithstanding any Action or Actions, Judgment or Judgments, Declaration or Declarations, Extent or Extents, by means of his late or present Misfortunes, or any thing, that may or shall happen to orarife therefrom} and that, in case this Deponent should fell, assign, or set

The First Resolution being read a Second time; Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That William A£lon, Clerk of the Prison of the Marshalsea, and Farmer of the same Gaol, and the Profits thereof, by Lease from Mr. John Darby, the Keeper of the said Prison, hath been guilty of many high Crimes and Misdemeanors in the Execution of his Office, and hath arbitrarily and unlawfully loaded with Irons, tortured, and destroyed, in the most inhuman, cruel, and barbarous Manner, Prisoners for Debt under his Care, in high Violation and Contempt of the Laws of this Kingdom.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time; Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That the Charities given by well-disposed Persons, for the Relief and Sustenance of the poor Debtors, confined in the said Prison of the foaifea, are notoriously and scandalously misappliedj and that the Keeper of the said Prison, and his Dependents, and Agents, instead of distributing the said Charities to the said poor Debtors, have mostunjuftifiably possessed themselves thereof, and wickedly perverted the same to their own Uses, to the great Fraud and Oppression of the said poor Prisoners in general, and to theftarving of many who have perilhcd in the said Prison, for Want thereof.
