The King'*' After which, his Majesty was pleased to make a most Speech? gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentle-mcn,

The Season of the Year, and the Di (patch you have given to the publick Business, make it proper for me to put an End to this Session of Parliament; which I cannot do, without expressing my Satisfaction at the just Regard you have shewn upon all Occasions, to my Honour, and to the true Interest of my People.

The Prudence and Temper, with which you have proceeded at this critical Conjuncture, have been very acceptable to me, and cannot fail of meeting with general Approbation. Your several Determinations upon Matters of the greatest Nicety, and Importance, have shewn you not insensible of the Difficulties we labour under, without suffering yourselves to be transported and carried into any unleafinable Warmths and Animosities. You have considered the Loftes of our Merchants with a becoming Compassion and Concern, and received their Complaints in such a Manner, as will bell conduce to the obtaining them Justice and Satisfaction; and you may be assured, no Endeavours shall be wanting on my Part, to answer the Expectations and Willies of my People.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Supplies, which you have granted me, and lb effectually raised, in a Manner, the lealt burthensome to my Subjects, are a new Proof of your Zeal, Affection, and Readiness to support me in the Defence and Protection of the Rights and Privileges of my Kingdom. It is a great Satisfaction to me to observe, that you have been thus able to supply the necessary Charges and Expences, that have unavoidably been brought and continued upon us, and at the same time to make a further Progress in lessening and reducing the national Debt.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have already acquainted you, that, it being necessary for me to visit my German Dominions this Year, I have determined to make the Queen Regent here, during my Absence} and I mull in a particular Manner recommend it to you all, to make her Administration as ealy as possible, by preferring the Peace and Quiet of the Kingdom in your several Stations and Countries, and by endeavouring to discountenance, and restrain, the vile and seditiousPraftices of railing unjuilClamours, and creating Discontents in the Minds of my People.

Th* King's Mr. Speaker reported, that the House had attended Speech re- his Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty

ported. was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the

Throne to both Houses of Parliament, of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to, prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House, and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is with great Satisfaction I acquaint you, that we have at length extricated ourselves from the many Difficulties and Inconveniences, that attended the uncertain State of Affairs in Europe, by having concluded an absolute Peace with the Crown of Spain.

This Negociation hath been carried on, and finished, with a perfect Union, Harmony, and Fidelity, between me and my Allies, with no other View, but to prevent the Miseries and Confusion of a War, which, if once kindled in Europe, it had been as hard to know the End, as to determine the Success of such a fatal Event.

As this Alliance is built upon the Foundation, and is agreeable to the Purport and Intentions, of former Treaties, without any Alterations in the principal Articles, but such, as tend to render more effectual what the contrafting Powers in the Quadruple Alliance were before engaged to fee performed, it is very justly to be presumed, that, from this happy Beginning, the great Work of a general Pacification will soon be perfect and complete.

But if, contrary to Expectation, and in Resentment of the present Engagements, any new Troubles, although with little Prospect of Success, should be raised in Europe, to oppose, or disappoint, the Execution of them, I am confident, I shall not want the Support and Assistance of my Parliament in so just a Cause, which hath the joint Concurrence of so many considerable Powers for the Honour and Credit of the present Measures, and their united Strength in Maintenance of our mutual Stipulations.

In the mean time I can assureyou, that I have made it my first Care to consult the immediate Interests of these my Kingdoms, preferable to any other Consideration, and at the Hazard of all other Events.

All former Treaties and Conventions, made with Spain, in Favour of our Trade and Navigation, are renewed and confirmed; not only afreeand uninterrupted Exercise of 17

ample Kestitution and Reparation for unlawful Seizures and Depredations are expressly stipulated and agreed to; in general, all Rights, Privileges, and Possessions, in any Manner belonging to me, and my Allies, are solemnly re-established, confirmed, and guarantied, and not one Conecflion is made to the Prejudice of me, or my Subjects.

By this Means a Foundation is laid, for removing all former Animosities and Misunderstandings between the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Spain; and it is not at all to be doubted, but that, by a faithful Execution of our reciprocal Engagements, a perfect Friendship betwixt Two Nations, united by the common Ties of mutual.

Interest, may be more strongly established and cemented, than ever.

And that my Subjects might reap the earliest Fruits of this advantageous Peace, I gave Orders for the immediate Reduction of a great Number of my Land Forces, and for laying up, and discharging, a great Part of my Fleet.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

This will make a cgnsiderable Saving in the F.xpence of the current Year; and I hope, it will give a general Satisfaction to my People, as it is a most sensible Pleasure to me. The proper Estimates shall be laid before you; and I make no doubt, but you will grant me the necessary Supplies, and enable me to make good my Engagements with my Allies, in such Manner, as shall be most effectual for the publick Service, and most easy to your Fellow-subjects.

Y ou will fee, by the Accounts, that will be laid before you, the Sate, Produce, and Application, of the Sinking Fund, as far as hath been hitherto directed by Act of Parliament; and you will not fail to take into your Consideration the further Disposition of the growing Produce.

You are the bed Judges, whether the Circumstances of the Sinking Fund, and of the national Debt, will, as yet, admit of giving any Ease, where the Duties are most grievous. I have the greatest Regard for the Sinking Fund, and I look with Compassion upon the Hardships of the poor Artificers, and Manufacturers: Ileave it to your Determination, what may reasonably, and with due Caution, be done upon this critical Consideration.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

That we may receive the natural Advantages of our present Situation, I mull, in the strongest Manner, recommend to you a perfect Unanimity among yourselves, such, as may intirely defeat the Hopes of our Enemies both at home, and abroad. The groundless Insinuations, Cavils, and Clamours, of some few ill-designing Persons, to (hake the Steadiness of those Powers, who are already my Allies, or to hinder others from becoming so, will by your Unanimity be rendered ineffectual; and I desire, that the Affections of my People may be the Strength of my Government, as their Interest hath always been the Rule of my AdVions, and the Object of my Wilhes.

The said Garrisons shall not meddle, directly or indirectly, under any Pretext whatsoever, in Affairs of the political, economical, or civil. those States, and in Safety from all Invasion, and other just Grounds of Fear, he will cause to be withdrawn from the Places in those States the Troops, which shall be his oWn, and not belonging to the Infante Don or to him, who shall succeed to his Rights, in such manner, that thereby thd said Succession, or Pofiession* may rest secure, and exempt from all Events.

The States General of the United Provirtces shall be invited to come into the present Treaty, and Articles: Such other Powers, as shall be agreed on, shall likewise be invited, and admitted, by Concert, into the same Treaty, and Articles.

Separate Articles.

Article tft.

ALTHOUGH, conformably to the preliminary Articles, it is laid in the Fourth Article of the Treaty, signed this Day, that the Commerce of the Nation

in America should be re-established on the foot of the Treaties and Conventions, antecedent to the Year 1725; however, for the greater Exactness, it is further declared by the present Article between their Britannick and Ca-tholick Majesties, which shall have the same Force, and be under the same Guaranty, as the Treaty, signed this Day, that under that general Denomination are comprehended the Treaties of Peace, and of Commerce, concluded at Utrecht the 13th of , and 9th of,

in the Year 1713, in which are comprized the Treaty of 1667,made at Madrid, and the Ced ulas therein mentioned; the latter Treaty, made at Madrid the 14th of December,

1715; as also the particular Contract, commonly called the

Affienlo, for bringing Negro Slaves into the Spanish , which was made the 26 th Day of March, in the said Year 1713, in consequence of the Twelfth Article of the Treaty of Utrecht; and likewise the Treaty of Declaration touch-

ing that of the Ajfiento, made the a6th of May 1716: All which Treaties, mentioned in this Article, with their Declarations, shall from this Day, even during the Examination by the Commissaries, be and remain in their Force, Virtue, and full Vigour; for the Observation of which his Catholick Majesty shall cause to be dispatched forthwith, if they have not been dispatched, the necessary Orders, and Cedulas, to his Vice-roys, Governors, and other Ministers, to whom it shall appertain, as well in Europe, as in the Indies, to the end that, without any Delay or Interpietation, they may cause them to be observed and fulfilled.

In like manner his Bdtannick Majesty promises and engages to publish the necessary Orders, if any be wanting, for ie-establishing the Commerce of the Subjects of Spain

in all the Countries under his Dominion, on the foot specified by the said Treaties, and for causing them to be exactly observed and fulfilled.

' Article ad.

Consequently, all Ships, Merchandize, and Effects, which shall not have been taken or seized on account of unlawful Commerce, and which shall now be proved, by authentick Proofs and Documents, to have been detained, seized, or confiscated, in the Ports of Spain, either in Europe, or in the Indies, and, namely, the Ship Prince Frederick, and her Cargo, if they have not been restored already, shall be immediately reftofed, in the same Kind, as to those Things, which shall be found still remaining in that Condition, or, in Default thereof, the just and true Value of them, according to their Valuation, which, if it was not made at the time, shall be regulated by the authentick Informations, which the Proprietors shall exhibit to the Magistrates of the Places and Towns, where the Seizures were made; his Britannick Majesty promising the like, on his Part, as to all Seizures, Confiscations, of Detentions, which may have been made, contrary to the Tenor of the said Treaties; their said Britannick and Catholick Majesties agreeing, that with respect to the like Seizures, Confiscations, or Detentions, on either Side, the Validity of which may not yet have been sufficiently made out, the Discussion and Decision of them shall be referred to the Examination of the Commissaries, to do therein according to Right, upon the foot of the Treaties here above mentioned.

The present separate Articles shall have the (ame Force, as if they were inserted word for word in the Treaty, concluded and signed this Day; they shall be ratified in the same Manner; and the Ratification of them shall be exchanged at the same time, as those of the said Treaty.

In Witness whereof, we, the under-written Ministers Plenipotentiaries of his Britannick Majesty, of his most Christian Majesty, and of his Catholick Majesty, by Virtue of our full Powers, have signed the present separate Articles, and caused the Seals of our Arms to be put thereto.

Done at Seville, the 9th Day of November 1729.

IV. Stanhope. Brancas. El Marq' de la Paz,

The Lord Fitz-william reported from the Committee, appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address, to be presented to his Majesty; that the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had direffed him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; vPz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our most humble Thanks for your most gracious Spceeh from the Throne.

We, cannot omit taking this first Opportunity to congratulate your Majesty upon your happy Return into these Kingdoms. The just and prudent Administration of the Government, during your Majesty's Absence, by the Queen, your royal Contort, ruling by your Authority, and governing by your Example, could alone compen-fate for the Want of your toyal Presence, and aulpicious Influence, among us.

The welcome News of your Majesty's having concluded an absolute Peace with the Crown of Spain, effected by a perfeff Union, Harmony, and Fidelity, between your Majesty, and your Allies, filled the Hearts of all your good People with inexpressible Joy and Satisfaction; and we should be wanting in Du;y to your Majesty, in Justice to ourselves, and not answer the Expeffatrms of those we represent, if we did not approach your Majesty, upon this happy Occasion, with Hearts full of Duly and Gratitude, and with the strongest Acknowlegements ot your Majesty's Goodness, Wisdom, and Resolution; your Wisdom and Resolution, in not suffering yourself to be diverted, by any falle malicious Clamours and Insinuations, from steadily pursuing the great and desirable Work of giving Peace to your People; your Goodnef, in consulting the immediate Interests of these your King*-doir.s, preferable to all other Considerations, and at the Hazard of all other Events.

This must convince the Woild of your Majesty's paternal Care and tender Regard for your Dominion?, when we fee all former Treaties, made in Favour of our Trade and Commerce, and for the Security of the Rights, Privileges, and Post'essions, belonging to your Majesty, renewed, and confirmed; when we lee the Crown of Spain under new and fresh Obligations to your Majesty, not only to permit to your Subjects a free and uninterrupted Exercise of their Trade and Commerce for the future, but to make just and ample Restitution and Reparation for all former unlawful Seizures and Depredations.

The Extension of former Engagements, without any material Alterations in the principal Articles from the

Purport

A Mrffs on

Kmo'i S; etch.

Geo. II. 14® — 15'

Purport and Intentions of former Treaties, in order to obtain these great and truly valuable Advantages, without one Concession made to the Prejudice of your Majesty,

or your Subjects, is a Confederation, that, to reject, had been losing the fairest Opportunity to recover the antient Freedom and Liberty of Trade and Commerce to these Kingdoms; and not faithfully to fulfil, and execute, what is stipulated, on your Majesty'* Part, to secure a reciprocal Performance, from your Majesty's Allies, of the Engagements, they have entered into, would be abandoning the particular Interests and Properties of your Majesty's trading Subjects, and to expose the Trade and Commerce of this Nation to all the Hazards and Incertainties which they have fb long laboured under.

These Blessmgs, secured to us, will sufficiently compensate all Inconveniencies, that can attend the Performance of your Majesty's Engagements; and as it is justly to be presumed, that a general Pacification and Tranquillity in Europe will be the Consequence of the present Treaty, the Prospect of seeing this soon complete, and perfected, adds greatly to our Satisfaction.

But if, contrary to Expectation, and in Resentment to your Majesty's just and prudent Measures, any new Troubles should be raised in Europe, to oppose, or disappoint, the Execution of the present Engagements, we think ourselves obliged by the strongest Ties of Duty, Affection, and Gratitude, to affine your Majesty, that we will stand by and support your Majesty against all Insults and Indignities, that shall be offered to your Majesty, and that we will enable you to make good your Engagements with your Allies.

The immediate Reduction of so considerable a Part of your Forces by Sea and Land, upon the first Notice of 1 the Confirmation of the Peace, is another Instance of your Majesty's Care and Attention to the Ease and Welfare of your People; and the recommending to our Consideration the State of the Sinking Fund, in so gracious and condescending a Manner, obliges us to proceed with all possible Caution and Prudence in an Affair of that Nicety and Importance, where the earlier Discharge of the national Debt on one hand, and the Hardships of the poor Artificers and Manufacturers on the other, require the greatest Regard, and deserve the most mature Deliberation.

From a due Sense of these many Proofs of your Majesty's unwearied Endeavours to consult the Happiness of your People, we think ourselves obliged toaffure your Majesty, that this House will, by the best and most easy Methods, effectually raise the necessary Supplies for the Service of the current Year; and by a proper Zeal and ! Concern for the Honour of your Majesty, the publick

Tranquillity, and the Good of your People, defeat the 1 vain Expedition of such ill-designing Persons, who may

flatter themselves with the Hopes of being able, by groundless Insinuations, Cavils, and Clamours, to shake the Steadiness of those Powers, who are already Allies to your Majesty, or to hinder others from becoming so.

! The said Address, being read a Second time, was,

upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Answer to Mr. Speaker reported, that the House attended his Address. Majesty Yesterday with their Address; to which his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I return you my Thanks for this very affectionate and loyal Address. The Assurances you have given me, and the Support of my Parliament, in enabling me to make good my Engagements with my Allies, will, I promise myself, greatly contribute towards settling the general Pacification of Europe.

You may be assured, that the Confidence, you repole in me, shall never be made use of, but for preserving the publick Tranquillity, for maintaining the Rights and Interests of my People, and in vindication of my Honour and Dignity.

In the Name of the most Holy Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Ghost, Three distinct Persons, and One only true God.

IX.

The introducing of Garrisons into the Places of heme, Por/o-ferraio, Parma, and to the Number

of Six thousand Men of his Catholick Majesty's Troops, and in his Pay, shall be effectuated without Loss of Time; which Troops shall i'erve for the better securing and preserving of the immediate Succession of the said States in Favour of thp most serene Infante Don , and to be ready to withstand any Enterprize and Opposition, which mighc be formed, to the Prejudice of what has been regulated touching the said Succession.

X.

The contracting Powers shall forthwith use all the Applications, which they shall judge to be confident with the Dignity and Quiet of the most ferenc Great Duke of Tuscany, and the Duke of Parma, to the end the Garrifor.s may be received with the greated Tranquillity, and without Opposition, as soon as they shall present themselves before the Places, into which they are to be introduced.

The said Garrisons shall take an Oath to the present Possessor, to defend their Persons, Sovereignty, Possessions, and States, and Subjects, in every thing, that shall not be contrary to the Right of Succession, reserved to the most lerene Infante Don Carlos; and the present Possessors shall not demand or exaftany thing, that is contrary thereto.

The said Garrisons shall not meddle, directly or indirectly, under any Pretext whatsoever, in Affairs of the political, economical, or civil, Government; and shall have most express Orders to render to the most serene Great Duke of Tuscany, and the Duke of Parma, all the Respects, and military Honours, that are due to Sovereigns in their own Dominions.

XI.

The Intent of introducing the said Six thousand Men of his Catholick Majesty's Troops, and in his Pay, being to secure to the moll serene Infante Don Carlos the immediate Succession of the States of , and

Placentia; his Catholick Majesty promises, as well for himself, as his Successors, that, as loon as the most serene Infante Don Carlos, his Son, or such other, who shall succeed to his Rights, shall be the quiet Possessor of those States, and in Safety from all Invasion, and other jud Grounds of Fear, he will cause to be withdrawn from the Places in those States the Troops, which shall be his own, and not belonging to the Infante Don Carlos, or to him, who shall succeed to his Rights, in such manner, that thereby the said Succession, or Possession, may red secure, and exempt from all Events.

XII.

The contracting Powers engage to edabliffi, according to the Rights of Succession, which have been dipulated, and to maintain, the most serene Infante Don Carlos, or him, to whom his Rights shall devolve, in the Poffclhon and Enjoyments of the States of Tuscany, Parma, and Placentia, when he shall once be settled there j to defend him from all Insult, against any Power whatsoever, that might intend to disturb him; declaring themselves, by this Treaty, Guarantees for ever of the Right, Possession, Tranquillity, and Quiet, of the most serene Infante, and of his Successors, to the said States.

XIII.

As to other Particulars, or Regulations, concerning the keeping up of the said Garrisons, once established in the States of Tuscany, Parma, and Placentia, as it is to be presumed, that his Catholick Majesty, and the most serene Great Duke, and Duke of Parma, will settle the same by an Agreement between themselves, their Britannick and most Chridian Majesties promise, that, as soon as that Agreement shall be made, they will ratify and guaranty it, as well to his Catholick Majesty, as to the most serene Great Duke, and Duke of Parma, as if it were inserted word for word in the present Treaty.

And whereas the said Lords the States General have always had a sincere Desire to continue, and drengthen, the good Intelligence and Friendship, wherein they have the Honour to live with their Britannick, most Chridian, and Catholick Majesties; and, as they desire to contri bute, as far as it depends upon them, towards the Preservation and Establishment of the Peace, and publick Quiet, without which, that of their Republick cannot be secure, they are very sensible of the obliging Invitation, which has been made them, to accede to this Alliance, being persuaded, that its Aim tends chiefly to bind themselves more dofely together.

And. as this Alliance, among other Ends, has that of establishing an intire Confidence between the contracting Parties, the States General suppose that the Allies will mutually communicate to each other, in all Confidence, their Thoughts as to the Ways and Means, which shall be judged the most effectual, in case of Need, to preserve and maintain the Possessions, and Rights, above mentioned in the Treaty, here before inserted, as well with respect to Commerce, as others, both within Europe, and without it: And whereas, in the firm Persuasion and Confidence, that this is the true Aim and Intention of their said Majesties, the said Lords and States General, to give an Indance of their Desire to unite themselves closely with them, and of the high Edeem they have for their Friend-ship and Alliance, have resolved to accede to the said Treaty, here above inserted; and for that Purpose they have named the Sieur Francis Funder Meer their Ambassador at the Court of Spain, and have furnished him with a full Power to agree upon this Accession with M.

If it should happen, that his Catholick Majesty should think fit to give at present, or hereafter, either publickly, or by secret Conventions, new Rights or Advantages to any Power whatsoever, with respect. to Trade, the same Rights or Advantages shall immediately be granted to their High Mightinesse, and to their Subjects, who shall be treated in every thing as those of the Nation the most favoured, as it is ffcipulated by former Treaties.

The Lords the States General having represented, that there may happen certain Cafes, wherein they may, out of Hatred for their Accession, signed this Day, be attacked, or troubled, in such manner, that they may be obliged to have immediate Recourse to Arms for their Defence, and that, in such Case, the Time, necessary for waiting for the Success of the Offices, which may have been employed, and after which only their Allies are obliged to furnish them with Succours, stipulated by the Second Article of this present Treaty, may be the Occasion of a considerable Prejudice to them, and leave them exposed to the most vigorous Attacks, without the Succours of the Princes, their Allies; his Britannick Majesty, his most Christian Majesty, and his Catholick Majesty, in order to give the States General a new Proof of the Share they take in the Preservtion of their Republick, have consented to engage and promite, that in the abovesaid Cafes, which might put the Republick in an evident Danger, they will furnish the Succours, stipulated by the Second Article above-mentioned, even without waiting for the Success of the Offices, and Instances, which they may have begun to employ with the Aggressor, for procuring the Satisfaction and Reparation required.

Supply. The House (according to Order) resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Sir Charles Turner took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir Charles Turner reported from the Committee, that they had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Monday Morning next.

Sir Charles Turner also acquainted the House, that he

was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Cftomiitew. Ordered, That all Committees be adjourned.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning next. Nine of the Clock.

loch*nd Sir John Stonekoufe reported from the Committee, to

U'mijoo whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Farmers, and Traders, in the County of , and also the Petition of the Mayor* Bailiffs, artd Commonalty, of the City of Oxford, and also the Petition of the Chancellor, Mailers, and Scholars of the University of Oxford, and allb the Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Farmers, and Traders, in the County of Oxon, were referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 26th of the lait Month, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said several Petitions, complaining of great Abuses of the Proprietors, or Under-tenants, of Locks and Wears upon the Rivers Thames and IJis, by imposing extravagant Rates for Water Carriage of Goods.

To make good the first Part of the said Petitions,

An Act of Parliament, passed in the Sixth and Seventh Years of the Reign of King William the Third, To prevent the Exactions of the Occupiers of Locks and Wears upon the River of Thames Wellward, and for ascertaining the Rates of Water Carriages upon the said River, was laid before the Committee.

That, in pursuance, of the said Act, the Rates, to be paid at the said Locks, were ascertained, and taken by the Occupiers thereof; but the said Act was made to continue for the Term of Nine Years only, and has not since been continued, or revived.

To prove the Exactions of the Occupiers of Locks on the River Thames, between London and Oxford, since the Expiration, of the said Act,

Robert Hooper was called; who said, that the Prices demanded, and paid, since the making of the said Act, for passing through the Locks, erected upon the River between London and Oxford, have been advanced so much that Mailers of Barges and other Vessels have paid at some of the Locks a fourth Part, and at fume half, and at others treble, more, than they were obliged to pay, during the Continuance of the said Act.

But Robert Hooper said, that the Mailers of the Barges and other Vessels agreed with the Occupiers of some of the Locks, to pay them a certain Price annually, whether they made use of the Locks, or not. —

To prove the Prices demanded, and paid, at the several Locks upon the River, above JoJim Hall was examined, and said, that he had belonged to the River Fifty Years; and that the Occupiers Vot. 21.

of the LtJcks on that Part of the River had raised the Mailers of Barges and other Vessels, at some of thd Locks a fourth Part, at others half, and at some treble* more, than was paid, when the said Act was in Force.

That the said Robert Hooper and Hall said, that the Occupiers of the said Locks imposing such extravagant Rates for Water Carriage of Goods, has been a very great Prejudice to the Navigation, and a great Diminution to the Trade in general of the several Counties, through which the said River runs, as also prejudicial to the Trade of the City of London, and Parts adjacent.

Robert Hooper, being further examined, said, that there was paid, in many Places, double the Price, that was paid , formerly, for Towing-paths, and for passing over the several Ferries and Bridges Upon the River, and that upwards of Threescore Men are now employed to each Barge to tow it, when Six Horses might be sufficient for that Purpose; and that would be of much lei's Expence to the Barge-masters, and less Damage to the Grounds, wherein the Towing-paths are: And also said, that, for Twenty Years together, he never paid any thing for towing his Barge below Kingsisn Bridge, but now is obliged to pay 5a. a Quarter.

Lazvrence Wyat, being examined, laid, that formerly Barge^mallers paid nothing for towing their Barges between Carryot's Wear and Stroud a little above the City of Oxford, but now pay conllanrly Two Guineas a Year for the lame.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to revive an Act, made in the Sixth and Seventh Years of the Reign of the late King William the Third, intituled,

Mr. Lyjler reported from the Committee, to whom Crackley the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto Bank and subscribed, appointed to put in Execution an Act, passed Shrewfbur/ in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King W 5 George the First, for repairing the Reids," therein mentioned, between Crackley Bank, in the Parish of alias Shiffnall, and the Town of Shrewsbury, in the County of Salop, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directecl him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, dated the Third Day of February instant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition;

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners laid before the Committee the Act of Parliament, mentioned in the Petition; whereby several Tolls and Duties were granted, for defraying the Expences of repairing the Roads, to continue payable for the Term of 21 Years.

And then

Mr. John Wyke was called; who said, that at the Time of passing the Act of Parliament, for repairing the Roads, the same were so very bad, that many Parts thereof were in the Winter Season dangerous to Passengers:

That the Roads, directed to be repaired by the said Act, being Thirty Miles in Length, and Materials, fit to amend the fame, lying at a great Distance, the Trustees, appointed to put the Act in Execution, borrowed Money on the Credit thereof, as they were impowered to do.

That it appeared to the Committee, the Trustees have borrowed, in the whole, the Sum of f. 3,000. and that the same has been applied according to the Directions of the Act; and, although the Money borrowed, and what has been collected by the Tolls, has been duly applied and laid out, yet the Roads are still very bad in several Places.

And the said John Wyke said, that the Money, collected by the Tolls, amounts to between Three and Four hundred Pounds per Annum; which being far short of die Sum necessary to be raised yearly for amending the Roads,

and Roger Jackson, Esquires, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and the other Trustees, appointed to put in Execution an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, intituled, "An Act for repairing " and widening the Road from Hill, near

" Buxton and Chapel in the Frith, in the County of " Derby, to Manchester, in the County of ,"

was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 2d of this Inllant proceeded to examine the Matterof the said Petition.

That the Act of Parliament, of the Eleventh of his late Majesty, mentioned in the Petition, for repairing the hid Roads, was laid before the Committee; whereby several Tolls were granted, and the said Act was to continue in Force for Twenty-one Years.

Then the Petitioners called Wm. Wright, Esquire; who said, that the said Roads, before the passing of the said Act, were so very bad in many Places, that they were almost impaflabie; and, in order to make the same passable, the Trustees borrowed several Sums of Money upon the Credit of the said Toll and Duties; and that there is now due upwards of £. 5,252. for Principal and interest:

That the greatest Part of the Toll has been raised by Horses, carrying Malt from Derby, and the Parts adjacent, into Cheshire-, but Malt has, since the Road was in part repaired, been chiefly carried by Carts, drawn with Two Horses; which has very much lessened the Profit of the Toll.

The same Witness further laid, that the Money, lo borrowed, cannot be repaid, nor the Roads amended, and kept in Repair, unless the Term, granted by the former Act, be enlarged, and the Toll augmented.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making more effectual an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing and widening the Road from brook Hill, near Buxton and Chapel in the Frith, in the County of Derby, to Mambefer, in the County of Lancaster\ and that Mr. Legh Master and Mr. Cholmondeley do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Sir John Dutton reported from the Committee, to Stroudwater whom the Petition of the several Gentlemen, Clothiers, Navigation, and other chief Inhabitants, and Traders, living in, or near, the Towns of Strowd and Bijley, and the several Townships, Hamlets, and Villages, of Chalford, wrth, and Woodchester, and other adjacent Places, in the County of Gloucester, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House:

And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 28th of January last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and, to prove the Allegations thereof, Witnesses were called, and examined; viz.

Mr. John Hoar ,being examined, said, that the River,

called Stroudwater, in the County of Gloucester, from the River Severn, near Framiload, to a Place called Wall-bridge, near to the Town of Strowd, is capable of being made navigable for Boats of about Sixty Ton:

That it is proposed to make Twelve Locks, each Seven Foot and an half wide, and one whereof to be made . sufficient effectually to prevent all Inundations. He laid, the Tide now flows up as far as Whitminster, which is j about a Mile and half: That the Cuts, being intended to be Thirty-three Foot wide, and Five Foot deep, will carry off Inundations much sooner, than they are now earned off: That there are Nineteen Mills between Wallbridge and the Severn-, and a Pipe of Four Inches Diameter, will be sufficient to supply the River, and that will not prejudice the Mills, for want of Water: That the whole Expence of making the said River navigable will be under Twenty Thousand Pounds, as well for making Satisfaction for Injuries, as for perfecting the intended Navigation, valuing the Land at Forty Shillings per Acre, and at Thirty Years Purchase: And said, the.

Length of the new Cut is proposed to be Eight Miles and a Quarter; which, when perfected, will be of great Benefit to the Land-owners adjacent thereunto, and be a Means to draw off the Water much sooner, upoa Floods, than it now runs off.

Mr. Edward Baghot, being examined, said, that the making this River navigable will be of great Benefit to all the Traders in the Woollen Manufactory in the County of Gloucester, particularly, by having Oils,

Dying Materials, and Wool, and Yarn, from Btiftol, at much cheaper Rates, than is now paid for the Carriage of the fame; as also Coals, great Quantities whereof are used in dying, as well as for the Use of the Families thereabouts. He said further, that great Quantities of Grocery Wares, Deals, and Timber, are brought from Bristol, for the Use of the Inhabitants; and that the Navigation will be of great Benefit to that Part of the Country, by bringing great Quantities of Corn from distant Places,

whereby the Poor will be relieved, and Provisions furnished at least Eight Pounds Centum cheaper, than they now are: And said, that the Price of Com is always Four Pence per Bushel dearer at Strowd, than in any other Markets in the County; which, if the intended Navigation is completed, will become as cheap, or cheaper, than it is sold at Gloucester, where it is generally sold at Six Pence per Bushel cheaper, than at Strowd: That the Land Carriage from Gloucester to Strowd is more expensive, than the Water Carriage from Brist to Gloucester; and that but Four Pence per Hundred is paid for Water Carriage from Bristol to Gloucester, being 30 Miles, and Eight Pence per Hundred for Carriage by Land from Gloucester to Strowd: That the Roads are so bad, that Wheel Carriages for Goods can't pals above Four Months in the Year.

John Crips, being examined, confirmed what Mr. Baghot laid; and further said, that Timber, for the Use of Mills, is Eight Pence per Foot cheaper at Bristol, than at Gloucester, besides the Expence of Land Carriage from

Gloucester to Strowd j and this Timber might, if the River is made navigable, be brought from the Koreft of Dean as cheap to Strowd, as it is brought to Bristol.

And he added, that about Ten thousand Ton of Coal will be furnished by this Navigation, at Four Shillings or Five Shillings per Ton cheaper thanusual; which will be of great Eale to the Poor, as well as others.

A Petition of the Ministers, Churchwardens, Overseers Worcester of the Poor, and principal Inhabitants, of the several Workhouse, Parishes of the City of Worcester, was presented to the &c-House, and read; alleging, that, pursuant to an Act, of the Second Year of the Reign of the late Queen Anne, by Poor's Rates upon the several Parishes of the said City, and by liberal Contributions of several charitable Persons, a large Workhouse was erected there, and the Poor of the whole City were set at Work, and maintained there, for some few Years; after which, the Governors, not being able to goon with the Workhouse, the Poor were returned back to their respective Parishes, and then the Common Council, called the Chamber of the City, took the Work-house into their Possession, and placed the Hop Market there, and set out several other Parts of the Workhouse for Dwellings, and Warehouses, of which none of the said Parishes have had any Benefit: And therefore praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for reviving, and continuing, the said Act, and establishing the said Workhouse for the future, or that the Rents and Profits of the said Workhouse, and the Benefits and Advantages arising therefrom, may be settled, established, and applied, to and for the Ule and Benefit of the several Parishes of the said City, towards the providing for, and maintaining their respective Poor, in proportion and according to their respective Quotas, which they severally raised, and paid, towards the building the said Workhouse, and letting the Poor at work, and maintaining them there, as aforesaid, with such Powers and Authorities, and under such restrictions, and in such Manner, as this House shall think fit.

Hugh Clopton, Esquire, said that he knows the Road,

leading from Stratford upon Avon, through Aldermarjion and Shipston, to the Top of Long Compton Hill, in the County of Warwick, which is about Twelve Miles in

Length, and that the same is become so bad, that in the Winter Seaton Horltrmen can't travel through the same without Danger, notwithstanding the Statute-work has been constantly performed, and Six Pence in the Pound raised.

The same Witness gave F.vidence, that, by reason of the Badness of the Road mentioned in the Petition, the Tradesmen of Shipston, a Market Town, and the Inhabitants of the several other Towns and Villages near the Road, within Ten Miles of Stratford upon Avon, in a plentiful Country for Corn and Grain, are in a great measure prevented, in the Winter Season, from carrying their Corn, and other Commodities, to Market, which is chiefly supplied from those Places; and they are also prevented from carrying from the said Market, Coals, and likewise Timber for building, as also such Merchants Goods, as come up the River Avon, and are landed at Stratford, with which they have been constantly supplied, and not only those Places, but a great many of such Parts of Oxfordshire, as lie near the Road.

And Mr. Clopton said, that the Trustees, appointed to act separately by the Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Roads, leading from Birmingham, through Warwick, to Warmington, and from Birmingham, through Stratford upon Avon, to Edghill, in the County of Warwick, have erected a Toll-gate on the Road from Stratford to Shipston, being one of thecross Roads, leading out

of the Highway or Road, by the said Act appointed to be repaired, at which the Inhabitants of the said several Towns and Villages, mentioned in the said Petition, pay a Toll, though they receive no Benefit from it: The laid Trustees are will-ng and desirous, that there may be but one Toll t:.k tup in the same Road.

Mr. Mafott, being examined, confirmed what was

said by Mr. Clopton; and also gave Evidence, that, as a Person travelled through the Road mentioned in the Petition, his Horse threw him near Shipston Toll-gate, and broke his Leg; and that the Badness of the Road was the Occasion thereof; and by that Fall loft his Life.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing the Road, leading from a Gate, called Shipston Toll-gate, at Bridgiown, in the Parish of Old Stratford, in the County of Warwick, through Alderminster and Shipston upon Slower, to the Top of Long Compton Hill, in the said County; and that Mr. Dig by, Mr. Compton, and Mr. William Bromley, junior, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The said most Christian King does further promise and engage, not to give Leave, at any Time hereafter, to the Person above-mentioned to return to Avignon, or to pass through any Territory of France, under Pretext of returning either to Avignon, or to Lorrain, or even to set foot upon any Part at all of the Dominions of the said most Christian King, much less to abide there by any Name, or on any other Pretence whatever.

III.

The said most serene Kings, and the Lords the States General, do likewise promise and engage reciprocally, to refuse all Manner of Entertainment and Harbour to that Ally's Subjects, who have been, or shall be. declared Rebels, as (oon'as a Requisition to this Purpose shall be made by that Party contracting, whose Subjects those Rebels are reckoned to be; and also to compel the said Rebels to depart their respective Dominions within the Space of Eight Days from the Time the Minider of the said Ally shall have made the above-mentioned Requisition in the Name of his Mader.

IV.

The most Chridian King being sincerly desirous to execute, fully and wholly, all that has formerly been di-pulated with the French Crown, in relation to the Town of Dunkirk, and to perform all other Things, which might appear necessary to the King of Great Britain, for effectually destroying the Harbour of Dunkirk, as also, that all Suspicion of making a new Harbour at the Canal of Mar dick may be entirely removed, or even of applying the said Canal to any other Ule, than for carrying off the Waters, which otherwise would overflow that Country, and for the Commerce, necessary for supplying with Provisions, and subsiding, the Inhabitants of that Part of the Netherlands, which is only to be carried on by Vessels, not exceeding Sixteen Foot in Breadth; his most Chridian Majesty undertakes, and promises, to cauie all Things to be put in Execution, which M.

V.

As the End and genuine Design of this Alliance between the said Kings and States General, is to preserve mutually the Peace and Tranquillity of their respective Kingdoms, States, and Provinces, which was edablifiied by the lad Treaties of Peace between the most serene Queen of Great Britain, the most serene most Chridian King, and the said high and mighty Lords the States General of the United Provinces, concluded and signed at Utrecht on the Eleventh Day of April, in the Year of our Lord 1713, it is agreed, and concluded, that all and Angular the Articles of the said Treaties of Peace, (o far as they relate to the Interests of the said Three Powers re-(pedively, and each of them in particular, as also the Successions to the Crown of Great Britain in the Protedant Line, and to the Crown of France, according to the said Treaties, shall have their full Force and Effect; and the said most serene Kings, and the Lords the States General, promise their mutual Guaranty, for the intire Execution

of

3 Geo. II. 19 — 20° Februariu 451

of all, that is stipulated in the said Articles, so far as they relate (as is aforesaid) to the Successions, and Interests, of the said Kingdoms and Provinces, as also for the maintaining and defending of all the Kingdoms, Provinces, Territories, Rights, Immunities, or Advantages, which each of the said Allies respectively shall actually possess at the Time of signing this Alliance; for which End the said Kings, and States General, have consented, and agreed, that, if any one of the said Allies shall be hostilely attacked by any Prince or State whatever, the other- Allies shall immediately interpose their good Offices with the Aggressor, to procure Right to be done to the Party injured, and to induce the said Aggressor to abstain intirely from all farther Hostility.

VI.

But if these friendly Offices should not have the desired Effect, by reconciling both Parties, and obtaining Satisfaction, and Reparation of Damages, within the Space of Two Months, then those of the Parties contracting, who shall not be attacked, shall be obliged to assist their Ally without Delay, and shall furnish the Party attacked with the Succours hereunder specified; that is to say.

The King of Great Britain Eight thousand Foot, and Two thousand Horse;

The most Christian King Eight thousand Foot, and Two thousand Horse;

The States General Four thousand Foot, and One thousand Horse.

But if the Ally, who shall be engaged in War, in the Manner aforesaid, shall desire to have assistance by Sea, or shall chuse Money, rather than Land or Sea Forces, it shall be freely at his Option, the Subsidies, to be furnished, bearing always Proportion to the Forces above specified. 4

And, that no Dispute may arise hereupon, it is agreed, that One thousand Foot shall be computed at Ten thousand Guilders, Dutch Money7, a Month, and likewise One thousand Horle at Thirty thousand Guilders, of the same Money, a Month, reckoning Twelve Months to the Year; the naval Succours to be valued in the like Proportion.

Vtl.

It is also agreed, and stipulated, that, if the Kingdoms, Countries, or Provinces, of either of the Allies, shall be disturbed by intestine Revolts, or Rebellions, on account of the said Successions, or any other Pretence whatsoever, that Ally, who shall be involved in such Troubles, shall haveaRight to demand of his Allies the Affiilanceabove-mentioned, or such Part thereof, as he shall judge expedient, and this at the Expence and Chargeof the Allies, who stand obliged to give the said Succours; the same to be fumished within the Space of Two Months, after they shall be required; the Party requiring still having his Option, as aforesaid, whether he would have those Succours in Land or Sea Forces, or ,in ready Money: The Charge of the Assistance, to be furnished by Virtue of this Article, shall be repaid to the Allies, who expended it, within the Space of a Year after those Disturbances shall be quieted and composed: But if the said Succours should not be sufficient, the Allies shall agree between them upon a further Help; and, it the same should require, shall even declare War against the Aggressors, and assist the Party injured with all their Forces.

VIII.

The present Treaty shall be ratified by his Britannick Majesty, his most Christian Majesty, and the Lords, the States General; and the Instruments of Ratification, in due Form, shall be reciprocally exchanged within Four Weeks from the Day or signing this Alliance, or looner, if it can be done.

In Witness whereof, we, the under-written, being authorized with full Powers by his Britannick Majesty, his most Christian Majesty, and the Lords the States General of the United Provinces, have, in the Names of all the forementioned, signed the presentTreaty with our Hands,

Mr Waller Bacon reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Sheriffs, Citizens, and Commonalty, of the City of Norwich, in Common-council assembled, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 4th of February instant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and, to prove the Allegations thereof. Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. Daniel Meadows, Mr. Nehemiah Lodge, and Mr. William Crowe; who, being severally examined, said, that, against the time of an Election of Members, to serve in Parliament, and also Mayors, Sheriffs, Aldermen, and Common-council-men, for the City of Nor-

wich, the Freedoms of great Number of poor Men have been purchased by other People, at a very low Price, in order to their voting at such Elections, as, they should be desired; which has been the Occasion of many unhappy ControversiCs in the said City:

That, against the Time of an Election for Aldermen, and Comtnon-council-men, great Numbers of the Freemen have removed out of one Ward into another, in order to vote; and at the last Election of Corqnion-council-men many voted for Three several Wards; and the City Gaol being in Two Wards, the Prisoners therein have been oftentimes removed out of one Part of the said Gaol into the other, purely to give a Vote for each Ward; and, in relation to the Hospital Men, the Dispute has been, whether they should vote for the Ward, where they formerly dwelt, qr in the Ward, where the Hospitals are.

The Petitioners, to make good the Allegations in the Petition, relating to the Charter of the said City, laid the same before the Committee; whereby it appears, that Sixty Common-council-men are to be yearly elected for the said City, on Four certain Days successively, therein particularly specified; viz. Twelve for the Ward of Conisford, Sixteen for the Ward of Muncroft, Twenty for the Ward of Wymer, and Twelve for the Ward beyond the Water.

That the same Persons gave Evidence, that it is usual and customary, in the Election of Common-council-men, to elect each Person singly; but the time, allowed by the said Charter, is not sufficient, when such Elections are controverted, to elect more than Four or Five in one Day, the Number of Eledors in each Ward being very numerous.

And the same Witnesses said, that there has beeagreat Disputes between the Court of Aldermen, and Comr mons, about their Right of voting in Assemblies, and such Disputes have caused them to break up; whereupon the publick Business of the City has been obstruded; and that there has not been an Assembly, to continue fitting to go through the Business of the Day, ever since lait May was Twelve-month.

That by a late Act of Parliament, for eroding a Work-house in the City of Norwich, the City is made one Parish; by which means the City are often at a Loss for want of Evidences, in Cafes of Removals of poor Persons, relating to their Settlement.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better regulating Elections in the City of Norwichy and for preserving the Peace, good Order, and Government, of the said City; and that Mr. Waller Bacon, Mr. Britiffe, Sir Edmund Bacon, of Garboldisham, and Mr. Harbord, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Alderman Child reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, and others, having Estates in Houses in and about the City and Liberty of Westminster, and Parts adjacent, in behalf of themselve9 and others, and also the Petition of several Gentlemen, Freeholders, and others, having Estates in Houses in and about the City of London, and Parts adjacent, in behalf of themselves, and others, were referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House.: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the Report and Resolution were read, and are as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date 10th February last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petitions; and, to make good the Allegations of the fame, called

Mr. Edward Sheppard; who, being examined, fiiid, that the Bricks, made since the passing of the late Acts of Parliament, are not lo good, as they formerly were; and that the Size, prescribed by the fiiid Acts, being larger than usual, they will not dry, or burn, lb soon and well;

17 and

Bricks and Tiles making.

3 Geo. II.

and that Bricks arc much dearer; for that Stock Bricks, before the passing of the said Act, were sold at Twenty Shillings per Thousand, delivered by Land, and now Thirty Shillings; and that formerly the Price of Place Bricks was Fourteen or Fifteen Shillings a Thousand, delivered by Land, and now Nineteen or Twenty Shillings; and that a Rod of Biick Work was formerly done for Five Pounds Ten Shillings, and now Seven Pounds:

And gave further Evidence, that, since the obtaining of the said Acts, he has made several Thousand of Bricks with Spanish, for his own Use, believing them to be better: And said, that the Bricks, madepurfuant to the said Acts, will not bind with old Bricks, and consequently are very inconvenient to use in repairing of old Buildings.

Mr. William Mason said, that the Brick-makers burn large Quantities of Brick in Clamps, which are not so good, as when burnt in Kilns; and that the Bricks, now made, are not so good, as formerly there were, the Size being too large; and that Bricks will fell cheaper, if they were made smaller; and he hath bought Place Bricks at Fifteen Shillings a Thousand, before the pading the said Acts.

Mr. Thomas Scott, being examined, said, that Five Chaldrons of Coals were formerly used in burning One hundred thousand of Bricks, but, since the said Acts, they are obliged to use between Fourteen or Fifteen Chaldron for One hundred thousand of Bricks, and the Bricks not so good, and well burnt, as before:

That he has made large Quantities of Bricks, pursuant to the said Acts, and has now by him as many of those Bricks, as amount to the Value of Two thousand Pounds, or thereabouts, and cannot dispose of them, as he could have done, if they had not been made pursuant to the said Ads:

That in the burning of Bricks it costs Six Shillings per Thousand more in Kilns, than in Clamps; and that Bricks may be very good, when burnt in Clamps; and that Place Bricks, made pursuant to the said Acts, are Sixteen Shillings per Thousand, delivered by Water, and Fourteen Shillings at the Clamp; Red Stocks Five-and-twenty Shillings per Thousand at the Kiln; and Grey Stocks Eighteen Shillings per Thousand at the Clamps: And laid, that Bricks, made with Spanish, are burnt better, than those without.

Mr. Andrew Godfrey laid, that Bricks were formerly better burnt, than now, by reason that the Size, prescribed by the late Acts, are too large to bum well; and that Place Bricks, made pursuant to the said Acts, by Water are sold at Sixteen Shillings per Thousand, and Stock at Thirty Shillings:

That he was appointed a Searcher in pursuance of the said Acts, and made Searches at Brentford, and several other Places, and found Bricks made contrary to the said Acts; but the Brick-makers, to avoid the Penalties of the said Acts, pleaded, that the Bricks were made by Contract, and not for Sale:

That the Size of Bricks, made according to the said Acts, have been found veiy inconvenient, when used with old Bricks; and that Bricks, proper for Use, should be Eight Inches and Five Eighths long, Four Inches One Eighth broad, and Two Inches One Fourth thick, when burnt; which were the Size Bricks were made of, before the passing of the late Acts.

That the Committee came to the following Resolution; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Act, made in the Twelfth Year of his late Majesty's Reign, intituled, <c An Act to prevent Abuses u in the making of Bricks and Tiles, and to ascertain the 4c Dimensions thereof, and to prevent all unlawful Combinations amongst any Brick-makers, or Tile-makers, " within Fifteen Miles of the City of London, in order u to advance or enhance the Price of Bricks or Tiles," and the Act, made in the second Year of his present Majesty's Reign, for explaining and amending the said Act, have occasioned the making of bad Bricks, and the enhancing the Price thereof,

inquiry Into Mr. Oglethorpe, from the Committee, appointed to theJ?‘at,c enquire into the State of the Gaols of this Kingdom, ac-Caos* quainted the House, that the said Committee, having entered upon their Enquiry, into the State of the King's Bench Prison* did find, that several indirect Pra&iceshad been ufetl, to prevent, and elude, such Enquiry s And he made a Report thereof to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table* where the same was read* and is as follows j viz.

That it appeared to the Committee, that George Gray> an Attorney at Law, wrote several Letters to Richard Mullins, Esquire, Marshal of the King's Bench, dated the 2d, 21ft, and 22d, of February last, demanding a Debt Of £.1. 8s. on behalf of one Richard Powell; and fug-gefting, that if he would not pay the said Money, Powell could give Informations against him arid intimating, that he, Gray, could be of Service to Mr. Mullins, as he had been last Year to Mr. Bambridgt, to whom he had given a full Account of the Measures to be taken against him, by means of his being then employed under one of the Solicitors, concerned against Bdmbridge and Huggins.

That Gray afterwards came, by Appointment, to Mr, Mullins % House, and acquainted him, that PoWell talked of informing the Committee of a Murder, committed by him the said Mullins; but that, if Mullins would give him Three Guineas, he would prevent Powell's giving any Information against him to the Committee: That Mr. Mackay was employed in drawing up Informations, to be laid before the Committee; and that, if he, Mullins, would place Five Guineas in proper Hands, it might be an Advantage to him, the said Mullins, in respect to Mackay.

That on the 23d of February, Gray, by a Letter, written by himself, but signed by him in the Name of John Mackay, acquainted the Committee, that Richard Powell, Robert Elliott, and other Persons, named in the Letter* could give an Account of the Charities, and Usage, of the Prison, and also an account of the Death and Murder of Thomas Denham, Mr. Allen, and others, through the Cruelty of the Marftials.

And Gray the same Day wrote a Letter to Mr. Mullins, giving him an Account of the Contents of what he had laid before the Committee, and that be had taken Powell away, and prevented his giving Evidence before the Committee and advised Mr. Mullins to fend Two Guineas, the Remainder of which, after letting Powell have 25 Shillings, he fays, he, Gray, should soon expend in Mullins's Service* and that he. Gray, designed that Evening to drink with Elliott, meaning the aforesaid Robert Elliott.

And by the general Tenure of all the Letters he undertakes to prevent Evidence being given to the Committee and he did actually convey away the said Richard Powell, and suppressed his Evidence; and this, in order to get Money from the Marshal, and render the Enquiry of this Committee ineffectual.

The Marshal of the King's Bench having laid the afore-mentioned Letters before the Committee, they ordered Gray to attend. He complied not with the Two first Orders; but wrote, the 26th of February, to the Marshal, that he had received them and that the Party on the Morrow would lay the Matter before the Chairman of the Committee, if the Matter proposed was not complied with.

It appeared to the Committee, that the said George Gray had tampered with feme Witnesses, in respect of their Evidence to be given to this Committee, and had hindered others from appearing, or giving Evidence; and the Committee ordered the said Trania&ions to be reported to the House.

Resolved, nemine contradicente, That George Gray, Attorney-at Law, having tampered with some Witnesses, in respect of their Evidence to be given to the Committee, appointed by this House to enquire into the State of the Gaols of this Kingdom, and having hindered others from appearing, and giving Evidence to the said Committee,

A. 1729*

is guilty of a high Crime and Misdemeanor, in Breach of the Privilege of this House, and in Contempt of the Authority thereof.

Ordered, That the said George Gray be, for his said Offence, committed Prisoner to His Majesty's Prisonof the Gatehouse; and that Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrants accordingly*

Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as low Election, it appeared to them, touching the Election for the Borough of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks, and the Refblution of the Committee thereupon: Which Report he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table where the same was read and the Report and Resolution are as followeth; viz.

Upon the Petition of Sir John Guise, Baronet, complaining of an undue Election and Return of John Clavering, Esquire, to serve for the said Borough:

"that the Right of Election was agreed to be in the Inhabitants, paying Scotland Lot, and not receiving Alms.

The Petitioner's Counsel alleged, that there was a Club set up, and encouraged, by the fitting Member's Agents, who combined together* and agreed among themselves to vote for any Gentleman to be their Representative in Parliament, that would deposit One thousand Pounds in some sure Hand, to be divided equally among them after such Election and that there were about Sixty Persons engaged in this Combination, who voted, upon the Promise of a Dividend out of the One thousand Pounds and objected against Thirty-five of the fitting Member's Voters, as being bribed, and concerned in the Combination: To prove which, they called

Thomas Keen and Robert Seers; who gave Evidence, that they were of the Club that they were Fifty, or upwards; that they signed a Paper, which was a Declaration of their Intent to vote for a fresh Member; and accordingly One thousand Pounds was offered by Mr. William Loftin, if they would choose any Gentlemen, he should fend for and the Money was to be lodged in the Hand of Mr. James Herman: That about Thirty, or more, met Mr. Clavering, at Mr. Brewer's and that Mr. Clavering promised to be as good as his Word: And named Twelve Persons of the Club, that voted for Mr. Clavering, on account of having an equal Share with the rest of the Club: That Mr. Brewer, Mr. Herman, Mr. Loftin, and Mr. Hammond, a died as Agents for Mr. Clavering:

That Mr. Clavering came there on a Swiday, and the Election was on the Wednesday following: The Society, about a Month before the Election, agreed among themselves to have Money for their Votes; and the Sum fixed was one thousand Pounds, to be divided equally among the Club:

That Mr. Herman gave Money to several; and Thomas Keen, one of the Witnesses, owned, he had Five Guineas; and that William With said, he had Three Guineas; and they were to have Share of the Thousand Pounds besides;

That the Paper subscribed was about Ten Days before the Election: That Herman told them, he had the Thousand Pounds ready; and that Mr. Clavering was by; and that the Money was to be paid, as soon as Mr. Chivering was returned: And Robert Seers said, the Intent of signing the Paper was, to choose any Gentleman, who would give One thousand Pounds; but could not say, he ever heard Mr. Clavering promise, or mention, the Sum. He said, he could read but very little, and he signed a Paper, that was not read to him; but said, his Intent, in signing the Paper, was, to have Share of the Thousand Pounds.

Alexander Jones said, he never was present at the Club; but that it consisted of about Fifty, or Fifty-six, Persons:

That Robert East, Thomas Stephens, Richard Webb, and Wm. Hollis, told him, tiiey voted for Mr. Clavering, on account of the Share of the Thousand Pounds, promised by Mr. Loftin and Mr. Herman for the fresh Member:

That lie collected the Land Tax; and that Samuel Bafney told him, when he demanded the fame, that Money was scarce; and that the Division, he was to have of the Thousand Pounds, for the fresh Member, would come to Twelve Pounds One Shilling a Man; and that they had been paid before that time, had not Sir John Guise petitioned the House of Commons: And that John Carter told him, about Seven Weeks ago, that he had Five Pounds for his Vote, but could not say, it was Part of the Money premised the Club; and that he gave no Note for the fame.

Being cross-examined, he owned, Sir John Guise was his Matter, but not at the time of the Election: That he asked Votes for him, and paid Reckonings at Andrew Trust's by Sir John Guise's Order: That he was his Agent: He thought, it was before the Election; could hot say, wheft the Liquor was drank: Paid about Eighteen Shillings at Hall's, some time before the Election, and paid at Hollis's, for Three Barrels of Beer, Six Pounds, about a Fortnight before the Election: That he paid Money to Samuel Dowley for Clock Cafes.

Charles Etheridge and John Philips owned, they had signed the Paper, and were promised by Mr. Brewer and Mr. Loft in, Agents for Mr. Clavering, One thousand Pounds for the Club: That the Division would be Twelve Pounds One Shilling a Man: That they called themselves the Flying Squadron: That Mr. Brewer was one of the Club; (eldom miffed; and that he told them, that anybody, who voted for the frefo Member, should have his equal Share 5 and that Sir John Guise's Petition prevented the Disposition of the Money: That John Butler, Mr. Brewer, John IVebb, Anthony Field, and Joseph Gray, agreed to vote, for the»r Share of the Thousand Pounds: And John Philips gave Evidence, that he worked for Mr. Herman, who told him, the Duke of St. Albans and Mr. Clavering had given a Note for the Thousand Pounds; and he, being desirous to see the Note, agreed to give a Pint of Wine for the Sight of it: Upon which Mr. Herman fetched it, and shewed it to him: That it was the 23d of August last was Two Years: That he set it down in his Pocket Book: That he flood dole by Mr. Herman; and that the Note began, " I f< promise to pay:" Said, he (aw Two Letters, which Herman told him, flood for the Duke of St. Albans' Name; and that Mr. Claveringhad signed it; and that it Was Security for the Money: Said, that the 1 and Three o's were Two or Three Lines below; and that Mr..Herman would not let him read it: That the Figures were intermixed among the Writing; and that Mr. Cla-verinr promised the Money before and on the Day of Election.

He said, that Lord Grandison was agreed at first to stand a Candidate, and they would have brought him in handsome; but, upon the Expectation of Five hundred Pounds to be distributed among them, he dropt their Interest.

William Buck, Richard Cock, Jeremiah Goodchild, Charles Carter, and Wm. Reading, gave Evidence, that they received Money for their Votes for Mr. Clavering, from Mrs. Brewer, Mr. Loftin, Mr. Herman, and Mr. Richard Lane; and that they were promised, besides, a Share of the Thousand Pounds.

Henry Williams, Thomas Pudsey, Wm. Hey croft, and John Burgess, gave Evidence, that they voted for Mr. Clavering, because they were promised an equal Share of the Thousand Pounds by Mr. Herman, Mr. Loftin, and Mr. Prat.

The fitting Member's Counsel observed, that the Evidence on behalf of the Petitioner had not proved Bribery, on the fitting Member; and alleged, that the Evidence given did not amount to a Proof of the pretended Note of the Duke of St. Albans and Mr. Clavering; and also alleged, that they should prove the Petitioner guilty of Bribery in many Circumstances: To prove which, they called

Andrew Trufi and Samuel Dowley; who gave Evidence, that they had Five Guineas each given them for their Votes Vol. 21,

for Sir John Guifi; and that John Bidet (lately dead) told him, he had Five Guineas likewise for his Vote; and that Sir John Guifi, when he few the Poll, said, it was a fair Poll, and did not object against the same: He said, Fifty-six or more, had agreed not to choose Sir John Guise: That they were of the Club, but signed no Paper: That they met, and spent their own Money: That they never heard of any Promise of a Thousand Pounds for their Votes, but were resolved to choose a new Member, because Sirjflfoi Guise and Mr. Waller had agreed, and given out, that they would keep out any body else* Andrew Trufi said, he kept a publick House; and that the Club did meet at his House in Turn, as well as others.

John Law said, that he knew one Oxland, that was an Agent for Sir John Guise; and that he gave Mark Hollis> a Neighbour of his, for a Sow and Pigs, Six Pounds, upon account of his voting for the Petitioner, though they were worth no more than One Pound Fifteen Shillings: That William Boverington told him, about a Year ago, that he had Twelve Guineas to vote for Sir John Guise, about Two Months before the Election: That he was Cryer of the Court; and that Sir John Guise said* the Election was very fair; and that Richard Hall, one of the returning Officers, told him, that Sir John Guise directed him to return the fitting Member.

John Prat said, he knew James Biggs $ Who told him, he had Nine Guineas for his Vote, of Sir John Guifi, or his Agents: That he was one of the Club, and never heard of a thou land Pounds promised by Mr. H&mdn, to return Mr. Clavering, nor never heard of such a Contract: Said, they resolved not to choose Sir John Guise> because his Tenants were hardly used by him: Said, there was a talk amongst a Parcel of Women, of a Chach-full of Money being lent down: And laid, he would take the Sacrament, that he never heard of any Money to be given for the Choice of a frefti Member: That he never was at the Club after the Election; and owned, he signed the Declaration for a fresh Member:

William Loftin, Esquire, gave Evidence, that he settled the Club against Sir John Guise, from some personal ill Usage he had received from Sir John: That at first they confided of about One-and-twenty Persons, and were called the Flying Squadron; afterwards they increased to about Seventy: That Lord Grandison offered to stand: That he promised him his Interest, if he would oppose Sir John Guife\ but his Lordship declined (landing: That since they had shewed their Teeth, and, upon talking with them, he found, he should have a Majority: That they promised to stand by him, and accordingly signed the Paper, as above-mentioned: That there was Talk of a Thousand Pounds to be given; but that it was never talked of in the Club, when he was present; but the First Report, he heard of it, came from Sir John Guise's House: He found, this Report encouraged his Party; and said, he did not think it his Business to un* deceive them: That they said, they would choose him, if he did not provide a Gentleman to represent them. And, being cross-examined, he said, when Mr. Ciavering came down, he was pretty much with him: That he never heard Mr. Clavering make any Promise: That Mr. Herman, Mr. Brewer, Mr. Hammond, and himfdf, met him on the Sunday before the Election: That the Election Day was the First time he heard of the Report of the Thousand Pounds Gratuity, to be given for choosing a Member: And he further said, that the Club confided of about Seventy Persons at the lead.

Then the Committee, in pursuance of an Order of Instruction to the Committee, for enquiring, why the Commissioners, for building 50 new Churches, had not rebuilt the Parish Church of St. Giles in the Fields, in the County of Middlesex> according to an Act of Parliament, passed in the Fourth Year of his late Majesty's Reign, proceeded to examine into that Matter.

That the Committee inspected the said Commissioners Books of Minutes, usually taken at their Meetings, but find no Mention made of rebuilding the said Parish Church.

That the said Mr. Philips, by Direction of the Commissioners, delivered a Paper to the Committee, containing the Reasons of the Commissioners for not having rebuilt the said Parish Church of St. Giles in the Fields; the Substance of which Reasons was, That the Commissioners had built, and finished, a Church in Bloomsbury, within the same Parish; and that they thought it their Duty to provide first for those Parishes, where Churches were most wanted.; and, in pursuance of this Rule, they had built several new Churches, repaired, and enlarged, several Chapels, and converted them into Parish Churches.

That it did not appear by any Entry in the Commissioners Books, or by any Papers in their Office, that any Application had been made to their Board for rebuilding St. Giles9s Church.

Whereupon the Committee ordered the Vestry Books of the Parish of St. Giles to be laid before them; wherein is an Order, dated the 21st Day of February 1718, directing, that Application should be made to the Commissioners, for rebuilding the said Parish Church of St. Giles: And the said Mr. Milner acquainted the Committee, that he, with other Parilliioners, had attended the then Commissioners, and desired, the said Parish Church might be rebuilt; but had in Answer from Doctor Hough (now Bishop of Worcester) who was in the Chair, to this Effe<ft, That the Commissioners did own their Obligation to rebuild the said Church; but that it was not then a fitting Opportunity, and that they should take some more convenient Time.

That by another Order of the said Vestry, made the 30th of July 1724, a Memorial was directed to be presented to the Commissioners, objecting to the DistridV assigned to the said new-intended Parish; in which Memorial Application is made, in express Words, to the Commissioners, to rebuild the said Parish Church of St. Giles.

That it further appeared to the Committee, by the Evidence of the said Mr. Milner, and Edward Liney, That the said Parish Church was in a ruinous Condition, very damp, and unwholesome, by reason it lies much lower than the Church Yard; and that the Parish ioners of the old Parish would, by this intended Division of the Parish, be utterly disabled from rebuilding, or supporting, the said old Parish Church, without some Assistance.

That Mr. Philips delivered to the Committee a List of such Churches, as were endowed, and of those, that were unendowed; one whereof is the Church in Bloomsbury.
