Mr. Alderman Perry reported from the Committee, importing to whom the Petition of several Merchants of the City of Salt into London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf ^tw York; of his Majesty's Colony of Nezv York in America, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Report and Refutation are as follows;

That the Committee, pursuant to the 0>der of the House, dated the 24th Day of February last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the Petition, and called the following Witnesses; viz.

Mr. Wm.Bryan, and Mr Charles Cromlake: And they,

being severally examined, said, that the Colony of Neztl York, in North America, is commodiously situated for the F.stablishment of a Fishery, there being great Quantities of BaJjj Shad, Heirine, Sardine, Sturgeon, and other kind of merchantable Fish; but that they are often in want of Salt, which is a great Hindrance to them in carrying on their Fishery; and, if the said Hland had the same Indulgence, as the Inhabitants of England and Newfoundland have, to ship and lade Salt in any Port of Europe, for their Fishery, the same would be of great Advantage to the Inhabitants thereof.

Then the Petitioners produced a Copy of a Report, made by the Corr.missioners of his Majesty's Customs to the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, wherein is the' following Paragraph: "That, for as much as there may " be a considerable Fishery on the Coast of New Torkf " we are humbly of opinion, so far as relates to the Customs, that, to prevent any Doubt, the like Liberties " may be given to carry Salt from any Part of Europe,

" for the Fisheries of New York, as have been granted to " New England, and Newfoundland, by a Clause in feme

" Act to be passed in Parliament."

And it appearing to the Committee, that the Petitioners had made good the Allegations of their Petition, the Committee came to the following llesolution;-viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That it will be of great Advantage to the Trade of Great Britain, and to the Inhabitants of the Colony of Nezo York, to import Salt from any Port of Europe, for Encouragement of the Fishery there.

The said Rdislution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon* agreed unto by the House.

That the present Annuity, or yearly Fund, of One hundred and Sixty thousand Pounds, payable to the East India Company, in respect to their capital Stock, or Debt from the Publick, of Three Millions and Two hundred thousand Pounds, be, from and after the Twenty-ninth Day of September, One thousand Seven hundred and Thirty, reduced to an Annuity, or yearly Fund, of One hundred and Twenty-eight thousand Pounds, redeemable by Parliament, on One Year's Notice, after the Fiye-and-twemieth Day of March, One thousand Seven hundred and Thirty-six, and on Payment to them of their said whole capital Debt ip one intire Payment, or on Payments from time to time, on fuel) Notices, as aforesaid, of any SumorSums, notlefsthanFivehundred thousand Pounds at a time, in Part thereof, till the whole be completed.

1. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the East India Company do and shall pay and advance into the Receipt of his Majesty's Exchequer, on or before the Twenty-fourth Day of , One thousand

Seven hundred and Thirty, the Sum of Two hundred thousand Pounds without any Interest, or Addition to their capital Stock, or Debt, for the fame, to be applied towards the Supplies, granted to his Majesty, for the Service of the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Thirty.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That in Consideration of the Content and Agreement of the East India Company to reduce their present Annuity, or Fund, and to advance and pay into the Exchequer the Sum of Two hundred thousand Pounds fertile Ule of the Publick, and to subject their Right, or Claim, to the whole and folc Trade to the East Indies, exclusive of all others, to be redeemable and determinable by Parliament, that all former Grants, made to them by any Act or Acts of Parliament, or any Charter or Charters, granted in pursuance thereof, of any Right or Title to be and conunut a Corporation, for trading to the East Indies with a joint Stock, and to hold and enjoy the whole and foie Trade to th tEast Indies, exclusive of all others, for ever, be

ratified and confirmed to them, freed and dischargpdfrom all former Provisoes, or Powers of Redemption, subject nevertheless to a new Provilb, or Power, for Parliament to determine their Right or Interest in the whole and foie Trade to the East Indies, exclusive of ail others, upon Three Years Notice alter the Twenty-fifth Day of March,

Upon the second-mentioned Petition.

Mr. Pibus, Mr. Wellard, Phineas Stranger, and others, were severally examined, and said, that the Road from Parham Downes to Dover Town's End is in the Winter Season very^bad, and dangerous for Carts and other Carriages, travelling through the fame, being deep and narrow; and, although the Inhabitants of the Parishes, wherein the Road lies, have done the Statute-work, and applied £.20. out of the County Stock, appropriated for that Purpose, and £ 10. given by the Dean and Chapter of Canterbury, and other Moneys, raised by Contribution, yet the fame, which hath been duly applied towards repairing the said Road, has proved ineffectual to put the Road into good Repair; and the Inhabitants of the Parishes, through which that Road lies, are so poor, that they are not able to do more, than has been done; and, unless some Assistance be given by Parliament, for repairing this Road, it will be impofGble for Carts and other Carriages to pass and repass through the same in the Winter Season, without Danger.

Upon the Third Petition,

John Derm and Richard Hollenbury, being examined, said, that the Road from a Place, called the Red Pump, in the said City of Canterbury, to Sturrey Bridge, about Two Miles in Length, and Part of the Road to thelfle of Thanet, is in so ruinous a Condition, that Carts and other Carriages can't travel through the fame, notwithstanding the Statute-work has been constantly done, and Six Pence in the Pound raised for 20 Years past, and duly applied towards repairing the fame.

The Witnesses further said, that about a Quarter of a Mile of the last mentioned Road, viz. from the said Red Pump to the Archbishop's Palace, is extraparochial; and that several Sums of Money have been given by the Dean and Chapter of Canterbury towards repairing and amending the same, but that has not been sufficient for that Purpose.

Mr. Pelham, of Lewes, reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, and other the Inhabitants, of the Towns of Lewesy Seaford, Brighthelme-Jlony Newhaven, and Places adjacent, in the County of Sussex, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 24th of February last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and to prove the Allegations thereof,

Captain Richard Lemon was called, and examined; who said, that he had known Newhaven Fifty Years, and upwards; and that there was a Timber Pier standing, when he first knew the Place, and so continued for about Thirteen Years after; and, during that Time, there was a good and safe Harbour, for the Reception of Ships of a considerable Burthen, which was very useful, and of great Advantage to Merchants Ships and Vessels, in order to carry Corn Coastways, and exporting the same into foreign Parts; and likewise would be very useful for conveying of Timber into his Majesty's Docks and Yards, great Quantities whereof are annually sent thither:

That, for want of some Provision to maintain and keep up the said Pier, the same is intirely gone to Decay, and the Harbour is become very bad; and the Mouth of it being stopped up, causes the Water to run into the Sea a great way to the Eastward of the Pier, to the great Damage of the Harbour, and Prejudice to the Merchants, and Persons living the reabouts.

Ben. Court, Gabriel Eyres, and Benjamin Swaine, being severally examined, said, that they had known this Harbour for several Years past, and have frequently seen Ships and Vessels (hut up and confined therein for several Months, by reason the Mouth thereof was stopped up, that the Ships and Vessels could not lall out, till the Mouth of the Harbour had been dug up, and opened.

Benjamin Swaine gave further Evidence, that he once knew the Price of Coals advanced from Two-and-twenty Shillings to Forty-five Shillings per Chaldron, by reason of the Harbour being intirely stopped up.

John Reynolds, an Engineer, laid, that he had viewed the Harbour and Pier; and that the same may be repaired, and made useful, for between Two and Three thousand

Pounds

Newbavea

Harbour.

3 Geo. II.

Pounds; and when put into'a good Condition, will be capable of receiving such Ships, as will draw Eighteen or Twenty Foot of Water, and will prevent the many Wrecks, that have frequently happened, and be a very useful and safe Port in time of War, and be of great Advantage to the Merchants, and Inhabitants, of the several Towns and Places, which lie near the fame.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for restoring, and rebuilding, the Haven and Pier of New-haven, in the County of Sussex; and that Mr, Pelham of Lewes, Mr. Pelham of Stanmore, Mr. Secretary at War, Mr. Butler, Sir William Gage, and Mr. Attorney-general, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Incorporation by Queen Elizabeth, and Grants from the / Crown, the Cursitors, who have their Offices for Life, are entitled to the foie making out all original Writs, and Writs of Summons in the Nature of original Writs, of which Nature are the civil Bills, and Summons thereupon, mentioned in the Bill depending before this House, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts; and prayiifg, that Regard may be had to the Preservation of their ancient Rights and Freeholds, and, in case the said Bill should oafs, that the Cursitors, for the Time being, in their respective Counties, by themselves, or Deputies at their Nomination, residing in the said Counties, and conforming in all respects to the Tenor and Meaning of the Bill, may be appointed to make out the Summons, which, they apprehend, are in the nature of their original Writs, and all the Process subsequent thereupon, or have such other relief, as to the House shall seem just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, be read a Second time.

A Petition of the Filazers of his Majesty's Court of Common Pleas at Westminster was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that the Filazers are ancient Officers for Life, and, in right of their Offices, they make out the mesne Proceisof that Court, and enter the Appearances of Defendanis, at a very small Charge, and have never been guilty of any Misdemeanor; but, if the Method, proposed by the Bill depending in this House, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, takes place, the Profits of their Offices will not answer the Expence of the due Execution of them: And therefore, relying upon the Justice of the House, to continue them the full Enjoyment of their Offices, or make them some reasonable Satisfaction for the Loss they willsustain by the said Bill, they pray, they may be heard by their Count'd, and be relieved, by being made Clerks of the civil Bills in their respective Counties, or otherwise, as to the House shall teem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, be read a Second Time.

The Committee came to the following Resolutions j viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the best Assize of Bricks, for Sale, is Eight Inches and Five Eighths long, Two Inches and a Half thick, and Four Inches and a Quarter broad, when burnt.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Twenty Load of Spanish, fifted through a Sieve of Half an Inch wide, not exceeding Thirty-six Bushels in each Load, be allowed to the making of One hundred thousand of Bricks.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Brick-makers be it Liberty, in burning of their Bricks, to join a Clamp of Stock Bricks to a Clamp of Place Bricks.

The said Resolutions, being severally retd a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Wigtown, Mr. Earle (according to Order) reported from the &c. Election. Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Election for the District* of Burghs of Wigtown, Whithorn, New Galloway, and Stanrawer, and the Resolution of the Committee thereupon: Which Report he read in his Place, and after-' wards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the said Repdrt and Resolution are as follows; viz.

Upon the Petition of the Magistrates, Town Council, and Clerk, of Wigtoun, complaining, that at the late Election of a Burgess, to serve for the District of Burghs of Wigtoun, Whithorn, New Galloway, and Stanrawer, John Dalrymple, Esquire, pretended to be elected at Stanrawer, whereas, by the Statute in that same provided, the Election ought to have been Voi,. 21.

at Wigtoun, and the Return made by the common Clerk of the said Butgli; and praying such Relief, as the House shall think fit.

The Committee have examined the Matter of thefald Petition.

The Petitioners Counsel alleged, that, according to the Act of Union, the Representative to‘Parliamen t, for the District of Burghs of Wigtoun, New Galloway, Stranrawer, and Whithorn, ought to have been chose, and returned, from the then presiding Burgh of WigtottH, according to the Order and Turn of the said Burgh, and in pursuancd of the said Act; and that the Return ought to have been made by the common Clerk of the said Burgh of Wigtoun, and not from the Burgh of Stranrawer, from which the fitting Member was returned, irt Prejudice to the Rights of Election in Scotland, so arixiously guarded b the said Act of Union.

The Counsel on behalf of the fitting Member alleged^ that the Return was good, and Three of the Commiifl-sioners for the said District of Burghs had voted for thd fitting Member; and that therefore the Commissioners of any of the presiding Burghs, in this Cafe, had not a Power to decide the Return, as if the Votes were equal, pursuant to the Act of Union.

And that therefore, if there had been any Mistake in relation to the Direction of the Writ to the proper Buigh in Turn, it ought therf to have been protested against, and Instruments indue Form taken thereupon: And infilled, that, as there was no proper Complaint made at the Time of the said Election, that the Return was good,' anti according to the Act 6® Anna, c. 6. for rendering‘the Union of the Two Kingdoms more intire and complete^" Which (amongst other Things) enacts, ' "

" And, in case a Vacancy shall happen in Time of " Parliament, by the Decease, or legal Incapacity, of " any Member, a new Member shall be elected in his " room, conformable to the Method herein before appointed; and in case such Vacancy be 6f a Reorefentative for any of the said Fourteen Classes of District

" of the said royal Boroughs, that Borough, which €‘ presided at the Election of the deceased, or disabled,

" Member, shall be the presiding Borough at such riew " Election."

Upon which, the Counsel for the Petitioner replied and infilled, that the Borough of Stranrawerwzs not th^ presiding Borough at the last Election, in Turn; and therefore, as the Sheriff had given an undue' Precedency, that was no Rule to go by, but ought to be settled in right Course here.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion this Committee, that Jahn Dalrymple, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the District of Burghs of Wigtoun, Whithorn, New Galloway, and Stranrawer.

Mr. Nicholas Masters and Ufeby ,being severally examined, said, that they have had very great Loflls, by the rotting of their Sheep, bad Crops of Corn, Trespatfes, and other inconveniencies: That the said common Fields are very fit and proper to be inclosed, and will be of great Advantage to the several Freeholders and Owners of the same: That the said common Fields are now let at Six Shillings per Acre, and, if the same were inclosed, would fetch Sixteen Shillings per Acre:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in lieu of the Duties and Revenues, now charged with the Fund, or Annuity, payable to the East India Company, an Annuity, or yearly Sum, of One hundred and Twenty-eight thousand Pounds, be charged on the several Duties and Revenues, commonly called the Aggregate Fund, to be payable to the East India Company from the Twenty-niath of September, One thousand Seven hundred and Thirty, for and as their new Annuity Fund, or Interest of their capital Stock, or Debt, of Three millions Two hundred thousand Pounds, subject to such Redemption by Parliament, as shall be enacted concerning the same.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Provision be made, that any Deficiencies, which may happen in the Fund, commonly called the South Sea Company's original Fund, short of what will be sufficient to pay the said Company their Annuity, or Allowances, charged thereon, shall from time to time be made good, quarterly, out of the Moneys arisen, or to arile, for the Duties and Revenues composing the Aggregate Fund.

James Gambier, Esquire, being examined, said, that he last Year accepted of the Office of Warden of the Fleet, during Pleasure, for the Life of Thomas Bambridge, upon the Belief, that the Tenure would be altered to good Behaviour, removeable by Address from either House of Parliament: That he grounded this Belief on a Bill, that had passed the House of Commons last Year, nemine con-tradicente, by which the Sense of the House appeared to be, that it was for the publick Good, that the Office of the Warden of the Fleet should be grantable by the Crown, during good Behaviour only, and the future Wardens be removeable, upon Address from either House of Parliament j and the said James Gambier was induced to

agree with the said Dougal Cuthbert for the Surrender of the said Patent, on the Payment of the Sum of £. 2,500. of which Sum he, the said Gambier, has already paid £. 500. to the end that such Regulations, as was intended,

should be made by Parliament, believing, that the Publick would pay the said £. 2,500.

Thomas Brafield, being examined, said, that, since the said Gambier hath held the Office of Warden, he hath been obliged to several Expences, for Repairs, and other Matters, which were absolutely necessary; particularly, that he hath rebuilt Part of the Womens Ward on the common Side, and "hath pulled down, and levelled with the Ground, the Dungeon on the Mailer Side, in which Ante perished: That he hath made several Reductions of Fees, and Chamber Rent; and that, from the former high Prices of Chamber Rent, he hath reduced the same to 2 s.6 d. per Week for each Room, fumished by him, and half of that Sum for each unfurnished Room, whether there be one or more Prisoners therein; so that, if there be Four Prisoners in a Room, furnished by the Warden, each pays j^d.per Week, and, if there be Four Prisoners in a Room, furnished by themselves, Ach pays the Half thereof; whereas formerly each Prisoner paid at the lead 2 s.6 d.per Head, though never so many lay in the same Room.

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

Resolved, That Mr. Richard Houghton be admitted to give Evidence of Persons having declared to him, that they would have voted for the fitting Member, if any, who were not sworn Freemen, had been allowed to vote.

The Counsel were again called in, and Mr. Speaker acquainted them therewith.

And the fitting Member's Counsel examined Mr. Houghton, and several other Witnesses.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

Strickland reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Owners and Matters of Ships, employed in the Coal Trade, belonging to the Port of Scarborough, in behalf of themselves, and many others, whose Names are not thereunto subscribed, and also the Petition of several Persons, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and others, Owners of Ships, employed in the Coal Trade, belonging to the Town of Whitby, in the County of York, and also the Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others, the Owners of Ships, employed in the Coal Trade, belonging to the Towns of Newcastle, Sunderland, &c. and also the Petition of several Persons, keeping Wharfs, and dealing in Coals, and other Goods, in the Cities of London, Westminster, and Parts adjacent, in behalf of themselves, and many others, and also the Petition of the Owners of Ships, employed in the Coal Trade, belonging to Great Yarmouth, in the County of Norfolk, were referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the lathe, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Report, and Resolutions of the Committee, are as follow; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Orders of Reference upon the several Petitions, proceeded to

examine the Matters, thereby complained of; and, to prove the fame, several Witnesses were called:

John Kitchingman, formerly a Matter, but now an Owner of a Ship, Henry Simpson, and John Lacy, who are Matters, and had belonged to the Coal Trade many Years, were severally examined, and said, that there are above One thousand Ships belonging to that Trade, 400 whereof trade to London; and that little Profit hath arisert by that Trade, for several Years part, there having not been made more than 1 and £ per Cent, for 12 Years, by reason there are not above 15 Persons, that buy a considerable Quantity of Coals, and those are Lightermen; and the Lightermen being incorporated, with exclusive Privileges and Powers, they raise and lower the Price of Coals, as they please, and prevent any other Persons from making use of any Lighters, or other Boats, for carrying Coals from or to any Part of the River of Thames:

That, the Coal Trade being under Discouragement, Ships have not of late been so well fitted out, and manned, as they were formerly; nor are the Matters of Ships able to take so many Apprentices; which prevents the bringing up of Seamen; and great Numbers of Matters have been reduced, by discouraging the Coal Trade: That, when Coal Ships have arrived in the River, the Matters thereof have been obliged, by the ill Usage of the Lightermen, to proceed to deliver their Coals into such Lighters, belonging to the Lightermen, before a Price has been agreed upon between such Matters, and the Lightermen, by reason it is in the Power of such Lightermen to prefer one Ship before another; which they often do: And that, since their Incorporation, they have demanded, and taken, a Premium of Six-pence, and sometimes Nine Pence, per Chaldron, for Coals; and have refused to give their Notes for Value received; and, when they have given their promissory Notes, such Notes frequently lie an unreasonable Time, after they are due; which is a great Prejudice to such Matters, who are the Endorsers, they being liable to make good any Loss, that happens, though it is 8 or 10 Months afterwards, such Notes not being protestable; but, if they were obliged to give their Notes for Value received, it would be an Encouragement in carrying on the Coal Trade.

John Kitchingman and Henry Simpson further gave Evidence, that they had made an Estimate of the Shipping, belonging to the Coal Trade at Wb tby, which amounts to near £. 170,000. but the Profit, made thereof, was no more than One and a half per Cent, per Annum, exclusive of Insurance; and to insure upwards and downwards amounts to 2 per Cent, per Voyage.

The same Witnesses gave Evidence, that, if the Ships had not observed some Regulation last Year, many Matters would not have been able to have brought their Ships to Sea again; which Regulation, they believe, was by reason of the Enquiry, made,- relating to the Coal Trade, the last Session of Parliament:

That the Ships, using the London Trade, are numerous, and without any Regulation; and it would be a Relief to them, if such Ships were obliged to deliver in Turn, as they arrive, and observe the like in failing; for, without such a Method be observed, the Lightermen can set Ships to work, that came last up to Market, in discharging their Loading sooner, than those, which arrived before them: A Turn is kept by all Ships, that load at Newcastle , and Lightermen, when they fend their Lighters on board, to load Coals, obfeive the like Method:

That Coals, brought to London, cannot be sold for less than 25 or 26 s.per Chaldron, to answer Insurance, and Interest.

Joseph Merryman, who is a Fadtof, or Crimp, being examined, said, that Thomas Jones, Anthony , and other Lightermen, would not buy Mr. Coals,

bccaufehc would not pay the Premium, and defued him, the said Merryman, to advise the Matter not to load them,

for if there were any other Coals of that Sort at Market, they would not meddle with Mr. s Coals; and that no Coals have been so often refuted, as Mr. s have been, notwithstanding his Coals are allowed to be as good of the Sort, as any that are brought to Market: That John Bromley, Lighterman, bought of George Ward a

Ship-load of Coals, belonging to Messieurs Richard and Nicholas Ridley, and were loaded for the Coast; and, being brought to London, he, the said Bromley, bought them, and teeing by the Certificate, to whom those Coals belonged, Bromley obliged the Matter to abate Six Pence per Chaldron, for the Premium.

John Tickner, who is a Dealer in Coals, said, that thd Lightermen have agreed among themselves, not to buy any Persons Coals without a Premium: That he, buying Coals of Mr. Gibson, applied to him for the Premium; but he refused to pay it; and has bought Colonel LyddePs and Mr. Bowes's Coals, without having a Premium: But Tickner con felted, that he had received Premiums of Mr. Horton, Agent for Mr. Wortley; and the

Lightermen having Information thereof, Horton told Tickner, he mutt expect no more Premiums, for fear of disobliging the Lightermen: And the Lightermen bought Part of a Ship-loading of Coals, and he, the said Tickner, bought the other Part; and when the Laghtermen knew it, they turned the Coals on the Matters Hands, because the Matters fold them to one who was not a Lighterman.

Philip Fruchard, Dealer in Coals, being examined, said, that since the Incorporation of the Lightermen into the Watermens Company, the Dealers in Coals, keeping Wharfs, have been rettrained from carrying Coals from and to any Part of the River of Thames in their own Lighters, or other Boats, except to their own Wharfs; whereby the Lightermen have monopolized and engrossed the Trade into a few Hands, and if they are suffered to go on, will in time exclude all other Persons, not being Lightermen, from dealing in Coals, half the Coals at present being bought up by a few Lightermen, who command the Market as they please; but, if there was a greater Number of Buyers, it would be more beneficial to the Publick, the Lightermen at present having it in their Power to hinder a Fleet of Colliers from discharging their Lading, when they please.

That it appeared by the same Evidence, that there are Abuses in the Admeasurement of Coals, which are frequently loaded from on board bare Measure, that is, 20 Chaldron, instead of 21, and so in Proportion; which can be with no other View, than to defraud the Buyer of his In-grain; in order to which, they carry the Coals to such Wharfs, or Docks, where they can be supplied with small Sacks, l'o that the Consumers may not be able to judge of their Measure; and many Persons, who keep Wharfs, to fell Coals on Shore, do not measure them at all, but fill them into Sacks, some of which do not hold more than Two Bushels and a half; by which Means the Buyer is defrauded of Four Bushels of Coals, if not more, in every Chaldron; which Abuse is about £.20,000. per Annum Loss to the Consumers; and the unfair Trader, who fells out but 32 Bushels to the Chaldron, has it always in his Power to undersell another, who gives the just Measure: And this is. very often done.

Mr. Samuel Okey and Mr. Thomas Smith, being severally examined, confirmed the Evidence, before given by Mr. Fruchard.

Mr. Richard Banbury, Merchant, who is a Dealer in Coals, said, that the Lightermen, who call themselves the Number of 16, have signed an Instrument, obliging them to bear an equal Charge in carrying on Prosecutions against such Persons, as shall keep Lighters, and buy Coals; and that he had been prosecuted, as such, and.

upon hearing a Matter in Dispute, in the Court of Chancery, between the Lightermen and himself, he had obtained a Decree in his Favour, with Costs of Suit:

And said further, that the Lightermen have endeavoured to hinder him from receiving of Premiums, and threatened to drive him from Billingsgate Market, he being not of the Body of Lightermen.

That it appeared by the Evidence of all the Witnesses, examined before the Committee, that if the Coal Trade was laid open, under certain Regulations, it would relieve the Navigation, and prevent the Abuses, complained of by the Petitioners.

And that, upon the whole Matter, this Petitioners having fully proved the Allegations of their several Petitions, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

I. Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the restraining Dealers in Coals from carrying the same from and to any Part of the River of Thames in their own Lighters, or other Boats, hath been very prejudicial to the Navigation, and to the Coal Trade.

a. Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Lightermen, since their Incorporation, have exacted unlawful Premiums, or Rewards, refused to give their Notes for value received, for such Coals, as they buy, and are become Crimps, or Factors, to the Matters of Ships, at the same time they are Buyers of Coals on their own Account, and have used other unfair Practices, to the Prejudice of the Coal Trade.

3. Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That such Proceedings of the said Lightermen have been detrimental to the Matters and Owners of Ships, employed in the Coal Trade, and tend to a Monopoly, and is highly injurious to the Publick.

4. Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That there have been great Abuses in the measuring of Sea-coal by many Dealers therein, whereby the fair Traders have been much injured, and the Consumers imposed upon.

The First of the said Resolutions, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The Second of the said Resolutions being reada Second time;

A Motion was made, and the Question being put,

>That the said Resolution be re-committed;

It passed in the Negative.

Then an Amendment was proposed to be made to the said Resolution, by inserting, before the Words " the " Lightermen," these Words, " some of."

And the same was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, so amended, That it appears to this House, that some of the Lightermen, since their Incorporation, have exacted unlawful Premiums, or Rewards, refused to give their Notes for Value received, for such Coals as they buy, and are become Crimps, or Factors, to the Matters of Ships, at the same time they are Buyers of Coals on their own Account, and have used other unfair Practices, to the Prejudice of the Coal Trade.

The rest of the said Refqlutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, pursuant to the said Resolutions; and that Sir Strickland, Sir Charles Turner, Mr. Chohnley Turner, Mr.

Crowle, and Mr. William Thompjbn, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

That the Committee, in pursuance of the Orders of the House,.have taken into Consideration. the feveril Petitions above-mentioned; and it appeared to the Committee,

That by virtue of Letters patent, bearing Date the 13th Day of July, 1714, Willi Trench, Esquire, deceased, was impowered to erect a Light-house on the dangerous Rock, or I Hand, called the near Holyhead,

in the County of Anglesey-, which being deemed to be of great Use and Benefit to the Navigation in those Parts, in Con6deration of the Expence, that the said Mr. Trench was to be at, in erecting and supporting such Light-house, and keeping a Fire therein, certain Duties were charged upon the Tonage of Ships, which should receive any Benefit by the said Light-house; that is to say, One Peny person in, and One Peny per Ton out, upon Natives, his Majesty's Ships of War excepted, and the like Sum upon Foreigners; and the said Mr. Trench was obliged to pay the Crown a Quit-rent, of Five Pounds per Annum:

That the said Mr. Trench, in pursuance of the said Grant, erected a Light-house on the said Rock, which is of about the Height of One hundred and Sixty Feet, and, being much exposed to the Winds, and Weather, is built very strong; and the Expence thereof was not less than Three thousand Pounds, he being obliged to fetch all the Materials from distant Parts, particularly, the Timber, and Iron, which was brought from Dublin; and One Ship, and Cargoe of such Materials, with the only Son of< the said Mr. Trench, was loft in ^oing to the said Bland.

That by the Will of the said Mr. Trench, bearing Date the 5th Day of June, 1725, the Debts of the said Mr. Trench, and a Legacy of jf.500. to Ruth Trench, his then Wife, are charged upon the Income of the said Light-house; and the said Sutton Morgan, and Anne, his Wife, are residuary Legatees of the said Mr. Trench.

And it appeared, that the said Light-house is of very great Use and Benefit to the Pacquet-boats, and all Ships failing Coastwise, and likewise to all others, failing through St. George's Channel, by Holyhead, for that between the Isle of Man and the llland of Skerries is but Eleven Leagues, and the said Light can be seen Six Leagues at Sea, except in hazy Weather; and that the Ships, belonging to the several Ports between Liverpoole and Scotland, frequently receive Benefit by the said Light-house in Stress of Weather, but not so often, as those, belonging to Chester, and Liverpoole-, and that the Mailers, and Owners, of several Ships, belonging to the Ports North of Liverpoole, have refused to pay the Duties, charged by the said Patent; and the said Letters-patent are not sufficient to enforce the Payment thereof.

That by all other Patents, for erecting Light-houses, there is charged upon Foreigners, Tome double, and others treble, Duties.

That the annual Expence of supporting and maintaining the said Light-house, and the Light therein, and the Rent of Twenty Pounds per Annum, payable to the Proprietors of the said Rock, or llland, has exceeded the annual Income of the Duties, collected for the Support thereof, and for these Twelve Years last pall above One hundred Pounds per Annum, which the said Sutton Morgan, since the Death of the said William Trench, has been obliged to pay.

Sir Charles Turner (according to Order) reported from Dispofmo* the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was lJlc referred to consider further of that Part of his Majesty's JJ® ua most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, which relates to the Disposition of the Sinking Fund, and the giving Ease to the Subject, where the Duties are most grievous, the Resolution, they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table-; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That out of the Moneys arisen, or to arise, for the Surplusses, Excesses, or overplus Moneys, commonly called the Sinking Fund, there be issued and paid to the South Sea Company the Sum of One Million, in Part of that Moiety of their whole increased capital Stock, as, being divided in pursuance of an Act, of the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, now remains the capital Stock of the said Company, and for redeeming a proportional Part of the Annuities attending thereon.

The said Resolution, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Gentlemen, who are to prepare, and bring in, a Bill for raising, by Exchequer Bills, a Sum, not exceeding Five hundred and Fifty thousand Pounds, to be circulated and exchanged at a Rate, not exceeding Three Pounds per Centum per Annum, that they do prepare, and add to the said Bill, a Clause, or Clauses, pursuant to the said Resolution.

Sir Nathanael Curzon (ac6ording to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the State of the Trade to Africa, the Resolutions, they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same were read, and are as followeth; viz.

ift, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Trade to Africa ought always to remain free and open to all his Majesty's Subjects.

zd, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the'Trade and Navigation to the Coast of Africa ought never to be taxed with any Duties whatsoever, for the Support and Maintenance of any Forts and Settlements there.

3d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa are necessary, for securing and preserving to Great Britain the Trade to those Parts.

4th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee. That an Allowance ought to be made towards the Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements.

The first of the said Resolutions, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

The Second of the said Resolutions being read & Second time;

Resolved, nemine contradicenie, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That the Trade and Navigation to the Coast of Africa ought never to be taxed with any Duties whatsoever, for the Support and Maintenance of any Forts and Settlements there.

The Third of tire said Resolutions being read a Second time, viz. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa are necessary, for securing and preserving to Great Britain the Trade to thoie Parts;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the said Resolution, by leaving out from the Word " necessary'* to the Word u those," and, instead thereof, to insert these Words, " to be maintained, as Marks of the Pof-

sessions of Great Britain in."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question £ut thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution so amended, that British Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa are necessary to be maintained; as Marks of the Possessions of Great Britain in those Parts.

The last of the said Resolutions, being read a Second time, was agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, that his Majesty, having been informed of the State and Condition of the British Forts and Settlements in Africa, had commanded him to acquaint this House, that this Majesty recommends to their Consideration the making such Provision, as this House shall think proper, towards the Support and Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements.

Ordered, That the royal African Company's full Establishment for their several Forts and Castles in Africa, with an Account of the Number, Names, and Qualities, of the Persons, who were actually upon the same Establishment the last Year, ending the Thirty-first Day of jDecember, One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty-nine, and the Charges of the fame, distinguishing, how much thereof is on Account of Trade, and how much for the Maintenance and Defence of the said Forts and Castles, be referred to the Committee of the whole House, who are appointed to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

A Petition of William Taylor, junior. Clerk of tile Hun- Recovery of dred and Forest Courts of Macclesfield, in the County Small Debt*. Palatine of Chester, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, that his Office is for Life, and he makes out all Process, and has the Benefit of all Proceedings, in the said Courts, which have Jurisdiction in, and try, Actions of Debt, and other personal Actions, of any Value, at a small Expence; but, if the Bill, depending in this House, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, should pass, he will be deprived of the greatest Part of the just Perquisites and Profits of his Office: And therefore praying, that, in case the said Bill should pass, he or his Deputy, conforming to the Tenor thereof, may, as a Recompence for the Loss in his Office, make out Summons, and be constituted Clerk of the civil or Bills, which shall be prosecuted against Persons within the said Hundred and Forest, and be appointed to enter and register all Petitions, Bills, and Appeals, and all Proceedings thereon, or have such other Relief, as to the House shall seem just and reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, is committed; and that the Committee, if they think fit, do make Provision in the said Bill for the Petitioner.

Proprietors and WatermCl1> O*vners of the several Ferry-boats, Row-barges, and Coal &c‘ Barges, employed between Kingston Bridge, in the County of Surry, and Windsor Bridge, in the County of Berks, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House:

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, dated the 26th Day of February lad, j*o-ceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and, to prove the Allegations of the lame,

The Act of Parliament, passed the last Session, for making more effectual several Acts passed, relating to Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lighterman, rowing on the River Thames, and for better ordering and governing such Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, was produced; and that Part of the said Act was read, which restrains all Persons, having not served seven Years Ap-prentiedhip to a Waterman, Wherryman, or Lighterman, from rowing or working any Boat, Wherry, Lighter, or other Vessel or Craft, upon the River, for Hire, or Gain, except Trinity Men, Fishermen, Ballastmen, and such, as are employed in rowing Western Barges, Mill Boats, Chalk Hoys, Faggot and Wood Lighers, Dung Boats, and Gardeners Boats.

That the Petitioners called Brent Reynell Spiller, Esquire, who, being examined, said, that he owns a Ferry-boat at: That,

since the passing of the Act of Parliament, his Ferryman and Servant were taken up, and carried before a Justice of Peace, for working the said Ferry Boat, having not served an Apprentice ship to a Waterman, or Wherryman; but, by reason Two Witnesses were not produced, to prove the fame, as the Act directs, they were not committed.

And he further gave Evidence, that one John Sedge-wick, who had worked Thirty Years in a flat-bottomed Boat, and his Son, were sent to the House of Correction for so doing, not having served an Apprenticeship to a Waterman, or Wherryman:

That Luggage Barges, commonly called Coal Barges, carry Corn, Meal, Malt, (Ac. to London, and bring back Coals, Deal Boards, and all other manner of merchantable Goods:

That, Mr. Reynell fays, he now gives his Ferryman Ten Shillings per Week, and Lodging, but he formerly gave no more than Three Shillings and Six Pence 10 a Man much more able; and he, by keeping up the Ferry, now pays Ten Shillings per Week to his Servant; so he is above Forty Shillings out of Pocket yearly, besides paying parochial Taxes for the fame.

That his Ferry-boat is u'ed to ferry over his own Cattle, Grass, and Manure for Land:

That the restrair.ing Men from working of flat Boats is very burthensome to his Majesty's Subjects.

Edward Goldkawk said, that it is very chargeable to the Owners of Ferry-boats being obliged to work their Boats by such Persons only, as have served an Apprenticeship; and, before the passing of the Act aforesaid, used to employ Persons, who had more Strength, and Judgment, to work the same with Poles: That the Price of carrying Goods is now advanced; for he paid One Shilling and Eight Pence per Load more now, than formerly; and, if such Persons, as have not served an Ap- prenticeship, were allowed to work, there would be as many, if not more, fit and able Persons, to serve his Majesty, and the Merchants; and since the making of the Act, several Persons have been forced to leave off their Trade, whereby they are destitute of any Manner of Business, whilst others carry it on.

John Sedgewick, aged Fifty Years, said, that he has

worked as a Bargemen for Thirty Years, but never served an Apprenticeship to a Waterman: That, since the Act passed, he was carried before a Justice of the Peace, and being not able to pay the Penalty of Ten Pounds, by the Act laid for working without having served an Appren-ship of Seven Years, was (ent to the House of Correction, and there confined for Fourteen Days.

Henry Saunders, being examined, confirmed Sedge-wick's Evidence; and said, he cannot work his Barge, fearing, he shall be fined, or sent to the House of Correction.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend a Clause in an Act,

An ingrossed Bill for continuing the Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, in that Part of Great Britain called England, and for granting to his Majesty certain Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, in that Part of Great Britaik called Scotland, for the Service of the Year 1730, was read the Third time.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass; and that the Title be, An Act for continuing the Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, in that Part of Great Britain called England, and for granting to his Majesty certain Duties upon Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, for the Service of the Year 1730; for exempting from the said Duties Cyder and Perry, used for distilling; for ascertaining the Bounty for Malt exported; for better preventing Frauds in the malting of Com for Exportation; for making good the Deficiency of a late Malt Act; and for giving further Time to Clerks and Apprentices to pay Duties, omitted to be paid for their Indentures and Contrafts.

A Petition of Thomas Brumell, of Newcastle upon Tyne, Hoaftman, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, that in October 1728, a Commission of Bankruptcy was issued against him, and, in Obedience thereto, he surrendered himself, and delivered up his whole Effects, from which would have arose to his Creditors above Eight Shillings in the Pound, and the Commissioners signed his Certificate within the Time of the late Act, concerning Bankrupts; but that Certificate not being returned into Chancery before the Expiration of that Act, the Commissioners apprehend, they cannot now make him the Allowance appointed by the said Act, for the necessary Relief of him, and his poor Family, who have continued ever since in a most neoeffitous Condition; and he is apprehensive, he is still liable to the Actions of his Creditors, and may, notwithstanding hehasactually delivered up his whole Effects, be thrown into Gaol: And therefore praying the Consideration of the House, and such Relief, as to the House shall seem reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Bill for the better Regulation of the Coal Trade, was read a Second time.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

A Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of the Company of Wherrymen, Watermen, and Lightermen, of the River of 'Thames, in behalf of themselves, and the said Company, was prel'ented to the House, and read; setting forth, that by the Act, of the Eleventh and Twelfth Year of the Reign of the late King William the Third, for incorporating the Petitioners, other Persons are restrained from carrying Coals, and other Goods, for Hire, on the River Thames-, but the said Restraint being in a great Measure taken off by some Clauses in the Bill, depending in this House, for the better Regulation of the Coal Trade, they apprehend, their Property, of being free Watermen, and Lightermen, will be evaded, and their Servitude of Seven Years to the said Employment will be rendered useless: And therefore praying, that they may be heard by their Counsel against so much of the said Bill, as tends to destroy the Privileges and Fran-chises of their laid Company, or that they may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the better Regulation of the Coal Trade is committed; and that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be heard by their Counsel before the said Committee, according to the Prayer of their Petition.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do admit Counsel to be heard for so much of the said Bill, as is petitioned against, at the same time.

A Petition of John Pope, one of the Messengers belonging to the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, was presented to the House, and read; expressing the utmost Sorrow for having been unhappily guilty of assaulting Arthur Tremayne, Esquire, a Member of this House, last Monday Night, in the Gallery of the House, at the Committee of Privileges and Elections, which Misfortune was occasioned by the Hurry and Consulion, which at that time happened by the great Crowd of Strangers, then attempting to fill the House, which he endeavoured to clear for the Eale and Convenience of the Members; and begging Pardon of the said Member, and of the House, for his said Offence; alluring, his future Demeanor shall be with the greatest Duty and Respects to the House, and to every particular Member of it; and praying to be discharged out of Custody.

Ordered, That the said John Pope, committed by this House to his Majesty's Gaol of Newgate on Tuesday lait, be brought to the Bar of this House Tomorrow Morning, in order to his being discharged out of Custody; and that Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrants accordingly.

A Petition of the Mayor, Burgesses, Freeholders, Gentlemen, and other the principal Inhabitants, of the Borough of Callington, in the County of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; complaining of great Decays in their Trades, occasioned by the clandestine Trade and Dealings, carried on by Hawkers, Pedlars, and petty Chapmen; and praying, that they maybe suppressed, or such other Relief given against them, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. 'Tothill and Mr. Allen:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for restraining Thomas Jervoise, junior, Esquire, a Lunatick, from marrying, or aliening, disposing, or incumbering, his Estate, during his Lunacy, and for railing Portions for his Sifter's Children, and for other Purposes therein mentioned j to which the Lords desire the Concurrence of this House;

And also, the Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better regulating Elections in the City of Norwich, and for preserving the Peace, good Order, and Government, of the said City, without any Amendment.

Mr. Cholmondeley reported from the Committee, to Remission of whom the Petition of Matthew Lyon, Executor of the Duty on da. last Will and Testament of Matthew Page, late of War- ma8e<J Salt. rington, in the County of Lancaster, Merchant, deceased, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House:

And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 28th of February last, had taken into Consideration the said Petition, and examined the Matter thereof.

That it appeared to the Committee, Matthew Page was a Proprietor of Rock Salt Pits in the Collection of Northwych, in the County of Chester', and, for the greater Conveniency and Encouragement of Trade, and Dispatch of Shipping, frequently lodged great Quantities of Rock Salt in Warehouses at Bank Key, in the County of Lancaster; and in the Months of , October,

November, and December, 1724, lodged several great Quantities of Salt in one of the Warehouses at Bank Key; during which time, there happened the greatest Flood or Inundation upon the River, that ever was known, occasioned by the high Spring Tide, violent Winds, and a great Fresh, which raised the River several Yards higher than ufoal; whereby all the said Rock Salt in the said Warehouse was totally destroyed, for the Duties whereof Matthew Page had given Bonds.

54*8 — *7

This Salt being so destroyed, the Petitioner, Matthew Lyon, in July, 1728, petitioned the Lords of the Treasury; which Petition they referred' to the Consideration of the Commissioners for managing his Majesty's Salt Duties, and to reporta true State of the Petitioner's Cafe,

with their Opinion, what was fit tq be done therein.

And the said Commissioners in November, 17*8, made their Report to the Treasury, which was laid before the Committee; whereby it appears, that 996 Bushels of, the said Page'i Salt Was totally dissolved and confilmed by the Accidents, mentioned in the Petition; and that the Petitioner's same was within the Intent and Equity, if not within the Letter, of the Clauses" in the Statutes, relating to Salt, or Rock Salt, loft, at Sea, or in any Ports, Harbours, or Rivers, of this Realm; but those Statutes mentioning only Losses at Sea, or in Rivers, where Salt has been shipped, to be carried Coastwise, could not extend to Losses, happening.in Warehotifes on Shore,

That, upon reading the said Commissioners Report, at the Treasury Board, the Lords of the Treasury directed the Prosecution upon the Bonds, given for the said Duties, to be suspended, until futh Time, as the J*arty concerned could have an Opportunity to apply to Parliament for Relief therein,: ' '>;

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Cofn-mittee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for taking off certain Duties on Salt, and for making good any Deficiencies in the Funds, that may happen thereby, is committed.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they have Power to receive a Clause, for the Relief of Matthew Lyon, Executor of Matthew Page, deceased, in respect of several Quantities of Salt, which were lodged in a vVarehouse at Bank Key, in the County of Lancaster, and were d^stroyed by the Overflowing of the River Mercy in the Year 1724.

Mr. Hughes (according to Order) made a Report from Enquiry into the Committee, appointed to enquire into the State of the Sure of the Gaols of this Kingdom, relating to a Matter, which Gaols‘ had been under their Examination, with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon: And he read the Report, in his Place, and afterwards delivered the same in at the Clerk's Table; where the said Report and Resolutions were read, and are as follows; viz

That the Committee, in the Course of their Enquiry,' received several Informations, tending to charge the Right honourable Sir Robert Eyre, Knight, Lord Chief Justice of his Majesty's Court of Common Pleas, and one of his Majesty's moll honourable Privy Council, with having personally visited Thomas B late Warden of the Prison of the Fleet, during the lall Sc (lion of Parliament, whilst he, the said Thomas Bambridge, was a Prisoner in Newgate, under a Commitment of the House of Commons, lor divers Crimes and Misdemeanors, committed in his Office of Warden of the , and charged with being guilty of the Murder of Mr. Robert

Cal ell,a Prisoner in his Custody, the said Sir Robert

Eyre being at that time in the Commission of Gaol Delivery for the Gaol of Newgate.

The Committee thought it their Duty to examine strictly into an Affair of so extraordinary a Nature; in consequence whereof, the following Persons appeared be; fore them, and endeavoured to make good the said Informations; viz. John Campbell, Anne Jones, James Brown,

Roger Johnson, Anne Johnson, (Wife of the said Roger Johnson) and Bel Anna Alinda Birnie; which Persons,

Enquiry into having been examined before the Cottirtvttcein the most the flat* foletttn Manner, grossly prevaricated in their Examina-of Gaols, tions, contradicted oneanother in several material Circum-ftaitces, and, as toother Fads, werefalfified by Persons, to whom they referred for the Truth of what they declared.

It Iikewile appeared to the Committee, that divers of the said Persons were Prisoners in Newgate, or the some of them of vile and infamous Characters, others actuated by a Spirit of Referttment, on account of Causes, determined against them before the said Lord Chief Justice, and all of them tampered with, and influenced, by the said John Campbell.

It further appeared to the Committee, that several of the said Persons had Meetings and Confutations amongst themselves, and had been guilty of divers evil Practices, in order to set on foot, and support, a Charge against the said Lord Chief Justice , relating to the Matters, contained in the said Informations.

That, after your Committee had spent several Days upon the said Enquiry, and had examined all the Witnesses above-named, the said John Campbell, having Reason to apprehend, that the Evidence given by them, could not be I'ufficient to impose upon the Committee, and to obtain Credit to the said Informations, didconfult With the said Mrs Birnieto fixa new Charge upon the said Lord Chief Justice Eyrenot mentioned before in any of

their Examinations, by giving Evidence of certain Circumstances, to create a Belief, that, about Three Days before the Time appointed for the Trial of the said Thomas Bam bridge for Felony, in the last long Vacation, the said 'Thomas Bambridge did fend a Letter to the said Lord Chiet Justice for Money, and that, in consequence ' thereof, he received One hundred Guineas.

Whereupon the Committee thought fit to re-examine both the said Campbell and Birnie who were not able to give the lead Co.our of Evdence, to support the said new Charge, and were flatly cuntr.ididled by the Evidence, to whom they referred; and, on their Examinations, the Committee, being convinced, that the said new Charge was only a Continuation of the former Conspiracr, and on considering the whole Matter, came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That there hath been a wicked Conspiracy carried on by certain infamous and profligate Persons, to vilify and asperse the Character of the Right honourable Sir Robert Knight, Lord Chief Justice of his Majesty's Court of Common Pleas.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Informations, given to this Committee against the said Lord Chief Justice Eyre, are false, malicious, scandalous, and utterly groundless.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That John Campbell, Anne Jones, James Brown, Roger Jon, Anne johnjon(Wile of the said Roger Johnson) and Bel Anna AlindaBirnie, were the Persons concerned in the said Conspiracy.

Resolved, nemine contradiThat the House doth

Resolved, nemine contradiccThat the House doth agree with the Committee, That the Informations, given to the said Committee against the said Lord Chief Justice Eyre, are false, malicious, scandalous, and utterly ground-ids.

Upon the Petition of Knox Ward, Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir James Thornhill, Knight, and William Betts, Esquire, to serve for the Borough of Weymouth and Melcomb Regis, in the Comity of

The Committee found themselves discharged, by Order of the House, from proceeding upon lb much of the said Petition, as relates to Sir James Thornhill.

And the Committee proceeded to examine the Matter of the Petition, as it relates to Mr. Betts.

The Counsel on both Sides agreed, that the Right of Election is in the Mayor, Aldermen, Bailiffs, and capital Burgesses, inhabiting within the Borough, and in Persons felled of Freeholds within the Borough, and not receiving Alms.

The Counsel for the Petitioner insisted, that Mr. Betts having not complied with the Afit of Parliament, which requires an Oath of Qualification, ttor with the Standing Orders of the House, which requires a Particular, in Writing, of his Qualification, to be left with the Clerk of the House, his Election is therefore void;

And that, by consequence, the Petitioner, having the next Majority on the Poll, was duly elected.

To prove the Demand of the Oath of Qualification* the Petitioner's Counsel called

Robert Loder; who produced a Copy of the Demand, made by Mr. John Ward, of Mr. Betts' Qualification, signed by Pour Elefilors, viz. John Ward, and Three others; and said, he believed, Mr. Betts was not at Weymouth, during the Time of the Election.

John Savage said, that he delivered to Mr. Betts, at

Epsom, a Paper signed by Four of the Elefitors, demand* hig his Qualification, and acquainted him, that it caine from Mr. John Ward -, to which Mr. Betts answered, that he never had any thing to do with Mr. Ward, nor ever would.

This Demand the Wilncfs made, and delivered to Mr. Betts, the 4th of October 1727.

Being cross-examined, he said, that Mr. Betts told him, he was not obliged to give an Answer: That he laid it down on the Table, and did not read it: That the Witness did not fee the Persons subscribe the fame, but they owned their Hands.

The Counsel for Mr. Betts admitted, that his Qualification is not sworn to, nor a Particular of it delivered; though they alleged, that he is qualified, and had served in former Parliaments; but is now grown infirm, and not able to attend the Service of the House: And insisted; that the Elefitors, being not appriled of this, ought to have an Opportunity of making another Choice.

The Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That William Betts, Esquire, is not duly elefited a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Weymouth and Melcomb Regis, in the County of Dorset.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Knox Ward, Esquire, is not duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Weymouth and Melcomb Regis.

Refohcd, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That William , Esquire, is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Weymouth and Melcomb Regis, in the County of Dorset.

The present Trustees are James Slann, a Footman to one of the Mortgagees, and John Wildey, a Scriver.er; which said Trustees, in pursuance of a verbal Order of Four of the Mortgagees, did, by Lfcafe, dated the Fourteenth Day of January One thousand Seven hundred Twenty-nine, let to Richard Mullens, Esquire, the Office of Marshal and Keeperof the Prisoners in the Kings Bench Prison, for Three Years; which Prisoners, as appears by the Commitment Books, are In Number Six hundred Fifty-seven, and are charged with One hundred Twenty-six thousand Four hundred Thirty-four Pounds, Twelve Shillings; besides gre.it Numbers, who are charged, with*-out Specification of the Sums, they being charged on Surrenders to Actions, the Number of which Actions amount to Three hundred Ninety-eight, and the Sums due may, probably, be very great. '

The Committee do not find, that any Security, except their own personal Security, hath been taken, or required, from any Marshal of the King's Bench, for the safe keeping of the Prisoners, either by the Trustees, or by any other; and the -Marshals, as well -as the Trustees; have, generally, been Men of very mean Circumstances; and the Mortgagees having thus fereened tbcmselves bo-hind Trustees, nominated at their own Request, deerti themselves not answerable. for -Escapes; so the Creditor hath no Person, of any Substance, to have Recourse to, in case of an Escape; the Consequence of which,

E. amongst many other Examples, appeared very evidently in the same of Mr. Poulter: He was indebted to Mr. William Wilson, in the Sum of Eighteen thousand Pounds, for which he was charged in Execution in the King's Bench Prison, and chose rather to make the Mar-flial a large Present, than to pay his own Debts. Mr.

Machen, who was then Marshal, accepted of the Money;

Poulter went to Holland; and Wilson sued, and recovered Judgment against, Machen, the Marshal; who, being an Insolvent, remained a Prisoner in his own Gaol; and Wilson applied to the Court of King's Bench, that the Profits of the Office might be sequestered for his Debt; but the Mortgagees made such a Claim, as to protest them; so that Wilson, having a Right, but no Remedy, and being by this Slight of Law intirely ruined, shot himself in Despair.

The Office of Marshal of the said Prison was let to the said Richard Mullens by a Trustee, by the Consent and

Direction of the Mortgagees, in Ja, One thousand Seven hundred Twenty-four, for the annual Rent of Seven hundred Pounds; he being, over and above, obliged to pay the annual Sum of Twenty-two Pounds, Ten Shillings, as a Fee-farm Rent; and also an annual Sum of Thirty Pounds to the Chamberlain, nominated by the Mortgagees; the Whole amounting to £.750. per Annum.

His Lease was renewed in January last.; and by Indenture bearing Date the Fourteenth Day Of the said Month, he covenants with James Slann and John , to pay

them £. 700 per Annum, clear of all Taxes; besides, which, to pay the Fee-farm, Rent, (i9c.although all the open and legal Profits, of which the said Mullens could give any Account to the Committee, amounted to about Three hundred and Fifty Pounds per Annum, and no more.

The high Rents of the said Office cannot be made up, without great Oppression; much less can the other Fees, with which it is loaded, be complied with; inso much that the Marshals generally continue but a short time in that Office, there having been Fifteen from the Year 1668 to the Year 1724; and sometimes, on a Prisoner's
