p being committed for a considerable Sum, the Mar-shal accepts of Money to grant him the Rules, and Suffers him to escape; and, if the Plaintiff recovers against the Marshal, he turns himself a Prisoner into his own Gaol, which is accompanied with a Kind of Gaol Delivery: The insolvent Marshal, being in this Condition, generally refuses to give his Successors any Account of the Prisoners, to whom he gave the Liberty of the Rules, and by this Proceeding the new Marshal does not apprehtnd himself to be charged or chargeable with them.

q On this Occasion a Rule of Court is Sometimes

granted, for the new Marshal to take all the Prisoners in the Rules, and Persons, who have eScaped; but the Marshal does not think himself obliged to re-take them, and it gives the new Marshal a Pretence to Squeeze great Sums of Money out of Such Prisoners, as enjoy the Rules.

VideD z Over and above the aforementioned exorbitant Rents, on a new Marshal's being Sworn, it hath been usual for him to pay One hundred Guineas to the Lord Chief Justice of the King's Bench, and Fifty Guineas to each of the Puifnc Judges of that Court. The present Marshal, when he was Sworn Marshal, in pursuance of a Lease, granted to him in 1724, gave a Purse of One hundred Guineas into the Hands of Sir , Knight,

then Lord Chief Justice of the King's Bench, and One other Purle, containing Fifty Guineas, to Mr. Justice Fartejcue, and the like Sum to Mr. Justice Pawn; and he offered the like Sum to Sir Robert , Knighr,

then One of the Puisne Judges of that Court, who refused the lame, saying, he did not know, any Such Fee was due, and that, if it was not a legal Fee, he would not take it; but that he would inform himself of the Lord Chief Justice, and the other Judges; and Some Days after he accepted the said Sum, having feea the Lord Chief Justice, and the other Judges of the said Court.

The said Richard Mullens was again Sworn into the said Office on the Twenty-fifth Day of , One thousand

Seven hundred Twenty-nine, his former Lease being then expired, and a new one obtained; on which Occasion Sir Rdbert Raymond, Knight, Lord Chief Justice of the King's Bench, and the other Judges of the said Bench, did not accept of any Fee whatsoever from the said Marshal.

Over and above these Fees, or Presents, paid by the Marshals, on their being Sworn into the said Office, they used to pay, every Christmas, to the Lord Chief Justice of the King's Bench Twenty Guineas, and to each of the Puisne Judges Ten Guineas, until Such Time, as the present Sir Robert Raymond came to be Lord Chief Justice: He then generoully refused to accept of any such Presents, and would never receive any Gratification whatsoever from the said Marshal; and he was imitated in this by Mr. Justice Reynolds, who, though he accepted the Ten Guineas, lent the fame, by his Clerk, to be distributed amongst the Prisoners of the said Prison; and all the Judges of the said Court have now followed this Example: At Chnjlmas 1729, they all refused to accept any Presents from the said Marshal. jl Not only the Marshals, but the Deputy Marshals, usually made Presents, on their Admittance, to the Lord Chief Justice of the said Court: Mr. John , who is now Deputy Marshal, on his buying that Office, besides the Purchase-money, paid by him for the said Office, made a Present to the Lord Chief Justice Holt of Twenty Guineas, which, as far as he remembers, he gave to him with his own Hands.

That, upon inspeding the said King's Bench Prison, it appears to be in very bad Repair, and not capable of containing a Third Part of the Number of Prisoners, even now in the Marshal's Custody, who amount to Six hundred and Fifty-seven; which Number is much Less, than used to be in that Custody, before the late Acts of Parliament against frivolous Arrests, and for Relief of insolvent Debtors: And it is remarkable, that not One Person, discharged by the said late Ad, for Relief of insolvent Debtors, hath been re-committed for any new Debt.

1730.

The common Side of this Prison is divided into little Cabins, or Lodges, the Floors of many of which are Six or Eight Feet below the Level of the Ground; the Mailer's Side is in a very bad Condition; and the Whole in no way adequate to the vast Rent paid for it.

Many Complaints were laid before the Committee, of Cruelties committed by former Marshals of the said Prison, particularly, of a Murder of one Allen, a Prisoner in the said Prison, in the Year 1723, when Machen was Marshal; and also Complaints of exorbitant Sums having been taken for the Liberty of the Rules.

But therequisite Attendances on other Services of the House have made it impracticable to go through the Examinations of these Complaints, before the Conclusionof this Session.

However, the Committee having examined all the Prisoners on the common Side, and many of those on the Mailer's Side, who are mostly new Prisoners, committed since the Beginning of the late parliamentary Enquiries into the State of the Gaols, it appeared by their Examinations, that no Violence or Cruelty hath been used to them by the present Marshal, but on the contrary, that he hath done many Acts of Compassion and Charity towards those on the common Side; by which, and by his free Confessions, and satisfactory Answers given to the Committee, upon his several Examinations before them, he hath rather entitled himself to Favour, than Blame.

The said Prisoners also declared, that they had heard of terrible Oppressions formerly, none of which have happened of late, the Ears of the present Lord Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench being always open to the Complaints of the Prisoners, and he having with great Patience heard all their Petitions.

Their chief Complaints, at present, are the great Distress, they are reduced to, the Charities not being sufficient for Maintenance of the poor Prisoners; and that the being admitted on the common Side, and thereby entitled to the Benefit of the Charities, which arc confined to that Side, is granted as a particular Favour, and not as a general Right; and that it is with great Difficulty a poor Wretch on the Matter's Side, though never so miserable, can be admitted on the common Side, to share in these Charities.

Vide E Marshal is chiefly enabled to pay his Rent,

'by permitting Prisoners, on Security, to live out of the Prison, any where within the Rules. The Strait-ness of the Prison, and its Incapacity tocontain the Numbers, thereto usually committed, occasioned the Prisoners Application to the Court of King's Bench for more Room; who took upon them to impowerthe Marshal to suffer his Prisoners to live out of the Walls of the Prison, be being answerable for their forth-coming. The Limits, within which such Prisoners were allowed to be, were fixed by the Court of King's Bench; and that space of Ground is called the Rules, and now deemed Part of the Prison. The Court of King's Bench hath taken on them to enlarge the said Space; particularly, in the Time, when Sir Prat, Knight, was Lord Chief Justice, the Court then declared, that it was in their Power to extend the Rules in such Manner, as they should think fit.

If this be Law, all England may be made One extended Prison.

The Prisoners make large Presents to the Marshal, for the Liberty of these Rules; and, being under his Protection, and in his Favour, may take Houses, or Lodgings, within the Rules, and live in a very easy Manner; whilst the poor honed Debtor, who hath paid away all his Substance, to satisfy his Creditors, is a dole Prisoner within the Prison: Thus the Debtor, who will not pay his Creditors, lives at Ease; and he, who cannot pay, suffers.

The Prisoners, enjoying the Liberty of the Rules, are, by the present Usage of the Court erf" King's Bench, in some Manner pro ted ed even in criminal Cafes; for if they are guilty of the greatest Crimes, or Dilbrders, they cannot, by the Opinion of that Court, be committed by any

Authority,

120 Mali.

3 Gfco. II. i2° M579

Authority, but that of the judges of the said Court of King'* Bench; so that, if a Murder, Riot, or Mutiny, should happen, whilst the said Judges are on the Circuits, or otherwise absent, there is no Power to commit to the County Gaol any, Prisoner in the Rules, who shall be concerned therein; for, should a Justice of the Peace, on Complaint made, commit a Prisoner in the Rules to the County Gaol, he would, it seems, by a late Opinion of the said Court, be deemed guilty of a Rescueand Escape, and be liable to tire Debts oif the Prisoner, whom the had so committed:

For it appears, that a Complaint was made, in December 1728, to Samuel Woodham, Esquire, one of his Majesty's Justices of the Peace for the County of Surry, against Humphry Heybord and Joseph , Two Prisoners in the Rules, for violently assaulting a Woman, and other Misdemeanors; and they not being able to find Security for their Appearance at the next Quarter Sessions for the said County, Mr. Woodham committed them to the said County Gaol: On this, the Marshal moved the Court of King's Bench for an Attachment against Mr. Woodbam; and the Matter being brought before the Court, the Court declared, that Mr. Woodham, in committing the said Heybord and Prisoner* in the

Custody of the Marshal, to the County Gaol, upon any Pretence whatsoever, notwithstanding the County Gaol was within the Rules of the Prison of the King's , was guilty of a Rescue: After which, the Court interposed, and prevailed with the said , the Marshal, to make up the Matter, on Mr. s paying Thirty-

one Pounds, Colts, for committing Two Prisoners, who had broke the Peace, and could not find Security.

The high Rent, paid by the Marshal, occasions exorbitant Fees, Extortions, and many other Inconveniences.

The Marshal hath one Shilling per Night, for every Prisoner, who lies in a Spunging-house; which may be a great Inducement to him to keep Prisoners from coming into the Prison.

The Prison Fees are exorbitant; and the Judges having met together, and proceeding to take the same into their Confident on, in order to their making a Reduction thereof, pursuant to the late Act, a Doubt arose, whether they could, or ought, to reduce the said Fees, because of the Property of the Mortgagees: And this Matter remains for the further Consideration of Parliament.

That no Security being given for lafe Custody of the Prisoners, and the artful Confusion of the Title between the Trustees for Lentball, and the Mortgagees, render the Custody of the said Prison unsafe, and precarious.

It appeared to the Committee, that, notwithstanding the Inconveniency, arising from the Claim of the Mortgagees, and the high Rent', paid by the Marshal, yet this Prison of the King's Bench is much better regulated, than any other Pnlon, the Committee had enquired into; which they cannot but aforibe to the Care of the Lord Chief Justice Raymond, who, not accepting of any Presents, or Fees, from the Marshal of the said Prison, hath kept the said Marshal strictly to the Performance of his Duty; and his Lordship bath heard, and redressed, the Complaints of the Prisoners.

It appeared to the Committee, that there are now in being some Books and Lists of Charities, belonging to this Prison; and also that there have been other Books, relating to the said Charities, which Books are not now forth-coming.

There is a Charity collected from the several Counties, and another, of Moneys collected in the Courts of Westminster-hall, called high Bar-money. In the collecting the First of the said Charities there is some Difficulty, full Powers not being given for the railing thereof; and K. it hath been represented to the Committee, that the latter, though Charity Money, doth belong to the lx>rd Chief Justice, and that he hath a Right to dispose of the lame, as he thinks fit.

> And it appeared to the Committee, that out of the small Charity, which yet remains unimbezzled, an

Vo 1. 21.

Attempt was lately made to deduct Money, to repair the Wards for receiving the Furniture, given to the lick Rooms by the present Lord Chief Justice; ami

that these poor Creatures, besides their great Fees, pay also for repairing Rooms in the Gaol, and they were induced to lign a common Seal for this Porpole:

That the poor Prisoners suffer greatly, by the applying of the Charity Money to Repairs, or to any other Uses, than dividing it among!! them, and by their not being admitted to the common Side, and the (haring the Charities.

That the prosecuting Justices of the Peace, for acting in Cales of Breaches of the Peace, committed by Prisoners of the King's Bench Prison, or within the Rules thereof, greatly tends to the encouraging of disorderly, riotous, and dangerous, Practices there.

By inl'pefting the Lists of Prisoners for Debt, transmitted from the various Gaols of this Kingdom, and the Gazettes, and other Authorities, the C -mmittee find, that near Six thousand Persons have been discharged out of the said Gaols by virtue of the Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for Relief of insolvent Debtors; and that Six hundred of his Majesty's Subjects, Fugitives for Debt, have returned, an I reaped the Benefit of that Act: And by the Returns of the Lifts from the Country Gaols, it appears, that many Hundred Persons are ftiil confined there, who were Prisoners for Debt before the Twenty-ninth Day of September 1728, from which Time the said Act took place.

The Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That effectual Provision be made, to prevent the Judges, their Clerks, and Servants, from receiving any Fees, Gifts, Presents, or any Gratuities whatsoever, from the Gaoler or Keeper of any Prison, or from any Officer, intruded with the Custody of the Prisoners, or any Person impowered by them.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That is is necessary to make further Provision, for the discovering, collecting, distributing, and accounting ior, the Charities, belonging to the King's Bench Prison.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is necessary to make further Provision for Creditors, for the more easy and effectual Recovery of Debts and Damages, on the Escapes of Prisoners from the King's Bench Prison.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is necessary to make further Provision, for the better Preservation of the Peace within the King's Bench Prison, and the Rules thereof.

Marshal of the King's Bench Prison, taken before the Committee of the House of Commons, appointed to inspect the Gaols of this Kingdom, this 21st Day of February, 1729, and 9th of April, 1730.

This Examinant faith, that he is Marshal of the King's Bench Prison, and appointed by the Proprietors, viz. Thomas Martin, William MJohn Alar tin, John Preston, and Joseph Studley, Esquires: That the said Proprietors have a Right to present a Marshal of the said Prison to the Court of King s Bench, who are to approve and confirm the said Marshal; and, after he is sworn in before the said Court, he is then in full Possession of the said Office. This Examinant further laith, that in the Year 1724 he applied to the said Joseph Studley, in order for to get the Office of Marshal to the King's Bench Prison, and by Meansof the said Joseph Studley was introduced to the other Proprietors, whom he, met at -

way'sCoffee-house towards the End of the Year 1724, where the said Proprietors, viz. Thomas Martin, John Martin, and Joseph Studley, Esquires, and, as he thinks, Wm. Martin, were present; who proposed to the said Examinant, that they, the said Proprietors, would present him to the Court of King's Bench, as Marshal of the said Prison, and grant him, Mullens, a Leaf* of the said Office and Prison for the Space of Five Years, with a Right of Renewal for Three Years, after the Expiration of the said Term, on Condition of paying to the said Proprietors the annual Sum of Eight hundred Pounds, and also the further annual Sum of about Twenty Pounds, as a Quit-rent, and to allow to the Chamberlain of the said Prison, appointed by the Proprietors, the usual Profits of the said Office, which he hath since compounded with the said Chamberlain, for the yearly Sum of Thirty Pounds; and that the said Proprietors further told him, that, over and above the said Sums, he, the Marshal, before he was approved of, and sworn into the said Office, mutt pay One hundred Guineas to the Lord Chief Justice of the King's Bench, and a further Sum of Fifty Guineas to each of the Three Puisne Judges of the said Court: That he, this Examinant, objected to all these Demands, as too exorbitant, from the Impossibility of fairly raising the said Sums; to which the said Proprietors answered, that, if he, Alullens, refused to take the said Office on these Conditions, many others would gladly accept of this Otter; and that the former Marshals had made a great deal of Money of the said Office, and, particularly, Mr. Machen, had got between Two and Three thousand Pounds by it: This Examinant replied, that ho Person could make such a Profit honestly; and if any one got so much Money in the said Office, it mutt be by giving Liberty to some of the Prisoners, and running away with them: To which the said John and Thomas Martin, or one of them, answered, that he, Mullens, mutt take his Chance for that, for he took the said Office with his Eyes open. And this Examinant further faith, that he agreed with the said Proprietors for the said Office and Prison, and a Grant of the same was made to him, and executed on the

Examination of Mr. Richard Mullens, Marshal of the Kings Bench Prison, 21 ft February, 1729.

About Five Months ago all the Judges or the King's Bench ordered Mr. Mullens to give the Proprietors Notice to attend them at the Lord Chief Justice's Chambers, and they all met accordingly. My Lord Chief Justice then told the Proprietors, the Occasion of fending for them was, to acquaint them, that they, the Judges, were of Opinion, that there would be a Parliamentary Enquiry into their Prison, as there had been of others; and, though, they apprehended, they had no direct Right to make any Order upon them, the Proprietors, yet they recommended it to them, the Proprietors, to alter the exorbitant Rent, they now let it at; and, though they imagined, they were secure under an Act of Parliament, yet it was their Opinion, that the Parliament would construe it, that by their letting it at such exorbitant Rents, and to People without sufficient Security, and obscure People permitted to covenant for it, that Escapes would be deemed voluntary in them, as if they had acted themselves as Marshal; that they themselves would be liable to make good the Escapes, and forfeit their Office.

R. Mullens.

E. Richard Mullens, Marshal of the King's Bench Prison, being examined this 9th Day of April, 1730, in the most solemn Manner, faith, that he, this Examinant, hath lived within the Rules of the said Prison, and been converlant therein, for the Space of Ten or Eleven Years; and that in or about the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty-three, one Poulter was committed to the Custody of Richard Machen, then Marshal, in Execution, for £. 18,000. and upwards, at the Suit of William Wilson; and that soon afterwards the said Macben gave the said Poulter the Liberty of the Rules, for 260 Guineas, or thereabouts, and took a Bond from the said Poulter's Brother, for £. 1,000. as the said Macben informed this Examinant, and in about Ten Days after the said Poulter obtained the Liberty of the Rules, he escaped to Holland, and there continues, as this Examinant is allb informed: And thereupon the said Wilson brought an Action, in the Court of King's Bench, against the said Machen, for the said Escape, and recovered Judgment for the said Debt; and afterwards the said Wilson moved the said Court, that the Profits of the Office of Marshal and Prison of the King's Bench might be sequestered for the said Debt; and the Court referred it to the Mailer of the King's Bench Office, to state the Account of the Mortgagees; and the said Mailer reported due to themjf. i8,oco. ap.d the said could not obtain any Satisfaction, and soon afterwards (hot himself, in Despair, at an Inn in Barnaby Street, which, this Examinant believes, was called St. Christophers. And this Examinant further faith, that the said Machen is now a Prisoner, in the Custody of this Examinant, at the Suits of Elizabeth and A me Wilson, the Administratrixes of the said Wm. Wilson, and also at the Suits of Benjamin Arnold and Christopher Thzvai/es; and that several other Prisoners, besides the said Poulter, did escape, during the Time that the said Blacken was Marshal; and that the Rent of the Office and Prison is so exorbitant, that no Person of good Substance would take the said. Office; and that it has been customary for former Marshals to suffer Escapes, to enable them to raise Money to pay their Ren.t, and to get their Livelihood.

R. Mullens.

The Examinations of Mr. Mullens, Marshal of the King's Bench Prison, taken 23d February, 1729, and 9th April, 1730.

This Examinant faith, that Knight and Surmait being possessed of Two Fifths of the Office of Marshal of the Prison of the King's Bench, as he is informed, Thomas Martin, Esquire, and Richard Bishop, Tipftalf of the Court of Common Pleas, purchased those Two Fifths of the Trustees of the South Sea Company, for the Sum of Sixteen hundred Pounds each, as this Examinant is also informed, and some time about Twelve Months since, Mr. Preston, Clerk of the Vintners Company, purchased Mr. Bijkop's laid Fifth; but knows not, what Sum of

Money was paid for it: That he computes the Fees, which he has actually received, as Marshal of the Prison, to amount to about Fifty Pounds annually, before they were lately reduced j and that he expects, very little will arise from those Fees for the future: That what induced him to take a new Grant of the said Office and Prison, at a Rent of Seven hundred and Fifty Pounds, was, from an Assurance given him by Mr. Studley, one of the Pro pri tors, of an Intention of the Proprietors to reduce h

Examination of Mr. John Morris.

H. John Morris, Deputy Marshal of the King's Bench Prison, being examined this 21st Day of February, 1729, fays, that he was appointed Deputy Marshal of the King's Bench, by Charles, Earl of above Twenty

Years ago, but hath not the Grant now with him, and paid Fifty Pounds to Thomas , for the said Earl, by way of Alienation, and a considerable Sum to him, the said Cook, who was then Deputy Marshal, and is since dead, for his surrendering to this Examinant; and that he paid a further Sum of Ten Guineas to one,

the then Marshal, and Twenty Guineas to the Lord

Vol. 21.

Chief Justice Holt, which, as far as this Examinant remembers, he gave to him with his own Hands.

Being asked, in what Manner the Office was furren-dered; fays, that Cook surrendered the Office to Lord Radnor, Two Days before Lord Radnor granted the Office to the Examinant.

Being asked, what was the Business of Deputy Mkr-shal; fays, that now the Business of Deputy Marshal is to attend the Court of King's Bench, with the Lord Chief Justice, wheresoever he goes; but formerly the Offices of Deputy Marshal, and Clerk of the Papers, were annexed; and now the Fees are given in jointly together.

Being asked, if he ever gave any thing, by way of Christmas Box, to the Judges, or any Officers under them; fays, that there was a Table kept in the Lord Chief Justice Holt's Time, and now he sometimes eats at the Lord Chief Justice's Table; and he has given at Half a Crown, orfo, to each Servant.

23d February, 1729. John Morris,

The Fourth Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That it is necessary to make further Provision, for the better Preservation of the Peace within the King's Bench Prison, and the Rules thereof

Ordered, That the said Report, with the Appendix, be printed; and that Mr. Speaker do appoint the Printing thereof j and that no Person, but such, as he Hull appoint, do presume to print the fame.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to Scarborough the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ, for Writ. the electing a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Scarborough, in the County of York, in the room of Sir William Strickland, Baronet, who, since his Election for the said Borough, hath accepted the Office of his Majesty's Secretary at War.

Ordered, That Mr. Thompson, of Scarborough, do Carry Coal Trade* to the Lords the Bill, intituled, An Act for the better Regulation of the Coal Trade; and acquaint them, that this House hath agreed to the Amendment, made by their Lordships thereto.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That effectual Provision be made, to prevent the Judges, their Clerks, and Servants, from receiving any Fees, Gifts, Presents, or any Gratuities whatsoever, from the Gaoler or Keeper of any Prison, or from any Officer intrusted with the Custody of the Prisoners, or.any Person impowered by them.

The Second Resolution of the Committee being read a Second time;

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee, in the said Resolution, That it is necessary to make further Provision, for the discovering, collecting, distributing, and accounting for, the Charities, belonging to the King's Bench Prison.

The King's After which, his Majesty was pleased to make a most dpctch. gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as tolloweth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Season of the Year, and the Dispatch you have given to the publick Business, make it proper for me to put an End to this Session; and I make no Doubt, but the Conduct and Behaviour of this Parliament, as it has answered my Expedations, will be equally Satisfadory to all my good and faithful Subjects.

The Support you have given me, in enabling me so effectually to make good my Engagements with my Allies, will, I persuade myself, have the desired Effect and, when it shall be seen, that the Allies of the Treaty of Seville are not only determined, but in a Readiness, to

execute their mutual Engagements, it is very much to be hoped, that a general Pacification will be the happy Consequence of this just and powerful Alliance.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I give you my Thanks, in particular, for the Supplies, you have raised for the Service of the current Year. It is a great Satisfaction to me, that you have had such a due Regard for the Ease of your Fellow-subjects, whole Welfare and Prosperity it shall always be my principal Care and Study to advance and promote.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I am very glad, that, for the general Satisfaction, you entered into a particular Consideration of the State of the Nation; a.nd it is a great Happiness, to fee, after so many unjust and unrealbnable Clamours, raised with all possible Art, Industry, and Malice, that, upon mature Deliberation, and the most solemn Debates, you were lb far from finding any thing worthy of Blame or Censure, that all Matters, which came under your Consideration, met with your Approbation.

This mull give all Mankind a just Detestation of those Incendiaries, who, from a Spirit of Envy and Discontent, continually labour, by scandalous Libels, to alienate the Affedions of my People, and to fill their Minds with groundless Jealoulies, and unjust Complaints, in Dif-honour of me, and my Government, and in Defiance of the Sense of both Houses of Parliament.

But I must rely upon vourPrudehce, and your Concern for the Peace and Happiness of your Country, to dif-countenance all such seditious Practices, and to make my People sensible, that these wicked Proceedings can have no other View, or End, but to create Confusion and Distraction among us.

Parliament And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty's prorogued. Command, Laid,

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty's royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to the Fourteenth

Day of July next, to be then here held; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Tuesday, the Fourteenth Day of July next.

Speech his Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty reported. was pieafet] to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House, and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen, 1

You cannot but be sensible, that the Measures formerly taken, and the Conclusion of the Treaty of have

prevented and dilappointed the dangerousConsequences, that were fojuftly apprehended from the Treaty of and we do not only fee that Union dissolved, which had alarmed all Europe, but the Allies of the Treaty of Hanover t strengthened by the additional Power of the Crown of Spain.

This Situation of Affairs gave us a reasonable Prospect of a general Pacification, and just Hopes of seeing the Conditions of the Treaty of complied with, with-'5

out the Necessity of coming to Extremities; and no Endeavours have been wanting, conformable to my Engagements with my Allies, to obtain that happy End; but this desirable Event having been hitherto delayed, the Treaty of Seville lays an indispensible Obligation upon all the contracting Parties to prepare for the Execution of it; and we must be in a Readiness to perform our Part, and, by continuing to pursue the proper Measures, convince our Allies, that we will faithfully fulfil our Engagements, and, as far as shall depend upon us, procure the Satisfaction due to them, either by such Means, as shall be most eligible, or by such, as shall be found absolutely necessary.

The present critical Conjuncture seems in a very particular Manner to deserve your Attention, and you need not be told, with what Impatience the Resolutions of this Parliament are every where waited for, and expected.

I am incapable of attempting to influence your Proceedings by groundless Fears and Apprehensions, and as incapable of amufingyou with vain Hopes and Expectations; but, as the Transaction % now depending in the several Courts of Europe, are upon the Point of being determined, the great Event of Peace, or War, may be very much affected by your first Resolutions. The Continuance of that Zeal and Vigour, which you have hitherto shewn, in Support of me, and my Engagements, must, at this Time, be of the greatest Weight and Importance, both with regard to my Allies, who cannot then think their Interest, and the common Cause, neglected, before the Conditions of their Treaties are accomplished, and with regard to those, who may be disposed, before the Sealon of Action is come, to prevent, by an Accomodation, the fatal Consequences of a general Rupture, which they will have little Reason to apprehend, if they find the Allies of Seville not prepared to do themselves Justice.

The Plan of Operations, for the Execution of the Treaty of Seville by Force, in case we shall be driven to that Necessity, is now under Confederation, and, until the Proportions of the confederate Forces, and the proper Dispositions for employing them, shall be finally adjusted, and agreed upon, it will not be easy to determine, how far the Expences, necessary for the Service of the ensuing Year, may, or may not, exeed the Provisions made for the Service of the last Year.

In the mean time, I am persuaded you will go on to give all possible Dispatch to the publick Business; and, if it shall be necessary, I shall not fail to alk the further Advice and Assistance of my Parliament, according to the Circumstances of publick Affairs, as soon as any proper Occasion shall require it.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I will order the proper Estimates to be prepared, and laid before you; and 1 can make no Doubt, but that dutiful Regard, which you have always shewed to me, and my Honour, and your just Concern for the true Interest of your Country, will induce you to grant me the necessary Supplies, and enable me to make good my Engagements with my Allies, with that Ciiearfulness and Afle&ion, which become a British House of Commons, tender and jealous of the Honour of the Crown, careful and solicitous for the Glory and Prosperity of the Kingdom.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Time draws near, which will admit of no further Delays. If the Tranquillity of Europe can be settled, without the Effusion of Blood, or the Expence of publick Treasure, that Situation will certainly be most happy, and desirable; but, if that Blessing cannot be obtained.

Honour,

Resolved, That, in case it shall appear, any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to' deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanor, and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

We cannot but tn G ratitude ackiiowlcdge your Majesty's Goodnels, in endeavouring to have the Conditions of the Treaty of Seville fulfilled and executed in such Manner, as might best secure a general Pacification, and be conformable to your Engagements with your Allies.

And, out of a just Scute of the Bletfings we enjoy, we think it our Duty to declare our intire Confidence in your royal Care and Concern for the Honour and Interest of your People, and our perfect Reliance upon your Majesty's Wil'dom and Justice, in doing every Thing, that shall depend upon you, to procure the Satisfaction, due to your Allies, by such Means, as shall be the most desirable, or, if they prove ineffectual, by such as shall be absolutely ftecellary.

We are firmly resolved to continue our utmost Zeal and Vigour in Support of your Majesty, and your Engagements, esteeming this the least Part of our Duty, when we consider, that those Engagements are the Effefit of your Vigilance for the Welfare of your Subjects.

We allure your Majesty, that we will give all possible Dispatch to the publick Dufinels, as it shall from time to time be brought before us, that, as your People feel the Ilappiness of your Reign, lb your Majesty may feel the Eale of it; and from a dutiful Regaril to your Honour and Dignity, and a just Concern for the true Interest of our Country, which we shall always look Upon as indil-penfible and inseparable Obligations, we have the greatest Satisfaction in*assuring your Majesty, that we will, with ell Chearfulness, grant such Supplies, as shall be necessary for the Service of the ensuing Year, and effectually enable your Majesty to make good your Engagements with your Allies.

Your Majesty's Goodness to your People is very apparent in your avoiding to brin»: any unnecessary Burthens upon them; and it is the leaftReturn we can make for it, to allure your Majesty, that, in case the Circumstances of publick Affairs shall oblige you to a fit the further Advice und Assistance of your faithful Commons, we will upon every Occasion, discharge our Duty to your Majesty, and those we represent, with that Chearfulness and Affection, which become a Bn House of Commons, tender and jealous of the Honour of the Crown, careful and felicitous for the Glory and Proi'perity of the Kingdom.

The said Address, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House, as are of his Majesty's most honourable Privy Council, do humbly know his Majesty's Pleal'ure, when he will -be attended by this House.

Ordered, That the Reverend Doctor Edward Littleton, be desired to preach before this House at St. Margaret's Westminster, upon the 30th Day of this instant January', and that Mr. Walpole and Mr. Longueville do acquaint him therewith.

RefAved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, take into Consideration his Majesty's most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of Sir William , Baronet, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that at the last Election of Members, to serve in this Parliament for the Borough of Honiton, com' Devon, Sir Wm. , Knight,

James Shepheard, Serjeant at Law, and the Petitioner, were Candidates: That Mr. Serjeant Shepheard, and his Agents, by Bribery, and other indirect Practices, procured several Votes, and prevailed on the Portreve to allow him several Votes, who had no Right, and tef disallow several Voters for the Petitioner, who had a Right to vote; and yet the Petitioner had a Majority of legal Votes, and ought to have been returned; but the Portreve hath returned Serjeant Shepheard, in Prejudice to the Petitioner: And praying the Justice of the House in the Premises.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Conficleration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do examine whether the said Petition be the fame, in Substance, with the Petition presented last &(fion, and make Report thereof in the First place, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Were severally presented to the House, and read; complaining of a general Declcnsion in the Woollen Trade, and the great Increase of the Poor, occasioned by the large Exportations of unwrought Wool from Great Britain and Ireland to other Nations; who, mixing it with their own Wool, make their Goods fit for Market, and thereby, and by the Cheapness of their Labour, are enabled greatly to undersell the British Merchants, to the Ruin of our Manufactures:

And praying the Consideration of the House, that the Duty may be takenoif Irish Yarn at Importation, and such Other Relief given, as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Committee to whom the Petition of several Mailers, and Members, of the Company of Weavers within the City of Bristol is refered.

Manchester A Petition of the principal Inhabitants, Traders, and

Workhouse. Land-owners, within the Town of Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaj, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of tliernselves, and others, the great-eft Part of the Inhabitants, Traders, and Land-owners, within the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitionees are informed, there is a Petition depending in the House, praying Leave to bring in a Bill for erecting a publick Woik-house in the said Town, for the better Maintenance and Employment of their Poor: That there is already a convenient Workhouse hired for that Purpose by the common Consent, at a publick Meeting of the said Town, and therefore, they apprehend, there is no Occasion for any other, which will prejudice their Trade, and render their -Rights and Properties very precarious: And praying, that they may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, before such Bill be brought into the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Petition of the several Inhabitants, Traders, and Proprietors of Land, within the Town of Manchester, in the County of easier, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and others, the Inhabitants, Traders, and Proprietors of Land, within the same Town, presented to the House the Twenty-third Day of January last, is referred; and that the Petitioners be heard by themselves, or Counsel, if they think fit, before the said Committee, against the said last mentioned Petition.

A Petition of the several Inhabitants, Land-owners, Mandril and Traders, within the Town of Manchester, in the Workbcote, County Palatine of Lancaster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others of the principal Inhabitants, Land-owners, and Traders, within the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioners find by the Votes of the House, that theie is a Petition, praying Leave to bring in a Bill for erecting a publick Workhouse in the Towr\ of Manchester, for the better Maintenance and Employment of their Poor: That there is already a convenient Workhouse hired for the Maintenance and Employment of the Poor? in pursuance of the present Laws, by common Confeat, at a publick Town Meeting, and there is no Occasion for any other; and that a Workhouse, as intended by the Petition depending in this House, praying a Bill for that Purpose, will prejudice the Trade and Interest of the said Town, and render the Rights and Properties of the Inhabitants, Traders, and Land-owners, therein, precarious and uncertain; and that the Terms proposed for building the Workhouse petitioned for, are disagreeable to the Town in general, and have been rejected at a publick Meeting: The Petitioners therefore pray the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that they may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, before such Bill be brought in.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the Petition of the several Inhabitants, Traders, and Proprietors of Land, within the Town of Manchester, in the County of ccfier, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and others, the Inhabitants, Traders, and Proprietors of Land, within the same Town, presented to the House the Twenty-third Day of January last, is referred; and that the Petitioners be heard by themselves, or Counsel, if they think fit, before the said Committee, against the said last mentioned Petition.

Harbour11 Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, *r our* and other the Inhabitants, of the Towns of Lewes,

haven, Brighthelmston, and Places adjacent, in the County of Sussex, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, that the Harbourof Newhavenh situate at the Mouth of a navigable River, about i8 Leagues from the Downs, Three from Beachy Head, and 15 from Portsmouth, and was once, by a Pier there erected, a late and convenient Harbour for Ships under Twenty Feet Draught, and a great Benefit to Merchants and Inhabitants thereabouts; but no Provision being made to support the lame, the Timber thereof hath been long since decayed, and the Harbour is now almost useless; nor has there been many Years any other Harbour, than such as the Inhabitants have occasionally cut through, at great Expence, to let out and in small Vessels, hired at excessive Freights, from the Incertaintv of its Continuance: That, were the old Pier rebuilt, and the Harbour restored, it would be the most convenient Place to receive out-ward bound Ships, that cannot reach the Isle of Wight, the only Means to prevent frequent Shipwrecks against Beachy Head, a safe Retreat for Merchant Ships in Time of War, and yfeful to drain many thousand Acres of Pasture Land, often overflowed, and the Produce of their own Country also exported, to their own Advantage, and of his Majesty's Revenues: And praying, that they may be enabled to collect a small Duty on the Goods and Vessels to be loaden or unloaden in the said Harbour, for and towards restoring and continuing the said Pier and Harbour, or that the House will grant such other Provision for the fame, as shall be thought meet.

MR. Roll* reported from the Committee, to whom Ilfordcombe the Petition of the Inhabitants of the Town and Hlrb<m-Borough of Ilfordcombe, with other Parts adjoining, in the County of Devon, and also of divers Justices of the Peace, and Gentlemen, dwelling near the said Town, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, hs it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, dated the Second Day of this instant February, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and, in order to prove the Allegations thereof, the Witnesses following were called; viz.

Mr. Henry Steevins; who, being examined, said, that the Key, or Pier, of the Harbour of Ilfordcombe is, by Length of Time, and the Violence of the Sea, very much funk and decayed, and the Warp, Light-house, and Boats, belonging to the Harbour, which is a very commodious one, are much out of Repair; by reason whereof the Navigation is almost loft, to the great Prejudice of his Majesty's Revenue, and the Trade of the said Town, the Harbour whereof is an ancient Place for fiflring and catehing of Herrings.

The said Henry Steevins further gave Evidence, that many Ships, and Persons, failing up and down the Brifol Chanel, have been preserved by the Affifiance of Boats, kept in this Harbour for piloting of Vessels distrelkd by contrary Winds; but, since the Harbour has been much decayed, a Ship was loft, and others have been in great Danger.

That the Committee find, several small Duties were laid, by a By-law, on Goods imported to, and exported from, the said Harbour, for maintaining and repairing, and keeping in Repair, the Key and Harbour, and the Warp, Warp-house, Light-house, and Boats, thereunto belonging; but there being no Power to enforce the Payment of the said Duties, not one half thereof Las of late Years been paid, notwithstanding the Light-house and Wharfs have been kept up.

That the Petitioners called ^Mr. John ,who,

being examined, confirmed what was said by Henry Steevins; and by their Evidence it appeared, that, unless Power be given for levying and collecting some Duties, to be ascertained, for maintaining, and keeping in Repair, the Key, Warp, Warp-house, Light-house, and Boats, the same will in a very little Time be ruined and destroyed, and the Town, which only depends on the Harbour and Pier, thereby very much impoverished.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for repairing, and keeping in Repair, the Pier and Harbour of Ilfordcombe, in the County of Devon; and that Mr.

Rolle, Mr. Tremayne, and Sir William Yonge, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

there was formerly a Pier, for making a convenient Harbour for Merchants Ships and Vessels, employed in exporting Corn, and other Goods, particularly large Quantities of Timber, lent to his Majesty's Docks and Yards; but the Pier being decayed, for want of a Provision made for repairing thereof, the Water runs into the Sea near Two Miles to the Eastward, whereby the Harbour is frequently stopped up, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners; which, being made a safe Harbour, may prevent many Wrecks at and be a Safety to

Privateers, cruiling on that Coast in Time of War: And praying, that they may l e enabled to coIlc«5t a small Duty on the Goods and Vessels, to be loaden or unloaden in the Harbour of Newhaven, for and towards restoring and continuing the said Harbour, and the Pier there, which are gone to Decay, but may be made of great Use to the Publick; or that this House will grant such other Provision for the fame, as shall be thought meet.

GEORGE the Second, by the Grace of God, King of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, Duke of Brunswick and Lunenburg, Arch-treasurer of the holy Roman Empire, and Prince Elector, ( 3c.To all, to whom these Presents shall come, Greeting. Whereas a certain Treaty, of a more intimate Friendship and mutual Defence, together with a separate Article to the same belonging, have been concluded between us, and the most serene and most high Prince Augustus William Duke of Brmjwick and Lunenburg Wo I-fenbuttel, and signed by the Ministers Plenipotentiaries, as well on our Part, as on the Part of the aforesaid most serene Duke, being furnished with full Powers and Authorities for that Purpose, in our City of Westminster, the Twenty-fifth Day of last past, in the Form

and Words following:

Whereas the most serene House of Brunswick Lunenburg has always endeavoured to preserve and cultivate an intimate Friendship between all its Branches, which has not only contributed to the Glory and Happiness of the

20

said moil serene House, but also to the Advantage of the Procestant Religion, the Interests whereof the said House has at all times had at heart; his Majesty the most serene King of Great Britain, Elector of Brunswick Lunenburg, and his most serene Highness the Duke of Brunswick Lunenburg Wolfenbuttel, judging, that it will be very proper, as well for the mutual Good of their House, as for that of the Protestant Religion, to strengthen the ancient Union by new Ties, made between his said Majesty and his said most serene Highness, with a View only to give each other a mutual Guaranty for their own Countries, and without the least Design to cause any Trouble, or to do any Prejudice, either to the Emperor, or the Empire, or to any other Power whatsoever; to this end they have on each Side given sufficient full Power, that is to say, his said Majesty the most serene King of Great Britain to his Privy Counsellors, Peter Lord Kin % , Baron of Ockham, High Chancellor of Great Britain, William Duke of Devonshire, President of his Privy Council, Thomas Lord Trevor, Keeper of his Privy Seal, Thomas Holies, Duke of Newcastle, one of his principal Secretaries of State, Charles Viscount Townshend, one other of his principal Secretaries of State, and Sir Robert Walpole, Knight of the most noble Order of the Garter, and first Commissioner of his Treasury, and his said most serene Highness the Duke of Brunswick Lunenburg Wolfenbuttel to the Sieur Conrad Det/eff, Count of De/tn, his privy Minister of State, President of the Chamber of Convents, Dean of the Chapter of St. Blaift at Brunswick, hereditary Cup-bearer of the Abby of

Ganderfheim, Lord of Wemdand Knight of the Danish Orders, and his Plenipotentiary to his Majesty of Great Britain-, who, having conferred together on the Means the most proper to attain the Ends above-mentioned, without doing Hurt to any one, have agreed upon the following Articles:

I.

That there shall be an intimate Friendship, and a sincere, firm, and unchangeable. Union, between the said King and the said Duke, their Heirs and Successors; which shall be so exactly and faithfully observed, that the contrafting Parties shall not only advance their mutual Interests, but shall also keep off from each other all Injury and Damage whatsoever, and shall traverse, as much as possible, every prejudicial Design, that may be formed against either of the said contrafting Parties, pursuant to the Treaties and Conventions, that are already subsisting betweeen the Two Branches of the said most serene House.

H.

That, by virtue of this drift Union, the said contrafting Parties do promise to assist each other mutually, by their Counsels, and by their good Offices, every-where, where it shall be needful; and, as the most serene King of Great Britain promises to guaranty to the said most serene Duke all his Countries and Dominions, so the said most serene Duke promises his Guaranty to the said most serene King, for the Defence of his Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland, and of his Countries and Dominions in Germany.

And whereas the Treaty concluded at Zell the 6th of May 1671, between the most serene Dukes of Brunswick Lunenburg, already obliges the most serene Duke to maintain always, as far as possible, the Possession of the Town and Fortress of Brunswi, for the common Security of the most serene House; his said most serene Highness renews hereby the whole Tenor of that said Article, and engages never to deliver his said Town and Fortress of Brunswick into the Hands, Possession, or Power, of any one whomsoever

III.

That, in same the abovesaid Countries and Dominions of either of the contrafting Parties be threatened with an Attack, or Invasion, then they shall concert together, without Loss of Time, the Means to repulse their Enemies, and shall regulate immediately, and without Delay, the Proportions of tire Succours to be given mutually; it

A Petition of the Justices of Peace, Gentlemen, and Language of Grand Juries of the West Riding of the County of Proceeding* York, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, 10La*‘ that it most frequently happens that none of the Grand Jury Men, serving at the Quarter Sessions, understand Latin, yet are obliged to make their Presentments, or Indictments, upon Oath, in that Language: That, when the Proceedings of Justices of Peace are removed by a Certiorari, the Returns are to be made in a Character, and Language, unknown to any, but the learned in the Law, which puts the Justices to great Expence in seeing Counsel to draw the same: That special Pleadings are found to be not only expensive, intricate, and dilatory, but highly prejudicial to the Property of the Subject, since many Persons have merely by the strict Rules of pleading, and uncertainty thereof, lost their Estates:

That, by some Mismanagement in the Execution of a late good and profitable Law, the Number of Attorneys continues still to be excessive, and Men of known infamous Characters have been lately admitted into the Courts, to practise in that Proftffion: And praying the House to take these Grievances into Consideration, and such Relief, as the House shall think fit.

Rewliaven Mr. Pelham, of Lewes, reported from the Committee, Harbour, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, and other Inhabitants, of the Towns of Lewes, Newhaven, Bright helmfion, and other Places adjacent,

in the County of Sussex, and also the Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, and other the Inhabitants, of the Towns of Sea/ord, , Wilming-

ton, Alfriston, and Places adjacent, in the said County, were referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, dated the 8th Instant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the Petitions; and the several Witnesses following were called;

Mr. Richard Lemon said, that he has known the Harbour of Newhaven for 50 Years, which lies at the Mouth of a navigable River, about 18 Leagues from the Downs, Three from Beachykead, and about x 5 from j

and, while the Pier remained good, it was a safe and convenient Harbour for Ships to come in, with 20 Feet Water at the Height of a Spring Tide, and was of great Benefit to the Merchants, and Inhabitants, of the Places adjacent; but for 40 Years part: the Pier hath been de-caying, there being no Provision to support it, whereby the Harbour is now become almost useless.

Mr. John Diplock, Mr. Gabriel , Mr. Benja. Swaine, Mr. Charles Harr if on, and Nix. John Whitfield,

being severally examined, confirmed the Evidence, before |>iven by Mr. Lemon; and further said, that the Pier being decayed, and the River unconfined, the River runs into several Places of the Beach, making a narrow Chanel, near Two Miles to the East<from the Pier; and the Mouth of the Harbour is frequently choaked up with Beach, and Sand, which the Farmers, and other Inhabitants, are often at great Expences in cutting through, to let finall Vessels in and out, hired at excessive Prices Vox.. 21.

for Freights, by reason of the Uncertainty of coming in and going out of the Harbour.

And they added, that about Two Months ago 13 Vessels were (hut up, loaded with Corn, which could not go out, till the Mouth of the Harbour was cut through, and cleared.

They farther gave Evidence, that, if the Pier was rebuilt, or a new one erected, the Harbour might be restored, and made as good a Tide Harbour, as any in England, be of great Service for receiving Ships, pafljBg between the Isle of Wight and the Downs, and prevent Losses by Shipwreck, often happening against head, and be a Preservation of Merchant Ships in time of War.

Mr. Gabriel Ayres and Mr. Benja. Swaine being asked, what would be the Expence of rebuilding the old Pier, or erecting a new onethey said, they believed, it would coll between Two and Three thousand Pounds; and that would make it as good a Tide Harbour, as any in England.

Mr. John Whitfield said, that, the Harbour being in a very bad Condition, the Freight of Timber is 4J. per Load more than it would be if the Harbour was made good; and that the Freight of other Goods is proportionable: And added, that he has known Vessels for that Reason go to other Harbours at a greater Distance, to unlade their Goods, and the Owners thereof have lent for them by Land Carriage, which has occasioned an Expence of above £. 15. per Cent, to them.

Mr. Benjamin Swaine, being again examined, confirmed the Evidence, given by Mr. in relation

to the excessive Prices of Freights.

A Petition of the Royal African Company of England, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, that this House having in the last Session, upon full Examination and Consideration of the State of the Trade to Africa, granted the Sum of Ten thousand Pounds towards the Maintenance of the British Forts and Settlements there, belonging to the Petitioners, the said Sum hath been applied accordingly; and it having appeared to the House, that the said Forts and Settlements cannot be supported, and the Trade preserved, without the Aid of Parliament, the Petitioners therefore pray, that such further Provision may be made in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr.Chancellorof the Exchequer acquainted the House, that his Majesty, having been informed of the Contents of this Petition, had been pleased to command him to acquaint this House, that his Majesty recommends it ro their Consideration, to make such turther Provision in the Premises, as the House shall think fit.

the Petition of the Owners and Proprietors of Lands, lying dispersed in the common Fieids and Grounds in in the County of Gloucester, whose names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf ol themselves, and other Owners and Proprietors of Land in the said common Fields and Grounds, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed lum to report the fame, as it appeared ter them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 13th Day of February instant, had taken into Consideration the said Petition; and, to make out the Allegations thereof,

The Petitioners produced the Articles of Agreement entered into by the Owners and Proprietors, for dividing and inclosing the said Common, comm n Ground, and Fields; by which it appealed, that all those who had tignecl the said Articles, were desirous that the said Common, and common Fields, might be divided, and inclosed.

That it also appeared to the Committee, that there are Five Proprietors who have not ligned the Articles; and such Proprietors have only a Sixteenth Part in the said common Fields and Grounds.

Then the Petitioners called Mr. Thomas Wells', who said, that he had acquainted the said Five Proprietors with the Contents of the said Articles, and that they laid, they would not of;*ofe such Inclosure.

Mr. Thomas Wells and Mr. Edward Baghott said, that if the said common Fields, and common Grounds, were inclosed, the same would be of great Benefit and Advantage to the Publick, and all Parties concerned therein; but such Inclosure cannot be effectually made, without the Aid of an Act of Parliament.

Mr. Alderman Perry reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants of the City of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others, trading to his Majesty's Colonies of Virginia and Maryland, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, in order to prove the Allegations of the said Petition, examined the following Witness; viz.

Mr. Thomas Colmore; who said, that about Two Months since he came from Maryland: That the Rivers, Coasts, and Seal?, adjoining thereto, abound with great Quantities of Shad, Sturgeon, Bass, Sardine, and several other Kinds of Fish: That he has salted several Barrels of Herrings, and sent them to has known leve-

ral Barrels of Fish spoiled, for want of good Salt: That, if Salt were permitted to be imported from Europe into the said Colonies, it would be a Means of establishing a

Fishery there, and tend to the advancing the Trade of Great Britain to those Places.

Mr. James Black down, one of the Clerks to the Turn* pike on the said Road, confirmed Mr. North's Evidence as to the Badness of the Road; and said, that the Proportion of the loll, allowed for keeping this Road in Repair, is so far from being sufficient to amend the fame* that it will require double the Toll::

Parish, are willing to pay double the roll they no* pay, provided the Road is sufficiently amended, and kept in Repair.

That it appeared to the Committee* that the Inhabitants of the several Parishes, through which the Road leads, have constantly done their Statute-work; and that* unless the present 'foil, taken at the Turnpikes on this Road, be doubled, the same cannot be amended, and kept in Repair.

Palatine of Lancaster, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others, the principal Inhabitants, Land-owners, and Traders, within the said Town, were referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read ihe Report in his Place, and after-Wards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the Report was read, and is as followcch; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the Twenty-third Day of January last, had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; andj to prove the Allegations of the First Petition, tncfics were called; viz.

Mr. Chrijicpher Byron, being examined, laid, that the Town of A.lanchejieris very large and populous, and the Poor numerous; and that within thele Five Years the Inhabit.ints have paid double of what they paid formerly, towards the Maintenance of the Poor:

That he applied to the proper Officer, who kept the Poor's Books, to inspetft, and take a Copy, or Extratft, from them, and was denied lo to do; but the Overseers of the Poor acknowledged to him, that the Poor's Rates were very much increased from what they used to be.

He further said, that, if a Workhouse was built, the Poor might be employed, and kept from rambling up and down; it would be an Eale to the Inhabitants, in the Poor's Rates, paid towards their Maintenance, and be of great Advantage to the Trade of the Town.

And he further gave Evidence, that about October, 1729, he was sent for to be at a Meeting of several of the chief and substantial Inhabitants of the Town, at which Meeting the Churchwardens, and other Officers of the Town, were present, and then received Instruction, in Writing, from one of the Churchwardens, to prepare a Draught of a Subscription Deed: Pursuant thereunto, he ptepared one accordingly, and attended them at another Meeting with it; when it was read, and unanimously agreed to by all, that were then present, and ordered to be ingrossed; and, after it was ingrossed, he law Fourteen of them lign it, which were all, that were present at that Meeting; Which Subscription Deed he delivered to the Committee; which was read; whereby it appeared, that Two thousand Pounds, and upwards, is subscribed, the Subscribers whereof are the chief Inhabitants of the Town.

And he laid further, that he was at a Meeting of some of the Inhabitants in June last, about Eight Months after the Subscription Deed was signed; when it was unanimously agreed, that a Workhouse should be hired for a Year only, for employing the Poor, until one could be built, pursuant to the Subscription Deed; and it was then agreed by the Churchwardens to apply to Parliament for an Act for creating a Workhouse:

That he was at the Workhouse, so hired, in December last, wherein were only Forty-five People taken in, and saw only One Perfirn employed at Work.

Mr. John Kay, being called, and examined, said, that he hath known the Town of Manchester about Four Years; and uioft of the Subscribers acknowledged to him, that their Names to the Subscription Deed was of their own Hand-writing} and he knew them to be Men of Subltaoce.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine the Matter of the Two Petitions, presented to the House the Second lnstant; and, to prove the Allegations thereof, Witnesses were called;

Mr. Bcwker; who laid before the Committee a Book of AiRfiments, made for a Poor's Rate in the Town of Manchester, which was signed by the Justices of the Peace

in June last, which is the usual Time of making the said A/Ieffments.

He is Overseer of the Poor, and hath been lo for Ten Years pa ft, for which he receives a Salary of Thirty Pounds per Annum :And laid, that a Book was produced

at a Meeting of several of the Inhabitants of the Town, and subscribed by great Numbers of them; but confessed, he never saw, or heard of, any such Book kept there, or of any such Meeting, before.

Mr. Jeffery Hart mid, that he had taken an Abstract of the Poor's Rate; and that it amounted to about £.1,333.

That the Inhabitants who have signed the Subscription Deed, and petitioned for a Bill for efedting a Workhouse, pay to the Poor's Rate £. 229. is. 9a. That the Petitioners against such Bill, who have subscribed the Deed, pay £.236. 14*. 2 d.and the rest of the Petitioners against the same pay £.506. 14*. 4 And he added, that at a Meeting, after the Subscription Deed was signed, it was then proposed to hire a Workhouse for a Year; and at another Meeting, the 2 2d of December last, a Paper was read, said to be a Subscription, which was rejected by those, that were then present.

Mr. John Byrom, being called, confirmed the Evidence, given by Mr. Hart, of a Proposal of hiring a Workhouse for a Year; and added, that he was at the Meeting on the 22d of December last, where about 190 of the Inhabitants of the Town were present; when it waspropoled to them to agree to the Subscription Deed, Which had been signed by several of the Inhabitants, for ere&inga Workhouse, a Copy of which, he said, was read at that Meeting; and they all declared against it: But, being asked, if he had examined that Paper, which was read to them, with the original Subscription Deed, he said, he never saw it: He hath a Family at but

could not say; whether or no he paid Scotland Lot.

That the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of the Committee,

That the Petitioners for a Bill for erecting a Workhouse in the Town of Manchester, have fully proved the Allegations of their said Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill for erecting a Workhouse in the Town of Manchester, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, for the better main- taming and employing the Poor of the said Town.

The House being informed, that Mr. Crookfhanks, Prcgre&of Secretary to his Majesty's Commissaries at the Court of Spain, attended at the Door, he was called in, and, at against^i*. the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to their Address to his Majesty, An Account of the Progress, which has been made by the Commissaries, appointed by his Majesty in consequence of the Treaty of Seville.

And then he withdrew.

And the Title of the said Account was read:

The said Account is as followeth; viz.

To the honourable the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses; in Parliament assembled.

In humble Obedience to his Majesty's Commands, signified to me by his Grace the Duke of Newcaft/e, one ©this Majesty's principal Secretaries of State, in pursuance of an Address of this honourable House, That his Majesty would be graciously pleased togive Orders for an Account to be laid before them, of the Progress, which has been made by the Commissaries, appointed by his Majesty and the King of Spain, in consequence of the Treaty of Seville, foradjufting the Demands, and Reparations, due to the Merchants of Great Britain, in the Matters to them referred, requiring me to lay before this honourable House an Account of the Proceedings of the said Commissaries, and what I, as their Secretary, have transiufted in the Execution of his Majesty's Commission for the Purposes above-mentioned, I humbly lay before this honourable House the following Account:

His Majesty having been pleased to name Benjamin Keene, Arthur Stert, and John Goddard, Esquires, his Commissaries for the Purposes aforesaid, and to order a Commission for them, in that behalf, to be prepared, and passed under the great Seal, the same was issued accordingly, and bears Date the ad Day of April, io the 3d Year of his Majesty's Reign; by which any One or Two of them may act in the Absence of the rest.

His Majesty's Pleasure having been signified, by a Letter from the said principal Secretary of State to the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, dated the Stli Day of the same Month, that they shouldgive Notice to the Merchants and others, who had any Claims to belaid beforethe said Commissaries, to bring them to their Board, with the necessary Proofs and Vouchers annexed, to be by them put into the Hands of the said Commissaries,

Care was taken, by publick Advertisements, dated the 9th and 23d of the same Month of April, inserted in the London Gazette, and frequently repeated, and by other proper Notices, to call upon the Merchants, and others concerned, to bring in their Claims to the said Lords Commissioners.

In the mean time Mr. Stert and Mr. Goddard, Twmof the Commissaries, attended the Board of Trade, to con-fult upon the most proper and regular Method of authenticating the Proofs and Vouchers, to be annexed to the said Claims; and, after several Confutations with his Majesty's Advocate-general, as well as with the Merchants, and others concerned, it was thought for the Advantage of the Claimants, that their respective Demands should be authenticated in the Court of Admiralty, according to the general Practice of other Nations in the like Cafes; and an humble Rep refen tat ion being made to the 17 King,

4 Geo. II.

26° Febru

King, of the Expence this would be to the Merchants, his Majesty was graciously pleased to take upon himself the Payment of the Fees for authenticating such Claims in the ("aid Court; of which publick Notice was also given in the Gazette the 23d of and that it would be necessary to have Spanish Translations of all Proofs and Documents annext to the

The laid Commissaries also attended the several Offices of the Secretaries of State, of the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, and the Directors of the South Sea Company, and had frequent Meetings with the Merchants, and other Persons concerned, to procure the proper Lights and Informations, for the better enabling them to discharge their Trull.

On or about the 23d of , Messieurs Stert and Goddard set out from London to Plymouth, where One of his Majesty's Ships of War was to take them on board, having, before their Departure, acquainted the several Offices before mentioned; and other Persons concerned, with their Design of setting out for and of leaving me behind, to receive the Claims, and bther Papers and Documents, and given me Orders, to use my utmost Endeavours for having every thing dispatched in the most char and authentick Method possible.

By Letter, dated the 27th of August, they inform me, that Three Days before they had received their instructions by a Messenger, and Orders to set out for the Court of Spain without Loss of Time; so that they only

waited the Arrival of the Hefl Man of War, then at PortJmoUth.

By Letter, dated Plymouth, the 27th of,

they advile me, that they should embark that Afternoon.

By Letter, dated from the Bay of the 20th of November, N. S. they advise me of having had a long Passage from Plymouth to Lisbon, and liom thence to that Bay.

On the 25th of November, N. S. they got to Seville-, and upon the 6th ot December, N. S. Mi. Keene and they wrote a circular Lerter to the British Conl'uls in Spain, for an Account of such Grievances as any Merchant in their respective Factories, or other British Traders, might have sustained by Infractions of Treaties subsisting between the Crowns of Great B. and Spain.

By Letter from Seville, of the 2111 of December, N. S. they advise me, that his Catholick Majesty had not yet named Commissaries, but had promised, it should soon be done.

Since the Departure of Mr. Stert and Mr. Goddard from London, I have pursued their Directions in the following Manner:

ill, In getting, from his Grace the Duke of Newcastle's Office, C >pies of all Treaties with from 1667 to

1729, inclusive, certified by a proper Clerk, and me, to have been collated with the Originals. Thele Copies made a large Volume, and hath since been sent from his Grace's Office by a Messenger to the Commissaries at Seville:

2cily, In getting, at the said Office, Copies of several Letters and Papers relating to the Spanish Ships taken by the English in 1718} in the same Manner collated and dispatched to Seville:

3d)y, In getting, pursuant to his Majesty's Orders to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, Copies of ail Letters and Papers in that Office, relating to the Prizes taken by, or from, the Spani, since the Peace at Utrecht-, which were compared by the proper Clerks, and myself, and certified to be true Copies, and have been in like manner sent from the said Secretary of State's Office to the Commissaries at Seville:

4thly, In attending on the Agents to the Captors of the Spanish Ships taken in 1718, for obtaining from them a full Account thereof, with authentick Vouchers, for settling that Matter; which Account, and Vouchers, have been lent to the Commissaries at Seville from the said Secretary of State's Office, in manner as aforesaid:

V01. 21.

5thly, In attending at DoHors Commons, on his Majesty's Advocate-general, for his Opinion in some Cafes which occurred; in waiting on his Majesty's Procurator-general, and the Examiner in the Court of Admiralty, with several Claimants, for the dispatching their Claims:

6th!y, In attending at the South Sea House, to receive the Company's Demands and Instructions; but the Papers, being very voluminous, were not in Readiness:

7thly, The Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations thought it proper to keep exact Copies of all the Claims, for Security of the Claimants, and for maintaining a regular Correspondence with the Commissaries in Spain; and, as the original Claims were to be delivered to me, upon my Receipt, their Lordships Secretary, and I, compared the Copies with the Originals, certifying them to be true Copies:

As Claims were brought in daily, a constant Attendance was requisite: Many of the Claims were very long, and one above 100 Sheets of Paper, being swelled with several Autos in Spanish, and sundry Documents in Italian, French, and other Languages; the Copies whereof, taken at the Office of the Lords Commissioners for Trade, make several large Volumes in Folio:

8thly, In comparing at the Office of the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, with the Originals there, several Memorials, Letters, and Papers, relating to the Trade to the Canary Islands, and several Places in Spain, &c. Copies whereof were made in Two Books in Folio, one containing 169 Pages, and the other 247 Pages, certified by their Lordships Secretary, and me, to be true Copies.

Upon the 30th of September last I received from the Secretary to the Lords Commissioners for Trade 48 Claims upon 37 Ships; which Claims, with the Two Books before mentioned, were sent by a Messenger from his Grace the Duke of Newcastle's Office to the Commissaries at Seville.

Upon the 16th of januetry last I received from the Secretary to the Lords Commissioners for Trade 54 Claims, 20 of which were upon Four of the said 37 Ships, and the remaining 34 Claims were upon 33 other Snips; which Claims have been in like manner forwarded to the Commissaries at Seville.

Upon the 25th of this instant February I received from the Secretary to the Lords Commissioners for Trade Eight Claims, Three of which were upon Three of the aforesaid Ships, Three upon Three other Ships, and the other Two for Effects and Prov.lions seized; which last mentioned Claims will be speedily conveyed to the said Commissaries at Seville.

London, 26th February, *730.

With humble Submission.

Jcr Crookjhanks Secretary to his Majesty's Commissaries at the Court of Spain.

Memorandum: The other Deductions out of the several Land Taxes do not appear at the Receipt of Exchequer; but by several Acts, granting the fame, there is to be allowed, by the Auditors, in passing the Receivers Accounts, the following Deductions; viz. id. per Pound to Receivers:

3 d.per Pound to Collectors:

1 id. per Pound to Commissioners Clerks:

As also Moneys discharged by Certificates from the Barons of the Exchequer, to reduce the double Tax to a single one, in Cafes, were Papists take the Oaths, or their Estates come to Protestants.

And likewise by the Act for Mutiny and Desertion, the Justices of the Peace, by their Warrants, are authorized to charge the Collectors of the Land Tax with the Payment of 20lh. for every Deserter apprehended within their respective Districts or Collections.
