Regulation The Lord Mayor of London reported from the Com-yf Broker* mittee to whom the Petition of the several Merchants, in London. an(j Traders, of London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Report, and Resolutions of the Committee, are as followeth;

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Allegations of the said Petition; and, to prove the fame, Witnessls were called 5 viz.

Mr. Philip Devifme; who said, that several act as Brokers, who have no legal Authority for so doing, and many of whom, under, or making use of, the Names of such Jews as are licensed; and such Jews, so acting without Authority, cannot be hindered, as the Law noiv stands, although not only prejudicial to the Merchants, but to such Brokers as are Chriflia

He further said, that about Twenty-two Years since an Order was made by the then Lord Mayor and Court of Aldermen, for admitcingTwelve Persons to be Brokers, although not free of the City; whereupon the French and Dutch Congregations here in London made Application to the Court of Aldermen, that Six , and Six Dutch, might be licensed to act as foreign Brokers; but such Application proved fruitless: Nevertheless, about that time Twelve Jews were licensed by the Court of Aldermen to act as Brokers, and were confined to that Number for several Years; but of late the Lord Mayor and Court of Aldermen have thought fit to admit, without Limitation, Persons to act as Brokers, to the Prejudice of Merchants and Traders; and that now there are great Numbers of Persons, who are neither licensed, or qualified; and such Persons frequently impole on the Merchants; but if all Brokers gave Security for their just and faithful Behaviour, the Merchant imposed upon, might have fotne Relief, and no Persons, but such as were of clear Characters, would be admitted Brokers.

Mr. Thomas Baynton, being examined, fad, that all Brokers, except the licensed Jews, are obiiged to be Freemen of the City:

That the Penalties, to be recovered by the Act of the Sixth of Queen Anne, touching Brokers, are thereby directed to go to the Use of the Lord Mayor, Commonalty, and Citizens, of L, but the Prosecutions are carried on in the Name of the Chamberlain, in behalf of the City; but the Person who is to give Evidence in this Prosecution. being a Freedhan, such Person must be disfranchised, before his Evidence will be received, in regard the Penalty, when recovered, is to go to the Use of the City; and restoring such Person to his Freedom again being attended with some Expence, and Trouble, many Prosecutions have for this Reason been dropt, or

?roved fruitless. He said further, that Freemen, upon a ury upon such Prosecutions, have been objected to, for being such; and, if Brokers are the Informers, it carries an Odium of an Informer:

That Merchants, or Traders, being Freemen of London, and subpoenaecl to give Evidence in Trials against any Person aiding as a Broker, and not duly licensed or admitted, such Freemen may refuse to be disfranchised, in order to give Evidence; so, consequently, the Prosecution mud drop. He further added, that these and other Inconveniences the Merchants and Freemen of the City of London labour under, by reason of the Defects of the Ad, made in the Sixth Year of her late Majesty's Reign.

Mr. Abraham Leftourgeon, Mr. isaac Mr. Wtn. Vaughan, Mr. John Walker, Mr. Theodore Van Rheden, Mr. Wm. Bearcroft, and Mr. being severally

called, and examined, confirmed the Evidence, given by Mr. Devifme and Mr. Thomas Baynton.

That, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committe.-, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of the said Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved, that Leave may be given to biing in a Bill for making more effectual the Ad, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for repealing the Act of the First Year of King James the First, intituled " An Act for the well garbling of Spices," and for granting an Equivalent to the City of London, by admitting Brokers.

Ordered, That the Establjfoment of the Royal African Company of England, for their several Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, with the Charges thereof for the Year 1730, distinguishing, how much of the same is on account of Trade, and how much for the Maintenance and Defence of the said Forts and Settlements, and also an Account how the Money, granted the last Session of Parliament towards the Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, hath been disposed of, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charges of the Royal African Company of England, for the Maintenance of the several British Forts and Settlements, belonging to the said Company on the Coast of Africa, for the Year 1731, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the State of the yearly Revenue and Expence of Greeenwick Hospital, be referred to the said Committee,

Ordered, That the Lift of the Widows of such reduced Officers of his Majesty's Land Forces and Marines, who died upon the Establishment of Half-pay in Great Britain and who were married to them before the 25th Day of December 1716, with an Estimate of the Charge thereof for the Year 1731, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Estimate of the Charge of the Out-pensioners of Chelsea Hospital, for the Year 1731, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of the net Produce into the Exchequer, for Three Years last past, of the additional Duties on stamp'd Vellum, Parchment, and Paper, which by an Act of the Ninth dnd Tenth Years of King William the Third, was, amongst other Things, charged with the yearly Fund of 160,000. payable in the united Company of Merchants of England, trading to the East Indies, distinguishing each Year, as also, what hath been charged upon the said additional Stamp Duties, and paid out of the fame, since the Twenty-fifth Day of March, One thousand Seven hundred and Thirty, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Petition of the Royal African Company of England be referred to the said Committee.

Mr. Richard Middlebrooh ‘ wild said* that there are Three Bridges on the new River, One called the Second Rawcliffe Bridge, and the Third New Bridge; which said Goo/ Bridge and Raw Bridge hinder Vef-

fels passing, each of them a Tide, or Twelve Hours, in calm Weather, and in stormy Weather much more: That the said Bridge, called Gool Bridge, is very prejudicial, and a great Hindrance, to the Navigation of the River, it (landing too near the Mouth of the River Where the Bottom is so very soft, that their Anchors often iari taking hold, and the Force of the Tides drive the Vessels against the Piles of the Bridge* and oflate Yeast Three or Four have been loft there, and several damaged: That at Low Water there are Eleven Feet Water, and About Twenty-eight Feet at High Water, at this Bridge* and that the Ground, whereon it (lands, is very sandy, and loose, and Vessels cannot be brought near it, to pass the fame, without great Difficulty, by reason of the Ra-pidness of the Tide from the River Owze; which would be prevented, if the Bridge was removed between Five or Six hundred Yards nearer to Bridge, at which

Place there is a Clay and firm Ground, to anchor in, and the River will be Five Feet deep there at Low Water: That, by reasons of these Inconveniences, Vessels have often been obliged to (lay a Tide, or m^re, before they could get through this B idge, which is Eighty Yards over and, when removed, it will b.* only Sixty Yards, but will be a Benefit to the Navigation, and maintained at a muchleL Expence, and no Detriment to Passengers, or to the House, now built at the Foot of this Bridge.

And he find further, that several Vessels have been loft at Gool Bridge; and that the Piles, drove there, arefome Forty-five, and some Sixty, Feet long, and Fourteen Inches, or thereabouts, thick: And laid, that Rawcliffe Bridge is of so little Use, that, if the same was taken away, it will be of great Advantage to the Navigation, and no Detriment to any body, as New Bridge lies as convenient to answer the Purposes of Rawcliffe Bridge: That the Removal of Gool Bridge higher up the R.ver is as convenient to the high Road to Hozvden, and will be no Damage or Hindrance to Passengers: That the Sides of the Banks at Gool Bridge are held up by Siathes: That . formerly there was a Bridge nearer the Mouth of the River Owze, where it is Sixty Yards wide, but that being a very bad Foundation, the same was taken down and, if the present Bridge is removed, the River will not be widened, if the Ends be left (landing: This Bridge has Thirteen Rooms, One whereof is Two:and-twenty Feet wide: That there was Two Meetings of the Land-owners at . DoncaJler, touching this Matter:

That in order to make the Navigation, several Cuts and Locks have been made, and the Navigation carried Seven Miles above DoncaJler, lor Vessels of Twenty Tons; and, to make this Navigation commodious, it will be proper to make a Cut on the North Side of the ' RiVer, upon a Marlb, called Thorp Marsh.

John Arthur said, that none of the Land-owners ligned the Petition, but only the Proprietors: And, being alkeS, if the Lord Irwin was not sent to in relation to this Matter, said, he believed, he was not sent to: And being further asked, whether the removing Gool Bridge would be of any Damage to my Lord, he said, it could be of no Detriment to his Lordship.

Richard Agar, Esquire, said, that Gool Bridge (land£ about One hundred Yards from the Mouth of the River Owze, but on very sandy and bad Ground *, and* if the same was removed higher, the same would be of great Advantage to the Navigation: That, about Twelve Years ago, there was several Jettees, which are since decayed, and almost gone: That there is a Road on the North Side of the River, and, if that Road was taken away, and another Road made on the South Side, it would be of very little Detriment to, or Inconveniencyto, Passengers: That the Participants are obliged to keep the Banks- in Repair, which the Vessels often break down: And added, that the Lord Irwin will not be damnified by removing the Bridge, called Gool Bridge.

Minufafiure. is called the great Handled; and for lopie Years past of Sail-cloth. great Quantities of foreign Sail Duck hath been imported into this Kingdom; particularly from Russia, which being made of Flax and Hemp of their own Growth, and ma-. nufactured, where Labour is exceeding cheap, a Bolt thereof, which is 36 Yards, costs but 5 6 d. making;

whereby small Quantities of British Sail-cloth have of late Years been made use of by the Merchants, the Manufactory whereof is in great Danger of being loft, and above -Jths Money is paid for Raffia Imports.

Mr. James Church further said, that in the Year 1743 many Thousands of poor People were employed in the manufacturing of English Sail-cloth, which was then allowed* though in its Infancy, to be very good, but are now arrived to a much greater Perfection in the making thereof.

Mr. John Butmaby further laid, that he exported 3,000 Bolts of English Sail-cloth to Spain, for the Service of their Navy, and it was allowed by them to be preferable to the belt Hollands Duck; and, if he could fell it so cheap, as they could buy foreign Sail-cloth, they had rather have it.

Mr. Samuel Gower, Sail-cloth-maker, said, that in the Year 1711a Contract was made, to furnish 30,000 Bolts of English Sail-cloth, and there was employed in the making thereof many thousand People, from Seven to Seventy Years of Age: And he added, that Ten People will make a Bolt of Sail-cloth, of 36 Yards, in a Week, the Labour whereof costs him 30 x. for the best Sort, and so in Proportion.

Mr. JVm. AJleR, Merchant, laid, that the Russia Imports are a Loss to this Kingdom near £. 200,000. per Annum, and the Exports to that Place, in February last, for One Year, did not amount to more than a Quarter of that Value: And he added, that the Russians now buy most Part of the Cloth they use, for clothing their Soldiers, of the Prussians, which they used to buy of the English, and have contracted with them for the present Year: And he also laid, that, notwithstanding Sail-cloth is dearer in Price, than foreign, yet it makes it up in Goodnels and Strength.

Captain IVm. Blakeway, Sail-maker, said, that, if J. 200,000. was paid for Sail-cloth, imported from Russia into this Kingdom, the Materials might be bought in Russia for -Jth of the Value, and manufactured at home, the Poor employed, and -Jths of that Money would be kept in the Nation, which in Proportion is sent t hit her.

Mr. Thomas Hyam further said, that Two Ships going to the East Indies, One of them used English Sail-cloth, and the other Hollands Duck; and, at their Return from the Voyage, the English Sail-cloth was belt, it being double Threads, made of Flax, and spun even; the Hollands Duck was a single Thread, made of Hemp, and not spun even, and (truck down with Tow, which they cannot use in making their Linen.

Sir Jacob Ackworth laid, that in his Majesty's Navy only English Sail-cloth is made use of, being better for Service, and preferable to the best Hollands Duck, the Thread being not so even spun, and the Shoot Yam in many Places very gouty, and little better than Tow, compared with the English: That, upon the Return of several Ships from foreign Voyages, the Officers have found, the Sails made of English Canvas, generally wore equal in all Places; the contrary of which has usually been observed of Hollands Duck, which is apt to fret into Holes.

Zepaniah Eadessaid, that Numbers of foreign Sails

are imported into England, for which no Duty is paid, and is a great Discouragement to the Manufacture of English Sail-cloth.

And all the Witnesses severally said, that, if a higher Dnty was laid on all foreign Sail-cloth, and Sails, imported into England, the Drawback taken off on Exportation, and the Duty taken off Flax, the Manufacture would be encouraged. Numbers of Poor may be employed, and enabled to support their Families, who are now a great Burthen to their several Parishes.

Vol. 21.

And several Pieces of English and foreign Sail-cloth were produed to the Committee; and it appearing to them, that English Sail-cloth was better thap foreign, and deserved Encouragement.

And that, upon the whole Matter* the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petitions.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Duties upon Flax are great Discouragcments to the making of British Sail-cloth.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That further Encouragement be given to the Manufacturers of British Sail-cioth, by discouraging the Importation of foreign Sail-cloth.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That some farther Discouragement be laid on the Exportation of foreign Sail-cloth.

Resolved, That-it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Use of foreign-made Sails is a Discouragemeot to the British Manufactory of Sail-cloth.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of this Report be put off to this Day Three Weeks.

Sir-John Rushout reported from the Committee, to whom the Petitition of several Merchants, Planters, and others, trading to,*and interested in, his Majesty's Sugar Colonies in America, in behalf of themselves, and many others, was referred; that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth;

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition, and, to prove the Allegations thereof, Witnesses were called;

Mr. Jonathan Sijfon; who said, that, (ince the Treaty of Utrecht, a considerable Trade has been carried on between New England, and other English Northern Colonies, and the French Sugar Colonies, especially at Martinique-, and that Horses, Lumber, Flour, and other Goods, are sent by the People of the Northern Colonies, and sold to the French, in Exchange for Molasses, and Rum, particularly Moialfes, of which the French make great Advantage, which.being formerly of lb little Ule to them, that they gave it to their Horses and H >gs, by Means of which Trade they have been enabled to enlarge their Plantations, and have cut down their W oods, to gain more Ground, being now supplied with Lumber, and other Plantation Necefl'aries, fromourNorthernColomes; vVherebv the French are greatly enriched, and the British Sugar Colonies impoverished; and this has caused the Necessaries, particularly Lumber, for the Plantations, to be very dear in the English Colonies, who can take off all

the Horses, and Lumber, they carry to Martinique: The French can't be supplied with those Necelfartes trom any other Place, by reason of the Navigation of Canada being so very difficult, and dangerous: The Northern Colonies may be supplied with Molasses, and Rum, from the English Sugar Colonies, at reasonable Prices; for Hum was fold the last Year at 11 d per Gallon, badoes Money, which is £.28 perCent. Difference between that and English Money.

He further said, that the French at Martinique fr ight English Ships from thence with Rum and Molasses on their own accounts, and fend the same to Boston, to their Factors or Agents there, the Produce whereof is laid out in the building of Vessels, and, when built, the Factors, Agents, or Builder, before they make a Bill of Sale to the right Owner, take an Oath before the Governor there, that they are not the Property of Foreigners, and that they are the true Owners thereof; upon which they obtain a Register in their ©wn Names, and the Oath taken, that they are not for foreign Service, is by these Means evadgd; and those Ships, and chiefly the small ones, are manned with English and Irish Sailors, hired by the French, and as they have Occasion, carry Molasses and Rum to the Northern Colonies, as well as to Cape Breton, from whence those Goods are carried in the New England coasting Vessels to Boston, and there disposed of, as before-mentioned. He added, that considerable Sums of Money were carried by those Ships from Barbadoes, and ourother Sugar Islands, to Martinique, in order to procure a more quick Dispatch to be given to their Loading of Sugars and Molasses, for which no more than £. 1. per Cent. Duty is paid, for the Produce of the French Islands, on Exportation; and that little else is carried to besides Molasses and Rum; but, if a Stop could be put to this Trade, a great Advantage would accrue to the English Sugar Settlements: Some of our Planters have' already removed to New Fork, and others are going, which, in a great Measure, is owing to this Trade: Formerly the Profits, arising to the Planter from Rum and Molasses at Barbadoes, was about One-third of the Value of the Produce of the Plantation, and generally paid more than the Charge of such Plantation.

Captain Richard Natijan, Captain Robert , and Captain James Nijbett, being severally examined, confirmed the Evidence, before given by Mr. Sijfon.

Mr. Sijfon further laid, that the French have at present 300 Men, fit to bear Arms, settled on the Island of St. Lucia, £00 on the Island of St. , and 500 on the

Island of Dominique, all Subjects of 5but these

Three Islands are included in the Commission of the Governor of Barbadoes; and that the French have more Men On the Island of Martinique, than the English have in all their Sugar Islands, excepting Jamaica:

That on the Island of Hijpani there are, the King's Troops excepted, 6,oooo Men, able to bear Arms; but on the Island of Jamaica there are not many more than half that Number.

He being asked, if the French could not have Horses from the Spaniards-, he said, they could only have Mules, and those were purchased at high Prices, and by a contraband Trade, and the meaner Planters, of which there are great Numbers, could not purchase:

That the Islands of Guardalupe and Grandterre are half as large again as Barbadoes, and there are on those Islands 5,000 white Men, fit to bear Arms:

That the Extent of the Island of Barbadoes is 28 Miles long, and 14 Miles broad; and that the Governor does not receive above ,£.1,100. per Annum out of 000. per Annum, granted for his Salary, the Gentlemen of the Assembly chusing to pay the Penalty of f.£o. each, for not collecting the Salary, which, by a Law there, they are obliged to pay, because the Inhabitants thereof, since this Trade has been carried on, are greatly impoverished in many Respects:

That the English Sugar Colonies are in a very declining State; and that the Fortifications at Barbadoes are quite decayed, the Walls in many Places cracked, the Carriages broke, and the Guns dismounted.

Captain Richard Nan/an said, that he was Mailer of a Ship, which failed from Cork in 1727, loaded with Provisions for St. Lucia, and in his Passage touched at badoes, where one of the Merchants lived, to whom the Cargo was consigned; and that Merchant obliged him to stay there, and fell Part of his Provisions for Money ro carry with him to St. Lucia, to purchase Sugars, by reason the French would not Trade with him without half Money; and gave 23 s.for each Pistole, when the current Price in Payment was but 6 That he carried 500 Pistoles with him, being Part of the Money for which he fold some of his Loading, and the remaining Part was sent after him to St. Lucia, which were 400 Pistoles more; where he purchased 237 Hogsheads of Sugars, which came from Martinique, and intended to have purchased 500; but a French Man of War coming into the Harbour, he, the said Nan/an, believing, the French Man of War to be an Enemy's Ship, fired at her, to make her shew her Colours; after which the Man of War made a Signal, for all Mailers of Ships in the Harbour to come on board her, and there to shew their Clearings from the English Ports; when and where they confined the Witness, till his Ship could be got ready to Jail, which took up Six or Seven Days, and then carried him to Fort Royal at Martinique, and put him into Prison; where he continued, till he was examined by the Judge of the Admiralty there; after which he was re-Jeased; but the Ship, and Cargo of Sugars, were condemned (a Copy of that Condemnation, which he had from the proper Officer, he laid before the Committee) and from that Sentence he appealed to the supreme Council of Martinique, setting forth, that St. Lucia was a neutral Island, and that he was not liable to that Judgment: Some short Time afterwards he had his Ship restored, when he bad been at an Expence of near .200. but the Sugars were publickly fold, and the Money deposited, till an Order could be had from the Court of France.

Captain Robert Taylor, being examined, confirmed the last Evidence, given by Captain Nan/an, he, the said Taylor, being taken by the French at the same time with him and some other English Vessels.

They further severally said, that, while they were at Martinique, 16 or 17 New England Vessels arrived there, loaded with Horses, Lumber, Flour, and other Goods, which were fold, and Molasses and Rum bought, but chiefly Molasses, to carry back with them; for which they had a Writing, purporting a Permission from the Governor, or General there, so to do, because the French can't be supplied with Horses and Lumber from any other Place, iiut the English Northern Colonies, the Navigation of Canada being so difficult and dangerous; nor can they carry on their Sugar Works without them; which has greatly increased the Price of both at our Sugar Colonies, where all the Horses and Lumber, they can supply them with, may be disposed of.

And they also said, that the Spaniards frequently goto the Island of Martinique, and purchase Part of the Flour, brought from New England and New York, with ready Moneys for which the New England People have only Molasses and Rum in Return; and that a Duty of no more than £. 1. per Cent, is paid on the Export of the Produce from all the French {(lands.

Mr. John Tomlinjon, being examined, confirmed the Evidence, given by Captain Nanfan and Taylor.

Captain James Nijbett said, that he was Mailer of a Ship, and went to St. Lucia in 1717, loaded with Provisions, in order to buy a Loading of Sugar, Ginger, and Cocoa, for Rotterdam: He was obliged to carry half Money, orelfc the French would not trade with him; and the Sugars were then not fogood, as the Sugars, made at the English Colonies; but that now they are very good: And further said, that he went to Martinique, in 1721, where he was Three or F8ur Months; and, during that Time, several Vessels arrived there from the English Northern Colonies, loaded with Horses, Lumber, and Provisions, to be sold, in order to buy Rum and Molaf* fes, of which the French make great Profit: In 1718 they made no Rum, but gave their Molasses to their Hogs and Horses: And that the French can't be supplied with Horses and Lumber from any other Parts; but, since this Trade has been carried on, the English Sugar Colonies have not been supplied with Plantation Necessaries in so good or cheap a Manner, and the Prices of Horses have been advanced there about 10 or £. 15. per Cent.

And he further laid, that the Mailers of English Vessels purchase new Permissions every Year, to trade to the French Sugar Islands, for which they pay in proportion to the Value of their Cargoes; and that he paid to the Governor of Martinique 1,000 Livres for a Permission to

Trade there:

And that the French, by vending their Rum and Molasses at the Northern Colonies, are able to make much greater Quantities of Sugar from the clear Profit of their Rum and Molasses, which is greatly increased by claying their Sugars; and a greater Quantity of Molasses is made, than otherwise they would have; and by this Trade the French are able to undersell the English very much, no more than £. 1. per Cent. Duty being paid on the Produce of the said Islands:

That he went to Guardalupe, to freight his Ship with Ginger for Holland, and a Vessel from New England come

in, while he was there, loaded with Horses and Lumber, with which he bought Molasses and Rum, and carried the same to Boston:

The French Islands are called Martinique,

Granada, Grandterre, Guardalupe, Hijpaniola, and the Saints Islands; but Martinique Island is larger than either of the English Sugar Islands, excepting Jamaica:

That in 1716 the French could raise on the Island of Martinique about 15,000 white Men; and their Sugar Colonies are greatly enriched, and also increased, by this Trade, and the Goodness of the Soil: That the Islands of Grandterre and Guardalupe are much larger than badoes, and are well peopled.

That he knows, Vessels have come from the Northern Colonies to Jamaica, and fell their Loading for Money, which they have carried to Hispaniola, to purchase Molasses; and that the French, to make the bell Advantage of their Molasses, wrote to him, to fend Coppers, and -Stills, to make Rum, to have the Benefit of that Manufacture.

Mr. Wm. Frazier said, that in November and December, 1729, he went from Barbadoes to Martinique, and St. Lucia, for his Health, and saw about 30 New England and Rhode Island Vessels there, loading with Molasses, and some Rum, for Boston; was personally acquainted with several of the Matters of those Vessels, being a Rum and Lumber Merchant himself at; and

that the Mailers of those Vessels informed him, that, if they brought in 60 Horses alive, they paid nothing for their Permission to Trade, Horses, and Lumber, being absolutely necessary for the French, as well as English Sugar Plantations: That those Vessels loaded chiefly with Molasses, in Return for the Horses, and Lumber; which Molasses they distil into Rum at Boston, where there are near 50 Distilling-houses, and thereby lower the Value of Rum, made in the Sugar Plantations, about £.25. per Cent, by fending the same to Maryland, Virginia, North and South Carolina, to the Newfoundland Fishery, and also some to Guinea:

That he has frequently bought Cargoes of Lumber of the New England People at which when

paid for, they have carried the Money to be laid out at Martinique, and have given Two and a half per Cent, for Money, called light Bitts, being what they gain most by between Barbadoes and Matiniq and that Horses and Lumber, for Seven Years last past, have been 25 or 30 per Cent, dearer at Barbadoes, by reason of such Quantities of Horses and Lumber being carried to Martinique; and that Barbadoes Rum is £. 25. or f. 30. per Cent, cheaper, by buying Molasses at Marti, of which Rum was made in Boston, and supplied the Places before-mentioned:

Mr. Patrick Blake Paid, that he lived on the Island of St. Christopher' % 16 Years, and has a Sugar Plantation there, and makes 500 Hogsheads of Sugar yearly, from which he distils about 2,000 Gallons of Rum, and, if Encouragement was given, he could make 20,000 Gallons; but, as the Trade is now carried on, the New England Traders will take little or nothing in Exchange for their Commodities, but ready Money or Molasses; which Molasses they carry to Boston, and there distil: That there is made yearly on the Island of St. Christopher's about 14,000 Hogsheads of Sugar, from which might be distilled great Quantities of Rum, in proportion to what he himself can make; and that several Vessels go, loaden with Horses, from New England to , to purchase Molasses; and that a Nezv England Sloop, wherein were about 35 Horses, and some Lumber, was, by contrary Winds, drove into , where he

Mr. Francis Blower and Mr. John Tomlinson, being severally examined, said, that. they were at Barbadoes in 1729; where was one Benjamin Duce, Commander of the Ship Lafcells, who had chartered his Ship to Mef-sieurs Blewett and Barret, to go from Barbadoes to Martinique, and from thence to Boson in New England, with a Lbad of Molasses and Rum; which Charter-party the said Blower, and Tomlinson saw: That he proceeded accordingly, and took in 480 Hogsheads of Molasses, and 80 Hogsheads of Rum, and carried the same to Boston, where there are several Distilling-houses, at the Risque of Monsieur Grangent ,a French Merchant, and delivered them to Captain Benjamin Clarke, who was employed there, as his Agent and Factor; and at the same time several other Ships went from the same Place, on the same Voyage, from 100 to to 250 Tons, loaded with Horses, Lumber, Cattle, Fish, and other Plantation Necessaries, and took in Rum, and Molasses; and that several Ships were building at Boston out of the Produce, arising from such foreign Rum, and Molasses: That some of the Ships were from 3 to 400 Tons Burthen; and several of them go from thence to Cape Briton, and are there made French Bottoms, and then go to to the Sugar lllands with Plantation'Necessaries; and that Duce was offered a Freight from Boston to Cape Briton, and the French Sugar lllands, which he refused; and that, when he, the said Duce, was at Martinique, several Spanish Vessels were trading the re, and among them was One large Ship, of about 300 Tons, which brought a great Quantity of Pieces of Eight, to purchase of the French Flour, which was brought from New York, and other Northern Colonies, and exchanged for Molasses.

Mr. Richard Harris, being examined, laid, that In 1730 Sugars fell in their Price 5 s. per Hundred Weight, and fell 2 or 3 s.per Hundred Weight the Year before, by reason of the great Importation of French Sugars into Europe; and that the French gain £ 25. per Cent, on their Molasses clear; which is a great Disadvantage to the English Sugar Colonies, the Produce whereof used to be worth to Great Britain about £. 1,500,000. per Annum.

That Mr. Popple, Secretary to the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations, laid before the Committee an Extract from a Representation, made by the Board of Trade upon the State of his Majesty's Plantations on the Continent of America, the 8th of September 1721, which is to the Effect following, under the Title of the -chujets Bay, That the Products of tins Country, proper for the Consumption of Great Britain, are Timber, Turpentine, Tar, and Pitch, Malls, Pipe and Hogshead Staves, Whale-fins, and Oi:, and some Furs:

That Spain, Portugal, and the fVeJi Indies, are supplied from the Northern Colonies with considerable Quantities of Fish, and Lumber; and that the Commissioners of Trade are informed, that there are in those Colonies Mines of several Kinds, which might be wrought, upon proper Encouragement.

That their Trade to the foreign Plantations in America consists chiefly in the Exportation of Horses to Surinam, and, as the Commissioners of Trade were informed, to Martinique*, and the other French islands, which is a very great Discouragement to the Sugar Planters in the British islands; for w'shout these Supplies neither the French, nor the Dutch, could?carry on their Sugar Works to any great Degree, and, in Return for their Horses, they receive Sugar,. Molasses, and Rum.

That a Letter from Captain George Prothero, Commander of his Majesty's Ship Bland ford, dated from Boston, in New England, the 14th December 1730, was produced, and read; alleging that the French carry on a great Trade from the West Indies to Boston, under borrowed Names, to the unspeakable Detriment of the Plantations in the West Indies.

Then the Laws of Barbadoes were laid before the Committee; wherein is an Act, paRed in that island the 12th of September 1663, For settling an Impost on the Commodities of the Growth of that island; which Act was read; whereby it appeared, that the Acknowlegment of £.40. of Cotton per Head, and other Taxes and Impositions, formerly raised to the then Eari of Carlifte, was held very heavy; and, for a full Remedy of all the Defects, and quieting the Possessions, and settling the Tenures, of the Inhabitants of that island, all the then rightful l'offeffors of Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, within that island, according to the Laws and Customs thereof, should at all times repair uiito their Governor for the full Confirmation of their Estates and Tenures, and then and there should and might receive such full Confirmation and Afl'urance under his Majesty's great Seal for that island, as they could reasonably advije or desire, according to the true Intent and Meaning of the Act:

That all Payments of £.40. of Cotton per Head, and all other Duties, Rents, and Arrears of Rents, were from thenceforth absolutely released; and that the Inhabitants should hold their several Plantations to them and their Heirs for ever, upon paying an Ear of Indian Corn to Vox.. 21.

his Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, in full Discharge of all Rents and Services for the future.

And, for defraying the necessary Charges and Expences of supporting the said island, and other Purposes, in the said Act mentioned, an Impost, or Custom, of Four and a Half in Specie, for every Five Score, was laid upon such native Commodities of that island, as should be shipped off the fame, and to be paid to his then Majesty, his Heirs and Successors, for ever.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better securing and encouraging the Trade of his Majesty's Sugar Colonies in America; and that Sir John Rushout, Mr. Bromley of Cambridgeshire, and Mr. do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Kettering, Tavstock, Oxon, Nezvport, New Sarum, Crediton, Ashburton, and Eastand West relating to the great Decay of the Woollen Manufacture, which the Petitioners attribute to fraudulent Exportations and funning of Wool from this Kingdom, and Ireland, and Woblleri Goods, thoroughly manufactured in Ireland, to foreign Parts, and also relating to Yarn, imported into this Kingdom, were referred, which Committee was also ordered by the House to consider of the Laws in being to prevent the clandestine Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland, and what further Provisions maybe necessary for preventing thereof; that the Committee had considered the said Laws, and had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afteN wards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the Report and Resolutions were read, and'are as followeth; vizf That, to prove great Exportations and Runnings of vast Quantities of unwrought Wool, as complained of, from this Kingdom, and of Wool, and Woollen Goods manufacture^, from Ireland into foreign Parts, contrary to Law, and of Woollen Goods, fraudulently manufactured for the Sake of the Wool only, tending to the Ruin of the British Manufactures, the following Evidence.was given:

Mr. Henry Diston said, that in August last he saw, in his Passage from Leige to Aix la Chapel/, several Waggons, loaden with Wool, which, as he was informed by the Inhabitants, was either English or Irish Wool,

Mr. John Murm said, that in 1726 he saw at Leiden several Skins with the Wool on; and in July 1726, he saw at Rotterdam several Packs of Wool, which he took to be Irish-, and was there informed, that 200 Todds of British or Irish Wool are usually worked up with the like Quantity of foreign Wool; which makes t eir Woollen Manufactures vendible. at a much higher Price, than otherwise they chuld be: That Flemish Wool is much coarser, than the English or Irish Wool, and cannot be worked up, without mixing it with ours: That between Menen and Lijle he saw Two Waggon Loads of English Wool, and also saw several Cheneys and Calitnancoes, which they cannot make without British or Irish Wool:

That he was lately informed in Ireland, that they could fend but very little Wool to England, it being 1 \d. per Pound dearer than English Wool; and that they should be glad, if Wool, and Woollen Yarn, might be imported from thence to England Duty-free: That Woollen Cloths are exported from thence to Holland, and France; and it is customary abroad to work up One-third of English Wool with Two-thirds of French; whereby they are

Mr. Thomas Vere said, that he is an Exporter of Woollen Goods; and that in the Year 1728, finding a Declension of the Sale of the English Woollen Manufacture at Lisbon, he procured an Account to be taken out of the King of Portugal's Books, at the Custom-house at Lisbon, of the Irish Camblets, that had been entered therefor that Year, the Amount of which appeared to be above £.33,000 Sterling; and that from January 1728, to October 1729, the Amount of the Goods, entered at the Custom-house at Lisbon from Ireland, was upwards of £.30,000 which paid a Duty of 23 per Cent. and that his Friends wrote him from thence, that by the Nature of the Package, they had reason to believe, that was not One-third of the Quantity, that had been imported into that Place, within that time, from Ireland, of Worsted Camblets only:

That it is not only Camblets, that are sent from Ireland, but several other Species of Woollen Goods, in large Quantities; which the Irish fell at Ljbon cheaper, than the English Merchants can buy them at home.

Mr. John Guertiey said, that there are several Goods made at Nonoich, partly for home Consumption, and

partly for foreign: The narrow Camblets are exported to Lisbon, but the said Manuftufture of late has been in a very declining Condition: That Sailors have Libertyof carrying some Goods from Ireland abroad, which, if prohibited, would be a Means to prevent their exporting greater Quantities, than they are now allowed by Law: That he had enquired in Ireland and Holland concerning the Exportation of Wool from Ireland to France, and other foreign Countries, and had received certain Information, that very great Quantities were constantly exported from that Nation That this was of such Service to the French and other Foreigners, in their Manufactories, that they could not work their own Wool into Stuffs without it; but that they could mix Two-thirds of French Wool with One-third of EngliOi or Wool, and with this Mixture could make Stuffs vendible at foreign Markets, to the Prejudice of those exported from England:

The Quantity of Wool, that has been exported from Ireland, is judged by Persons, that have made particular Enquiry, and leen a great deal of it abroad, to be 200,000 great Stone a Year; but if there be but Half that Quantity, and they, mix Two thirds of their own with One-third of Irish, that it will make 300,000 great Stone, or that Mixture, which being combed, and lpun into Yarn, and that Yarn made into Worsted Stuffs, their Worth is at lead £.450,000 Sterling, of which the Labour of the

That the Manufacturers in and Norfolk lie

under such a Hardship, as the Law now stands* respdCting the Importation 01 Irish Wool and Yarn, by reason of the Duty paid for it, and the Land Carriages irom the Pork of Importation, to which it is now confined* that, unless they have ionic Relief in that particular, they-arc not able to item the Tide of the Irish Manufactures in foreign Markets; for the Land Carriage, and other Charges, that now attend them, on the Importation of Irish Yarn, is at least Six per Cent, more, than it would be, if they could bring it either to the Port of London, or Yarmouth, directly from Ireland, and on the Importation of Wool, at the present Prices of Wool in Ireland, about 1 "J per Cent, and at the usual Prices, which it bore fouac Years since, about 25 or 30 per Cent.

To prove which, he produced several Computations.

Mr. Richard Champion said, That what he offered to the Committee, was as an Englishmen, and not as a Tradcfinan of any particular Place: That he thought, the opening die Ports, for Importation of Wool, would be of dangerous Consequences, and what had been formerly rejected, upon Applications of that Sort: That the bringing of Wool from Ireland to the Eastern or Northern Parts of England will give the Irish People an Opportunity of more ealy running it into France, Flanders, and Holland-, for they will pretend to be drove into the French or other Ports by Strci's of Weather, when they are only seeking a better Market.

That they will be tempted to defraud the Insurers; and that the Yarn, if it lies long on board, will heat, and sufi'er great Damage: That it is more for the Advantage of the Manufacturers in Norfolk to have the Yarn from Cork to Bristol, and so to j Norfdian it is to bring it directly from Cork to Yarmouth.

To prove which, he also produced several Computations.

Mr. Joseph Hitchcock fa id, That he had been Masterof

a Ship, and was well acquainted with the Coast of England and Ireland: That, if the M ind is at South-weft, that Wind will carry Ships directly from Ireland to Bristol: That there arc Twelve Points of the Compals, which will carry a Ship from Cork to Band but Three, that

will carry a Ship from Cork to Yarmouth: That in a South-weft Wind a Ship cannot get out of to double

the Lizard, or the Ifiupd of Sci That the Wind is in the South-weft Corner Two-thirds of the Year; and, if diat is the Cafe, it is Two-thirds of the Chance of the "Wind, and Three-fourths more of the Compals; then putting those Numbers together, with Four times the Distance, makes it not less than Twenty-four to One; and allowing, he was doubling Two Days to Bristol, he should be Forty-eight to Yarmouth; and, if the Wind was not fair, he might be Three or Four Months going to Yarmouth.

Mr Thomas Eades said, That the longer Yam lies.on

board a Ship, the worle it is, because, when it is heated, it will not work well, and it lofps, the Colour; and, if it lies but a Month's time, it will be damaged; and, as

soon as it heats, it damages: Yarn will not heat'by lying in a Room; and, when a Pack is opened, it is ealy to difeern, whether it is new I'am, or has lain any time:

Mr. Robert Devere! said, That he had dealt'in Yrarn several Years, and had never any Meat, after he had it, if it had not been heated on board, before it came to his Hands;

Mr. Henry Torige, a Manufacturer of Bristol, said, That he had made Observations several times, that, w hen' Yarn, Imported at BriJlbt, had a short Passage, it came over ip good Quality, and without Damage; on the Contrary, when i,t had been, on board Three Weeks, or upwards, and heated in the itold, it w as One-eighth less in Valuer and, when continued longer on board, be had known it hast decreased much more in its Value; so that it would nqt, make so good a Fabrick when manufactured, and he would not purchase the Yarn upon aby Terms, by reason the Poor could not get their Bread by it: That, if lie lived at Norwich, he should rather chuie to have the Yarn imported into Bristol from Ireland, and brought by I^ind

Carriage to Norwich, thpn to have it imported from Ireland to Yarmouth-, and that there-is not one and a half per Cent. Difference, exclusive of die Hazard of Damage by heating on board Ship, nor Three-fourths per Cent. when manufactured; which, he conceived, was not an Equivalent for the Hazard of a Wreck upon the Coast of France.

It appeared to the Committee, upon the Examination of some of the Commissioners of the Customs, and their. Officers, that great Care has been taken to prevent i'rau^ dulent and clandestine Exportations and Running of Wool, contrary to the Laws now in being; and that great Quantities have bpen discovered, and seized.

Estimates were laid before the Committee, by the Commissioners of the Customs, of the Quantities of Wool, -and Woollen and Bay Yarn, imported from Ireland to this Kingdom for several \7ears past, with the Duties thereon.

And several Schemes, or Proposals, for remedying the Mischiefs complained of, were laid before the Committee.

And, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to, the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the lait Clause in the Act, made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of the Reign of King William the Third, for continuing several Laws therein mentioned, and for explaining the Act, intituled, "An Act to prevent the " Exportation of Wool, out of the Kingdoms of Ireland " and England, and into foreign Parts, and for the Encouragement of the Woollen Manufactures in the Kingdom of England,"be further explained, or repealed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a most properWay to prevent the running Wool from Ireland, will be by encouraging the Importation of Worsted, Woollen and Bay Yarn, from thence into this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the enforcing die Act, of the Thirtieth Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, for burying in Woollen, by augmenting the Penalty, and extending it to the Plantations in America, and the Islands, will be very much for the Advantage of the Woollen Manufacture of Great Britain.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of Heads for a Bill for more effectual preventing the Exportation of Wool from Great Britain, and of Wool, and Wool manufactured, from ' to

foreign Parts.

The Order, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the w hole House, to consider of the Petition of the Gunpowder-makers, and of several Merchants, Traders in, and Exporters of Gunpowder to divers fereign Parts, being read;

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they have Power to consider of the Duties upon Salt-petre and Brimstone.

Dundee A Petition of the Noblemen, and landed Gentlemen, Toward of the Counties of Angus and Perth, in the Neighbourhood 4rtour* of the Burgh of Dundee, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, that, unless the Duty of Two Penies Scots on the Pint of Ale, fold within the said Town, be farther continued, as prayed by a Petition from the said Town, presented to this House for that Purpose, the said Town must inevitably go to Ruin, and thereby the Petitioners will not only lose the Benefit of a Harbour, which will tend to the Destruction of Trade, but also their Rents will be diminished; which for the most Part are consumed in that Town: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant such Relief to the said Town of Dundee, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of the Company of Watermen and Lightermen, of the River of Thames, in behalf of themselves, and others; and also,

A Petition of the Watermen and Lightermen, inhabiting in the City and Liberty of Westminster, in behalf of themselves, and others; and also,

A Petition of the Watermen and Lightermen, working on the River Thames, in flit-bottomed Boats, Barges, and other Vessels, between Kingston Bridge, in the County of Surrey, and Windsor Bridge, in the County of Berks, on behalf of themselves, and others;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; alleging, that, by having served Apprenticeships on the River Thames, they are legally entitled to the Liberty and Privilege of working on the said River, for the Maintenance of themselves and Families, and get their Living by working in Boats, Lighters, Barges, and other Vessels, on the said River, from London to Windsor, in carrying Passengers, Goods, Luggage, and other Things; and that, if the Bill, depending in this House, to explain and amend a Clause in an Act, passed in the Second Year of his Majesty's Reign, for making more effectual several Acts, relating to Watermen, fcsV. should pals, it will give Power to Persons, who have not served Apprentice-ships, to work and use Ferry-boats, flat-bottomed Boats, Barges, and Vessels, upon the said River; which will not only lay the Navigation of the River under the like Disorders, Mischiefs, and Damages, it was subject to before the Act of the nth and 12th of King Willians the Third, but the Petitioners will be highly injured, and their Families muftcome to their Parishes, their Apprentices will leave them, and none, for the future, will serve an Apprenticeship to any Waterman, or Lighterman, and consequently no Regulation can be enforcedon the said River: And therefore praying, that they may be heard by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill, before any thing be done to the Prejudice of their Rights, or that they may have such other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet,

Ordered, That the said Petitions do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to explain and amend a Clause in an Act, passed in the Second Year of the Reign of his present Majesty King George the Second, for making more effectual several Acts passed, relating to Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, rowing on the River Thames, so far as the same relates to Ferry-boats, and flat-bottomed Boats, be read a Second time and that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be then heard by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill.

The Translation of the said Treaty is as followeth; viz.

-*. WH EREAS tire most serene and most jx>tent Prince,

'James the Second, King of Great Britain, and the most serene and most potent Prince, Lewis the Fourteenth, the most Christian King of France and have

hi nothing more at Heart, than daily to strengthen more and

more the mutual Friendship between themselves, and the if: sincere Union and Corresponde>nce between their King-

doms, Dominions, and Subjects; and whereas they have thought fit, with that View, to enter into a Treaty of Peace, good Correspondence, and Neutrality, in America, by which all Controversies and Differences, which should happen to arise between the Subjects of both Crowrs m those remote Parts, may be prevented, as much as pose; fible; the most serene Kings have appointed Plenipotentiaries on both Sides, to treat and assemble upon this Matter; to wit, the above-mentioned King of Great Britain, the Lords, George Baron Jeffreys of IVem, Great Chancellor of England, Lawrence Earl of Rochester, High Treasurer of England, Robert Eaiiof Sunderland, Proficient of the Privy Council, and one of the Principal Secretaries of State, Charles Earl of Middleton, another of the principal Secretaries 6f State, and Sidney Lord Godal-phin, his Majesty's Privy Counsellors, and the above-mentioned most Christian King, the Lord cf Amoncourt, Marquis of an ordinary Coun-

fellor in his Counsel of State, and his Ambassador Extraordinary; who, after duly exchanging their full Powers; have agreed on the following Articles:

1.

It is concluded and agreed, that from this Day forward there be a firm Peace, Union, Amity, and good Corre-| spondence, as well by Land, as by Sea, between the Bri-

iifh and French Nations in America, as well Northern, at

Southern, and within the Wands, Colonies, Forts, Cities* and Governments (without Exception of Places) belonging to the most serene King of Great Britain, or to the Irtoft serene most Christian King, in America, and which ' are under the Jurisdiction of either King respectively.

It is provided and agreed, that this present Treaty shall not in anywise derogate from the Treaty, concluded between the said most (erene Kings at Breda the -f 'r Day of July, in the Year of our Lord 1667; but that all and Angular the Articles and Clauses of that Treaty shall remain in Force, and be observed.

That all Treaties or Articles, at any Time heretofore made and concluded between the said Nations, about the Island of St.Chrtfiopker' % , or other Places in shall be in Force, as formerly, and shall be observed on both Sides, as heretofore, unless where they shall be found to be contrary to this present Treaty.

21.

Lastly, It is agreed and concluded, that this present Treaty, and all and Angular the Matters therein contained, shall, as soon as may be, be ratified and confirmed on both Sides, and that the Ratifications thereof (lull, within the Space of Two Months from the Date of these Presents, be reciprocally and duly exchanged between both Parties, and within the Space of Eight Months, or sooner, if it may be, be published in all the Kingdoms, Dominions, and Colonies, as well in America, as elsewhere, of both the Kings.

In witness whereof, we, the Plenipotentiaries, have Agned and sealed this present Treaty. Given in his Majesty's Palace of Whitehall the W Day of November 1686.

Press 7. L. 11. After " away" to insert " or."

L. lad. After " Building" to insert " or from or out of any Garden, Orchard, Court-yard, Fence, or Outlet, belonging to any Dwelling-house, or other " Building."

Mr. Cary (according to Order) reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whpm it was referred to consider of Heads for a Bill for the more effectual preventing the Exportation of Wool from Great Britain, and of Wool, and Wool manufactured, from Ireland, to foreign Parts, and also to consider of the Duty upon Woollen and Bay Yarn, imported from Ireland into England, the Resolutions, they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table j where the same were read, and are as followeth; v

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Provision be made for preventing the fraudulent Exportation of Wool from Great Britain, under Pretence of being manufactured.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Wool, Woolsells, Mortlings, Shortlings, Wool-flocks, Worsted, Bay or Woollen Yarn, in Great Britain or Ireland, shall be packed up into any Box, Barrel, Caik, Cafe, Gheft, or any other Package, »but in Linen, Woollen, Canvas, and Pack-cloth, only.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Statute, of the Seventh and Eighth Years of the Reign of King Williamthe Third, by which the inhabitants of the respective Hundreds, Port, or Places, out of or through which any Wool, Woolsells, Mortlings, Shortlings, Wool-flocks, Worsted, Bay or Woollen Yarn, is carried, or exported, contrary to the said Act, are subject to certain Penalties, be further enforced, and extended to Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Security, given for carrying Wool, and Woollen Goods, Coastwise, in Great Britain and Ireland, be made more effectual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That some further Provision be made, more effectually

Mr. Earle (according to Order) reported from the Nrfcp Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Complaint, made to the House the Twenty-fourth Day of March last, again!!

Charles Bass, and John Metcalfe, and others, for entering, in a forcible Manner, into Part of the Estate of Francis Annefiey, Esquire, a Member of this House, and

(eizing, and carrying away, divers Goods, distraiacd by him for Rent due, in Breach of the Privilege of this House, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Report, and Resolutions of the Committee, are as followeth;

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the Complaint, That Charles Bass, John , (who

pretended to be an Attorney, of Bernard's Inn) Elizabeth Langford, Thomas Paine, and Cooke, Bed-stead-maker, with divers other Persons, assembled in a riotous Manner, did on Sunday, the 21st of Match last, in the Time of divine Service, in a forcible Manner, enter into the George Inn on Snow-hill, in the Parish of St. Sepulchre's, London, Part of the Estate of Francis Ann, Esquire, a Member of this House, and did seize, and carry away, divers Goods, distrained by the said Mr lor Rent

due to him.

The Committee examined several Witnesses, who gave Evidence, as follows; viz.

John Day, being examined, said, he had enquired and searched for Charles Bass, Elizabeth , Thomas

Paine, and Godfrey Cooke, and that he had been at their Lodgings, and at all the moll likely Places, and Publick-houses, where they used, but could not find them; but that he had found John Metcalfe, who was attending at the Door.

Mr. Thomas Basham, being examined, proved the Counterpart of the Lease, from Mr. Annejley to of the George Inn, dated 23d Day of December 1725, for the Term of 12 Years; in which there is a Converunt, that, if it happen, that a Year's Rent at any one Time, during the said Term, be behind, or unpaid, it should be lawful for the said Francis Annejley under his Hand and Seal, to determine and make void the said Lease; and that, when Charles Bass should be served with such Instrument, or Wrijing, the said Lease should from thenceforth cease, and be void:

And gave Evidence, that the Rent was 140. per An-

num, and that there is now due /. 314. 5 s. allowing the Taxes.

John Day, being again called in, gave Evidence, that Mr. Aldersey served Mr. Bass with Mr. Annejley s Order, to make void the Lease; that he was by, wiien it was served, and took a Copy of it; and that Bass, when served, spoke very slightly of his Landlord, and how little he valued his Proceedings: That he seized the Goods by the Order of Mr. Hinton: That he entered the 27th ol February last, and took Possession; and he took it to be by Mr. Annejley's Order:

That on Sunday, the 21st of March last, Mr. Bass came into the Yard, and went into the Stable, and drove

Four Saddle Horles, which were seized for Rent, out of the Stable: That he attempted to flop them; upon which Bass pulled out a naked Cutiafs from under his

Coat, and swore, he would do him forne Mischief, if he offered to interrupt the carrying off the Horses: That then Bass drove the Horles away: That in the Afternoon, in Sermon-time, he came again, with about twenty Persons more, and then, with many wicked Oaths, threatened, in a violent Manner, to cut him in two in the Middle, if he offered to relilt him, or to call any body to his Aid and A Alliance.

That John Metcalfe was there, and threatened him

Violence, if he refilled, and to turn him out of Possession; and pretended to be an Upholder; afterwards to be an Attorney, of Bernard's Inn; but, upon Enquiry, is an

That Thomas Paine, Godfrey , and Elizabeth

Langford, assisted them likewil'e, in the same Manner, to carry off the Goods, as Beds, Linen, Pewter, and other Goods, and were concerned and a fulling in the riotous Proceedings on the said Sunday in the Afternoon:

That Charles Bass threatened, that Mr. Annesley should never have his Lease, and that he would make him know it j and threatened to pull down his Houses, and to bring Carts, and carry away the Materials.

Mr. Joshua Hinton gave Evidence, that he acted by Authority under Mr. Annesley'* Hand: That he distrained the 27th of February lait, and put John , and another Person, into Poliession, by Content of Mrs. , who was in the House, and ill ahove-ltairs; who sent him word, ihe did consent, that Persons should be put intoPossession on the behalf, and for the Use, of Mr. Annesley.

Alter which, his Majesty was pleated to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as fol-Ioweth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The King's It is a great Pleasure to me, that, at the Close of this Speech. Session of Parliament, 1 am able to acquaint you, that the Hopes I had conceived, and given you, of seeing very suddenly a happy Period put to the Troubles and Difor-ders, which had been so long apprehended, are no\y by the Treaty, ligned at Vienna, answered and accomplished.

A Project of a Convention betwixt the Emperor and the Maritime Powers, for accommodating the Differences and Disputes, that were fubliffing, having been formed, the Treaty is concluded, and ligned by me, and the Emperor, and is now under the Consideration of the States General, the Forms of that Government not admitting a previous Concert m a Negotiation of this Nature; and, as this Treaty principally regards the Execution of the Treaty of Seville, it is likewise communicated to the Courts of France and Spaas Parties to the Treaty of Sevillej and I have just received Advice, that the Ratifications between me and the Emperor are exchanged.

The Conditions, and Engagements, which I have entered into upon this Occasion, are agreeable to that necessary Concern, which this Nation mull always have for the Security and Preservation of the Balance of Power in Europe-, and, as the uncertain and Violent State of Affairs, to which Europe was reduced, and the Mischiefs of an immediate general War, which began to be thought unavoidable, are now removed, this happy Turn duly improved, with i just Regard to our former Alliances, which it shall be my Care to preserve, gives us a favourable Prufpeft of seeing the publick Tranquillity re-established.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,.

I return you my Thanks for the effectual Supplies, which you have granted me for the Service of the present Year, and for the proper Disposition you have made of the publick Funds, towards lessening and discharging the national Debt. The remarkable Dispatch, and Unanimity, which you have shewn at this critical Conjuncture, has added very much to the Credit and Weight of your Proceedings, and you shall find as great a Readiness on my Part to ealc the Burthens of my People, as soon as the Circumstances and Situation of Affairs will admit of it, as you have shewn to raise the Supplies, necessary for the Service of the Publick.

mon the Benefits of the present happy Establishment;

And let your Good-will to one another be as extenfivf, as my Protection, which all my good and faithful Subjects have an equal Right to, and may equally depend upon.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

My Lords, and Gentlemen.

I hope, at your Return into the Country, you will find all Aitempts to raise a Spirit of Discontent among my People, by unjust Clamours and Mifreprdentations, vain and ineffectual. All malicious Insinuations, to the Prejudice of my Measures, must lurely vanish, when it shall appear, that my firstand principal Care has been for the Interest and Honour of this Kingdom. Let it be your Endeavour to remove all groundkfs Jealousies and Apprehensions; that the Satisfaction of the Nation may be as genera', as it is my earned; Desire, that their Happiness may be: I.et all my People, let all Orders of Men, enjoy quietly, and unenvied, the Rights, Privileges, and Indulgences, which by Law they are entitled to: Let no Innovations disturb any Part of my Subjects in the Possession of their legal Property: Let all, that are zealous in the Support of me, and my Government, partake id Cornea

A MESSAGE from his Majesty, by Sir Charles Dalton, Gentleman-usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty immediately in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend his Majesty:

And being returned;

Several Members, returned upon nets Writs, took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration, and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, pursuant to the Laws made for those Purposes.

A Bill for the more effectual preventing clandestine Outlawries, was read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

Mr. Speaker reported, that the House had attended his Majesty in the House of Peers; where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy; Which he read to the House, and is as fol-Ioweth;

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is a great Pleasure to me, that I am able to acquaint you, that the Expectations, which I have from time to time given you, of seeing the general Tranquillity of Europe, restored, and established, are now fully answered.

The Shaie of Credit and Influence, which the Crown of Great Britain has had in bringing about this difficult and desirable Work, and which redounds so much to the Honour and Interest of this Nation, as it is universally confeifed abroad, wi'l, I am confident, be agreeable to my People, and acknowledged with Gratitude by you.

It is well known, tin;, from the lime of concluding the Quadruple Alliance, the several Courts of Europe have been employed in finding Means to execute, what the principal Powers had agreed to, for the Succession of Tuscany and Parma in (avour of an Infant of Spain; but the various jarring and contending Interests, hard to be reconciled, and united, in effectuating a Point of so much Importance, the extended Views, and Hopes, of obtaining, on every Side, further Advantages, and the natural Jeaioufies and Distrusts, arising among the several Powers concerned, from such opposite Principles and Purposes, had kept in Suspense, and unexecuted, what the Court of Spain had very much at Heart, and occasioned such Troubles and Disturbances, as embarrassed the Affairs of Europe for many Years, and particularly affected the Interests of this Nation.

You have from time to time been informed of the different Measures and Negotiations, that have on all Sides been carrying on, during this long unsettled State of Affairs; and you have enabled me to persevere in maintaining the Rights and Possessions of this Kingdom, and in Preserving the Peace and Balance of Europe.

The preliminary Articles, and the subsequent Transactions thereupon, not answering the Expectations of the Court of Spain, and creating a Coolness and Diflht is faction among the contracting Parties of the First Treaty cf Vienna, laid the Foundation of the Treaty of Seville, and thereby dissolved that Union, which had raised so many Apprehensions, and so long alarmed the World.

The Execution of the Treaty of Seville was the great Difficulty, that (till remained; and this, unfurmouniable as i( was thought, I have, by your Support, and by the Confidence you repoled in me, been able to overcome, by just and honourable Treaties, without coming to Extremities, and without the Hazard and Expence of a general Rupture, or kindling a War in any Part of Europe.

Parma and Placentia are now in the actual Possession of the Infant Don Carlos', the Six thousand Spaniards are quiety admitted, and quartered, in the Duchy of Tuscany to secure, by the express Consent and Agreement of the Great Duke, the Reversion of his Dominions j and a Family Convention is made between the Courts of Spain and Tuscany, for preserving Peace and Friendship between those Two Houses, during the Life of the Great Duke.

Tor perfecting and finishing this tedious Work, conducted through a Series of infinite Changes and Viciffi-tudes, and incumbered with all the different Views of Intervft and Ambition, 1 concluded the late Treaty of Vienna-, wherein I have entered into no Engagements contrary to former Treaties, or tending either to aggrandize, or reduce, the Power or Weight of any Potentate; calculated purely for preserving a due Balance, and to avoid such Confusion, as new Changes and Convulsions, upon future Events, would unavoidably create, and wherein Great Britain Could never stand by, and be an idle Spectator.

When this shall be duly confiJcred, and it shall be seen that the Wounds, which have been long bleeding, are intirely healed, groundless Jealousies will cease, ill Humours will subside, and Peace and good Harmony return together; all Diffidence and Diltruft, the natural Effect of repeated Delays, artfully instilled, and industriously improved, and aggravated, will be removed, and mutual Satisfaction be the Consequence of the punctual and Effectual Performance of all Engagements on our Side; which will ever be remembered with great Regard and Honour to this Crown and Nation, and leave an imlifpenfable Obligation upon those, that are immediately concerned, to make such Returns, as Honour and Justice call for, and demand.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

The Estimates, for the Service of the current Year, shall be prepared, and laid before you; which you will observe to be considerably less, than those of former Years. It is a Pleasure to me to give Ease to my Subjects, whenever the Welfare of the publick will admit of it. You have seen the happy Effects of your former Zeal, and Resolution: Success has attended my Measures, and you reap the Fruit of my Endeavours, and your Confidence in me; and it mud be aSatisfaction to you to reflect, that all the Expences, you have lately made, are amply recQmpenled by preventing and avoiding far greater.

My Lords, and Gentlemen*

This happy Situation of Affairs, I promise myself, will inspire you ail with such Temper and Unanimity, and such a seasonable Zeal for the publick Good, as becomes a Parliament, sensible of the great Blessings they enjoy. The Duty and the Affections of my Subjects are all the Return I desire for my paternal Love and Concern for them. My Government has no Security, but what is equally conducive to your Happiness, and to the Protection of my People; and your Prosperity has no Foundation, but in the Defence and Support of my Government: Our Safety is mutual, our Interests are inseparable.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; to declare our highest Satisfaction in seeing the general Tranquillity of Europe restored, and established, by his Majesty's Credit and Influence, with so much Glory to the Crown of Great Britain, and Honour to this Nation; to acknowledge, with Gratitude, his Majesty's unwearied Endeavours for the Happiness of his People, and his Goodness in pursuing, with Steadihefs and Constancy, such Measures as best conduced to the preserving the Rights and Possessions of thele Kingdoms; to express our just Sense of his Majesty's great Wisdom, in being able to l'ur-mount the various Difficulties, that so long embarrassed the Affairs of Europe, and particularly affected the Interests of Great Britain, and, by pacifick Measures and Negociations, to bring to a happy Conclusion the several Disputes, that for many Years had been subsisting and depending, and by just and honourable Treaties to settle and re-establish the publick Tranquillity, without the Hazard and Expence of a general Rupture, or kindling a War in any Part of Europe; and to assure his Majesty, that this House, sensible of the happy Effects of the Confidence, so justly reposed in his Majesty, and the Blessings we enjoy under his Government, will with Chearfulness grant the Supplies necessaryfor the Service of the current Year, for the Defence and Support of his Majesty's Government, and for the Security and Protection of his People.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed, to draw up an Address, to be presented to his Majesty, upon the said Resolution:

The Lord T yrconnelreported from the Committee appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address, to be presented to his Majesty, that the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had directed hitzi to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as follows;

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty's most loyal and dutiful Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our most humble Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

It is the highest Satisfaction to your faithful Commons, to see the general Tranquillity of Europe restored, and re-established, by your Majesty's Credit and Influence; which reflects the greatest Glory to the Crown, and, of consequence, to the Nation, the Honour

and interest of which are always mutual and inseparable.

We are fully persuaded, that the Treaties, your Majesty has entered into, were made with no other View, than to preserve the Balance of Power in , and

fee. re the Possessions of the Crown of Great Britain, and all the Rights and Privileges we are entitled to; and we acknowledge, with Gratitude, your Majesty's Wisdom and Goodntfs, in procuring for us all theie Advantages, without the Expence and Hazards of a War.

We are very sensible of the many Difficulties, your Majesty laboured under in bringing this great and glorious Works to so happy a Conclusion. The many Obstacles, anting from various Pretensions and Jealouties, during the Course of these Transactions, unsurmountable as they have been thought, are by your Majesty's Steadi-ness and Prudence intirely removed; and, at a time, when a War seemed unavoidable, the Settlement of the Succession of Don Carlos to the States of and

Parma has been peaceably accomplished, and the general Tranquillity of Europepreserved, by the Weight and Credit or your Majesty's Negotiations.

Thus has your Majesty extricated, not only this Nation, but all Europe, out of the uncertain State, wc for many Years laboured under, and that by Means most honourable to your Majesty, confident with all former Engagements, and without the least Injury to any Prince or Power in Europe,

Mr. Speaker reported, that the House attended his Majesty on Saturday last with their Address; to which his Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I return you my Thanks for this dutiful and loyal Address.

I make no Doubt of the Continuance of your Duty, Afledtion, and Confidence in me; and you will always find, that all my Views tend to the Honour, Interest, and Security, of my Crown, and People.

The House (according to Order) resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Motion, made on Saturday last. That a Supply be granted to his Majesty.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair

Sir Charles Turner took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir Charles Turner reported from the Committee, that they had come to a Resolution, which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Mr. Thorowkettle, licensed Pilot, laid, that, when he has gone on board foreign Ships, to pilot them up the River, he has been threatened by the Mailer to be thrown over-board, and, if he (laid, he should have nothing to eat; and, when the Ship has been brought up the River by his Care, expected to receive £. 5. but the Matter would pay no more than £. 3. upon which he applied to the Trinity-house for a Summons, and served the Matter with it; who would not obey such Summons: That, upon his Application to them again for Relief, he was informed, the Corporation could not oblige Foreigners to take Pilots; and advised him to take the £. 3. the Mailer had offered him.

Wm.Kilwick and Zachary Mason, licensed Pilots, severally confirmed the Evidence given by Thorowkettle, of Foreigners refusing to take Pilots, and of their threatening to throw them over-board.

Robert Boyce, John Peterson, Thomas Buckingham, and Wm. Kilwick, severally said, that the English Ships are obliged to take Pilots at Norway, Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Hambrough, and Holland, and pay Pilotage, if they have not a Pilot on board.

Edward Holliday said, that at St. Sebastians and they take Pilots, to carry Ships into those Harbours, and cannot go in without.

And he further said, that the Corporation have 93 Alms-houses, wherein are 26 Pilots, or their Widows, who receive from them £. 346. per Annum; and about 77 monthly Pensioners, Pi.ots, and their Widows, who are not in Alms-heufes, and receive about 234. Annum-, which makes the whole, paid to them, about £.580. per Annum; and the Poundage, paid by the Pilots, amounts but to £. 50. per Annum, upon a Medium, for about 40 Years past:

That the Number of monthly Poor, who ate Pilots, Seamen. Mariners, their Widows, and Orphans, maintained, and paid monthly, by the said Corporation, exclusive of the Poor in the Alms-houses, amounts to near 2,000 Persons, besides £. 160. per Annum, paid to accidental Poor.

And he further testified, that the whole Money, paid to all their Poor annually, amounts to near £. 5,500. exclusive of Cloth Gowns, once in Two Years given to the Poor in Alms-houses, and 20J. per Annum to each Alms-house, for Coals.

But said, that some of their poor Brethren received but £. 3. per Annum, which was not suffi.ient to keep them from starving.

Petitioners are unable to come at the Knowlege of their Combinations, or to bring them to Justice, without Aid of the Power and Authority of this House: And therefore praying, that the House will vouchtafe to enquire into the State of the said Corporation, and the Conduct of those who have had the Care and Management of their Affairs, and*give such Relief to the Petitioneis, as to the House shall seem meet.
