Lombe'* Mr. Alderman Perry reported from the Committee, to

or whom the Petition of Sir homas Lombe was referred; Orgaozinc that the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, together with the Resolution of the Committee thereupon, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the Report and Resolution were read, and are as follow:

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, dated the a8ih of January instant, proceeded to examine into the Matter of the said Petition; and, to prove the Allegations of the fame, called the following Witnesses; viz.

Mr. Daniel Booth, Si k Weaver; who said, that the fine Italian Organzine Silk is a Commodity, absolutely necessary to carry on the Siik Weaving Trade in this Kingdom; and that in Times pall the Merchants have been forced to buy this Organzine Silk with our Money, ready worke I in Italy, for want of the Art of making it here: That, since the Petitioner, Sir Thomas has set

up his Engine, it has reduced the P'ice of Italian Organzine Silk, which is now Five Shillings per Pound cheaper, than it usually used to be, and is now about 20 Cent. cheaper than it has been, at a Medium, for these Twenty Years last pall; and that he has bought as good Organzine Silk, madd by the Petitioners Engine, for 20 a Pound, as he formerly gave 25 s. for; and that there has been a very great Increase of the Siik Manufacture of this Kingdom, since the said Engine was ereCled, and the Price thereof very much reduced: And said, that Org xnzine Silk can't be thrown by Hand, but is now perfectly done by the Petitioner's Engine; and that this Organzine Silk is absolutely necdlary for making the Warp of all fine Silks; and that the Silk, thrown here by the Silk-throwers, is only fit for the Shute; and that, without a constant Supply of this Italian Organzine Silk, the Silk thrown by the Silk-throwers in England could not be used.

And the same Witness, being further examined, laid, that it is but very lately, that the Petitioner has brought his Organzine Silk to Perfection; and that Luftrings, Alamodes, and several other of our Silk Manufactures, are wholly made of this Organzine Silk, and can't be made of any other; and that no Silks can be made by the Weavers of the Siik thrown here by the Silk-throwers, without having a proper Proportion of this fine Italian Organzine Silk, to mix with it, and serve as a Warp to cover the said Silk thrown here.

Then the said Witness produced to the Committee several Samples and Patterns of Organzine Silk, and of the Silks thrown here, and demonllrated the Difference between them; and also produced several Patterns of woven Silks and Sattins, and distinguished to the Committee, what Pa-t thereof was made with the said Organzine Silk, and what with the Siik thrown here by the Silk-throwers; and likewise produced some Patterns of fine Velvet, and Mantua Silks, made intirely with the said Organzine Silk.

Mr. Wm. Seltvyn, who is an Importer of Italian Organzine Silk, and Trader in other Sorts of Silks, laid, that he has imported from Italy great Quantities of the said Voj.. *1.

Italian Organzine Silk, foi* many Years pall, and has known several Mills I'er up, but never knew any that could work the said Italian Organzine Silk to Perfection, as the said Sir Thomas Lombe's Engine does; and that there is great Profit arising to the Nation by bringing over the Silk raw, and working it into Organzine Silk in England.

Mr. Roger Drake, Italian Merchant, laid, that he has bought several Quantities of Organzine Silk in which he always paid for in Money, either by remitting it to Italy, or being drawn upon from thence: That he

has seen the said Sir Thomas Lombe's, Engine, and that there is not such another in England; and that Organzine Silk cannot be thrown by any other Mill; and that the said Engine, he believes, has been the Occasion of lowering the Price of Silk in Italy.

Captain Peter Lekeux, Weaver, being examined, said, that he has imported Organzine Silk from Italy, and has paid for it 27 s.per Pound; but, since Sir Thomas Lombe's Engine has been let up, the Price has been reduced 5 or 6 s. per Pound; and that Sir Thomas Lombe's Organzine Silk is now as good in Quality a; the Italian; which said Organzine Silk is absolutely necessary to make all Sorts of plain and flowered Silks, Gold and Silver Silks, and Brocades; and that the making of such Organzine Silk has not been brought to Perfection by Sir Thomas Lombe above a Year or Two, at most, fie himself having often; before thar Time, found it defective, and complained thereof to Sir Thomas Lomb; and that, without the said Organzine Silk, the Siik Weavers can't make any Piece ot Silk:

And that the said Sir 7 ToomasLombe's Engine employs

our own Poor, in making a new Manufacture in England, and is of great Advantage to the Nation.

Then the Petitioner laid before the Committee his Patent, bearing date the 8th Day of September, 1718; whereby it appeared, that the foie making and using the said Engines, and all Benefit arising the reby, was granted to him for the Term of Fourteen Years:

And likewise produced to the Committee the Law, printed in Italian, and the Translation thereof; whereby it appeared, that the disclosing, or attempting to discover, any thing relating to the making the Engines, or the working the said Organzine Silk, is by the said Law prohibited in Italy, on Pain of Death.

And it further appeared to the Committee, that the said Sir Thomas Lombe has with the greatest Hazard and Difficulty found out those Arts, and brought them here into England, and at a very great Expence of his own Money, and but lately brought the ManulaClure to Perfection.

And that, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a further Term of Years be granted to Sir Thomas Lombe, his Executors, Admindhators, and Assigns, beyond the Term of Fourteen Years, granted to him by his late Majesty King George, for the foie Privilege, Power, and Authority, of exercising, working, making, using, and enjoying, his new Invention of Three Sons of Engines, or Machines, found out, brought into England, and, since the granting of the said Patent, erected by the said Sir Thomas Lombe on the River Derwent, in or near, the Town of Derby, for making Organzine Silk, and all Benefits arising by the said Invention.

Charitable A Petition of the Creditors, whose Names are thereunto Corporation, subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and other the Creditors by Notes and Bonds, of the Charitable Corporation, for Relief of industrious Poor, by assisting them with small Sums, upon Pledges, at legal Interest, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, that the Petitioners have lent large Sums of Money on their Notes and Bonds, at legal Interest only, without any farther Views of Profit without which, as the Petitioners apprehend, the said Corporation could not have been able to have made the Dividends, which they have thought fit to make on their Shares, at the Rate of Ten Pounds per Cent, per Annum, and other considerable Advantages: And complaining, that by unparalleled Frauds, and Mismanagement, the greatest Part of the Capital of the said Corporation has, as the Petitioners have great Reason to believe, been embezzled and consumed, and the Effects belonging to the fame, are thereby become scarce sufficient to answer the Petitioners Demands; and that not the lead Notice has been taken, by the present Managers and Inspectors of the said Corporation, of the said Demands, though Money has been issued out, as the Petitioners are well allured, for other Purposes; and the Goods of the Corporation are in the mean time differed to lie spoiled in their Ware-houses: And therefore praying, that, since they have Vo L. 21.

little or no Prospect of Relief, without the Aid and Assistance of this House, that the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ships of considerable Burthen, laden, can't venture m, but near the Tops of Spring Tides, and Ships of lesser Burthen, about an Hour and an Half before high Watety and an Hour and an Half after: That, in caie the said Addition be made to the said Pier, as desired, near Seven Foot Water will be gained in the Harbour; and then Ships, which at present can come in only at Three Quarters Flood, and until a Quarter Ebb, may come in Four Hours and Half before high Water, and Four Hours and Half after high Water; and the largest Ships laden now, belonging to the Coal Trade, may then safely enter-the Harbour: That the present Pier being veryTmall, and so full of such Ships as are laid up in the Winter Season, it is almoll impossible then to get in; but, after the proposed Addition shall be made, there will be room for near Two hundred Sail of Ships more.

That the same Witness laid before the Committee an Estimate of the Expence of making the proposed Addition, which amounts to £.11.490. 4*. and laid, that the desired Addition was Four hundred and Forty Foot in Length, the greatest Part of which to be built Six Foot, and upwards, in the Water, at low Water, and to be Twenty Yards broad at the bottom, Ten at the Topi and Thirty-live Foot high, and to be built all with Slone.

appointed to inspect, and settle, the Fees, to be taken by Officers of all the Officers, and Servants of the House, and to exa- l^e 1Iou^c* mine w hat Salaries, or Allowances, they have from the Government, the Matter, as it appeared to them, with the llefelution of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Resolution of the Committee is as followed);

ReJ'olved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all Fees to be demanded or taken by any Officer or Servant of the House, be fixed according to the Rale of the Lift of Fees, entered in the Journals in the Year 1700; and that Tables of the fame, being first peruled by Mr, Speaker, be printed, and hung up in the Speakers Chamber, in the Lobby, and in the Clerk's Office; and that the Clerk take care to renew such printed Tables from time to time, as Occasion shall require, and to pre-lcrvc them always fair and legible.

The said Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, nominecontradicente, That the House doth

agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That all Fees, to be demanded or taken by any Officer or Servant of the House, be fixed according to the Rate of the Lift of Fees, entered in the Journals in the Year 1700; and that Tables of the fame, being first perused by Mr. Speaker, be printed, and hung up in the Speakers Chamber, in the Lobby, and in the Clerk's Office; and that the Clerk take care to renew such printed Tables from time to time, as Occasion shall require, and to pre-lerve them always fair and legible.

ReJ'olved, nomine contradicente, That, if any Officer or Servant of this House shall prel'ume to demand, or take, any greater Fee, than what shall be contained in the said printed Tables, this House will proceed against such Officer or Servant with the utmost Severity.

Ordered, That the said Resolutions be Standing Orders of the House.

Ordered, That the said Reiblutions be printed with the said Tables of Fees.

The said Report, and Appendix thereto, being too long to be conveniently inserted in this Journal, is bound up with the other Papers of this Srifion.

The Serjeant at Arms attending the House, being called upon, to give an Acc unt what had been done in relation to the taking of John Thompson, lateWarehouse-keeper to the Charitable Corporation, the Messenger, who was sent in Search of him, acquainted the House, that he had withdrawn himself, and was not yet taken.

And the House being informed, that the said John Thompson had withdrawn himself to Parts beyond the Seas;

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do enquire as to the Time, Manner, and other Circumstances, of the said John Thompson withdrawing himself into Parts beyond the Seas; and that they do report the same specially to the House, with all convenient Speed.

A Petition of the licensed Pilots of the of

Deptford Strond, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, 0fPite,u in behalf of themselves, and others, licensed Pilots of the said House, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, that several Clauses, contained in the Bill nowdc* pending before the House, for the better Regulation and Government of Pilots, licensed by the Corporation of Trinity-house of Deptford Strond, in the County of Kent, and to prevent Mischiefs and Annoyances upon the River of Thames below London Bridge, are, as the Petitioners apprehend, contrary to the Liberties and Privileges of free-born Subjects; and that the said Bill, if passed into a Law, will tend to the great Prejudice, if not the utter Ruin, of the Petitioners, and others: And therefore praying, that the Petitioners may have Leave to be heard by themselves, or Counsel, against such Parts of the said Bill, or have such other Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for the better Regulation and Government of Pilots, licensed by the Corporation of Trinity-house of Deptford Strond, in the County of Kent, and to prevent Mischiefs and Annoyances upon the River of Thame below London Bridge, is committed; and that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be heard before the said Committee by their Counsel, according to the Prayer of their Petition.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they do admit Counsel to be heard at the same time, in favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

That the back Water, with proper Means used tocon-fineit to the Channel, will also wash away the Sand in such Channel; fothat, should the Winds at any Time raisethe Tides, or should any Land Floods meet with spring Tides, the Water will go off much quicker, than it now does, from the River's being made deeper, and from the Fall of the Waters being increased between 10 and Feet; and the Motion of the Waters being quickened, will cause the Lands above the Causeway to be more securefrom being overflowed, than what they now are; for that the present Windings of the Channel are an Obstruction to the back Water, and the Current above the Causeway is very flow; and the confining the Water to this new Channel will have no Influence on the Swell of the Tide, or raise the Water any higher.

And the said Witness further said, that the Depth of the Water in the Channel, at the Ebb, will be in Proportion to the back Water; and that the Sand, through which the new Channel is proposed to be made, is a looie Sand, and will be washed away by the Weight of the Water:

' That the Expence of this Undertaking is estimated at between 40 and £. 50,000. which is proposed to be raised by a Tonage on Vessels, laden with Good* to and from Chester, to be paid according to the Distance of their Voyages; and the Sands, which in time will be gained thereby, computed at about 6,000 Acres, are to be appropriated towards this Expence; but that it will be 20 Years, before such Sands can be made use of.

And the feme Witness further said, that the said River is to be made navigable, before any Benefit is to accrue thereby to the Undertakers thereof.

Tl)at the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the 17U1 Instant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and, to prove the Allegations thereof, Witnesses were called: Mr. Anthony Mead; who laid, That he had been a Hat-maker Thirty-five Years; and he had seen several Hats, made in foreign Parts; but that they are not so good as those made here in England-, and that a considerable Trade was formerly carried chi with the Plantations in America for Hats, in Exchanges for Beaver Skins.

Richard Turner, Hat-maker, said, That he has, often fold great Quantities of Hats for Exportation to the said Plantations in America;and that they were altogpthor for-

merly supplied with the same from England; but that they are npw chiefly from A7etc York, and New England; and has been informed, that Ten thousand Beaver Hats are yearly made there.

Air. Anthony Mead, being further examined, said, That the Price of 1 leaver is considerably cheaper in America, tiian in England, as not being chargeable with Custom, Freight, or iiazard of the Sea; and that the Skins being their own Produce, they have Advantage of being supplied with the best, and can afford Hats 5 cheaper there, than here in England; and said, that the Skins, imported from thence, arc not so good as they were formerly, and are fold here for 4s. 6d. per Skin.

Then the Book of Rates, fr om the Commissioners of Customs, was produced, and laid before the Committee; whereby it appeared, that there is a Duty, of about Sixpence per Skin, paid for all Skins imported into England.

Ibraham Jaques, Hat-maker, said, That he was at ton, in New England, about a Year and half since, and worked there with a Matter Ilat-maker, who commonly iinithed Forty Beaver Hats in a Week; and that Four or Five Apprentices were employed in the Trade, besides Journeymen; and that Three of the Apprentices came from Jvrfey, anil were bound only for Two, Three, or Four, Years; and that there were lli Hat-makers in the Place, and that most of them kept Four or Five Apprentices; anil that the Wages of making a Hat there is but 1 s. 31/. Eng/ijk Money, hut, if made in England, 46d. or

Edmund Pinneger, Hat-maker, said, That he worked

some time since at Newport, and Rhode with one

H in Pinneger, who had Apprentices, Four whereof were

bound to him for Two, Three, or Four, Years only; and was informed, that it was a common. Practice, for Matters there to take Six Apprentices, and to hind them only for Two Years; and that a great many Hats are sent from thence to Jamaica, Barbadoes, South and

tinico; and that very tew Ships go to Jamaica from thence without Hats.

Captain George Wane said, That he had followed the Madeira Trade 14 or 15 Years; and that he has seen several Parcels of Hats shipp'd from York, and New England, to Madeira, for Prieits, and Jefoits, who were formerly supplied with the same from England; and tl«at the said Hats are fold for Six Mill Rees a Hat, but* if made in England, could not be afforded to be sold for leis than Ten Mill Rees a Hat; and said, that there is a constant Trade carried on with Jamaica for Hats.

John Hawkins, Gun-maker, said, That in the Year 1722, when he was at Virginia, a Sloop brought in Tw o

Boxes of Hats from Nezo England; and that he bought one for himself, which was a very good Beaver; and said, that in North Carolina, about 1723, several Sloops came from New England with Hats for Sale; and that commonly all the Sloops, that came from thence, brought some for that Purpose to North Carolina; and that Beaver Hats cost 12s. Sterling at Nero England; *nd said, that he had Two Beaver llats lenthim from South Carolina, which cost 17 s.3 d.Sterling; and that he fold them here in England for 28 s. which were sent to him about Three Years since, for a Sample, but did not encourage the lending any more, it being out of his Way of Business.

Mr. Docminique, from the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, presented to the House, pursuant to their Order, A Report of the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, of such Methods, as have been thought of by them, for preventing the running of Wool from England and Ireland for the future.

And the Title of the said Report was read.

The Report is as follows; viz.

To the honourable the Commons bf Great in Parliament assembled:

PURSUANT to an Order of this honourable House, dated the 29th of the last Month, directing us to lay before you l'uch Methods, as have been thought on by us, for preventing the running of Wool from England and Ireland for the future, we take Leave to represent, That, having for some time had this Matter under our Consideration, we did give publick Notice in the,

of the 12th Day of June last, that we were ready to receive any Proposals, which should be made to us on this Head, from all Persons whatsoever.

Since the Publication of this Advertisement, which was often repeated in the Gazette, and other publick Papers, we have been attended by several Persons, and many Schemes have been transmitted to us from different Parts of this Kingdom, and from Ireland, containing various Proposals upon this Subject; and it has been with great Satisfaction, that we have observed the Zeal, with which io many Persons have applied themselves to consider of proper Methods for putting a Stop to a Practice, fovery pernicious to the trading Interest of their Country.

Thole, who seem to have most maturely considered this Matter, concur in Opinion, that nothing can put lb ef-

*7

A. 1731.

fectual a Stop to this Evil, as the finding out some certain Method of knowing the whole Quantity of Wool, that may be in the Kingdom, whether in Warehouses, or on the Sheeps Back, and of tracing it through the Hands of the Wool-ftapler, and all the Traders, who deal in this Commodity, till it shall be finally wrought up by the Manufacturer.

In order to this, it has been proposed, that Ware* houses should be erected, at the publick Expence, in such Counties of England and Ireland, where conGderable Numbers of Sheep may be fed, or where the Woollen Manufacture may be carried on in any great Extent, into which the Wool of the Two Kingdoms should be brought within a certain Number of Days, after it is Ihofn, in or* der to be afterwards transported, under proper Regula* lations, from Ireland to England, and from one County of England to another, in proportion to the Demand, that there may be for it amongst the Manufacturers.

Others have proposed, that general Registers should be established ih England and Ireland, for entering the eia& Numbers of Sheep and Lambs, with the yearly Quantity of Wool shorn from them, or pulled from Skins, together with the Natnes of all such, as deal in this Commodity.

In addition to the Proposition for publick Ware* houses, it has been offered by anothet hand, that all the Wool, produced in the Kingdom, should be bought in the King's Name, at certain Prices, to be ascertained at a Medium, upon the different Growths of Wool for so many Years past, and that the Produce of the First Years Growth and the Value of the Stock in Hand, should be paid for by a final! Land Tax, of Three Pence, of Six Pence, in the Pound; by which Means the Growers would receive ready Money for their Wool, which would be very beneficial both to Landlords, and Tenants; but, if this should be thought impracticable, it is further proposed by the same Person, that Payment for the Wool may be postponed, till it be fold, in part, or in the whole, or that the Gr6wers should be left at Liberty to fell it themselves to the Manufacturers, provided they delivered it to the Storekeepers, under proper Regulations.

Many of the Proposers concur in Opinion, that the bed Method of preserving an exact Knowledge of the Wool, in its Progression from the First Grower to the last Manufacturer, will be, to put it under the inspection of the Officers of Excise; and different Methods have beta suggested, for putting this Proposal in Execution.

it has been laid under this Head, that all Dealers in Wool may be obliged to enter the Warehouses, and Store-rooms, wherein they keep this Commodity, with the Excise Officer of their Division, into which the Officer should have free Admission at any time; and that no Wool should be brought into the Warehouses, before Notice be given of it to the Excise Officer, under a certain Penalty:

That every Owner of Sheep shall give Notice, when he intends to (hear his Ffock, that the Officer maybe present, to take an Account of the Number of Sheep, and Weight of the Wool fhom; and that every Fell-monger may be obliged tb inform the Officer of his Division of the Weight of the Wool, which he shall pull from Skins; and in general, that all Dealers in Wool shall be obliged to give ati Account to their Excite Officer of all the Wool in their Possession:

That no Wool shall Be removed from Warehouses, lo entered, except by virtue of a Permit from the Excise Officer, to be renewed, as often as the Wool shall pass from Qije Dealer to another, till it comes into the Hands of the last Manufacturer.

It has been likewise suggested, that the Excise Officer may take a Bond from the first Buyer, whereby he should oblige himself to manufacture the Wool, he buys; but, if the Purchaser be not a Manufacturer, that then Notice should be given to the Officer of the Division, whenever the Wool shall be refold, either in the whole, or in part, and fresh Bonds be given by the Buyers, till the fame

5 Geo. II.

6" Martii.

«33

1#

ft

y

fame shall be finally manufactured j and some have thought, that for the better Security of this Matter, the Manufacturer should be obliged to make Oath, that he will manufacture the Wool, he buys.

Without Doubt, the keeping Sight of the Wool, from the time it is (horn, till it is brought into the Hands of the last Manufacturer, might greatly contribute to the putting a Stop to the running of this Commodity; but, as all the foregoing Fropolals would probably be attended with Multiplicity of Accounts, besides other Difficulties, and great Expence, we are of Opinion, some other Methods, which seem liable to fewer Difficulties, might be very conducive to the Cure of this Grievance.

With regard to Great Britain, we would propose, that the Law, now in force in Kent and Sussex, passed the 9th and 10th of William 3d, intituled, An Act for the Explanation, and better Execution, of former Acts,

made against the Transportation of Wool, Fullers Earth, and scouring Clay," may be extended to all Parts of the united Kingdom within Ten Miles of the SeaCoaft:

That no Wool be brought or imported from Ireland into this Kingdom, or earned Coastwise in except in Vessels, registered and appointed solely for that Purpose; and that all Wool, shipped on board any other Vessel, shall be liable to Seizure by the Captains of his Majesty's Ships of War, by the Commanders of the Register Ships, the Custom-house and Excile Officers, and by all other Persons, duly authorised; and that Officers be appointed, to put the Laws in Execution against the running of Wool, with ample Encouragement to Informers, easily to be recovered, and proportionable Penalties laid on Offenders.

But, as every thing, that may be proposed for the Cure of this Evil in Great Britain oniy, would be far from answering the Design upon the whole, unless proper Methods should at the same time be found, to prevent the Exportation of Wool, and of Woollen Manufactures, from Ireland to foreign Parts, so, many of the same Persons, who have considered this Matter with respect to Great Britain, have also extended their Thoughts to

Ireland.

And some of them have proposed to apply the foregoing Expedients of County Warehouses, general Registers, and the Inspection of the Custom-house Officers, as proper to be put in Practice in Ireland; with this Addition, that certain Staple Towns should be appointed in that Kingdom, for the Reception of Wool grown there.

But we are of Opinion, that the moll likely Means, and most attainable, for these Purposes, would be, absolutely to prohibit the shipping of Wool in except in Ships and Vessels, registered and appointed for that Service only, and that no Wool Licences should be granted, for Shipping of Wool on board any other Vessels:

That the explanatory Clause contained in an Act, passed in the 11th and iath of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act for continuing 4‘ several Laws therein mentioned, and for explaining " the Act, intituled, An Act to prevent the Exportation *4 of Wool out of the Kingdoms of Ireland and England into foreign Parts, and for the Encouragement of the Woollen Manufactures in the Kingdom of Eng-4‘ land," whereby Leave was given to every Mariner, or Passenger, on board a Ship, to furnish himself with the Woollen Manufactory of Ireland, to the Amount of Forty Shillings, may be repealed, since it is highly probable, that, under this Pretence, the Woollen Manufactures of that Kingdom first found their way to foreign Markets in large Quantities:

That the Captains of English Men of War and Sloops, as well as the Commanders of the Register Ships, and all Officers of his Majesty's Customs and Excile, may be invested with full Power and Authority to seize all Irish Woollen Goods, which they shall find on board any Ship or Vessel whatsoever, and all Wool, which shall Vox.. 21.

be found on board of any other but the said Register Rannioi Vessels. of Wool.

And these Provisions are the more necessary, because we have been credibly informed, that of late Years British Merchants have given no small Encouragement to the Irifl) Woollen Manufactures, by buying up, and exporting, great Quantities from that Kingdom, on their own Account to foreign Parts.

And, provided an effectual Stop could be put to the Exportation of Irish Woollen Manufactures, and of Irish Wool, to foreign Parts, we should conceive, that ii would be highly for the Advantage of Great freely, and without Duties, to admit the Importation of their Yarn.

And, in order to make this Benefit more extensive, we would beg Leave to submit to the Consideration of this honourable House, whether it may not be proper to open all the Ports of Ireland and England, for the Exportation and Importation of Irish Woollen Yam, but more particularly the Ports of Gallway and London; for we are in-? formed, that great Quantities of the bell Wool in Ireland are produced within Thirty Miles round the Town of Gallway, winch is above One hundred Miles distant from any of the Ports now open for the Exportation of Wool from that Kingdom; so that the Land Carriage in Ireland creates an Addition of about Six per Cent, upon the prime Coll of the Wool, before it comes to any of the Ports, from whence it can be sent to England, as the Law now Hands; and, in the same manner, the Charges of bringing a Pack of Irish Yam from the Port of Bristol to Colchester, or Norwich, has been computed to be no

leis than Five per Cent, at a Medium, upon the prime Coll of the Yarn, and the Charge of carrying a Pack of Irish Wool between those Places is computed at near Fifteen per Cent, upon the prime Cost of the Wool; which being impartially considered, we conceive, it will appear unreasonable to this honourable House, that the Manufactures in one Part of this Kingdom should remain under the Necessity of working up of the Irish Wool and Yam near Ten per Cent, dearer, than others; a Difficulty, that would be intirely removed by opening the Port of London which lies conveniently for tbpiplying the Manufacturers of Essex, and of the adjacent Counties.

These are the principal Matters, that have occurred to us upon this Subject; to which we would beg Leave tp add, that such of these Provisions, as shall be approved of, and more particularly, what relates to the Register Ships, may be extended to the Illes of Man, G'uernfey,

Jersey, Alderney, and Sark.

All which is humbly submitted to this honourable House.

Whitehall, March P. Dominique,

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the Second Instant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition; and, to prove the Allegations thereof, Witnesses were called: Mr. James Laws-, who said, that the said Island of Jamaica is at present very thinly inhabited by white People; but, if Encouragement was given to the Produce of Coffee on the said Island, it will be ofgreat Service to the Inhabitants thereof, and be aMeans to bring in the poorer Sort of People there, which is very much wanted:

And, being examined as to the Produce of the Coffee

Woollen A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common- ,

ment of forte Coffee, that grew in the Garden there, he Found the same to be tolerably good, which encouraged him to try the planting of it in his Plantation: And produced to the Committee some Samples of Coffee, that tame from his Estate in Jamaica; and said, that he had shewed them to several Druggists in and they all

agreed, that they were very good:

Said, that he has been informed, that the Trees will not bear Coffee Berries under Four or Five Years Growth, and that a Tree will not last longer than Fout or Five Years: And said, that about Four hundred Trees may be planted on an Acre of Ground, and that each Tree will bear one Pound of Coffee in a Plantation, and in a Garden between Two and Three Pounds; and that he had Seven hundred Weight of Coffee from Six hundred Trees:

Said, that the Trees are very precarious, and subject to be destroyed by Vermin; and that, if the Produce of Coffee was encouraged in the said Iffand, it will employ several poor Persons, to watch and preserve the same from being destroyed: And said, that the Ground and Latitude of the said Hland is a very proper Soil for Coffee, and lies near the same Latitude as Mochoa:

And, being further examined, said, that the Coffee grows better upon the Mountains, than low Land, by realbri of its being well supplied with Rain, which is of great Service to the Growth thereof:

That, if the Produce of Coffee was encouraged in the said Iffand, the Plantations of Sugar will not be decreased, but will rather be increased, by reason, as the poor People get Money by the Produce of Coffee, they will be encouraged to ered Sugar-works: And said, that Coffee will grow upon some Part of the Mountains, which are too deep and laborious for Sugar; and that the same will not grow in many Places, as Sugar does, it being a more tender Plant, and requiring more Rain to preserve it.

And being asked, if the Dutch did not produce Coffee at Surinam, said, he had been informed, that they did,

and that 200,000 Weight had been imported from thence into Holland in a Year; but it is not so good, as Coffee from Mochoa.

Mr. Richard Harris said, that it had been the constant Practice of the Legislature, for the Encouragement of and Commodity of our own, to abate the Customs thereof in its Infancy; and enumerated several Instancesof the like Kind, as Sugar, Tobacco, and Ginger; which paid higher Duties upon Importation, when a foreign Growth, than from our own Plantations: And said, that, if Encouragement was given to the planting of Coffee, it would be a great Advantage to this Nation, and increase the poorer Inhabitants of that Iffand, and not only save the Nation a great Sum of Money, annually exported for the Purchase of the said Commodity, but would enable it to supply their Neighbours with the fame.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Friday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

to the Plenipotentiaries of his Majesty, 16th April 1727; and a Translation thereof: And also,

An Estimate of the several Sums of Money, that have become due and payable to the King of , by virtue of his late Majesty's Declaration to that Purpose, for the Agio, or Difference, of the Subsidies, payable to the Crown of Denmark in pursuance of the Treaty between his late Britan nick Majesty, the most Christian

The said Translation of the said Declaration, and tbf said Estimate, are as follows; viz.

TV WHEREAS a Difficulty had ariie;, which retarded the Conclusion of the Convention, signed this Day betw een their Britannick, Danish, and most Christian Majesties, on account, that his most Christian Majesty offered the Payment of the Subsidy of Three hundred and Fifty thousand Itix Dollars, stipulated in the said Convention, in the current Money of Demark, and that his Danish Majesty infilled upon having it in Bank Money of Hamburgh, in Specie; we, the underwritten, by virtue of the full Power, communicated this same Day, do declare, in the Name of his Britannick Majesty, that he will employ his good Offices with his most Christian Majesty, to dispose him to pay the said Sublidv in Bank Money of j

Hamburgh; and that, if his Britannick Majesty cannot ui

fuQceed, in engaging his most Christian Majesty to fatidy the King of Denmark on that Head, then his said fyri-tannick Majesty, to contribute towards the Advantage of the common Cause, and out of a particular Frietulship for his Majesty the King of Denmark, is willing to charge himself with the Difference between the current Money of Denmark, and that of the Bank, in Specie; which he will pay in the Manner, and at the Times, mentioned in the said Convention.. In witness whereof, we have signed the present Declaration, and have lit the Seal of our Arms thereunto, at Copenhagen, the itith of April, in the Year 1727.

Mr. Thomas Tmcer reported from the Committee, who were appointed to inspect what Laws are expired, or near expiring, and to report their Opinion to the House, which of them are fit to be revived, or continued, that they had inspected the Laws accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read die Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

lft, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, " An " Act; for the better securing the lawful Trade of his Majesty s Subjects to and from the East Indies, and " for the more effectual preventing all his Majesty's Subjects trading thither under foreign Commissions," which by an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty King George, was continued in force to the End of the Session of Parliament now lait past, when the said Act expired, is fit to be revived. Vol. 21.

2d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, "An Act for the better regulating the Manufacture of " Cloth in the West Riding of the County of York," which was to continue in force for the Term of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and is near expiring, is fit to be continued.

3d, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for " the better Encouragement of the making of Sail-cloth " in Great Britain," which Act, by several Acts, made in tire Fifth and Tenth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, was from time to time continued in force to the End of the Session of Parliament now lait past, when the said Act expired, is fit to be revived.

4th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act to prevent frivolous and vexatious Arrests," which was to continue iti force for the Term of Five Years, and from thence to the End of the next Session of Parliament, and is near expiring, is fit to be continued.

5th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, "An Act for the better viewing, searching, and examining, " all Drugs, Medicines, Waters, Oils, and Compositions, used or to be used for Medicines, in all Places, " where the same shall be exposed to Sale, or kept for

7th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, "An Act for the more effectual disarming the Highlands in " that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and for the " better securing the Peace and Quiet in that Part of the " Kingdom," which is near expiring, is fit to be continued.

9th, Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, "An Act for repealing the Duty laid upon " Snuff, by an Act made in the Eighth Year of her late Majesty's Reign, and for ascertaining the Rates, according to which the remaining Duties are to be paid, " and for giving further Encouragement to the Greenland " Fishery," as relates to the encouraging his Majesty's British Subjects to import Whale-fins, Oil or Blubber of Whale, Seal Oil, Seal Skins, or any other Produce of Seals, or other Fifti, or Creatures, taken or caught in the Greenland Seas, or in Davis's Straits, or in any other Parts of the Seas adjoining or adjacent thereunto, which is expired, is fit to be revived.

A Petition of Thomas Tomkyns was presented to the Tomb' House, and read; setting forth, that the Petitioner was, on the Eleventh Day of July 1718, arrested, and has from tw*1 that Time been confined in Prison, upon an Extent, for an Arrear, which he (lands charged with to his Mijel'y, for the Use of the Publick, as having been Cashier to the late Commissioners for licensing Hawkers, Pedlars, and Petty Chapmen: That, having been afflicted with Sick-ness, he should have wanted the common Necessaries of Life, if he had not been assisted by his Friends, by whom his Wife, and Four firtall Children, have also been supported: That he hopes, by their A Alliance, or by feme other Way, if he should procure an Act of Parliament for a Discharge from his Imprisonment, to be enabled, in Time, to raise a Sum of Money, to compound his laid Debt: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, that a Bill may be brought in, to impower the Lord High Treasurer, or Lords Commissioners of his Majesty's Treasury, for the Time being, to compound the said Debt with the Petitioner.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, that the Petitioner's Cale having been humbly represented to his Majesty, his Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, that his Majesty gives his Consent, that the House may do therein, as they think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, refoive itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

Growing Mr. Alderman Perry (according to Order) reported Coffee in from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it 'lantxtioM. was refcrretj to consider of the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Planters of, and Merchants trading to, the Island of Jamaica, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others, concerned in the said Island, was referred, the Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House; and which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth;

Resolutions Resolved, nemine contradicente. That it appears to this on undue House, that on the 30th of July, 1723, Matthew White, Practices of Esquire, was declared the Purchaser of an Annuity of £ 200. during the Life of Charles Radcliffe, issuing out of the Estate of James, late Earl of Derwentwater, with all the Arrears thereof from his Attainder, for £. 1,201. 1 s. without due Notice of Time or Place for exposing such Annuity to Sale, and without the Presence of a sufficient Number of Commissioners and Trustees, as required by die Ad, appointing such Commissioners and Trustees.

Rejclved, nemine contradicente, That it appears to this House, that William Smith, Esquire, did on the 1 ith Day of July 1723, for the Consideration of £. 1,060. contract for an Estate of James, late Earl of ,mentioned in a Particular, published by the said Commissioners and Trustees, to be of the annual Value of 5,013. subject to the Annuities and Incumbrances in the said Particular mentioned, and to be sold, during the Continuance of an Estate in Tail Male, verted in Charles Radcliffe in Remainder, Expedant on the Death of John Radcliffe under Age, and without Issue Male; which Contract: was on the 30th of the same July vacated, and torn out of the Book of Contracts, and a new one then procured, and dated as on the Eleventh, by which the said William Smith not only obtained the said Remainder in Tail, but also the Reversion in Fee, of the said Estate, for the same Sum of £. 1,060. although a sufficient Number of Commissioners and Trustees, as required by Act of Parliament, was not present, either on tire nth or 30th of the said July, nor had any Notice been given of exposing to Sale the Reversion in Fee of the said Estate.

Resolved, nemine contradicente. That it appears to this House, that Matthew Whi, and William Esquire,

were present on the 30th of the said July, when Samuel Allen, Secretary of the said Commissioners and Trustees, signed the Names of Sir Thomas Hales and Sir John Eyles to the respective pretended Contracts, made with the said White and Smith on the said 30th of , when no Commissioner and Trustee, but Denis Bond, Esquire, and John Birch, Serjeant at Law, were present.

Resolved, nemine contradicente. That the con trading for the Sale of the aforesaid Estates by aless Number of Commissioners and Trustees, than Four, and the not giving Fifteen Days Notice, at lead, of such Sales, was a manifest Violation of the Act of Parliament for the Sale of the said Estates, highly injurious to the Publick, and a notorious Breach of the Trust, reposed in such Commissioners and Trustees.

Fraudulent Sale of Der-weotwater's Eftaie;

A Member reprimanded.

Sir John Eyles attending in his Place (according to Order) Mr. Speaker called upon him by his Name: And Sir John Eyles {landing up in his Place, uncovered, Mr. Speaker, fitting in the Chair, covered, spoke to him to the Effect following:

Sir John Ey/es,

The House have come to a Resolution, That you are guilty of a great Irregularity, as a Commissioner and Trustee for Sale of the forfeited Estates for the Use of the Publick, by impowering Mr. Samuel Allen, Secretary of the Commissioners and Trustees for the Sale of the said Estates, to sign your Name, when absent, in order to make up the Number of Commissioners and Trustees, required by Act of Parliament to Matters of Form in Proceedings under the said Act:

And-have imposed a Command upon me, which is the only one, I can truly say, that I ever received with any Uneasiness in the Place I now fit, not from any Doubt of the Justice of the Command, nor from any Unwilling-ness in me to obey an Order of the House, but because you, Sir, are unfortunately the Subject of it, for whom I have always had the greatest personal Regard.

The Offence, you are guilty of, having come within the Notice of the House, it was impossible it should escape their Censure, as it had a Reference to a Trust re-posed in you; reposed by Parliament, the highest and most sacred Authority, any Subject of this Kingdom can aft under; and with a particular Confidence in you, and the others joined with you, because of the Relation you bore to the Parliament; a Trust of great Importance, and which required great Pains in, and Attention to, it; and for that a very considerable Recompence was assigned to you out of the publick Treasure. The Recompence, Sir, you enjoyed; but the Pains and Attention expected from you, you failed in; and illegally delegated your Trust, in Instances, where a false and fraudulent Use has been made of it. But, happy for you, Sir, it appears to the House, to have been a Matter, rather of evil Example, than of evil Intention; for which Reason the Resolutions of the House, on this Occasion, have a Mixture of Justice and Mercy; and, as your Offence will always justify the Censure of the House, let it be your Care, Sir,

that your future Behaviour always justify their Lenity:

Let the Justice of the House make you fear, and the Clemency of the House make it a Matter of Sorrow in you, to offend again.

This Sense, 1 persuade myself, you will have of the Judgment the House has passed upon you; which is, That I reprimand you for your said Offence: — And Ido reprimand you accordingly.

Whereupon Sir John Eyles said.

Sir,

I am very much ashamed of an Offence, that has drawn upon me the Animadversion and Censure of this House; an Offence, which, at the Time of committing it,

I had scarce an Idea of being subject to Blame for. I an now made truly sensible of it; and the strong and lively Colours in which you. Sir, have drawn it, will be to me an everlasting Memento of future Caution.

The Judgment, the House has passed upon me, I endure with a dutiful Sub million; and you, Sir, having shewn that Tenderness and Humanity, which is agreeable to your Nature, in your kind and indulgent Manner of pronouncing it, and thereby, in feme Degree, abated its Rigour, I cannot but express my grateful and sincere Acknowledgements to yourself, and also to the House, for their Favour, in not carrying this Censure to any further Consequence.

Resolved, nemine contradicente. That the Thanks of this Wc$ House be given to the Lord Viscount Gage, a Member of this House, for the great Service he hath done the Publick, in detesting the fraudulent Sale of certain forfeited Estates of James, late Earl of Derwentwater, and of a forfeited Annuity, issuing out of the fame, which were vested in Commissioners and Trustees, to be sold for the pfeblick Use.

And Mr. Speaker gave him the Thanks of the House accordingly, as follows:

My Lord Gage,

The House have come to an unanimous Resolution, That the Thanks of the House be given to your Lordship, for the great Service you have done the Publick, in detesting the fraudulent Sale of certain forfeited Estates of James, late Earl of Derwentwater, and of 1 forfeited Annuity, issuing out of the fame, which were vested in Commissioners and Trustees, to be sold for the publick Use.

And the Manner of your Lordship's making this DiP covery, has shewn your disinterested Regard to the publick Service, as the Effect of it may be greatly to the publick Benefit.

The applying the forfeited Estates to the Use of the Publick being one of the principal Reasons for making it thereby impossible, they should ever be given back to the unfortunate Families, they once belonged to, the House of Commons could not, without Uneasiness, think of this pretended Sale, which has thrown into private Hands, no ways allied to the Estate, Co large a Share of Profit, due to the Publick, with a very low, and almost the bare Appearance only of a, Consideration for one Part, and not so much as even that for another.

But your Lordship's seasonable Detection of this injurious Transaction will very likely produce Justice and Restitution to the Publick; and for this Service your Lordship is now receiving a Reward, that, I an answer for your Lordship, you esteem among the greatest, and most honourable, you can acquire, and which, my Lord, will not only, remain with you, but will derive a lading Honour to those who may come after you:

An Honour, my Lord, the House has always beeo most tender of in the Way, and for the Reason, they confer it upon you, and, if I may use the Expression, is a Sort of Bounty, they have ever been most frugal of granting. Few are the Instances of it: Not, that publick Services have not frequently been performed, but, that the Thanks of the House of Commons are never given

A Petition of the Justices of the Peace, Gentlemen, Merchants, and Clothiers, Makers of Kerseys, Plains, and other narrow Cloths, in the West Riding of the County of York, was presented to the House, and read; complaining, that by a Clause in an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for the better regulating the " Manufacture of Cloth in the West Riding of the County of York," the Makers of narrow Cloths were restrained from making broad Cloths, though the broad Clothiers are allowed to make narrow Cloths: And therefore praying, that Provision may be made by the Bill for the Continuance of the said Act, for restoring the narrow Clothiers to their ancient Privilege of making broad Cloths, or any other Cloth, and for preventing the Distress, which they will inevitably be exposed to, if not relieved by a Repeal of the said Clause, or by such other Means, as to the House shall seem fit.

Ordered That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of me Crown, to make out a new Writ, for the electing a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Poole, in the County of Dorset, in the room of Denis Bond, Esquire, expelled this House.

Resolved, nemine contradicents, That George Robinfen, Esquire, having been charged in Parliament with being privy to, and concerned in, many indirect and fraudulent Practices, in the Management of the Affairs of the Charitable Corporation, for Relief of industrious Poor, by affiffine; them with small Sums upon Pledges, at legal Interest, and with having got into his Hands very large Sums of Money, belonging to the said Corporation, and being returned a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks, and having never attended the Service of this House, although required so to do, is guilty of a high Contempt of the Orders and Authority of this House.

Resolved, nemine contradicente, That the said George Robinson, Esquire, be, for his said Offence, expelled this House.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ, for the electing a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks, in the room of George Robinson, Esquire, expelled this House.

The House proceeded to take into Consideration the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Elias Turner, and Company, and Lewis on

behalf of themselves, and such others, as are in their Cafe, was referred.

And the said Report was read, and is as followeth; viz.

That the Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 29th of February 1731, took into Consideration the said Petition, and do find the Matter thereof to be as follows; viz.

That by an Act, of the Ninth Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, the Sum of £. 103,003. 11 4 was given

to such of the Proprietors, and Inhabitants, of the Islands of Nevis and Saint Christophers, as had or should resettle on the said Islands, in Consideration of the great Losses they had sustained, by the Invasion and Depredations of the French on those Islands, for which the then Commissioners of Trade and Plantations were to make forth Debentures, for their respective Shares of such Money, to bear Interest after the Rate of £.6. per Centum per Annum, to be registered, and paid, in like Manner, as the unsatisfied Debentures, charged on the forfeited Estates in Ireland, were:

That by another Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of her said late Majesty, taking notice, that the Bounty aforesaid would amount but to one Third Part of the Losses, so sustained, the Commissioners of Trade and Plantations were authorised to issue out Debentures for such Third Part of their Losses: And by those Acts the Debentures were directed to be made payable to the said Proprietors, or to their certain Attorneys, Executors, Administrators, or Assigns, respectively, and were to be delivered to such Persons, as those, who were entitled thereunto, should respectively authorise.

Pees taken in Courts of Justice and by Law Officers.

892 18

Mr. Wyndhain reported from the Committee, to whom

the several Lists of the Officers, and their Deputies, belonging to the several Courts in /, and else-

where, with the Lifts, Accounts, and 'l'ables of Fees, claimed by them, which were presented to this House in the last and present Session of Parliament, and allb the Lifts, Accounts, and Tables of Fees, of the Officers, and Servants, belonging to the Judges of the several Courts in ll\stminster-hull, and the Circuits, the Associates, and Clerks of Assize, presented to this House in the Session of Parliament preceding the last, were referred, the Matter, as it appeared to them, with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, which they had directed him to report to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read; and the Report and Resolutions are as follow; viz.

The Committee, taking into Consideration the great Number of Officers, and Clerks, who have presented to this House Lists of Fees, thought itnecefi'ary to examine into the Fees of the Officers of each Court separately, and to begin with the Court of Chancery, which is a Court always open, and which exercises the most extensive Jurisdiction, and abounds with Clerks, and Officers.

The Committee enquired, of w hat Officers the Court of Chancery did anciently, conlift, and what Regulation of their Fees had been made, and what Methods uted, to prevent the Increase of unnecefiiuy Officers, and the Exaction of illegal Fees.

It appeared to the Committee, that Commissions, to enquire into the Behaviour of Officers in Courts of Justice, ecclesiastical and civil, were frequently ifi'ued, in former Times, to several great Officers of the Kingdom, and others, with Power to correct Abuses, and with Direction to certify their Proceedings, either to the King in Council, or into the Court of Chancery.

The Inrolment of Two such Commissions in the Reign of James the First, and of Four in the lteign of Charles the First, were produced, to the Committee, from the Records in the Chapel of the Rolls; but no such Commission has issued since the Restoration of.1 the Second.

Another Method of reforming Abuses in the Courts of Justke was, by the Presentment of experienced Prafitifers, upon Oath, appointed by the Judges of the several Courts to enquire, what Fees had been exacted, other than the ancient and uiual Fees.

A Preferment, upon Oath, of Fifteen Persons, in the Fortieth of Elizabeth, for the better Reformation of sundry Exactions and Abuses, l'upposed to be committed by Officers, Clerks, and Ministers, in the;High Court of Chancery, was flic wed to the Committee; by which Preferment it plainly appeared, who were the Officers of the Court at that Time, and what were their legal Fees.

But, as the Officers of the Court of Chancery are exceedingly increased since that Time, by Patents and :Grants, and many Secretaries and Clerks, and other honorary Attendants upon the Judges of that Court, appear now to claim large Fees, whose Services were unknown to the ancient Prafitifers in the Fortieth of Elizabeth, the Committee thought it proper to make a List of such Offices, as appear to be ancient, and necessacy to the Justice of the Court; and a List of such, as have since grown up insensibfy into Office of great Profit, and much increased the Expence of the Proceedings of the Court.; which Lifts are hereunto annexed, Appendix, N° 1. and 2.

By the Presentment of Fees in the Fortieth of Elizabeth, -and by the Lists of pees, lately presented to this House, 'j it appears, that many Fees of several ancient Officers, then allowed, continue the same to this Time; particularly, of the Examiners, the Cursitors, the Clerk of the Subpoenas, the Clerk of the Chapel of the Rolls, the Cleiksof the Petty Bag, the Six Clerks, and others; whiUi flit Committee think very observable, and consider 3.- . J ] 6t of a good Regulation, once established,

hr . been able to preserve itself for above One

rilis. / A. 1732.

hundred and Thirty Years against the Incroachments of Officers on all Sides in the same Court.

'l he Abolition of the Court of Star-chamber, and of the Court of Wards and Liveries, together with all the Writs and Proceedings of thofef Courts, has extinguished some Offices, and reduced the Profit of feme uncieut Officers of the Court of Chancery; and the Alteration, which Time has introduced into the Practice of the Court, has greatly raised the Profits of other Officers, who are concerned in the Proceedings in Equity, by the multiplying of Petitions, Bills, Answers, Plcadings, Examinations, Decrees, and other Forms, and Copies of them, and extending them frequently to an unnecessary , Length.

It appeared to the Committee, that the Charge of drawing and entering an Order in the Court of Chancery anciently was but One or Two Shillings, and never exceeded Three Shillings, until the Time, that the Office of Ilegifter was erected, and a Grant made of it, and that all Orders, Dismissions, and Decrees, were eudorsed upon the Pleadings. The Fee of Three Shillings and Six Pence for each Side in all Causes, and of Seven Shillings a Side in Causes by Consent, now claimed by the Ilegifter, and his Deputies, appear to the Committee to be a heavy Burthen upon the Client, especially, considering the long Recitals in Decrees and Orders of late Times, which tire Deputy Ilegifters did acknowledge to eonfift frequently of Twenty, Thirty, Forty, or more, Sides, and considering, that other Forms in the same Court are charged Eight Pence, or at most Tw elve Pence, a Side.

The Charge of Eight Pence a Side for Copies, received by the Masters, and by the Six Clerks, is an ancient Fee, w here Copies are necessary; but the Committee were informed, that Copies are frequently forced upon the Client, contrary to his Desire, and claimed by Officers, as due to them, or charged by Solicitors, though neither claimed, or paid; which, considering the prodigious Length of some Forms, and that tire whole Proceedings in Causes conlift often of several Thousand Sheets, is a grievous Abuse, that ought to be reformed.

The Masters in Chancery claim Two Shillings for every Summons, which the Committee admit to be reasonable; but are informed, that Abuses have been often committed, by a great Number of Summons ilfuing, without any Attendance of the Clerks, or Solicitors, who uevertheleis may charge their Clients for such Summons, and their Attendance, because few Bills are regularly taxed before the Masters; which Mr. Halford and Mr. Eldc Masters, in Chancery, did affirm to be a principal Occasion of the Increase of Expence in Causes, the Solicitors generally taking upon themselves to tax one anothers Bills, and making what Allowances they think fit.

The Committee apprehend, that the Fees of the Secretaries, Clerks, anil other Officers, w ho do not appear to have been known formerly to the Court, have never undergone any publick Examination; that many different Offices render the Business of the Court very inconvenient to the Suitor, and greatly encourage the Demand of new Fees.

It appeared to the Committee, that Orders had sometimes been made, for the Officers to hang up publickly Lists of their Fees; most of which Lifts are since withdrawn, or have been suffered to decay, and become lb useless, that the Officers themselves seemed often doubtful, what Fees to claim, and most of them relied upon no better Evidence, than some Information from their Predecessors, or the Deputies of their Predecessors, that such Fees had been demanded, and received.

Among the various Claims of those, who now call themselves Officers of the Court of Chancery, none appeared more extraordinary to the Committee, than the Fee of tire Secretary and Clerk of the Briefs; who, upon Grants, to enable Persons to beg and collect Alms, claim, and frequently receive, a Fee of Forty, Fifty, or Sixty, Pounds; and the Ilegifter takes, besides, Twelve or Thirteen Pounds, for stamping and telling the Briefs; which Fees,

5 Geo. II.

with other great Charges upon the Collection, devour Three Parts in Four of what is given for the Relief of Persons, reduced to extreme Poverty by Fire, or other Accidents.

The Clerk of the Lunaticks and Ideots informed the Committee, that he had never seen any Account of his Fees, till lately; he believes, not till a List of them was ordered to be laid before this House: That Mr. Lewis, who had been his Deputy in his Office for Thirty-four Years, had constantly refuled to shew any List to Mr. Bennett his Predecessor; and that he had no other Rule in the Demand of his Fees, for Three or Four Years, but Receipts, and loose Papers, which he found in his Office; but that the Fees, which be took, appear to agree exactly with the Fees contained in the Lift, which he has so lately discovered.

Such were the Accounts of Fees, which the Officers gave the Committee , who took into ConOderation the great Difficulty they had even to discover, of what Officers, Clerks, and Ministers the Court of Chancery does at present consist, or in what Terms to describe their Offices and Employments, lb as to make them discover themselves} and observing, how little able, or willing, many Officers were to give any satisfadiory Account of the Fees they claim, and receive, came to the following Resolutions: Resolved.That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the long Dilute of publick Enquiries into the Behaviour of the Officers, Clerks, and Ministers, of the Courts of Justice, has been an Occasion of the Increase -of unnecessary Officers, and given Encouragement to the taking illegal Fees.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Interest, which a great Number of Officers, and Clerks, have in the Proceedings in the Court of Chancery, has been a principal Cause of extending Bills, Answers, Pleadings, Examinations, and other Forms, and Copies of them, to an unnecessary Length, to the great Delay of Justice, and the Oppression of the Subject.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Table of all the Officers, Ministers, and Clerks, and of their Fees, in the Court of Chancery, fljould be' fixed and established by Authority; which Table should be registered in a Book in the said Court, to be at all Times inspected gratis, and a Copy of it, signed and attested by the Judges of the Court, should be returned to each House of Parliament, to remain among the Records.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled: '

Having received the Commands of the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury to lay before this honourable House, pursuant to an Order, of the 19th Instant,

Copy of a Representation to the Lords of the Treasury, relating to the Importation of Brandy from with the Directions given by the Treasury thereupon;

Wehumbly acquaint this honourable House, that there has been no Representation made by this Board to the Treasury concerning that Matter; but we herewith lay before you. Copy of a Report to their Lordships, dated the 24th March, 173?, on a referred Petition of Thomas EUis, relating to a Parcel of Brandy, imported by him from Dunkirk, which he entered as Flemish, and the Offi-

cers, by our Orders, seized the lame, as French Brandy; and their Lordships, upon Consideration thereof, were of Opinion, that the Prosecution should go on; and we proceeded accordingly; but, on a Trial in the Court of Exchequer, a*Verdict was given for the Defendant.

Which is humbly submitted. Custom-house, London, Evelyn,

21 April, 1732. T. Walker, Charles Peers.

May it please your Lordships:

In Obedience to your Commands, signified to us by Mr. Frecker, on the annexed Petition of Thomas Ellis, setting forth that he has lately imported from Dunkirk a Parcel of Brandie-, and paid Duty for them as which are seized as French; that, for Seven Years lall pad, Brandies have been permit ted to come from paying the Flemish Duties; and that in the same Ship, in which these came, there was 130 Tons of Brandy permitted to pal's, on paying the Flemish Duty, without being seized, although sold at the Custom-house Keys for French Brandy; praying he may be put upon the same foot with the rest of the Merchants, and have his Brandy restored, and Satisfaction for the Damages he has sustained; your Lordships directing us to consider the fame, and report a State of the Cafe, with our Opinion, what is fit to be done therein;

We humbly report, that it is true, as the Petitioner alleges, that considerable Quantities of Brandy have been imported at this and other Ports from Dunkirk, for some Years part, and entered by the Merchants as Flemish Brandy, and passed, as such, by the proper Officers at the Water-fide, they not having sufficient Proof to the contrary; but we have constantly given them Directions, that, whenever they had Proof, the Brandy, entered as Flemish, was really French, to seize it.

Wefurtheracquaint your Lordships, that the Petitioner having, in the Newspapers, advertii'ed the Sale of French Brandy, just landed at the Keys, and being informed, that Part of that Parcel of Brandy, which the Petitioner had imported, and entered as , had been sold by

him for French Brandy upon the Keys, we directed the

Land Surveyor to seize it there; which wc thought our Duty to do; but not having the same Information, and Proof, against the rest of the Brandy, imported in the same Ship, we did not direct the Officers to seize that.

All which is humbly submitted to your Lordships Consideration.

Custom-house, London, Hill,

24 March, 173?-. J. Stanley,

Copy. T. Walker,

Cha. CarkeJJe, Secretary. C. Peers.

The House proceeded to take irrtofurther Consideration the further Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Proprietors of the Charitable Corporation, for Relief ofindustrious Poor, by assisting them with small Sums upon Pledges, at legal Interest, assembled in their general Court, is referred.

And Part of the said Report, relating to the Examination of Mr. John Harrison, Accomptant to the Petitioners,

and the Account, by him produced, was read.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that the Money paid in upon the capital Stock of the Charitable Corporation, for Relief of industrious Poor, by a(Tifling them with small Sums upon Pledges, at legal Interest, was, upon the Fifteenth Day of February 1731, Three hundred and Fifty-three thousand Eight hundred and Seventeen Pounds, and Ten Shillings, and the Notes and Bonds, issued by the Committee and Assistants of the said Corporation, and then standing out, were for One hundred and Forty-five thousand Five hundred and Fifteen Pounds, amounting in the whole to Four hundred and Ninety-nine thousand Three hundred and Thirty-two Pounds, and Ten Shillings, and that the Pledges and Securities, to make good the lame, amount to no more than Seventy-seven thousand Five hundred and Seven Pounds, Three Shillings, and Two Pence Three Farthings; so that there remains a Loss of Four hundred and Twenty-one thousand Eight hundred and Twenty-five Pounds, Six Shilling?, and Nine Pence Farthing-

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that by the Charter granted to the said Corporation, the Choice of Officers, making of By-laws, and the Management of the Affairs and Business of the said Corporation, are directed to be by the general Court.

Several Parts of the said Charter, relating to the several Powers vested in the general Court, and the Committee, of the said Corporation, were read.

And a Resolution of the general Court of the said Corporation, on Tuesdaythe Second of November 1725, was read.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that under Colour of a Resolution of the general Court of the said Corporation on Tuesdaythe Second of November 1725, impowering. the Committee of the said Corporation to begin and proceed in lending Money upon Pledges, and in order thereto, to chuse proper Officers, and agree upon Houses, and to prepare By-laws, to be laid before the general Court, and to do and perform all such other Matters and Things, as relate to the carrying on the Business of the said Corporation, the Committee of the said Corporation, have from that Time, taken upon them to appoint Officers, and to make Orders, for the Direction and Management of the Affairs of the said Corporation, without communicating the same to, or having the Approbation of, general Courts.

Resolved, That it appears to this House, that Three hundred Ninety-six thousand and Sixty-nine Pounds, Eleven Shillings, and Eight Pence Farthing, is charged to be lent out, upon Pledges, at the Offices, belonging to

the said: Corporation, iff Fenthurch-Sheet and Laurence Pounlney Hill, though no more Goods are to be found, to answer the fame, than what upon a Valuation, amount to Forty thousand Pounds.

The Third particular Instruction to the Cashierof the said Corporation, relating to the Deposit Money, contained in the Appendix to the said Report, was read.

And some Parts of the said Report, relating to the Proceedings of the Committee, with respect of one of the Keys of the Warehouse at the House in Fenchurch-freet, were read.

Resolved, That the taking the Key of the Warehouse in Fenchurch-street out of the Hands of Mr.

the Accomptant of the said Corporation, who had given large Security for his good Behaviour, and.ordering the same into the Hands of Nathanael Lovell, their Mefien-ger, who had given no Security, was one of the principal Causes of the great Loss sustained by the said Corporation.

An Order of the general Court of the said Corporation, on the Twentieth Day of March 1718, relating to the Warehouse-keepers of the said Corporation, contained in the Appendix to the said Report, was read.

And the particular Instructions to the Surveyor of the Warehouse of the said Corporation, contained in the Appendix to the said Report, were read.

And several Parts of the said Report relating to the Directions, given by the Committee of the said Corporation to Mr. Clarke, Surveyor of the Warehouse in

Fenchurch-street, to makeparticularObservationsupon the Value of Pledges, and some Entries in a Minute Book of the Committee of the said Corporation, relating to the same Matter, and an Entry in the said Minute Book, relating to the Discharge of the said Mr. Clarke from his Office of Surveyor of the Warehouse, were read.

Resolved, That the discharging Mr. Clarke, the Surveyor of the Warehouses belonging to the said Corporation, after he had made Observations upon the Insufficiency of the Value of Pledges at the Warehouse in Fenchurchfreet, without examining into the Truth of the said Observations, and the not appointing another Surveyor in his Room, gave a great Opportunity to John Thomson, Warehouse-keeper to the said Corporation, to defraud the Corporation, and was one other principal Cause of the great Loss they have sustained.

The First particular Instruction to the Warehouse-keeper of the said Corporation, contained in the Appendix to the said Report, was read.

And Part of the said Report, relating to an Orderof the Committee of the said Corporation, allowing Borrowers to negociate their Business by Brokers, was read.

And Part of the Examination of Thomas Warren and Richard Woolley, contained in the said Report, relating to Money, borrowed by them of the said Corporation, as Brokers, was read.

Resolved, That the permitting Borrowers to negociate their Business in the Names of Richard Woolley, and Thomas Warren, and other Agents and Officers of the said Corporation, as Brokers, and not in their own Names, has been the Occasion of many Frauds, and very great Loss to the said Corporation.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Report be adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Eleven of the Clock.
