Mr. Wimington reported from the Committee, appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address, to be presented Litw.7. to his Majesty; that the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly, which they had dire died him to report to the House: And he read the same in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the same was read, and is as followeth; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty's most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, having taken into our Consideration the great Collection of valuable Records, belonging to this Nation, and the Necessity of transmitting them down fafeand intire, for the Use of our Posterity, humbly beg Leave to represent to your Majesty the State in which we found them, together with the Inconveniences, that may arise from their remaining in their present Situation.

A great Part of the Cottonian Library, with the Variety of curious and useful Matters therein contained, has, notwithstanding the late Fire at Ashburnham House, by the great

W Thrfe Wordi ‘of bii Majesty'i Customs to the Commissioncn," are here omitted, 11 also li the tevcral Entries of this Older upoa the 28th of Anrii, and the 3d of Mty preceding.

5 Geo. II. 10° — n ° Mail.

9*9

Cottonian great Diligence and Attention of the Trustees, been pre-Library. served; and, that the Publick may not, for want of due Care, be gradually deprived of lo noble and generous a Benefaction, we beg Leave to recommend it, in the most particular Manner, to your Majesty's Consideration, Favour, and Protection.

The several Places, assigned for the Preservation of all these inestimable Monuments of Antiquity, are too narrow and confined for their Reception, and feme of them in a very ruinous and dangerous Condition.

We find also some Records, not deposited in their proper Offices, but either remaining in private Hands, or in Places not assigned for publick Records, nor under the Care of any Rated Officer.

Nor has the ancient Method of removing Records from the Offices, wherein they are originally formed, to such Places, as are appointed to preserve them, been duly observed, chiefly for want of Room in the present Offices, allotted for their Reception.

Great Inconveniences have arilen to the Enquirers after this useful Knowledge, not only from these Difficulties, but also from the undistinguished and confused Manner, in which some of the Records of this Kingdom have been kept, there being no general Calendars, or Indexes, to the Whole; which, with proper Encouragement, maybe completed by Persons of Skill, and Ability, and would probably bring to Light many material Remains of Antiquity, which, from the Difficulty of Access, have long laid unknown, and neglected.

The present short Inquiry, imperfect as it is, has produced an Instance of this, by discovering amongst the ancient Records, that Directions for Works of this Kind have been formerly given by your Majesty's royal Predecessors.

Your faithful Commons beg Leave further humbly to represent to your Majesty, that, as the publick Interest is concerned in providing more secure and decent Repofi-tories for the Records of this Kingdom, so the publick Faith is engaged for the better Reception and Preservation of the Cottonian Library, so generously given for thepub-Jick Service.

And, as there is at present little or no Allowance to the Keeper of the said Library, we humbly submit it to your Majesty's Consideration, whether, if a proper and reasonable Stipend were granted to him, it would not engage him to perform his Duty with greater Care and Diligence.

Having thus, with the greatest Humility, laid the State of the Records of this Kingdom, and of the Cottonian Library, before your Majesty, we assure ourselves, that it will be entirely agreeable to your Majesty's gracious Dif-position to transmit to future Ages these Monuments and Remains of Antiquity, so necessary and useful to the Knowledgeand Preservation of our excellent Constitution, which, we hope, will go down to Posterity, together with the Family, under which it now flourifties, as in-separableand perpetual Blessings to this Nation.

Your faithful Commons do therefore most humbly beseech your Majesty, that you will be graciously pleased to give such Directions, as your Majesty in your great Wisdom shall think fir, for the better Reception, and tnore convenient Use, of the publick Records of this Kingdom, and of the Cottonian Library.

And we beg Leave further to assure your Majesty, that, whatever extraordinary Expences are incurred by the Directions, your Majesty in your great Wisdom shall think fit to give on this Occasion, shall, with great Cheerfulness and Unanimity, be provided for, and made good, by your faithful Commons.

The said Address being read a Second time.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by such Members of this House as are of his Maiellv's most honourable Privy Council.

AP ETITIO N of Sir Alexander Murray, of Stanhop, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that on Friday, the 28th of April last, being the Day appointed for eleding a Knight of the Shire, to serve in Parliament for the County of Peebles, in room of the honourable Mr. John Douglas, deceased, Sir James Nasmith, of Pojfo, and the Petitioner, appeared as Can* dictates; when Alexander Murray, of Cringlety, the last elected Commissioner now living, pursuant to the Act of Parliament, made in that behalf, put the Question, for the Choice of a Praefes, and a Clerk; and, upon the Question so by him severally put, the honourable Mr. William Carmichael was duly elected Prsfes, and Alexander Shaw duly elected Clerk, by the Majority of legal Voters; but that Sir Alexander Murray, of Black -rory, Sheriff, appointed since the Date of the Writ, tho' retrained by his Commission from naming a Sheriff Clerk, and though there was another Sheriff Clerk then existing, and lawfully entitled to ad, appointed Wm. Veilch to be Sheriff Clerk, who, by Order of the said Sheriff, put the Question, for the Choice of a Praefes, and Clerk; and that the said Sheriff, and the fiud William Veilch, by his Direction, voted in the Election of Praefes, tho neither of them were inrolled in the Roll of Freeholders: That the Petitioner required the whole Meeting to qualify, by taking the Oaths appointed by Law; and tho' he, and his Friends, did accordingly qualify, the said Sheriff, and his Adherents, who appeared in the Interestof Sir James Nasmith, refused to qualify; and that the Roll of Electon was partially made up, by inserting the Names of Persons, not entitled to vote, and deleting the Names of such as had been duly inrolled, and had voted in former Elections: That tho* the Petitioner protested against this Proceeding, and was duly elected by a Majority of legal Voters, the said Sheriff has taken upon him to return the said Sir James Nasmith, as duly elected, to serve in this present Parliament for the said County of Peebles, in Violation of the Freedom of Elections, and the Righc of the Freeholders: And alleging, that the said Sir Nasmith is not only unduly elected, but that his Return is void, his Election not having been certified by the proper Clerk, nor the Election carried on under the Conduct of the Prsefes, lawfully elected, but contrary to the Voices of the Majority of habile Voters: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Confederation, and to afford the Petitioner such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. John Bennet and

Mr. Lighthoun:

Vo 1.21.

And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table j where the Reasons were read, and are as follows; viz.

To all the Amendments, made by your Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act for continuing an Act, of the Eleventh Year of his late Majesty's Reign, intituled,

" An Act for more effectual disarming the Highlands " in that Part of Great Britain called Scotland, and for " the better securing the Peace and Quiet of that Part "of the Kingdom," except the last, the Commons do agree.

To the last Amendment, made by your Lordships, being Clause B, the Commons disagree;

ift, Because the Clause makes an xmreasonabie Distinction between the different Parts of the united Kingdom, by making it penal to wear in one Part of it that Dress, that may lawfully be Worn in the other:

2dly, Because it seems more unreasonable, in the same Parish, to leave it lawful for one Part of the Inhabitants to wear what Dress they please, whilst the other, and the most considerable, Part, are subject to Penalties, if they make use of the same Habit; so that a Distinction of Ten Shillings Rent may make a Man subject to, or free from,

Penalties:

3dly, Because it seems of dangerous Consequence to subject any Person to be imprisoned for Six Months, upon the occasional wearing, or putting on, any Part of the Higland Garb, even in his own House, on the Oath of One Witness only:

4-thly, Because the Dress prohibited is extremely well suited to the Circumstance of the mountainous Country, in which it is now wore, serving for a Covering by Night, whilst at the same time it is very light, and easily carried, by Day:

5thly, Because, whilst the Bill itself, by disarming the Highlanders, distinguishes them from others his Majesty's Subjects, it does not seem proper to give them any Disgust, by depriving them of that Dress, which, in their Circumstances, appears highly convenient, if not absolutely necessary, for them:

6thly, Because the changing of the Dress must occasion an Expence, which will be burdensome to Persons of so finall Fortunes, as those described in the Clause, and probably an Introduction to Luxury:

7thly, Because discharging the Use of Bonnets will be injurious to several Incorporations of Bonnet-makers, lawfully constituted within divers royal Boroughs in that Part of the Kingdom called Scotland.

The said Reasons, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That a Conference be desired with the Lords Conference upon the Subject-matter of the Amendments, made by with the their Lordships to the said Bill. Lord*.

Ordered, That Sir Edmund Bacon, of Gillingham, do go to the Lords, and desire the said Conference.

Your Committee being informed, that Sir Robert Sutton had received a Letter from Mr. Robert Arbut knot, a Banker in Paris, in which was inclosed a Letter from Mr. John Angelo Belloni,a Banker at Rome, directed to your Committee, or, in case they did not subsist, then to Sir Robert Sutton, Sir John Walter

Esquire, Doctor John Mowbray, or any of them, they ordered the said Sir Robert Sutton to attend them with the said Letter;which he accordingly did; and hedelivered to your Committee a Letter, dated, Paris, May aid x 732, from the said Mr. Robert Arbuthnot, to his Brother, Doctor John Arbuthnot, acquainting him, that he had procured John Thomson to be arrested, pursuant to a Request, long lincemade to him by SwRobertSutton, and likewise another Letter of the same Date, from the said, Mr. Arbuthnot to the said Sir Robert Sutton, acquainting him, that his Correspondent at Rome, Mr. John Angelo Belloni, had got John Thomson arrested, and made Prisoner in the Castle St. Angelo, and had engaged him to make a full Difeo-very of all his Effects, and to give a full Account of his Behaviour: That Mr. Belloni had sent to him the Information, and a Memorandum, with Papers, and

his Orders to his Friends, to deliver up his Effects; but at the same time he had promised Thomson, that the said Papers should remain as a Deposit in the said Mr. not's Hands, and not be given up, till the Conditions in the said Memorandum should be agreed to, and absolutely secured; upon which he, the said Mr. Arbuthnot, should fend large Discoveries of great Sums, with Orders to Thomson's Correspondents to make them effectual; but, if these are not complied with, he is to return the said Papers back to Mr. Belloni. The Conditions are as follows; viz.

Memorandum, which I humbly beg may be stipulated, and made the Conditions for delivering up the Books and Papers.

lft, That my Sureties may have their Bonds up, in all for X-S*oooo.

2d, That Launcelot Ord, Esquire, who (old me a small Estate, the Value of £.1,300. after paying a Mortgage upon it, in Consideration of an Annuity I was to pay him, for his Life, be allowed to take quiet Possession of his Estate again, as I am not in a Capacity to pay him his Annuity. I left his Papers with a Friend of his, for that Purpose.

jd, My Father having taken a Bond, in my Name, from Mr. Blackwood, though the Money was his own, I desire, upon his giving Proof of that, that he may be allowed to receive it upon a Power of Attorney, 1 lent him for that Purpose, and that they will not put him to Trouble, because it happens to be in my Name.

4th, There is somewhere a Bond of my Brother Samuel's; I desire, it may be delivered up, because he is not in a Capacity to pay it.

5th, I desire, that those, that have had my Books and Papers in keeping, may have no Trouble, upon their surrendering them, in case the Act, that passes, any Penalty is annexed to that.

6th, I desire, I may be enabled to pay about £. 2,700. private Debts I owe to number of People.

7th, What is thought proper for myself, I submit it; and I only observe, that I have at present discovered, of my own private Effects, which will appear, upon catling up the Accounts, the Sum of £. 26,000. and my Books and Papers will discover a much larger Sum.

J. Thomson.

Mr. Gybbon reported from the Committee, to whom it was referred to draw up Reasons, to be offered to the Lords at a Conference, for disagreeing to one of the Vol. 21.

Amendments, made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act to prevent the committing of Frauds by Bankrupts j that they had drawn up Reasons accordingly, which they haddirested him to report to the House: And he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table; where the Reasons were read, and are as follows; viz.

The Commons do agree to all the Amendments, made by your Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act to prevent the committing of Frauds by Bankrupts, except to the Amendment Press 41. Line 13. to which the Commons disagree;

1 ft, Because no Provision is made by your Lordships for the safe Custody of the Records, when this Act, which is temporary, shall expire:

2dly, Because it is not probable, tho* a Law of the like Nature with this, should hereafter be made, that the same Persons would enjoy such Office, and therefore the Records, by being removed, may be loft, or damaged j whereas the Place, proposed by the Commons, is an ancient known Office, which will continue on other Accounts, and the Records remain there in Safety, and ail Persons know where to find them, notwithstanding the Expiration of this Act:

3dly, Because it is not likely that such new Officer, who1 must provide a House, and probably, a Deputy,

should inroll such Commissions, and Proceedings, on as easy and reasonable Terms, as may be expected from Persons, used to such Business, who have an Office provided for them, and whose Fees are as subject to be ascertained by the Lord Chancellor, as those of such new Officer, proposed by your Lordships.

The Commons decline, at this Time, offering any other Realons, believing, these may be sufficient to prevail with your Lordshipsnot to infill upon the said Amendment, that a Bill, so necessary, may not be loft.

The said Reasons, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question kverally put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Mr. Sandys reported, that the Managers had met the Lords at the Conference, which was managed, on the Part of the Lords, by the Lord President j who acquainted them, that the Lords having taken into Consideration the Reasons, given by the Commons, at a Conference on Wednesday last, for their disagreeing with one of the Amendments, made by their Lordships to the Bill, for continuing an Act, of the Eleventh Year of his late Majesty's Reign, intituled, An Act for the more effectual disarming the Highlands in that Part of Great Bii*

" tain called Scotland, and for the better securing the " Peace and Quiet of that Part of the Kingdom," their Lordships do infilt on their Amendment; for which they, gave their Reasons: Which he reported to the House:

And the Reasons are as follows; viz.

1 ft, Because the whole Foundation of this Bill is to render the Inhabitants of the Highlands more civilized, and to induce them to live in the like Manner, as the rest of his Majesty's Subjects:

2dly, Because the Highland Drefshas been one of the chief Reasons, why the Peace of that Part of the Kingdom has been so often broke, and so many Injuries done to the Country adjoining to the Highlands, by its being lb commodious for marching, and lying abroad in the Fields: jdly, Because it is much easier for the Inhabitants of the Highlands to be guilty of Insurrections, in Disturbance of the publick Peace, when they wear the Highland Habit, than if they were dressed in the like Manner, as the rest of the Kingdom:

4thly, Because this Clause is confined to Gentlemen, and others, who have no Pretence to any Necessity of wearing the said Habit.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Morning.

The Order of the Day being read;

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee, to Examining whom the Bill for reviving an Act, made in the Tenth Drugs* Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, "An Act for the better viewing,

" searching, and examining, all Drugs, Medicines,

Waters, Oils, Compositions, used or to be tiled for " Medicines, in all Places, where the same shall be ex- poled to Sale, or kept for that Purpose, within the City of London, and Suburbs thereof, or within Seven " Miles Circuit of the said City,"..... be taken into Consideration on Monday Morning next.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

After which, his Majesty was pleased to make a most TVKW gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

You having now dispatched all the publick Business, that it was practicable for you to go through with at present, and the Season of the Year being so far advanced,

I believe, it will not be disagreeable to you, that I give you an Opportunity of retiring into the Country, by putting an End to this Session of Parliament, '

It is unnecessary for me to represent to you the happy State and Situation of publick Affairs, both at home and abroad. You mull all be fenfibie of what is universally leen, and felt, in the full Enjoyment of a general Peace.

The Concurrence of the States General in the late Treaty of Vienna has perfected the Establishment of the publick Tranquillity, as far as human Prudence can foresee, or provide; and a faithful Observance and Execution of the Treaties and Alliances, now subsisting among the several Princes and Powers of Europe, free from Groundless Jealousies, and void of all ambitious Views, will be the moil effectual Means to continue and preserve these Blettings to us.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

1 return you my Thanks for the Provisions you hive

made, for the Defence and Security of the Kingdom, and for carrying on the Service of the current Year. It is a great Satisfaction to me to fee, you have turned your Thoughts towards railing the necessary Supplies by such Methods, as may be the least burthensome to my People; and, as this cannoc but be received in the Country as a moll grateful and acceptable Service, I hope it will encourage you to pursue such Measures for the future, as may on all Occasions render the Supplies, that shall be necessary, as equal, and easy, as is possible.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It being necessary for me to visit my German Dominions this Year, I have determined to leave the Queen Regent here, during my Absence; and I doubt not, but it will be your Endeavours to make the Government as easy to her, as, I am confident, it will be her Care, by a just and prudent Administration, to deserve your Duty and Regard. I recommend to you all, in your several Stations, to study and consult the Preservation of the Peace and Quiet of the Kingdom.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty's Command, said.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty's royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued toTAur the Twenty-seventh

Day of July next, to be then here held; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to the Twenty-

seventh Day of July next.
